developed, engineers lack the necessary parameter 
inputs or operational data to validate the models 

Risk Categorization and Mitigations 
To  determine  the  proper  mitigation  to  address  each  of  the  gaps  discussed  in  this  paper,  the  relevant  risk  was 
categorized by likelihood and impact. Existing NERC registered entities cannot address many of the risks to the BPS 
from  emerging  large  loads.  Requirements  are  needed  for  additional  entities  (such  as  large  loads,  LSEs,  or  similar 
entities) to adequately address the risks, especially due to the severity of the risk. 

Critical Reliability Recommendations 
To  ensure  that  large  loads  can  be  reliably  integrated  into  the  BPS,  the  LLWG  recommends  updating  Reliability 
Standards and NERC registry criteria to reflect the electric grid of today and the future. Registry criteria for large loads 
and LSEs should be considered so  that NERC  Reliability Standards can be directly applicable. Reliability Standards 
modifications should be made for existing registered entities and large load entities. As discussed in this paper, many 
gaps exist in areas such as interconnection requirements, operations and balancing standards, and load modeling. 
Without updates to registry criteria, large loads and LSEs are not subject to Reliability Standards.  

The  LLWG  recommends  a  combination  of  Reliability  Standards  updates,  registry  criteria  revisions,  educational 
material/guidance,  and  coordination  with  relevant  stakeholders  to  help  address  the  gaps  identified  in  this  white 
paper. The solution to address the gap may not always be to update the specific NERC standard, requirement, or 
process that has the gap. To tailor risk mitigation, the LLWG recommends a holistic and nuanced approach for the 
design of mitigation measures to ensure that the grid is ready to safely and reliably integrate emerging large loads. 
This approach needs to consider the likelihood of impact to the BPS from the risk and the severity of the impact. The 
NERC  Framework  to  Address  Known  and  Emerging  Reliability  and  Security  Risks140  document  provides  direction 
regarding how the risks from emerging large loads should be addressed. The LLWG recommends that this document 
be utilized to determine appropriate risk mitigations. Applicable stakeholders should consider the gaps discussed in 
this paper and implement risk mitigations to address the risks posed by emerging large loads. 

The following recommendations are offered as guidance to ensure the reliability and security of the BPS.141

Recommendation 1: Because there are multiple high-impact risks to the BPS from large loads that NERC registered 
entities cannot adequately address, the LLWG recommends that NERC pursue registration of a type of entity (or types 
of entities) that is able to perform the following regarding large loads:142 

•  Provide accurate short-term demand forecast data 

•  Provide  sufficient  data  for  applicable  entities  (e.g.,  RC,  TOP,  and  BA)  for  the  development  of  short-term 

demand forecasts and operating plans  

•  Provide accurate load model data and ongoing model updates 

• 

Inform the TO and/or other applicable entities of any pertinent changes to the characteristics of the load 
before and after energization 

•  Perform  real-time  (and  operations  planning  time  frame)  coordination  with  the  TOP,  BA,  and/or  RC,  as 

applicable 

•  Comply  with  operating  instructions  from  the  TOP,  BA,  and/or  RC,  as  applicable,  and  ensure  appropriate 

training for receiving those instructions 

•  Ensure compliance with disturbance ride-through requirements 

•  Ensure compliance with ramp rate requirements (down ramp and up ramp) 

•  Provide accurate information (as accurate as possible and as early as possible) regarding large load dynamic 

model to support interconnection and transmission planning studies 

•  Provide  TOs  and/or  other  applicable  entities  with  accurate  information  necessary  for  performing 

interconnection studies 

•  Coordinate with TOs and/or other applicable entities to establish a comprehensive commissioning process 

that ensures operational readiness 

•  Adhere to necessary operating protocols, communication protocols, etc. 

•  Ensure  compliance  with  performance  requirements  (such  as  requirements  from  the  TO,  TP,  or  PC)  to 
minimize and mitigate unintentional local area or interconnection-wide power oscillation interaction during 
normal and post-event conditions 

•  Provide utility with site vulnerability/risk assessment and mitigate issues discovered in this assessment

Appendix A: Phasor/Time  Domain  Simulation  Tools,  Modeling 
Terminology, and Applications 

The use cases of various simulation tools are provided in Figure A.1. 

Figure A.1: Simulation Tool Applicability Based on Dynamics Being Simulated 

Terminology related to models and modeling platforms is provided below: 

1.  Phasor Simulation Tools and Models: 

a.  Purpose: Used to study reliability risks related to slower local and inter-area oscillatory dynamics, angular 
and voltage stability, and unacceptable voltage and frequency excursions resulting from unexpected loss 
of large load during grid disturbances and unexpected load ramps. 

  Characteristics: These tools use simplified models to study bulk system reliability impacts, which are 
generally  slower  frequency  events. Models in positive sequence platforms need to be reasonably 
accurate without being computationally burdensome. For example, the composite load model, with 
about 130 parameters, already slows down simulations for large interconnections. New large load 
models  should  not  significantly  add  to  the  existing  computational  burden  while  still  accurately 
modeling the phenomena of interest. 

2.  EMT Simulation Tools and Models: 

a.  Purpose: Used to study reliability risks related to faster dynamics, such as subsynchronous resonances 

and interactions, ferroresonances, switching transients, and harmonic stability assessments. 

b.  Characteristics: EMT models are significantly more detailed than phasor models, including faster controls 
and  the  switching  of  power  electronic  devices  for  certain  evaluations.  EMT  studies  typically  involve 
detailed models of the local system connected to an external system. Due to their high level of detail, 

NERC | Assessment of Gaps in Existing Practices, Requirements, and Reliability Standards for Emerging Large Loads | March 2026 
56 

 
 
 
 
 
Appendix A: Phasor/Time Domain Simulation Tools, Modeling Terminology, and Applications 

EMT models and tools are generally not used for bulk system analysis, although some utilities maintain 
EMT models for their entire footprints. Most utilities use EMT studies for screened parts of the system 
where the  reliability  challenges  can only be captured by modeling  the faster dynamics systems, (e.g., 
phase-locked loop instability for weak grids, subsynchronous interactions). 

3.  Generic and Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) Models: 

a.  Generic Models: Representations of power system equipment based on the basic physics of the device 
being  modeled,  covering  key  stability  and  control  features  common  to  most  manufacturers.  These 
models do not include proprietary control methods and are well documented. They are useful for long-
term  transmission  planning  studies  where  equipment  manufacturers  are  not  yet  decided.  OEMs  may 
parameterize  these  models  to  reflect  their  device’s  dynamic  performance  and  submit  them  to  the 
relevant TP. 

b.  OEM Models: Developed by OEMs to reflect the controls and dynamics of their own equipment, including 
proprietary  controls.  These  models  are  often  black-boxed  to  protect  intellectual  property  and  are 
submitted as user-defined library-linked models, with modeling details hidden from the TP. OEM models 
are used when generic models cannot sufficiently replicate the behavior of the equipment. OEM models 
can be in either the phasor domain or EMT. 

NERC | Assessment of Gaps in Existing Practices, Requirements, and Reliability Standards for Emerging Large Loads | March 2026

Level 2 Alert Report 

R E L I A B I L I T Y   |   R E S I L I E N C E   |   S E C U R I T Y  

P O W E R I N G   T O D A Y .   P R O T E C T I N G   T O M O R R O W .  

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Aggregated Report on NERC Level 2 Industry 
Recommendation: Large Load Interconnection, 
Study, Commissioning, and Operations 

Summary  
The Alert was published on September 9, 2025, and required Transmission Owners (TO), Resource Planners 
(RP),  Transmission  Operators  (TOP),  Transmission  Planners  (TP),  Balancing  Authorities  (BA),  Planning 
Coordinators  (PC),  Distribution  Providers  (DP),  and  Reliability  Coordinators  (RC)  on  the  NERC  Compliance 
Registry (NCR) to respond by January 28, 2026. 

The purpose of the Alert was to recommend and encourage the following to facilitate the integration of large 
loads with the bulk power system (BPS) in a manner that supports continued reliability: 

•  TOs, in collaboration with relevant TPs, PCs, RCs, TOPs, and BAs, should establish clear facility design 

and performance criteria in their interconnection requirements for large loads. 

•  TPs  and  PCs  should  establish  a  comprehensive  interconnection  and  system-wide  study  process  to 

assess the reliability impacts of large loads. 

•  TOs should enhance their load commissioning activities to establish a comprehensive commissioning 

process that ensures operational readiness for large loads. 

•  TOs should establish operating protocols and the necessary communication infrastructure to support 

reliable ongoing operations after large load facilities enter into commercial operations. 

•  TPs,  RPs,  and  PCs  should,  in  consultation  with  their  appropriate  regulatory  bodies,  identify  and 
implement a process to include large loads in their long-term transmission planning horizon demand 
forecasts as well as their near-term transmission planning horizon demand forecasts. 

The full text of the Alert has been posted to the NERC website.1 Responses to this Alert have informed NERC 
of the extent of the condition of the rapid and unprecedented rise in large electronic loads (sometimes also 
referred to as computational loads). Additionally, this Alert raised industry awareness of the potential reliability 
concerns associated with such large loads and provided recommendations to TOs, RPs, TOPs, TPs, BAs, PCs, 
DPs, and RCs to mitigate these concerns. 

Background 
The purpose of this Alert is to expeditiously address the risks observed from the analyzed large load behavior 
and assess the status of industry preparedness in relation to large loads.  

As part of its normal course of business, NERC often either discovers, identiﬁes, or is provided with information 
that is critical to ensuring the reliability of the BPS in North America. In order to eﬀectively disseminate this 
information,  NERC  utilizes  email-based  “alerts”  designed  to  provide  concise,  actionable  information  to  the 

1 https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/programs/bpsa/alerts/2025/nerc-alert-level-2--large-loads.pdf  

R E L I A B I L I T Y   |   R E S I L I E N C E   |   S E C U R I T Y  

P O W E R I N G   T O D A Y .   P R O T E C T I N G   T O M O R R O W .  

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
electric  industry.  As  deﬁned  in  its  Rules  of  Procedure,  NERC  alerts  are  divided  into  three  distinct  levels,  as 
follows: 

1. 

Industry  Advisory:  Purely  informational,  intended  to  alert  registered  entities  to  issues  or  potential 
problems. A response to NERC is not necessary. 

2.  Recommendation to Industry: Recommends specific action be taken by registered entities. A response 

from recipients, as defined in the alert, is required. 

3.  Essential Action: Identifies actions deemed to be “essential” to BPS reliability and requires NERC Board 
of Trustees approval prior to issuance. Like recommendations, essential actions also require recipients 
to respond as defined in the alert.  

NERC issued the Level 2 Alert with the present recommendations based on the results of its eﬀorts under the 
Large Loads Action Plan.  

Key Takeaways and Next Steps 
NERC identiﬁed the following key takeaways based on the responses to the Alert: 

•  Many entities at the time of this Alert do not have specific procedures to handle the unique challenges 

associated with large loads.  

•  Many  entities  do  not  have  a  process  to  coordinate  with  TOs  and  DPs  to  establish  protection 

coordination and post-disturbance recovery requirements for large loads. 

•  Many entities report waiting on or coordinating with a separate entity, primarily their independent 
system operator (ISO) or regional transmission organization (RTO), before changing their procedures 
to address the reliability concerns in the recommendations of this Alert. 

•  Many entities have not developed a list of detailed modeling data, settings, and parameters needed 

from large loads. 

•  Entities did not contact their large load entities to respond to this Alert even if they have established 

strong contacts with the large load customer. 

•  Entities do not have a standardized requirement for operational ramp limits in a post-disturbance state 

to address the reliability concerns raised in Recommendation 1. 

•  Entities  report  not  being  able  to  gather  modeling  information  to  represent  large  loads  as  raised  in 

Recommendations 1 and 2.  

•  Entities  generally  do  not  have  a  commissioning  process  to  address  the  concerns  discussed  in 

Recommendation 3. 

•  Entities broadly do not have a direct level of coordination with large load entities as they either do not 
have large load entities or a problem arose that prevented communication in their established process. 
These are issues that are addressed in Recommendation 4. 

•  Entities do not have a good way to capture large loads in the near- or long-term transmission planning 

horizons as recommended in Recommendation 5. 

Aggregated Report on NERC Level 2 Industry Recommendation: Large Load Interconnection, Study, Commissioning, and Operations 

2 

 
 
 
 
 
As  explained  in  the  report,  these  key  takeaways  demonstrate  that  additional  steps  are  needed  to  reliably 
integrate computational loads (including, for example, data centers). Such next steps range from coordination 
to  revisions to standards and NERC registry criteria, to ensure that relevant parties take essential actions to 
maintain BPS reliability. NERC plans the following next steps: 

• 

Issue a Level 3 Alert by May 2026 with essential actions to ensure BPS reliability and integration of 
computational load with the grid. 

•  Explore and draft starting in the second quarter of 2026:  

 

 

(i) registry criteria updates to address the integration of computational load and  

(ii) develop new and update existing Reliability Standards applicable to new registrants and existing 
registered entities. 

•  Release a reliability guideline in mid-2026 to share best practices as developed by the Reliability and 
Security Technical Committee’s Large Loads Working Group. This guidance as well as the Level 3 Alert 
will be crucial for entities as they will immediately share methods to improve reliability.  

To stay current with updates, follow NERC’s Large Loads Action Plan initiative webpage.2 

Overview of the Report 
The Alert required registered entities belonging to the TO, RP, TOP, TP, BA, PC, DP, and RC functional groups to 
respond to a total of 105 questions. The distribution of questions among the groups was as follows:  

•  TOs and DPs – Questions 1–44 (total of 44) 

•  TPs and PCs – Questions 45–67 (total of 22) 

•  RCs, BAs, and TOPs – Questions 68–95 (total of 27) 

•  RPs – Questions 96–105 (total of 9)  

The  questions  were  a  combination  of  multiple  choice,  Yes/No,  and  requests  for  free-text  narratives.  The 
requirement to answer certain questions was contingent on the entity’s previous answers. Additionally, the 
uploading of a Data Submission Spreadsheet was mandatory for entities that answered “Yes” to Question (3) 
(Do you have Large Loads or are you expecting to integrate Large Loads by 12/31/2027 within your footprint? 
[Yes/No]).  

The worksheet information indicated that for TOs and DPs that currently have large loads on their system or 
are expecting to integrate large loads by the end of 2027, major load growth is anticipated during the next ﬁve 
years. Forecasts collected from the worksheet information indicate that load may increase by 300 GW between 
2028 and 2030, with the bulk of this increase represented by data centers.

Furthermore,  the  Alert  asked  for  model  data  ﬁles  to  be  submitted  representing  the  large  load.  These  data 
submittals were in ﬁle formats (e.g., a sav, dyd, or dyr ﬁle format) for specialized industry engineering software. 
Analysis  of  these  ﬁles  indicates  that  some  entities  use  advanced  load  models  such  as  the  PERC1  (power 
electronic reconnecting and ceasing load model) or EV1 (electric vehicle) models to represent their loads. Some 
entities  use  the  complex  load  (CLOD)  or  composite  load  (CMLD)  dynamic  models,  primarily  for  traditional 
industrial  loads,  with  generic  representations  for  large  loads  on  the  system,  thereby  using  similar 
representations for computational load consumption. One entity’s response indicates that some organizations 
may  be  using  the  user-deﬁned  model  functions  of  their  software  to  implement  industry  models  as  their 
software  platform  currently  does  not  have  the  model  implemented  in  their  standard  library.  These  are  all 
expected outcomes and align with the need to represent large loads in planning studies; however, they were 
the minority.  

Roughly  three  quarters  of  all  data  center  load  models  are  insuﬃcient  to  represent  data  center  dynamic 
behavior, reﬂected in the dynamic model ﬁles included in the response to this Alert. Nearly 33,282 MW of 
currently operational data centers were evaluated. For “type of PSPD (power system protection device) model 
the large load submitted to represent their facility,” entities indicated “None” for 10,536 MW of data center 
load. Another 14,968 MW of data center load had a blank response. This means that 25,504 MW of data center 
load  relies on  the  inherent  ZIP  (constant  impedance  (Z),  constant  current  (I),  or  constant  power  (P))  model 
representation in stability software. Only 7,641 MW of data center load was indicated to use the CMLD (or 
CLOD) model, and 137 MW was indicated to use a user-deﬁned model (to leverage the recently released PERC1 
or similar EV1 model).

respondent anonymity, regional breakdowns are not presented for questions when a region only has a single 
respondent. When this occurs, data is presented in aggregate. Furthermore, there was a signiﬁcant portion of 
entities  registered  as  TOs  excluded  from  analysis  as  they  have  only  point-to-point  HVdc  lines  and  are  not 
impacted by the content of this Alert.6

This question was shared among all entities that received this Alert (see Questions 46, 69, and 97). The analysis 
for all responses is below as there was no signiﬁcant diﬀerence in responses. Nearly two-thirds of all submitting 
entities indicated a lack of experience in integrating modern data centers or other large loads. Of those that 
have experience, a third had less than ﬁve years of experience, a third had six or more years of experience, and 
a third had experience only serving “traditional” industrial large loads.   

The large share of entities submitting a lack of experience indicates that they either have no large loads or have 
not yet completed (but may have received) interconnection requests for this category of load. The entities that 
have a concentration of large load experience (six or more years) typically also reported that their experience 
from traditional loads has informed them for their approach to current large loads and that they have either 
adapted their traditional process or crafted new requirements based on disturbance ﬁndings or to address risk 
observed in their own or similar systems.

4.  In  the  free  text  field  provide  how  you  are  contacting,  interacting,  or  otherwise 
coordinating with Large Loads that are operational or nearly operational (i.e., 2 years or 
less) to collect information or resolve ongoing issues that arise. - TO, DP 

This question was shared between TOs, DPs, TPs, and PCs (see Question 47). There was no signiﬁcant diﬀerence 
in responses across the diﬀerent entity types (e.g., TO and DP vs RP). Roughly half of the responses indicate 
that  the respondents have  recurring  contacts  with  procedurally  deﬁned entities  during  the  interconnection 
process  and  provide  a  “key  accounts  manager,”  “customer  accounts  manager,”  or  similar  title/position  to 
continue to engage with operational or nearly operational large loads.  

In the responses, NERC found that TOs, in concert with their load-serving entities (LSE), contact data centers 
directly. That is, the TOs and LSEs are the ones that collect information and supply it to the TP, PC, RC, or other 
functional entity. Some TOs are also “coordination only” when collecting or resolving ongoing issues as they 
coordinate with either the large loads or the LSE to gather information. In general, the entities that have large 
loads have great contact with them either directly or through the LSE; however, many reporting entities do not 
have large loads.  

The other half of reporting entities did not have this direct level of coordination among large loads for a variety 
of reasons. Some do not have large loads on their system, and others had erroneous contact information (in 
processes  like  the  above)  or  did  not  receive  a  response  from  the  large  load  entity  through  their  typical 
communication methods 

5.  In  the  free  text  field  provide  any  challenges  experienced  while  coordinating  with 
operational  Large  Load  entities  for  the  process  development  and  data  submittals 
necessary  to  respond  to  this  alert.  Enter  “Not  Relevant”  if  your  organization  did  not 
coordinate with Large Load entities to respond to this alert. - TO, DP 

Roughly  all  (~85–90%)  respondents  indicated  that  they  did  not  coordinate  with  large  load  entities  when 
responding to this Alert. This ﬁnding is counter to the expectation that entities work with their large loads to 
gather the information requested in the Worksheet. Some entities (<5%) indicated that they had no issues with 
coordinating and gathering information to ﬁll out this Alert.   

Those that did reach out to their large loads indicated that their challenges included conﬁdentiality of the data 
between the customer and the Alert response, resource adequacy to serve end-use customer demand, and 
modeling  challenges.  Some  reported  that  their  large  load  entities  are  fatigued  by  the  multitude  of  data 
requests, and others have reported challenges with gathering any information from their contacts.  

This indicates that while entities may have set up avenues to gather information, these are simply not eﬀective 
vehicles  to  gather  information  to  address  emerging  risks  associated  with  this  technology  as  reported  by 
entities. One TO in an area with a high penetration of large loads mentioned that out of ﬁve entities contacted 
for a dynamic model, only one was able to provide a dynamic model. The original data request for the dynamic 
model was from a recent request for information sent before this Alert was issued.

6. In the free text field provide any comments you wish to provide to help explain your 
answers to these questions. - TO, DP 

This question was shared among all entities that received this Alert (see Questions 48, 70, and 100). There was 
no signiﬁcant diﬀerence in responses. Many entities did not provide information in this column; however, those 
that did used this ﬁeld to share more about their current practices, discuss potential challenges with contacting 
or  getting  information  on  large  load  entities,  or  explain  how  they  plan  to  engage  with  their  PC,  RC,  BA,  or 
another  entity  to  align  their  internal  processes  to  the  recommendation.  Common  themes  included  the 
following: 

•  Many entities expressed that they did not or do not expect in the next two years to interconnect any 

large loads. 

•  Many entities highlighted concerns with the hypothetical load that burdens their processes.  

•  Many entities stated that they defer to the ISO or RTO for additional work and implementation of the 

Alert Recommendations. 

•  Entities reiterate that they have limited experience with these loads. 

•  Some  entities  stated  they  use  steady-state  models  and  studies  only  and  do  not  perform  dynamic 

studies. 

•  Some entities shared using a CMLD model to represent data centers in transient studies. 

•  Some entities stated they rely on consultants to study or perform some of their duties. 

•  Some entities stated that tariff revisions are ongoing to solidify their work. 

•  Some  entities  use  a  loss  of  load  expectation  (a  probabilistic  measure  of  energy  adequacy)  study  to 

determine if additional requirements or changes are needed from large load entities. 

•  A minority of entities indicated that they have large load-specific interconnection processes. These are 

ones with more significant experience or that have proactively acted.

7. Have you established clear facility design, modeling, and performance criteria in your 
interconnection requirements for Large Loads? [Yes/No] - TO, DP 

Most  respondents  have  not  established  clear  facility  design,  modeling,  and  performance  criteria  in  their 
interconnection requirements. Clear load facility performance criteria are expected for any loads, even if the 
design, modeling, and performance criteria are generic to all interconnecting loads.  

Clear facility design, modeling, and performance criteria in an entity’s interconnection requirements ensures 
that  any  end-use  facility  design  will  include  speciﬁcations  that  improve  reliability.  In  this  context,  these 
requirements form the design parameters and basis for a facility’s construction. Without these clear design, 
modeling, and performance criteria, entities may not design (and thus operate) their facilities in a way that is 
consistent with BPS reliability.

9. Describe in the free text field a summary of the relevant Large Load language in your

This question was only required of the 55 entities that answered “Yes” to Question 7. The entities that attached

requirements.  Many  explained  that  their  requirements  also  included  a  Data  Center  Information  Collection 
Questionnaire that the NERC Load Modeling Working Group (LMWG) developed, indicating that the entities 
that have interconnection requirements are leveraging available industry documentation to help standardize 
the  information  requested  of  large  loads.  Some  entities  explained  that  they  mirror  the  Small  Generator

These interconnection requirements include relevant language on the following:  

•  Power system oscillations 

•  Load ramps 

•  Voltage ride-through or expected performance 

•  System protection 

•  Some include operating protocols and operational readiness 

•  Factors that trigger a qualified change, including the following: 

  Growth of the load facility in the future 

  Changes to energy consumption

20. Describe the disturbance recording equipment for Large Load and where such devices

24. Have you established a Large Load commissioning process to help ensure operational 
readiness for Large Loads? [Yes/No] - TO, DP 

A  large  majority  of  entities  do  not  have  an  established  commissioning  process  that  ensures  operational 
readiness for large loads. Those that do have varied degrees of complexity, outlined in the response to further 
questions. 

Commissioning processes enable entities to identify any inconsistencies from their designed plans that occur 
during a large project’s construction. These checks ensure that the installed equipment matches the studied 
designs and that resulting models and performance from the equipment will meet reliability objectives. A lack 
of speciﬁc commissioning process to ensure operational readiness decreases the certainty that equipment will 
operate in a reliable manner.  

Aggregated Report on NERC Level 2 Industry Recommendation: Large Load Interconnection, Study, Commissioning, and Operations

25. Enter how you are consulting with RCs, TOPs, and BAs in this commissioning process. 
Enter “Not coordinated” if this process does not exist. - TO, DP 

This question was only required of the 35 entities that answered “Yes” to Question 24. Many entities coordinate 
with their RCs, TOPs, and BAs when performing their commissioning practices for large loads. Some entities 
claim that they have no formal process to perform this coordination; however, they typically follow either an 
ad-hoc process or an “energization checklist” given to them by the RC, TOP, and BA. This indicates that some 
level of commissioning coordination for large loads already occurs with the RC, TOP, and BA.  

One  unique  consideration  is  that  many  vertically  integrated  entities10  stated  that  they  have  robust  internal 
coordination and provided details. These entities indicated that coordination was facilitated by the relevant RC, 
TOP, or BA being part of the same company. This unique consideration is in line with the generic response that 
if an entity has established strong requirements in its TO function, it will be more likely to have a commissioning 
process to follow from its RC, TOP, or BA.  

26. Describe your process to verify on-site settings and verify the as-built model. Enter 
“Not performed” if this process does not exist. - TO, DP 

This  question  was  only  required  of  the  35  entities  that  answered  “Yes”  to  Question  24.  Most  responses 
indicated that no model veriﬁcation is performed against on-site settings to verify the as-built model of the 
load facility. The small minority that do perform this action are also split between veriﬁcation of only protection 
settings versus veriﬁcation of the entire facility dynamic model.  

Model veriﬁcation of as-built facilities is a crucial step in improving the accuracy of dynamic models. Model 
veriﬁcation processes capture changes that occur between the design and construction phase of any large-
scale project. The lack of a veriﬁcation process during commissioning increases the uncertainty that planners 
and operators have in their models reﬂecting these facilities. Decreased dynamic model accuracy increases the 
risk of instability in real-time operations.  

27. Describe your process to validate performance of Large Loads to adhere to the design 
criteria  and  interconnection  requirements  after  energization.  Enter  “Not  performed”  if 
this process does not exist. - TO, DP 

This question was only required of the 35 entities that answered “Yes” to Question 24. Nearly all entities do 
not validate performance after energization. Of those that do, some are split between monitoring the point of 
interconnection with the large load via SCADA telemetered values versus oﬄine download of data recorded in 
a power quality meter.

Model validation is a key step to ensure that a facility’s model is aligned with real performance. The lack of 
validation increases uncertainty and poses a risk that the model may be unable to predict small- or large-scale 
behavior against disturbances.  

28.  Describe  your  process  to  update  as-planned  modeling  information  and  coordinate 
with TPs and PCs to perform additional analysis during commercial operations of Large 
Loads. Enter “Not performed” if this process does not exist. - TO, DP 

This question was only required of the 35 entities that answered “Yes” to Question 24. Almost all entities did

interconnection stage, the MOD-032 processes do not cover model submissions as the FAC-002 standard covers

29. Describe your process to review performance and modeling at different points of time 
for multi-year load growth Large Load projects or as major equipment updates are made. 
Enter “Not performed” if this process does not exist. - TO, DP 

This question was only required of the 35 entities that answered “Yes” to Question 24. Almost all of the entities 
indicated that they did not have a process to review performance and modeling during a multi-year load growth 
for large load projects. The entities that did have this process indicated that the commissioning process handles 
the  multi-year  buildouts  and  that  the  review  of  performance  and  modeling  is  not  performed  for  buildout 
updates. Furthermore, these entities that do have a process to review performance and modeling for multi-
year load growth indicate that many of the changes happen during the study phase of the process rather than 
throughout the construction of the various phases.

38. Describe the method the Large Load entities provide operational load forecasts. Enter 
“N/A” if this does not exist. - TO, DP 

This question was only intended for the 90 entities that answered “Yes” to Question 34. Nearly all these entities 
did not indicate how the large load entity provides operational load forecasts or indicated that the process 
does not exist. The entities that do have a process for large loads to provide operational load forecasts primarily 
receive these forecasts through customer account representatives or other formal tariﬀ procedures. Not all 
entities ask for the same granularity of forecasts or for the same periodicity. Some entities, albeit a minority of 
entities, receive these forecasts seasonally, monthly, weekly, or daily through contact to the operating ﬂoor. 
Some of these forecasts are hourly demand expectations for the large load. 

Some responses seemed to indicate that the question was asking for long-term transmission planning forecasts 
and not expected load consumption during real-time to day-ahead operations.

40. Describe the process by which a Large Load entity notifies you, the BA, TOP, RC, or a

a coordination one with joint and sole responsibilities to interface with the large load customer and the BA, 
TOP, or RC. Each structure, while unique, highlights that those with deﬁned interconnection requirements for 
large loads have processes in place for major equipment status changes.

42.  Describe  the  coordination  process  Large  Loads  will  follow  in  System  Emergency 
operating conditions with BAs, TOPs, or RCs (E.g., telemetry via SCADA or operator calls). 
Enter “N/A” if this does not exist. - TO, DP 

This question was only intended for the 90 entities that answered “Yes” to Question 34. Entities answered this 
question largely the same as Question 41 with only a few notable exceptions, typically around the content of 
the operator calls, issuing of operating instructions, and other items necessary to maintain the stability of the 
BPS. One entity mentioned that the RC has telemetry set up so that they can issue curtailment commands 
directly  to  the  load.  Similarly,  some  entities  included  real-time  management  capabilities;  however,  most 
entities expected operating calls and issuing of operating instructions.  

These  points  emphasize  the  importance  of  the  Alert  Recommendation  to  establish  coordination  with  large 
loads to return the BPS to normal operations. 

43.  Describe  the  coordination  process  Large  Loads  will  follow  in  the  post-Disturbance 
period following a Contingency with BAs, TOPs, or RCs, (E.g., Operator calls). Enter “N/A” 
if this does not exist. - TO, DP 

This question was only intended for the 90 entities that answered “Yes” to Question 34. Many entities answered 
this question with the same category of response as Question 41 with some notable diﬀerences. The same 
emphasis on the need for operating calls was raised by responding entities, but some emphasized the need for 
direct calls to operating personnel prior to reconnecting the large load following a system disturbance. These 
details,  as  in  Question  42,  also  emphasize  the  importance  of  the  Alert  Recommendation  to  establish 
coordination with large loads to return the BPS to normal operations following a system disturbance. 

44. Describe any plans you have within 2 years to include revisions to address the issues 
raised  in  Recommendation  4.  Enter  “No  plans”  if  you  do  not  have  plans  to  revise  your 
operating protocols and the necessary communication infrastructure. - TO, DP 

This question was expected for all TOs and DPs responding to the Alert. Roughly half of entities did not have a 
plan to revise their processes to address the items raised in Recommendation 4. For those that did include 
plans to revise, a majority were waiting on a separate entity to proceed before revising their internal processes. 
The entity for which most respondents were waiting was their ISO or RTO. Only a few entities planned to align 
within the two-year time frame raised in Question 44. Given the communication needs of operators, the TOs 
and DPs looking to their ISO or RTO (i.e., their BA, PC, or RC) is an expected outcome to ensure coordination 
among these large loads.

50.  Describe  how  you  distributed  these  requirements  for  detailed  modeling  data, 
settings, and parameters to TOs and DPs. Enter “Not distributed” if this process does not

This question was only intended for the 48 entities that answered “Yes” to Question 49. Most entities indicated 
that they distribute their modeling requirements publicly through mechanisms like an Open Access Same-Time 
Information  System  (OASIS)  or  similar  distribution  system.  As  some  entities  were  also  the  TO  or  DP,  they 
indicated  that  internal  coordination  accounts  for  the  distribution  of  detailed  model  data,  settings,  and 
parameters. Some entities did not distribute modeling data, settings, and parameters to their TOs and DPs.  

51. Describe how these model requirements discussed in Questions 49 and 50 address 
acceptable  model  types,  structures,  necessary  parameter  values,  out  of  range 
parameters, and other reasonability checks on data. Enter “Not addressed” if this does 
not exist. - TP, PC 

This  question  was  only  intended  for  the  48  entities  that  answered  “Yes”  to  Question  49.  Most  entities 
responding to this question indicated that they only check for acceptable model types, structures, parameter 
values,  and  other  reasonability  checks  on  data  when  a  model  is  submitted.  Few  entities  perform  a  full 
veriﬁcation or validation of the model to identify any unreasonable responses. Many entities also indicated 
that  they  are  focusing  their reasonability  checks  for  large  loads  on  the  composite  load  model.  This  type  of 
model is largely updated for reasonable parameters and values by Interconnection-wide model builders.  

This  demonstrates  that  many  of  the  reasonability  checks  on  submitted  models  may  be  coming  from  the 
Interconnection-wide model building context, which contains a diﬀerent scope than local reliability studies like 
an interconnection request for large load entities. 

52. Describe any plans you have within 2 years to include revisions to address the issues

your modeling data, settings, and parameter requirements as well as whether you plan 
to establish an independent set of model requirements for Large Loads. - TP, PC 

This question was required of all TPs and PCs responding to the Alert. Roughly half of the entities responding 
indicated  that  they  had  no  plans  to  address  the  issues  raised  in  Recommendation  1.  Of  the  entities  that 
indicated they have a plan to address the issues raised in Recommendation 1, the processes to ﬁnalize the 
changes may take longer than the two-year period seen in Question 52. Some entities indicated that they are 
waiting on another organization (primarily their ISO or RTO).

53. Describe in the free text box how you are coordinating with TOs and DPs to establish 
performance-based post-Disturbance recovery requirements for Large Loads. Enter “Not 
coordinated” if this process does not exist. - TP, PC 

This question was required of all TPs and PCs responding to the Alert. Nearly all entities responding to this 
question indicated that there is not a process to coordinate with TOs and DPs to establish post-disturbance 
recovery requirements. The very limited number of entities that do have a process for this purpose shared that 
this is done via a formalized process like a tariﬀ or that the TO and DP is the same company as the TP or PC. 
Most of the largest, non-vertically integrated PCs indicated that they have an open stakeholder process that 
takes  input  from  TOs,  DPs,  and  many  other  relevant  stakeholders  to  establish  post-disturbance  recovery 
requirements for large loads. 

54. Describe in the free text box how you are coordinating with TOs and DPs to establish 
protection  coordination  requirements  for  Large  Loads.  Enter  “Not  coordinated”  if  this 
process does not exist. - TP, PC 

This question was required of all TPs and PCs responding to the Alert. Nearly all entities responding to this 
question  indicated  that  there  is  not  a  process  to  coordinate  with  TOs  and  DPs  to  establish  protection 
coordination requirements for large loads. The entities that do have a process for this purpose shared that this 
is done via a formalized process like a tariﬀ or that the TO and DP is the same company as the TP or PC. Some 
PCs  indicated  that  they  have  an  open  stakeholder  process  that  takes  input  from  TOs  and  DPs  to  establish 
protection coordination requirements. These coordination requirements typically are focused on voltage ride-
through and known mitigations to address ride-through performance. 

55. Describe in the free text box how you are coordinating with TOs and DPs to establish 
design  requirements  to  minimize  and  mitigate  power  oscillation  interactions  during 
normal operations and in the recovery post-System Disturbance requirements for Large 
Loads. Enter “Not coordinated” if this process does not exist. - TP, PC 

This question was required of all TPs and PCs responding to the Alert. Nearly all entities responding to this 
question indicated that there is not a process to coordinate with TOs and DPs to minimize and mitigate power 
oscillations for large loads. However, more entities explained that there is some coordination to reduce power 
oscillations than in Questions 52 (for model requirements), Question 53 (for post-disturbance recovery), and 
Question 54 (for protection coordination).  

The entities that do have a process for this purpose shared that this is done via a formalized process like a tariﬀ 
or  that  the  TO  and  DP  is  the  same  company  as  the  TP  or  PC.  Some  PCs  indicated  that  they  have  an  open 
stakeholder process that takes input from TOs and DPs to establish protection coordination requirements. A 
handful of entities also have established screening tests or have put into place a taskforce to understand and 
implement power oscillation mitigations concerning large loads.

59. Describe the accuracy of the models mentioned in Question 57 and 58 to reflect the 
Large  Load  facility  in  the  post-Disturbance  period,  including  its  recovery  performance. 
Include in this description the ability to assess any interaction with other loads or System 
protection devices. Enter “No models” if no Large Load models exist. - TP, PC 

This question was only for the 56 entities that answered “Yes” to both Questions 57 and 58. Responding entities 
were split between indicating that the models were accurate enough for their studies versus indicating that 
the models were not accurate to depict known performance of large loads. This was apparent in one region 
where most of the TPs claimed that their models were accurate enough, but the PC for that area stated that 
most models are not when compared to real system events. Furthermore, some entities indicated that their 
planning area does not contain enough large loads to include a requirement to assess the accuracy of large 
load models.  

The entities that indicated that their models were accurate primarily use the CMLD model for representing 
large load facilities. However, the composite load model’s structure is unable to capture the key features of 
computational load performance.  The  entities  that  indicated  that  the  models were  inaccurate  claimed  that 
their model did not use site-speciﬁc (generic or user-deﬁned) parameters or settings and supported new model 
development. There is evidence of disagreement forming between TPs and PCs on the accuracy of the model 
to be used in their studies. 

60.  Describe  how  the  models  mentioned  in  Question  57  and  58  are  validated  with  as-
designed,  as-built,  or  as-studied  parameters.  Enter  “Not  validated”  if  no  Large  Load 
models are validated or do not exist. - TP, PC 

This question  was only  for  the  56  entities  that  answered  “Yes”  to  both Questions  57  and  58.  Most  entities 
indicated that they were unable to validate the large load model either due to a lack of models or a lack of 
process. Some entities indicated that this activity is done at the commissioning phase of the facility compared 
to  the  studied  model,  with  a  few  indicating  that  this  activity  is  done  following  event  analysis  through 
mechanisms like disturbance playback. While most entities have indicated that they were unable to validate 
the model, a large number of entities also indicated that ongoing exercises are at work to ensure large load 
model validation.  

These entities are working toward validation of large load models; however, even these entities have yet to 
execute model validation to their satisfaction.

61. Describe how the post-Disturbance Large Load frequency and voltage performance 
related  to  the  included  Large  Load  model(s).  Include  in  this  description  the  largest 
aggregate  loss  of  load  and  the  largest  single  load  loss  due  to  the  most  severe 
Contingency. Further explain any change to these losses expected in the next five years. 
Enter “Not performed” if you do not evaluate post-Disturbance Large Load frequency and 
voltage performance. - TP, PC 

This question  was only  for  the  56  entities  that  answered  “Yes”  to  both Questions  57  and  58.  Most  entities 
reported that there is no evaluation of post-disturbance large load frequency and voltage performance for the 
single largest aggregate loss of load. This was generally either due to a lack of post-disturbance analysis or due 
to a contingency deﬁnition not including aggregate load loss but rather singular loss of a given load facility. 
Some entities stated that they are studying aggregate load-loss impacts, but such eﬀorts were not ﬁnalized or 
completed at the time of the entity response. Of those that evaluated the frequency and voltage performance, 
entities performed ad-hoc studies or annualized data quality reviews. Some indicated that their criteria only 
contain studies for the loss of the largest single load and not aggregate load loss.  

One  PC  collects  large  load  models  that  demonstrate  post-disturbance  frequency  and  voltage  performance. 
Each  facility  has  unique voltage  sensitivity  and  post-disturbance recovery  performance. The  PC uses  all  the 
mentioned models in interconnection-wide studies to identify any major eﬀects of aggregate load loss from 
large load facilities that trip oﬀ-line from voltage disturbances and do no reconnect. The study is ongoing, and 
the PC plans to present its results at a future public stakeholder meeting.

indicated that no EMT study was performed when integrating large loads. Some entities indicated that they 
will run a study if their ISO or RTO requires the study or if other screening studies coupled with engineering 
judgment indicate an EMT study is necessary.

71.  In  the  free  text  field,  describe  your  process  or  needs  to  include  Large  Loads  into 
Undervoltage  Load  Shed,  Underfrequency  Load  Shed,  and  Manual  Load  Shed  plans. 
Indicate in this response how you have communicated this need and associated capability 
to TOs and DPs in your footprint. Enter “No shedding” if you do not see a need to include 
Large Loads into these programs. - RC, BA, TOP 

This question was required for all RCs, BAs and TOPs responding to this Alert. Nearly all entities indicated that 
large  loads  are  not  included  in  automatic  load-shedding  programs.  Some  indicated  that  their  manual  load 
shedding schemes may consider large loads, but they are weighted against all industrial-level loads and depend 
on various real-time conditions before shedding the load. Roughly half of entities also reported that their load-
shedding schemes are based on studies to prove their eﬀectiveness, including underfrequency load shedding 
(UFLS) and undervoltage load shedding (UVLS). In these studies, the entities reported that the large load is 
evaluated  for  potential  inclusion  or  exclusion.  Entities  have  also  reported  that  they  follow  NERC  Reliability 
Standards for coordination and communication to the TO or DP for these study results and potential inclusion 
of large load entities in automatic or manual load shedding schemes.

Loads  enters  service,  exits  service,  or  operates  during  normal  operations.  Enter  “No

This question was required for the 20 entities that answered “Yes” to Question 77. Nearly all entities reported 
that these limits do not exist for normal operations. Some entities that do impose these limits indicated that 
this  is  worked  out  through  the  contractual  agreements  with  the  large  loads  during  interconnection  and 
imposed via operating instructions in real time. Some entities (of which not all were required to respond to 
this question) also shared that they are looking for their ISO or RTO to implement or impose these limitations. 
Some entities mentioned that their ISO or RTO has two diﬀerent load disconnection limits: one for any given 
P1–P7  contingency  as  part  of  the  TPL-001  process  (e.g.,  1,000  MW  per  Point  of  Interconnection),  and  the 
second one is a system operating limit based on frequency stability (e.g., 2,600 MW of aggregate loss). The 
second limit for frequency stability considers all load in an area that may disconnect from a transmission fault 
in a dynamic simulation.  

79. Describe how these limits are shared to TOs within your footprint. Enter “Not shared” 
if these limits are not shared to TOs. - RC, BA, TOP 

This question was required for the 20 entities that answered “Yes” to Question 77. Nearly all entities reported 
that these limits are not shared to the TOs in their area. Where they are shared, most entities reported that 
they  provide  user  manuals,  operational  guides,  tariﬀ  language,  or  other  instructions.  Some  entities  also 
indicated that they are the same company as the TO and share internally. Some entities (of which not all were 
required to respond to this question) also shared that they are looking for their ISO or RTO to implement or 
impose these limitations. One ISO/RTO company mentioned that it also discusses these limits and any updates 
to the studies that inform the limits at a regular stakeholder meeting. 

80. Describe how these limits are shared to DPs within your footprint. Enter “Not shared” 
if these limits are not shared to DPs. - RC, BA, TOP 

This question was required for the 20 entities that answered “Yes” to Question 77. Nearly all entities reported 
that these limits are not shared to the DPs in their area. Where they are shared, most entities reported that 
they  provide  user  manuals,  operational  guides,  tariﬀ  language,  or  other  instructions.  Some  entities  also 
indicated they are the same company as the DP and share internally, but this is a signiﬁcantly fewer number of 
entities than in Question 79. Some entities (of which not all were required to respond to this question) also 
shared that they are looking for their ISO or RTO to implement or impose these limitations.

Conclusions and Next Steps  
From  the  responses  to  the  Recommendations  in  the  Alert,  NERC  has  found  a  few  key  principles  that 
demonstrate how industry is responding to reliability concerns with interconnecting, commissioning, studying, 
and operating large loads. These key ﬁndings are as follows: 

•  Many entities at the time of this Alert do not have specific procedures to handle the unique challenges 
associated with large loads. Some do not plan to implement changes to address the risks associated 
with  the  Recommendations  in  this  Alert.  Entities  that  are  creating  requirements  are  mostly 
coordinating with higher-level entities like PCs and RCs in stakeholder processes. 

  For  entities  that  do  have  strong 

interconnection  requirements  for 

large 

loads,  these 

interconnection requirements adequately address most reliability concerns with large loads. 

  Some evidence exists that entities were unable to report consistent numerical load capacities as 
indicated in the Alert worksheet. For example, some load forecasts for in-service by year end of 
2025 did not equal the sum of all reported in-service large loads (within a margin of acceptable 
error).  

  Some entities do not have or do not plan to have large loads interconnecting to their system, which 

explains this type of entities’ lack of plans to address the Recommendations in this Alert. 

•  Many  entities  do  not  have  a  process  to  coordinate  with  TOs  and  DPs  to  establish  protection 

coordination requirements for large loads. 

•  Many  entities  do  not  have  a  process  to  coordinate  with  TOs  and  DPs  to  establish  post-disturbance 

recovery requirements. 

•  Many  entities  report  waiting  on  or  coordinating  with  a  separate  entity,  primarily  their  ISO  or  RTO, 
before changing their procedures to address the reliability concerns in the Recommendations of this 
Alert. 

•  Many entities have not developed a list of detailed modeling data, settings, and parameters needed 

from large loads. 

•  Entities did not contact their large load entities to respond to this Alert even if they have established 

strong contacts with the large load customer. 

  Typically, this coordination was performed through the TO and the associated LSE for the large load, 

if not done directly.  

  Many  entities  that  did  contact  their  large  load  entities  used  customer  account  managers  to 

coordinate and communicate. 

•  Entities do not have a standardized requirement for operational ramp limits in a post-disturbance state 

to address the reliability concerns raised in Recommendation 1. 

•  Entities  report  not  being  able  to  gather  modeling  information  to  represent  large  loads  as  raised  in 

Recommendation 1 and 2.  

  Many entities report not having the authority to gather the modeling information. 

Aggregated Report on NERC Level 2 Industry Recommendation: Large Load Interconnection, Study, Commissioning, and Operations 

65 

 
 
  Some entities report a lack of knowledge on what modeling information to gather to represent the 

large load facility. 

•  Entities  generally  do  not  have  a  commissioning  process  to  address  the  concerns  discussed  in 

Recommendation 3. 

  Most entities do not have processes to require large loads to provide and update modeling data 

based on design changes, upgrades, and disturbance-based model validation. 

  Entities  that  do  have  a  commissioning  practice  do  not  include  model  verification  or  model 

validation to support BPS reliability.  

  Many entities report not coordinating the findings of the commissioning to other entities. 

•  Entities broadly do not have a direct level of coordination with large load entities as they either do not 
have large load entities, or a problem arose that prevented communication in their established process. 
These are issues that are addressed in Recommendation 4. 

•  Entities do not have a good way to capture large loads in near-term or long-term transmission planning 

horizons as recommended in Recommendation 5. 

  Some evidence in the data shows that RPs are not themselves determining the capacity needs for 

their area. 

The data collected in this Alert underscores the importance of recognizing the reliability concerns around large 
loads and proactively addressing the associated challenges. NERC recommends continuing collaboration with 
industry to drive a continued focus on these risks.  

To do so, NERC recommends taking targeted actions, including the following: 

• 

Issue a Level 3 NERC Alert by June 2026 with essential actions that address the most significant gaps 
and concerns identified from this Level 2 Alert analysis. 

•  Explore and draft starting in the second quarter of 2026:  

  Registry criteria updates to address the integration of computational load and  

  Develop new and update existing Reliability Standards applicable to new registrants and existing 

registered entities. 

•  Release a reliability guideline mid-2026 to share best practices. This guidance as well as the Level 3 

Alert will be crucial for entities as they will share methods to improve reliability.

P O W E R I N G   T O D A Y .   P R O T E C T I N G   T O M O R R O W .  

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Incident Review 
Considering Simultaneous Voltage-Sensitive Load Reductions 

Primary Takeaways 
Operators  and  planners  of  the  Bulk  Electric  System  (BES)  should  be  aware  of  the  risks  and  challenges 
associated  with  voltage-sensitive  large  loads  that  are  rapidly  being  connected  to  the  power  system. 
Specifically, when considering data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities, entities should be aware 
of the potential for large amounts of voltage-sensitive load loss during normally cleared faults on the BES. 
Voltage-sensitive  data  center-type  loads  have  increased  on  the  system  and  are  predicted  to  continue 
growing  rapidly.  The  2024  NERC  Long-Term  Reliability  Assessment  (LTRA)  documents  and  discusses  this 
potential growth of data center-type loads. This vignette highlights this load-loss potential based on analysis 
of  a  recent  event  in  the  Eastern  Interconnection  and  offers  some  considerations  for  BES  operators, 
planners,  and  regulators  concerning  identifying  and  mitigating  the  potential  reliability  effects  and  risks 
presented by these large voltage-sensitive load losses for future operations.  

Summary of Incident 
A 230 kV transmission line fault led to customer-initiated simultaneous loss of approximately 1,500 MW of 
voltage-sensitive load that was not anticipated by the BES operators. The electric grid has not historically 
experienced simultaneous load losses of this magnitude in response to a fault on the system, which has 
historically been planned for large generation losses but not for such significant simultaneous load losses. 
Simultaneous large load losses have two effects on the electric system: First, frequency rises on the system 
as a result of the imbalance between load and generation; second, voltage rises rapidly because less power 
is flowing through the system. In this incident, the frequency did not rise to a level high enough to cause 
concern. The voltage also did not rise to levels that posed a reliability risk, but operators did have to take 
action to reduce the voltage to within normal operating levels. However, as the potential for this type of 
load loss increases, the risk for frequency and voltage issues also increases. Operators and planners should 
be aware of this reliability risk and ensure that these load losses do not reach intolerable levels. 

Incident Details  
At approximately 7:00 p.m. Eastern on July 10, 2024, a lightning arrestor failed on a 230 kV transmission 
line  in  the  Eastern  Interconnection,  resulting  in  a  permanent  fault  that  eventually  “locked  out”  the 
transmission line. The auto-reclosing control on the transmission line was configured for three auto-reclose 
attempts staggered at each end of the line. This configuration resulted in 6 successive system faults in an 
82-second period. The protection system detected these faults and cleared them properly. The shortest 
fault duration was the initial fault at 42 milliseconds, and the longest fault duration was 66 milliseconds. 
The voltage magnitudes during the fault ranged from .25 to .40 per unit in the load-loss area.

Load Details 
Discussions were held with data center owners to understand the specific cause of their load reductions. It 
was determined that the data centers transferred their loads to their backup power systems in response to 
the disturbance. Data center loads are sensitive to voltage disturbances. The data center protections and 
controls are designed to avoid equipment outages for voltage disturbances. In addition to the computer 
equipment  at  these  facilities,  cooling  equipment  is  also  critical  to  the  operation  of  the  data  center  and 
sensitive to voltage disturbances. To ride through voltage disturbances on the electric grid, data centers 
employ uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems that will instantaneously take over providing power to 
the data center equipment when a grid disturbance occurs. The differing types and designs of these UPS 
systems cause differences in the characteristics of the data center responses to a voltage disturbance. A 
centralized design uses UPS systems at the load-center level that are typically in the range of 2–5 MWs. The 
UPS uses power electronics to switch the load to a battery bank connected to the UPS. These battery banks 
are not designed to supply the load for long periods of time but rather to power the load for the short time 
periods of disturbances or—in the case of a complete electric grid outage—long enough to start a backup 
generator that will then provide power to the UPS. The decentralized UPS design uses many smaller UPSs 
at the rack level. These rack-mounted UPSs are typically in the range of 3–4 kW. The decentralized UPS 
systems operate similarly to the centralized UPS systems, just on a smaller scale. Another type of UPS is a 
dynamic/diesel  rotary  uninterruptible  power  supply  (DRUPS).  These  systems  use  a  flywheel  to  provide 
uninterruptible power and a clutch system to quickly start and connect a diesel engine upon a disturbance 
on the electric grid.  

Incident Review – Considering Simultaneous Voltage-Sensitive Load Reductions 

4

Figure 6: DRUPS 
[Source: Schneider Electric White Paper 92]

Figure 7: Typical Centralized UPS Power Distribution 
[Source: Uptime Institute Journal] 

The load characteristics of these types of UPS systems differ in response to a transient disturbance on the 
electric grid. For the static centralized and decentralized UPS systems that utilize batteries, the load will be 
taken over by the battery when the transient voltage disturbance occurs. Since it is a transient disturbance, 
such as a temporary fault on the electric grid, the grid voltage will typically return to normal in milliseconds. 
Once the grid voltage returns to normal, the load will then be transferred back to the grid. A typical load 
characteristic for these types of static UPS systems, as seen by the grid, is shown in Figure 8. Upon detecting 
the transient voltage disturbance, the DRUPS system will immediately transfer the load to the flywheel/ac 
generator  and  start  the  engine  that  will  act  as  the  prime  mover  for  the  generator  before  the  flywheel 
exhausts its kinetic energy. This system will not quickly transfer the load back to the grid after the transient 
disturbance has cleared and the grid voltage returns to normal. Typically, transferring the load back to the 
grid from the DRUPS system must be done manually. A typical load characteristic for a DRUPS system, as 
seen by the grid, is shown in Figure 9. As can be seen in these figures, the typical static UPS system load 
characteristic, as seen by the grid, is a short-duration loss of load that returns quickly after the transient 
disturbance clears. The typical DRUPS system load characteristic, as seen by the grid, is a loss of load that 
does not return quickly after the transient disturbance clears.

Figure 8: Static UPS Load Characteristic 

Figure 9: DRUPS Load Characteristic 

Discussions with the data center owners also identified another protection/control scheme that impacts 
the response of data center load to voltage disturbances on the grid. The scheme detects and counts voltage 
disturbances on the grid. If a certain number of voltage disturbances are seen within a certain time, the 
data  center  will  transfer  its  load  to  the  backup  system,  and  it  will  remain  there  until  it  is  manually 
reconnected to the grid. The typical number of voltage disturbances that trigger this scheme is three, and 
a  typical  time  is  one  minute.  As  such,  three  voltage  disturbances  within  one  minute  will  result  in  data 
centers using this protection/control scheme transferring their load off the grid and staying off until they 
manually transfer back. This scheme can be deployed on both centralized and decentralized UPS designs. A 
load characteristic for this type of data center control scheme can be seen in Figure 10. 

Incident Review – Considering Simultaneous Voltage-Sensitive Load Reductions 

7 

 
 
 
 
 
 
Figure 10: Voltage Disturbance Counting Scheme Load Characteristic 

While these three load characteristics were predominant in this event, many load characteristic variations 
exist. These characteristics are determined by the numerous vendor-supplied equipment controls within 
the data center, including the vendor-specific UPS controls. Additionally, controls under the purview of data 
center owner/operators,  such  as  a  certain  number  of disturbances  within  a  certain  period  of time,  also 
determine the characteristic response to system disturbances. 

Most  of  the  sustained  load  reduction  occurred  simultaneously  with  the  third  voltage  depression,  which 
coincided  with  the  third  automatic  reclosing  attempt.  At  that  time,  approximately  1,260  MW  of  load 
dropped  off  the  electric  grid  and  did  not  return  for  hours.  Most  of  the  load  loss  in  this  event  can  be 
attributed to the interaction between the automatic reclosing sequence on the faulted transmission line 
and the data center’s protection/control scheme that counts the number of voltage disturbances within a 
specified period of time. 

While  this  incident  did  not  present  any  significant  issues  with  the  reconnection  of  the  large  loads,  the 
potential  exists  for  issues  in  future  incidents  if  the  load  is  not  reconnected  in  a  controlled  manner. 
Significant amounts of load being reconnected to the system present challenges to Balancing Authorities 
(BA)  and  Transmission  Operators  (TOP).  Ramp  rates  for  load  connection  are  just  as  critical  to  system 
operations  as  generation  ramping.  Voltage  management  and  maintaining  balance  between  load  and 
generation are considerations that need to be given for load reconnection ramp rates. 

This incident has highlighted potential reliability risks to the BES with respect to the voltage ride-through 
characteristics of large data center loads. Similar incidents have occurred in other  Interconnections with 
cryptocurrency mining loads as well as oil/gas loads. While these loads are different than the data center 
loads  in  this  incident,  they  present  the  same  challenges  to  the  operators  and  planners  of  the  BES. 
Understanding the changing dynamic nature of load is critical to the future operation of the BES. 

Future Considerations 
While this disturbance did not cause significant operating issues with the grid at this location and at this 
time, as data center loads continue to grow rapidly, the risk could quickly increase. Actions that TOPs and 
Transmission Planners (TP) should start taking to avoid significant issues in the future are listed below: 

•  Require dynamic response models of large loads in their facility interconnection requirements

Incident Review – Considering Simultaneous Voltage-Sensitive Load Reductions
