Section  VI  —  NERC  Organization  Registration  Appeals 
Process 

Purpose and Scope 
This  section  describes  the  process  that  any  organization  must  use  to  seek  review  of  its  listing  and  functional 
assignment on the NCR. 

Overview 
NERC has established documented procedures to ensure a fair and impartial appeals process.  No one with a direct 
interest in a dispute may participate in the appeals process except as a party or witness.  See Figure 3, Organization 
Registration Appeals Process Overview. 

Organization Registration Appeals Procedure 

1.  Any  Registered  Entity  included  on  the  NCR  may  challenge  final  decisions  regarding  its  listing,  functional 
assignments,  and  determinations  regarding  the  applicability  of  a  sub-set  of  Reliability  Standards  (which 
specifies the specific Reliability Standards and may specify Requirements/sub-Requirements). 

2.  All registration appeals must be filed in writing to NERC, via electronic and registered mail.  Appeals are sent 

to:  

Organization Registration and Certification 
Main: (404) 446-2560 
Facsimile: (404) 446-2595 
Email: Communications@NERC.net 
Address: As posted on NERC.com 

3.  Each party in the appeals process shall pay its own expenses for each step in the process. 

4.  A stipulation of invoking the appeals process is that the Regional Entity or Registered Entity requesting the 
appeal agrees that NERC (its Members, Board, committees, subcommittees, and staff), any person assisting 
in the appeals process, and any company employing a person assisting  in the appeals process, shall not be 
liable for, and shall be held harmless against the consequences of or any action or inaction or of any agreement 
reached in resolution of the dispute or any failure to reach agreement as a result of the appeals proceeding. 
This  “hold  harmless”  clause  does  not  extend  to  matters  constituting  gross  negligence,  intentional 
misconduct, or a breach of confidentiality. 

5.  Parties retain the right to seek further review of a decision in whatever regulatory agency or court that may 

have jurisdiction. 

6.  All appeals must be received within 21 Days of receipt of the NERC determination that is being appealed.  The 
appeal must state why the Registered Entity believes it should not be registered or should be deactivated 
based  on  the  NERC  ROP  and  the  NERC  Statement  of  Compliance  Registry  Criteria  or  why  its  compliance 
obligations  should  be  limited  only  to  a  sub-set  list  of  otherwise  applicable  Reliability  Standards  (which 
specifies the Reliability Standards and may specify Requirements/sub-Requirements).  A copy of the appeal 
must be concurrently served on the Regional Entity. 

7.  After receipt of the appeal, the Registered Entity has a 30 day period to work with the Regional Entity to 
resolve the appeal, if possible.  NERC may extend such deadline in its sole discretion.  If the appeal is resolved, 
the Regional Entity will notify NERC with the details of the resolution and NERC will close the appeal. 

Public 

 
 
Public 

Section VI — NERC Organization Registration Appeals Process 

8.  At any time through this appeals process, a Registered Entity may agree with the decision and/or agree to 
close the appeal.  NERC shall notify the involved parties and the NERC BOTCC that the appeal is resolved and 
update the NCR as applicable. 

9.  NERC will notify the Registered Entity and the applicable Regional Entity(ies) regarding the appeal with the 

following expectations: 

a.  The  Registered  Entity  will  provide  NERC  and  the  applicable  Regional  Entity(ies)  any  additional  data 

supporting its appeal within 10 Days of the date of the NERC appeal notification. 

b.  The applicable Regional Entity(ies) will provide a copy of its assessment directly to the Registered Entity, 

as well as to NERC, within 20 Days of the date of the NERC appeal notification. 

c.  The Registered Entity may submit a response to the Regional Entity(ies) assessment, with copies to the 

Regional Entity(ies) and NERC, within 30 Days of the date of the NERC appeal notification. 

d.  To ensure there is no confusion with respect to the rights and responsibilities of the Registered Entity 
during the appeal process, the notification will confirm whether the Registered Entity will remain on the 
NERC Compliance Registry and will be responsible for compliance with approved Reliability Standards 
applicable to the function under appeal during the appeal. 

e.  NERC may extend the timelines for good cause shown.  Requests should be sent to the Registration email 
address, found on the Registration and Certification page on the NERC website.  NERC shall notify the 
Registered Entity and the Regional Entity of such time extensions. 

10. Hearing and Ruling by the BOTCC 

a.  The BOTCC will resolve Registration disputes and apply a de novo review. 

b.  The BOTCC may request additional data from NERC, the relevant Regional Entity(ies) or the Registered 

Entity, and prescribe the timeframe for the submitting the requested data. 

c.  The BOTCC will provide a written decision regarding any appeals, along with the basis for its decision. 

d. 

e. 

If the BOTCC upholds the appeal, NERC will: 
•  Notify the Registered Entity and Regional Entity(ies) that the appeal was granted. 
•  Update the NCR. 

If the BOTCC does not uphold the appeal, NERC will: 
•  Notify the Registered Entity and the Regional Entity(ies) that the appeal was denied. 
•  The  Registered  Entity  may  appeal  to  Federal  Energy  Regulatory  Commission  (FERC)  or  another 

Applicable Governmental Authority within 21 Days of the notification of the decision. 

f.  A record of the appeals process shall be maintained by NERC.  Confidentiality of the record of the appeal 

will be based on the NERC ROP Section 1500. 

Public 

 
Public 

Section VII — NERC Organization Certification Appeals Process 

Purpose and Scope 
This section describes the process for an organization to appeal the Certification decision that was determined in the 
Certification process. 

Overview 
The  NERC  Organization  Certification  Program  provides  a  key  means  to  fulfill  NERC’s  mission.  In  conducting  this 
program, NERC has established documented procedures to ensure a fair and impartial appeals process.  No one with 
a  direct  interest  in  a  dispute  may  participate  in  the  appeals  process  except  as  a  party  or  witness.  See  Figure  4 
Organization Certification Appeals Process Overview. 

Organization Certification Appeals Procedure 

1.  Appeal for an Organization Certification finding. 

2.  Any entity can appeal an Organization Certification decision issued as a result of the Certification process. 

3.  Requirements and Conditions for Appeals. 

a.  For all appeals under the NERC Organization Certification Program, the appeals process begins when an 
entity notifies the NERC via the Certification email address, found on the Registration and Certification 
page of the NERC website that it wishes to use the NERC appeals process. 
•  The Director of Compliance is the main contact for all parties in all steps of the appeals process. 
• 

If an appeal is not filed within 21 Days of the date that the Certification report or finding is issued, or 
the final Regional Entity appeals process ruling is made, the finding shall be considered final and un-
appealable. 

b.  Each party in the appeals process shall pay its own expenses for each step in the process. 

c.  A stipulation of invoking the appeals process is that the Regional Entity or entity requesting the appeal 
agrees that NERC (its Members, Board, committees, subcommittees, and staff), any person assisting in 
the appeals process, and any company employing a person assisting in the appeals process, shall not be 
liable, and shall be held harmless against the consequences of any action or inaction or of any agreement 
reached  in  resolution  of  the  dispute  or  any  failure  to  reach  agreement  as  a  result  of  the  appeals 
proceeding.  This  “hold  harmless”  clause  does  not  extend  to  matters  constituting  gross  negligence, 
intentional misconduct, or a breach of confidentiality. 

d.  Parties retain the right to seek further review of a decision in whatever regulatory agency or court that 

may have jurisdiction. 

4.  At any time through this appeals process, an entity may withdraw its appeal. 

5.  Hearing and Ruling by the Compliance and Certification Committee. 

a.  Within 28 Days of receiving notice from the NERC Director of Compliance, the CCC will conduct a hearing 
where  all  the  parties  or  representatives  of  the  disputing  parties  will  present  the  issue  in  question,  in 
accordance  with  CCC  procedure  CCCPP-005,  Hearing  Procedures  for  Use  in  Appeals  of  Certification 
Matters, which is incorporated in Appendix 4E of the ROP. 

b. 

If the appeal is upheld, NERC notifies the entity and Regional Entity(ies), updates the NCR, and issues any 
appropriate letter and certificate to the entity. 

c. 

If the appeal is denied, NERC notifies the entity and Regional Entity(ies). 

Public 

 
 
Public 

6.  Hearings and Ruling by the BOTCC. 

Section VII — NERC Organization Certification Appeals Process 

a.  The BOTCC will be asked to resolve a dispute related to the NERC Organization Certification Program if 

any party to the appeal contests the CCC final order. 

b.  The BOTCC may request additional data from NERC, Regional Entity(ies) or the entity and prescribe the 

timeframe for submitting the requested data. 

c.  At  the  next  regularly  scheduled  BOTCC  meeting,  or  at  a  special  meeting  if  the  Board  determines  it  is 
necessary, the Chair of the CCC will present a summary of the dispute and the actions taken to the BOTCC. 
•  Each party will have an opportunity to state its case. 
•  The BOTCC will then rule on the dispute. 

d. 

e. 

If the BOTCC upholds the appeal, NERC will: 
•  Notify the entity and the Regional Entity(ies) that the appeal was upheld. 
•  Update the NCR. 
• 

Issue a Certification letter and a certificate to the entity as applicable. 

If the BOTCC does not uphold the appeal, NERC will notify the entity and the Regional Entity(ies) that the 
appeal was denied. 
•  The entity may appeal to Applicable Governmental Authorities within 21 Days of the issuance of the 

decision. 

f.  A  record  of  the  appeals  process  shall  be  maintained  by  NERC  and  available  upon  request. 

Confidentiality of the record of the appeal will be based on the NERC ROP Section 1500.

Statement of Compliance Registry Criteria (Revision 89)  

Summary 
This document describes how the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) will identify organizations 
that may be candidates for Registration and assign them to the Compliance Registry. 

NERC  and  the  Regional  Entities1  have  the  obligation  to  identify  and  register  all  entities  that  meet  the  criteria  for 
inclusion in the Compliance Registry, as further explained in the balance of this document. 

Organizations will be responsible to register and to comply with approved Reliability Standards to the extent that 
they are owners, operators, and users of the Bulk Power System (BPS), perform a function listed in the functional 
types identified in Section II of this document, and are material to the Reliable Operation of the interconnected BPS 
as defined by the criteria and sections set forth in this document. NERC will apply the following principles to the 
Compliance Registry: 

• 

In order to carry out its responsibilities related to enforcement of Reliability Standards, NERC must identify 
the owners, operators, and users of the BPS who have a material impact2 on the BPS through a Compliance 
Registry.  NERC  and  the  Regional  Entities  will  make  their  best  efforts  to  identify  all  owners,  users  and 
operators who have a material impact on the BPS in order to develop a complete and current Compliance 
Registry list. The Compliance Registry will be updated as required and maintained on an on-going basis. 
•  Organizations listed in the Compliance Registry are responsible and will be monitored for compliance with 
applicable  mandatory  Reliability  Standards.  They  will  be  subject  to  NERC's  and  the  Regional  Entities’ 
Compliance Monitoring and Enforcement Programs. 

•  NERC and Regional Entities will not monitor nor hold those not in the Compliance Registry responsible for 
compliance with the Reliability Standards. An entity which is not initially placed on the Compliance Registry, 
but which is identified subsequently as having a material impact on the BPS, will be added to the Compliance 
Registry. Such entity will not be subject to a sanction or Penalty by NERC or the Regional Entity for actions or 
inactions prior to being placed on the Compliance Registry, but may be required to comply with a Remedial 
Action Directive or Mitigation Plan in order to become compliant with applicable Reliability Standards. After 
such entity has been placed on the Compliance Registry, it shall be responsible for complying with Reliability 
Standards  and  may  be  subject  to  sanctions  or  Penalties  as  well  as  any  Remedial  Action  Directives  and 
Mitigation Plans required by the Regional Entities or NERC for future violations, including any failure to follow 
a Remedial Action Directive or Mitigation Plan to become compliant with Reliability Standards. 

•  Required compliance by a given organization with the Reliability Standards will begin the later of (i) inclusion 
of that organization in the Compliance Registry and (ii) approval by the Applicable Governmental Authority 
of mandatory Reliability Standards applicable to the registered entity. 

Entities responsible for funding NERC and the Regional Entities have been identified in the budget documents filed 
with  FERC.3  Presence  on  or  absence  from  the  Compliance  Registry  has  no  bearing  on  an  entity’s  independent 
responsibility for funding NERC and the Regional Entities. 

1 The term “Regional Entities” includes Cross-Border Regional Entities that have footprints in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, as applicable. 
Applicable Governmental Authorities in Canadian jurisdictions may have adopted their own Rules of Procedure and Compliance Registry 
requirements. Registered Entities may be subject to the Compliance Monitoring and Enforcement Programs (CMEP) in their respective 
jurisdictions, in accordance with applicable laws and regulations. 
2 The criteria for determining whether an entity will be placed on the Compliance Registry are set forth in the balance of this document. At 
any time a person may recommend in writing, with supporting reasons, to the Director of Compliance (or an equivalent position) that an 
organization be added to or removed from the Compliance Registry, pursuant to NERC Rules of Procedure Section 501.1.3.5. 
3 Budget documents are submitted to Applicable Governmental Authorities in Canada for information. 

Public 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Statement of Compliance Registry Criteria (Revision 89) 

Public 

Background 
The initial Registration process began in January of 2006.  Registration of new entities is an ongoing process.  If a 
Registered Entity’s information changes, these changes must be submitted to the applicable Regional Entity(ies). 
Based on selection as the ERO, NERC’s Organization Registration program4 is the means by which NERC and the 
Regional Entities plan, manage, and execute Reliability Standard compliance oversight of owners, operators, and 
users of the BPS. Organizations listed in the Compliance Registry are subject to NERC’s and the Regional Entities’ 
Compliance Monitoring and Enforcement Programs. 

Statement of Issue 
As the ERO, NERC intends to comprehensively and thoroughly protect the reliability of the grid.  To support this goal 
NERC will include in its Compliance Registry each entity that NERC concludes can materially impact the reliability of the 
BPS. 

NERC will identify those entities that may need to be listed in its Compliance Registry. Identifying these organizations 
is necessary and prudent for the purpose of determining resource needs, both at the NERC and Regional Entity level, 
and  for  communicating  with  these  entities  regarding  their  potential  responsibilities  and  obligations.  Candidate 
entities can be identified at any time, as and when needed. The Compliance Registry is available on NERC’s website. 

Resolution 
The potential costs and effort of registering every organization potentially within the scope of “owner, operator, and 
user  of  the  BPS,”  while  ignoring  their  impact  upon  reliability,  would  be  disproportionate  to  the  improvement  in 
reliability that would reasonably be anticipated from doing so. 

NERC and the Regional Entities have identified two principles they believe are key to the entity selection process. 
These are: 

1.  There needs to be consistency between Regions and across the continent with respect to which entities are 

registered; and 

2.  Any entity reasonably deemed material to the reliability of the BPS will be registered, irrespective of other 

considerations. 

To address the second principle the Regional Entities, working with NERC, will identify and register any entity they 
deem material to the reliability of the BPS. 

Registry Criteria 
In order to promote consistency, NERC and the Regional Entities use the following criteria as the basis for determining 
whether particular entities should be identified as candidates for Registration. All organizations meeting or exceeding 
the criteria will be identified as candidates. 

The  following  criteria  (Sections  I-V)  plus  the  statement  in  Section  VI  will  provide  guidance  regarding  an  entity’s 
Registration status: 

I.  Owners, operators, or users of the BPS are candidates for Registration.5   

4 See NERC ERO Application; Exhibit C; Section 500 – Organization Registration and Certification. 
5 See NERC Rules of Procedure Section 501.1 NERC Compliance  Registry — NERC shall establish and maintain the NCR of the BPS owners, 
operators, and users that are subject to approved Reliability Standards.  For purposes of this Section I, users, owners, and operators of the BPS 
includes: 1) entities that use, own, or operate Elements of the Bulk Electric System (BES) as defined in Appendix 2 of the NERC Rules of Procedure 
and NERC Glossary of Terms; as well as 2) entities otherwise defined in the Registry Criteria in this Appendix 5B.

III.  Entities identified in Section II above as being subject to Registration as a Distribution Provider, Computational 
Load Operator, or Computational Load Owner should be included in the Compliance Registry for these functions 
only if they meet any of the criteria listed below: 

III(a)   Distribution Provider: 

III.a.1  Distribution Provider system serving >75 MW of peak Load that is directly connected to the BES;7 or 

III.a.2  Distribution Provider is the responsible entity that owns, controls, or operates Facilities that are part 
of any of the following Protection Systems or programs designed, installed, and operated for the 
protection of the BES:8 
•  a required Undervoltage Load Shedding (UVLS) program and/or 
•  a required Special Protection System or Remedial Action Scheme and/or 
•  a required transmission Protection System; or 

III.a.3  Distribution  Provider  that  is  responsible  for  providing  services  related  to  Nuclear  Plant  Interface 

Requirements (NPIRs) pursuant to an executed agreement; or 

III.a.4  Distribution Provider with field switching personnel identified as performing unique tasks associated 

with the Transmission Operator’s restoration plan that are outside of their normal tasks. 

III(b)   Distribution Provider with UFLS-Only assets (referred to as “UFLS-Only Distribution Provider”) 

III.b.1  UFLS-Only  Distribution  Provider  does  not  meet  any  of  the  other  registration  criteria  in  Sections 

III(a)(1)-(4) for a Distribution Provider; and 

III.b.2  UFLS-Only  Distribution  Provider  is  the  responsible  entity  that  owns,  controls,  or  operates  UFLS 
Protection System(s) needed to implement a required UFLS Program designed for the protection of 
the BES. 

The Reliability Standards applicable to UFLS-Only Distribution Providers are: (1) any version of PRC-005 and 
PRC-006 applicable to UFLS-Only Distribution Providers, (2) any regional Reliability Standard whose purpose 
is to develop or establish a UFLS Program, and (3) any Reliability Standard that lists UFLS-Only Distribution 
Provider in the applicability section. Reliability Standards that apply to Distribution Providers will not apply 
to UFLS-Only Distribution Providers, unless explicitly stated in the applicability section of these Reliability 
Standards and in future revisions and/or versions. 

7 Ownership, control or operation of UFLS Protection System(s) needed to implement a required UFLS Program designed for the protection of 
the BES does not affect an entity’s eligibility for registration pursuant to III.a.1. 
8 As used in Section III.a.2, “protection of the Bulk Electric System” means protection to prevent instability, Cascading, or uncontrolled 
separation of the BES and not for local voltage issues (UVLS) or local line loading management (Special Protection System) that are 
demonstrated to be contained within a local area.

III(c)  Computational Load Owner or Operator: 

III.c.1   Computational Load Owner of a Computational Load Site with a total connected Load greater than 
or equal to 50 MW that is supplied through electrical equipment connected at a voltage level greater 
than or equal to 100 kV from one or more points of connection. 

III.c.2  Computational Load Operator of a Computational  Load Site with a total connected Load  greater

greater than or equal to 100 kV from one or more points of connection. 

IV.  Joint Registration Organization, Coordinated Functional Registration and applicable Member Registration. 

Pursuant to FERC’s directive in paragraph 107 of Order No. 693, NERC’s rules pertaining to joint Registrations and 
Joint Registration Organizations, as well as Coordinated Functional Registrations, are now found in Section 501, 
507, and 508 of the NERC Rules of Procedure. 

V.  If NERC or a Regional Entity encounters an organization that is not listed in the Compliance Registry, but which 
should be subject to the Reliability Standards, NERC or the Regional Entity is obligated and will initiate actions to 
add that organization to the Compliance Registry, subject to that organization’s right to challenge as provided in 
Section 500 of NERC’s Rules of Procedure. 

Determination of Material Impact9 
An entity that does not meet (i.e., falls below) the criteria may nevertheless be registered if it can be demonstrated 
that the entity has a material impact on the reliability of the BPS. Similarly, an entity that meets the criteria may be 
excluded if it can be demonstrated to NERC that the entity does not have a material impact on the reliability of the 
BPS. Such Registration decisions regarding materiality must be made by the NERC-led Registration Review Panel in 
accordance  with  Section  III(D)  of  Appendix  5A  to  the  NERC  Rules  of  Procedure.  In  order  to  ensure  a  consistent 
approach to assessing materiality, a non-exclusive set of factors (“materiality test”) for consideration is identified 
below;  however,  only  a  sub-set  of  these  factors,  or  other  additional  factors,  may  be  applicable  to  a  particular 
functional registration category or specific entity, as appropriate: 

1. 

Is the entity specifically identified in the emergency operation plans and/or restoration plans of an associated 
Reliability Coordinator, Balancing Authority, Generator Operator or Transmission Operator? 

2.  Will intentional or inadvertent removal of an Element owned or operated by the entity, or a common mode 
failure of two Elements as identified in the Reliability Standards (for example, loss of two Elements as a result 
of  a  breaker  failure),  lead  to  a  reliability  issue  on  another  entity’s  system  (such  as  a  neighboring  entity’s 
Element  exceeding  an  applicable  rating,  or  loss  of  non-consequential  load  due  to  a  single  contingency)? 
Conversely, will such contingencies on a neighboring entity’s system result in issues for Reliability Standards 
compliance on the system of the entity in question? 

3.  Can the normal operation, misoperation or malicious use of the entity’s cyber assets cause a detrimental 
impact (e.g., by limiting the operational alternatives) on the operational reliability of an associated Balancing 
Authority, Generator Operator or Transmission Operator?

UVLS,  Special  Protection  System,  Remedial  Action  Schemes  and  other  Protection  Systems  protecting  BES 
Facilities)  cause  an  adverse  impact  on  the  operational  reliability  of  any  associated  Balancing  Authority,

American Electric Power’s Comments on Proposed Revisions to 
NERC Rules of Procedure for Computational Load 

American Electric Power (AEP) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the proposed 
revisions to the NERC Rules of Procedure (ROP) pertaining to Computational Load. AEP supports NERC’s 
objective of safeguarding the reliability of the Bulk Power System (BPS) from risks associated with large 
Computational Loads and recognizes the importance of establishing Registration Criteria for entities that 
own or operate such sites.  

AEP appreciates NERC's consideration of stakeholder feedback throughout this initiative and 
acknowledges the revisions made in response to prior comments. AEP believes these revisions reﬂect a 
thoughtful eﬀort to address stakeholder concerns while advancing NERC's reliability objectives. 

AEP Proposes the Following Modiﬁcations: 

Appendix 2 (Deﬁnitions Used in the Rules of Procedure) 

The proposed deﬁnition updates provide important clarity and consistency for the Computational Load 
framework. NERC's eﬀorts to better deﬁne key terms strengthen the foundation for the associated 
Registration Criteria and support a common understanding across stakeholders. AEP appreciates the 
thoughtful approach taken to improve clarity within the Rules of Procedure and supports the proposed 
revisions. 

Appendix 5A (Organization Registration and Certiﬁcation Manual) 

The revisions to Appendix 5A are a constructive enhancement to the registration process for 
Computational Loads. The proposed updates improve transparency and provide useful guidance on how 
the registration requirements will be applied. 

Appendix 5B (Statement of Compliance Registry Criteria) 

AEP supports the proposed Registration Criteria and appreciates NERC's eﬀorts to establish a clear 
framework for identifying Computational Load facilities that may present reliability risks to the Bulk 
Power System (BPS). AEP believes the proposed revisions provide a practical path forward and supports 
their adoption.

Ameren comments on the Proposed Computational Load ROP Revisions 

Ameren supports the proposed revisions to the NERC Rules of Procedure to incorporate 
computational loads into the registration and reliability framework. Ameren also 
recommends that NERC consider whether future revisions should address large loads 
more broadly, including MW, interconnection voltage, and load type, because aggregated 
emerging large-load categories may present similar reliability considerations.

Comments for Computational Load ROP Revisions
Friday, September 18, 2026 6:59:40 PM

Definitions in Appendix 2:
ATC feels that the definition for Computational Load Site (CLS) may be too broad since “One 
or more buildings, structures, or installations at a single location” may not appropriately 
represent every CLS. For example, a single campus with multiple interconnections evaluated 
separately may not be classified as one CLS as some may interpret “a single location” as one 
POI or substation which can be too limiting.

There are also concerns for coordinated multi-sites that are separate CLS under different 
CLOs that are operated as one aggregate computation load. For example, data center owners 
have stated that a single” job” can be run on multiple data centers with different owners. This 
job will act in synchronism at the different locations so that load characteristics, such as 
variability, ride-through, etc. will affect the system the same as if they had been at one 
location with a single owner. The job could even be terminated for job-related reasons, 
affecting all sites involved simultaneously. This would be very difficult to monitor and audit for 
compliance.

Additionally, the definitions for Computational Load Owner and Computational Load 
Operator, when used in conjunction with CLS, is too simplistic a definition that does not 
clearly establish the responsible entity for a campus served through multiple substations or 
POIs.

Criteria in Appendix 5B:
ATC believes that the Computational Load Sites definition should apply to a voltage level 
greater than or equal to 60 kV as even these locations with a high enough load could easily 
impact the BES/BPS.

Thank you,

Amy Wilke
Reliability Standards Compliance Analyst  l PWK l

Please see below BPA’s comments on the Computational Load ROP Revisions. We

BPA believes the NERC Rules of Procedure definitions must be strengthened to
ensure Registered Entities such as Transmission Owners (TO), or currently non-
registered entities that have computational loads on their systems, would not be
able to apply Bulk Electric System (BES) exclusions E1 or E3 to areas that contain
Computational Load Site(s) (CLS). If the CLS or Computational Load Owner (CLO)
is interconnected to the Bulk Power System (BPS), and for that portion of the BPS
the TO uses BES exclusions such as E1 or E3, the Transmission Planner would not
receive modeling data for that portion of the TO system under the exclusion. In
the model, this would create an island for CLS data. BPA recommends exclusions
E1 and E3 not be allowed when there is embedded CLS within such networks.
Please see the attached document (E1-E3-LN Example.pdf), which helps clarify
our concerns in a visual format.

BPA suggests two potential solutions for consideration:

1. (Preferred solution) Revise the current definition of Bulk Electric System

(BES) in Appendix 2 to include a new I6 specific to Computational Load Site
and conforming revisions to Exclusions E1 and E3 (see attached Word Doc
‘Proposed Solution to Modify Appendix 2_Definition of BES_For
Computational Loads_BPA Comments). Or,

2. Modify MOD-032 to allow for data gathering to be applied for all BES and

BPS elements connected to Computational Load Sites.

Additionally, BPA recommends Appendix 5B be revised to align with language
used in Appendix 2, as show below.

Appendix 5B (Statement of Compliance Registry Criteria):
Computational Load Owner or Operator of a Computational Load Site with a
total connected Load greater than or equal to 50 MW that is supplied through

 
electrical equipment that is connected at a voltage level greater than or
equal to 100 kV from one or more points of connection to the BPS.

Appendix 2 (Definitions Used in the Rules of Procedure):

“Computational Load Site” means one or more buildings, structures, or
installations at a single location that

1. Primarily contains information technology infrastructure used for:
creating, executing, and delivering software applications and
services;
artificial intelligence training, deployment, and delivery;
cryptocurrency mining; or
other computational activities at a data center; and
2. is supplied through electrical equipment that is connected to the

BPS.

Appendix 2 
“Bulk Electric System” or “BES” means unless modiﬁed by the lists shown below, all 
Transmission Elements operated at 100 kV or higher and Real Power and Reactive Power 
resources connected at 100 kV or higher. This does not include facilities used in the local 
distribution of electric energy. 

Inclusions: 

•

•

•

•

•

•

I1 - Transformers with the primary terminal and at least one secondary terminal
operated at 100 kV or higher unless excluded by application of Exclusion E1 or E3.

I2 - Generating resource(s) including the generator terminals through the high-side
of the step-up transformer(s) connected at a voltage of 100 kV or above with:

a) Gross individual nameplate rating greater than 20 MVA. Or,
b) Gross plant/facility aggregate nameplate rating greater than 75 MVA.

I3 - Blackstart Resources identiﬁed in the Transmission Operator’s restoration plan.

I4 - Dispersed power producing resources that aggregate to a total capacity greater
than 75 MVA (gross nameplate rating), and that are connected through a system
designed primarily for delivering such capacity to a common point of connection at
a voltage of 100 kV or above. Thus, the facilities designated as BES are:

a) The individual resources, and
b) The system designed primarily for delivering capacity from the point where
those resources aggregate to greater than 75 MVA to a common point of
connection at a voltage of 100 kV or above.

I5 - Static or dynamic devices (excluding generators) dedicated to supplying or
absorbing Reactive Power that are connected at 100 kV or higher, or through a
dedicated transformer with a high-side voltage of 100 kV or higher, or through a
transformer that is designated in Inclusion I1 unless excluded by application of
Exclusion E4.

I6 - Computational Load Site(s) with a total connected Load greater than or equal to
50 MW that is supplied through electrical equipment that is connected to the BPS.

Exclusions: 

• E1 - Radial systems: A group of contiguous transmission Elements that emanates

from a single point of connection of 100 kV or higher and:
a) Only serves Load, not identiﬁed in Inclusion I6. Or,
b) Only includes generation resources, not identiﬁed in Inclusions I2, I3, or I4,
with an aggregate capacity less than or equal to 75 MVA (gross nameplate
rating). Or,

c) Where the radial system serves Load, not identiﬁed in Inclusion I6, and

includes generation resources, not identiﬁed in Inclusions I2, I3 or I4, with an
aggregate capacity of non-retail generation less than or equal to 75 MVA
(gross nameplate rating).

Note 1 – A normally open switching device between radial systems, as depicted on 
prints or one-line diagrams for example, does not affect this exclusion. 
Note 2 – The presence of a contiguous loop, operated at a voltage level of 50 kV or 
less, between conﬁgurations being considered as radial systems, does not affect 
this exclusion. 

• E2 - A generating unit or multiple generating units on the customer’s side of the

retail meter that serve all or part of the retail Load with electric energy if: (i) the net
capacity provided to the BES does not exceed 75 MVA, and (ii) standby, back-up,
and maintenance power services are provided to the generating unit or multiple
generating units or to the retail Load by a Balancing Authority, or provided pursuant
to a binding obligation with a Generator Owner or Generator Operator, or under
terms approved by the applicable regulatory authority.

• E3 - Local networks (LN): A group of contiguous transmission Elements operated at
less than 300 kV that distribute power to Load, not identiﬁed in Inclusion I6, rather
than transfer bulk power across the interconnected system. LN’s emanate from
multiple points of connection at 100 kV or higher to improve the level of service to
retail customers and not to accommodate bulk power transfer across the
interconnected system. The LN is characterized by all of the following:

a) Limits on connected generation: The LN and its underlying Elements do not
include generation resources identiﬁed in Inclusions I2, I3, or I4 and do not
have an aggregate capacity of non-retail generation greater than 75 MVA
(gross nameplate rating);

b) Real Power ﬂows only into the LN and the LN does not transfer energy

originating outside the LN for delivery through the LN; and

c) Not part of a Flowgate or transfer path: The LN does not contain any part of a
permanent Flowgate in the Eastern Interconnection, a major transfer path
within the Western Interconnection, or a comparable monitored Facility in
the ERCOT or Quebec Interconnections, and is not a monitored Facility
included in an Interconnection Reliability Operating Limit (IROL).
d) Limits on connected loads: The LN and its underlying Elements do not

include Computational Loads identiﬁed in Inclusions I6.

• E4 - Reactive Power devices installed for the sole beneﬁt of a retail customer(s).

CenterPoint Energy Houston Electric, LLC (CEHE) Comments on NERC Rules of 
Procedure Revisions for Computational Load Registration 

To whom it may concern, 

CenterPoint Energy Houston Electric, LLC (CEHE) is supportive of the registration effort for 
computational loads. The Computational Load “Owner” and “Operator” structure that NERC 
proposed is appropriate and echoes tried-and-tested registration frameworks (such as the 
Transmission  “Owner”  and  “Operator”  structure).  CEHE  also  agrees  with  the  expanded 
narrative definition of a Computational Load Site, as proposed in the changes to Appendix 2 
of  the  NERC  Rules  of  Procedure,  but  supports  EEI’s  recommendation  that  guidance  is 
provided clarifying that cloud storage sites are intended to be included under the definition. 

CEHE  does  recommend  that  NERC  provide  additional  guidance  on  the  types  of 
Computational Load Site configurations that would be subject to registration requirements. 

Many  Computational  Load  Sites  in  excess  of  50  MW  are  interconnected  via  fully-fledged 
breakered customer substations. At said customer substations, the voltage is stepped down 
to  distribution  level  voltages,  such  as  35  kV,  before  Computational  Load  Site  padmount 
transformers further reduce the voltage to a level appropriate for computational equipment 
(e.g.  480  V).  Because  the  customer-owned  substation  takes  transmission  service,  it  is 
unambiguously part of the BPS per the registration criteria.  

However, in other cases, a utility may interconnect a Computational Load Site in excess of 
50 MW via a dedicated distribution feed and own the padmount transformers on the outside 
of the Computational Load Site. The utility thereby provides 480 V distribution service to the 
Site. Would the registration criteria in such instances be applied to the point of connection 
at the primary transformers feeding the site (the distribution padmount transformers), or the 
transformer(s)  that  the  dedicated  feed  comes  from?  Figure  1  below  illustrates  such  an 
example.  

Page 1 of 2 

Figure 1 

Additionally, some Computational Load Sites in excess of 50 MW may be interconnected on 
radial distribution feeds, as illustrated in Figure 2 below. In such instances, would the radial 
nature of the point  of connection preclude registration  (per the  7-Part Test established in 
FERC Order 888), or would the proposed registration criteria still apply?  

Figure 2 

Guidance and/or a NERC registration webinar to answer these questions would help reduce 
ambiguity  for  both  Computational  Load  Site  Owners/Operators  and  interconnecting 
Utilities.

Constellation Comments on Proposed Revisions to the NERC Rules of Procedure NERC Rules of 
Procedure Appendix 2 (Definitions Used in the Rules of Procedure); Appendix 5A (Organization 
Registration and Certification Manual); and Appendix 5B (Statement of Compliance Registry 
Criteria): 

While Constellation supports the creation of two new functions, Computational Load Owner 
(CLO) and Computational Load Operator (CLOP), further clarification is needed on the intent and 
scope of the CLOP.  The FAQ document developed to provide additional guidance on connection 
point(s) to the BPS and examples of defining a Computational Load Site boundary does not 
provide enough clarity on what “operational” activities could be performed by the CLOP.  
Without revision, it is not clear what reliability functions will apply to the connecting 
Transmission Owner, Distribution Provider or Generator Owner serving the Computational Load 
or what reliability functions would apply to the CLOP.  For example, in the case of a GO/GOP 
that connects to a Computational Load directly or via a Co-Located Load arrangement, if the 
GO/GOP operates the breakers supplying the Computational Load in response to an Operational 
Instruction to divorce the load it could inadvertently and unnecessarily require the GO/GOP d to 
register as a CLOP. 

Per the revised definition of an Operating Instruction: 

(Modified) Operating Instruction: 
A command by operating personnel responsible for the Real-time operation of the interconnected 
Bulk Electric System to change or preserve the state, status, output, or input of an Element of the 
Bulk Electric System or Facility of the Bulk Electric System or a Computational Load Site. [emphasis 
added] 

The Technical Rationale for CLO-003-1 does provide some example scenarios on the potential 
ownership of the main power transformer(s) of the Computational Load Site and additional 
clarity on how the CLOP may be applied; however, Technical Rationale documents are 
informational only and not submitted to the FERC for approval.  The drafting team should 
remove ambiguity regarding the assumed demarcation between the CLOP and the GO, DP 
and/or TO because it is not clearly described within the definition of the CLOP or the associated 
draft CLOP Standards.

Data Center Coalition comments on NERC Proposed Rules of Procedure and Registry Criteria 
Friday, September 18, 2026 4:31:23 PM

Good Afternoon,        

See below, the Data Center Coalition (DCC’s) comments on NERC’s proposed Rules of 
Procedure and Registry Criteria, due today. Please confirm receipt of our comments as 
appropriate.

DCC Comments on the NERC Rules of Procedure Updates 
On the Computational Load Definitions/Registration Criteria
Submitted 9/17/2026

The Data Center Coalition (DCC) is pleased to submit these comments on NERC’s 
updated proposed Rules of Procedure definitions and registration criteria for 
Computational Loads.
Like all customers, the data center industry depends on a reliable electricity grid in order 
to fulfill its role as a vital backbone of our modern economy. In turn, data centers offer a 
number of reliability benefits to the grid, including significant investments in new energy 
resources and next-generation technologies. Data centers can also serve as grid assets 
that help promote reliability during energy emergencies caused by extreme weather.
It is critical to ensure proposed definitions and registration criteria by NERC are based 
on complete evidence, the technical capabilities and specifications of data center 
equipment, and do not disregard important developments or information from the 
industry. The DCC’s comments below aim to provide the challenges and concerns with 
the proposed definitions and registration criteria in applying accurately and fairly across 
the country, while also giving recommendations to improve the definitions and criteria to 
address the stated issues.

Proposed ROP Definition

DCC requests that NERC confirm that it intended to use the term “BPS” in defining
Computational Load Site as "supplied through electrical equipment that is
connected to the BPS."  The NERC registration model has historically been based
on the BES definition, as NERC/REs determine whether or not entities are "Users,
Owners, and Operators" of the BES for purposes of registration.  Yet Section 215 of
the FPA uses the term "BPS," not BES.  FERC has said that, even though NERC

uses BES, the fact that FPA Section 215 uses BPS is evidence that Congress
actually intended to give FERC authority beyond NERC's BES definition. See, e.g.,
Mandatory Reliability Standards for the Bulk Power System, 118 FERC P 61,218 at
P 76 (2007) (“Therefore, the Commission confirms its statements in the NOPR that
the Bulk-Power System reaches farther than those facilities that are included in
NERC's definition of the bulk electric system.”).  DCC requests clarity on the intent
and purpose of using BPS, and how this use relates to the exclusion in FPA Section
215–namely that the BPS “does not include facilities used in the local distribution
of electric energy.”
DCC is particularly concerned about the potential for confusion regarding the
definition of “Computational Load Operator” as the entity that “operates” a
Computational Load Site, and the definition of Computational Load Owner as the
entity that “maintains” a Computational Load Site.  Given the diversity of business
models and responsibility configurations among distinct legal entities that may
exist at a given Computational Load Site, it may be unclear where one entity’s
“operation” of a site ends, and where another’s “maintenance” begins.  DCC
suggests striking the phrase “or maintains” from the definition of Computational
Load Owner to avoid this potential confusion. In addition, the use of the word
“owns” in the Computational Load Owner definition should also be clarified that
this is the owner of the physical equipment of the site (UPS, cooling systems,
electrical infrastructure, controls/relays, etc.), rather than say owners of the real
estate/land.
The Computational Load Site definition covers one or more buildings, structures,
or installations at a “single location, “ and how that term and the term “one or
more buildings” are read decides whether a phased campus generates one
registration or several. The term should be defined to track how campuses are
actually built, since buildings may be separated by roads or parcel lines, energized
years apart, and fed from different stations while sharing cooling and auxiliary
load. If it stays undefined as it currently is in the proposed definition, the same
physical campus can be read as one location or several depending on the
reviewer, and each reading carries a different registration count and compliance
cost, which is the highest leverage cost driver in the package. DCC asks NERC to
either define single location by reference to the published factors, or to replace it
with new text such as the following: “buildings, structures, or installations that
share common electrical infrastructure or a coordinated operating function
constitute a single Computational Load Site, without regard to parcel boundaries
or phased in service dates.”

Proposed MW Threshold Criteria

DCC recommends NERC increase the proposed registration threshold from 50
MW to 75 MW while retaining the 100 kV criterion. NERC's own technical analysis
provided with the ROP changes shows that a 75 MW threshold would still capture
approximately 63,960 MW, or 80%, of current/forecasted computational load,
compared to 68,288 MW, or 86%, under the proposed 50 MW threshold. The
proposed 50 MW threshold therefore captures only approximately 4.3 GW of
additional load nationwide, representing less than 6% of total current/forecasted
computational load. DCC does not believe this incremental increase in coverage
materially changes aggregate BPS reliability risk, and a 75 MW threshold would
provide a more appropriate balance between reliability and regulatory burden.
In addition, the term “connected Load” in the CLO/CLOP registration criteria
should also be clarified to ensure it is the contracted load identified/agreed upon
in the interconnection agreements such that any behind-the-meter generation is
accounted for that impacts the total load seen by the grid.

Clarification of the term “Primarily”

NERC should revise the proposed Computational Load Site definition to replace
the subjective term "primarily" with a measurable threshold. Unlike other
jurisdictions, the proposed definition does not specify what percentage of facility
demand must be attributable to computational load activities. For example,
ERCOT defines a Large Computational Load as a facility where 50% or more of
demand consists of computational load, while MISO uses a threshold based on at
least 25 MW of IT equipment demand (essentially the same as a 50% threshold).
Establishing a clear percentage or MW-based criterion would improve consistency
of the registration criteria across Regional Entities.

Proposed Voltage Threshold Boundary Concerns

NERC should clarify the application of the 100 kV criterion by establishing a clear
boundary for when a Computational Load Site is considered to be "supplied
through" electrical equipment connected at or above 100 kV. As currently drafted,
it is unclear whether a facility interconnected at 34.5 kV remains subject to
registration simply because the serving distribution circuit ultimately traces back
to a 100 kV or higher transmission source (all distribution eventually traces back to
a transmission source). Additional guidance is needed to distinguish between
facilities served by dedicated feeders directly connected to a neighboring
transmission substation and facilities served through traditional distribution
systems with many customers.
The proposed ≥100 kV criterion creates ambiguous and inequitable outcomes for

data centers connected at distribution voltages. Many facilities take service at
sub-100 kV (e.g., 34.5 kV) through Distribution Provider infrastructure that
connects upstream to the transmission network at 100 kV or above. In these
configurations, the Computational Load Owner has no control over, and often no
visibility into, how the Distribution Provider connects to the transmission system
or what other loads share the same bus. The NERC FAQ diagrams suggest that
registration may hinge on whether other loads happen to be connected to the
same distribution bus, yet Distribution Providers routinely move loads, open bus
ties, and swap feeders without notifying connected customers. A facility's
registration status could therefore change overnight through no action of its own.
DCC requests that NERC clarify: (1) how applicability is determined when the
distribution bus serving a data center also serves other customers; (2) what
notification obligations the Distribution Provider has when network changes affect
a facility's registration status; and (3) whether the FERC Order 773 seven-factor
test for local distribution exclusion applies to large loads consuming power at
distribution voltage, given that the only sub-100 kV inclusion precedent in that
order was for generation injecting power, not load withdrawing it. DCC also asks
NERC to further clarify and define the phrase “common point of connection,”
which Figures 2 and 3 in the FAQ both use and treat as distinct from the point of
connection to the BPS without defining either.

Co-located Campuses & Buildings

NERC should clarify how registration applies to campus developments with
multiple Computational Load Owners. Under the proposed framework, it is
unclear whether registration is assessed at the Computational Load Site level, the
individual owner level, or both. For example, if a campus exceeds 50 MW in
aggregate but consists of multiple building owners, including some responsible for
less than 50 MW of load, it is unclear whether all owners would be required to
register.
The industry needs clarity up front prior to these new definitions and registration
criteria getting approved in place, as the industry and future registered entities
need to understand exactly how these roles and responsibilities will apply to their
facilities and existing commercial agreements such that flexibility and appropriate
planning of these compliance responsibilities can be made well in advance of the
official NERC registration dates.
Similarly, many Computational Loads operate in a co-located tenant model. It is
unclear whether tenants are CLOPs in all circumstances or only when they
exercise operational control over computational equipment. As an example, if a
300 MW Computational Load Site contains ten Computational Load Operators,

including operators responsible for less than 50 MW each, it is unclear whether all
ten operators would be required to register or whether registration would apply
only to those entities with a material ownership or operational role at the site. Any
compliance framework should align responsibilities with the entity that owns or
controls the relevant equipment and data. NERC should also recognize that
colocation providers are often subject to confidentiality and commercial
agreements that limit their ability to obtain, verify, or disclose tenant-specific
operational information, and should avoid imposing compliance obligations that
require one entity to report information controlled by another. 
To illustrate the range of delivery models the registration criteria must
accommodate, DCC offers the following to NERC staff:

DCC’s members develop power infrastructure using the delivery model best
suited for each location. On some campuses, the serving utility owns and
operates the substation and provides medium voltage service (typically 34.5
kV or 12.5 kV) directly to the owner’s facilities. On other campuses,
particularly large hyperscale developments requiring significant capacity,
the owner takes service at transmission voltage (typically 100 kV and above)
and owns the high voltage substation that transforms power to medium
voltage for campus distribution. In these cases, the owner owns and
manages the transmission interconnection, substation assets, and medium
voltage distribution infrastructure. Power is delivered to the tenants at low
voltage (typically 480 V), and each tenant controls only their own
computational workload.

Single Registration Language in ROP

NERC should clarify the treatment of multi-tenant facilities and expressly identify
when a single entity may serve as the accountable Computational Load Operator
for an entire Computational Load Site in the ROP. While NERC has indicated that a
centralized or shared operating function may serve as the single accountable
Computational Load Operator at a multi-tenant site, that concept is not reflected
in the proposed registration criteria or supporting definitions.

This matters because a campus is typically owned by one legal entity,
operated by staff or an affiliate or a shared services entity, and leased to
tenants who control only their own workloads, so without a stated rule,
affiliates or tenants risk being pulled onto the Compliance Registry alongside
the owner. Left as drafted, a registrant cannot tell a tenant with confidence
that the tenant is outside the registry, which complicates leasing. DCC
requests that NERC clarify where owner and operator functions are split,
when a single accountable operator may register as CLO for the entire site,

and provide confirmation that a tenant controlling only its own workload is or
is not itself a Computational Load Operator where a shared operating
function has registered

Phased Campus Buildouts

NERC should also clarify how these requirements apply to phased campus
developments. Registration obligations should be clarified on how current
energized and operational capacity may be phased over time leading to the
ultimate buildout capacity, as campuses are commonly developed and placed
into service over multiple phases and years. Clear guidance is needed to ensure
consistent treatment of multi-owner campuses while allowing registration and
compliance obligations to align with the actual load that is in service.

Making the FAQ Document Binding Text

NERC’s FAQ says helpful things, that two or more sites can sit behind the same
supply equipment, that a single site can be fed from separate stations, and that
there can be more than one owner and more than one operator of a single site, but
an FAQ is not enforceable and can be revised or ignored by whoever runs a given
registration review. For an owner and operator, that means the difference between
one registration and several registrations for a phased campus is based on
informal guidance rather than on the criteria themselves, and registration is the
gateway to every obligation in all three proposed Reliability Standards. If the draft
stays as written, each campus gets reviewed on its own facts with no binding text
to point to, so outcomes vary region to region. DCC recommends NERC to convert
the FAQ answers into binding text in Appendix 5B or some other enforceable
document to keep consistency across the entire ERO.
NERC has identified factors – such as ownership, shared or common
infrastructure, and coordinated use of the computing infrastructure – that bear on
how a site is delineated, but they currently function as informal guidance rather
than as a published test. A published test is what lets an owner model registration
outcomes at the design stage, when it is deciding whether phases share a
substation, share cooling, or are separately metered. Without it, the registrant has
no certainty in advance and invites inconsistent results across regions. DCC asks
that the factors NERC lists be published as the governing test for site delineation,
with the further point on how the connected load is measured at the site compared
against the future maximum build out of load studied in the interconnection
process, and how those differences will apply for registration and NERC
requirements while the projects are built out over time.

FAQ Expansion

DCC requests that NERC add various campus examples to the FAQ illustrating
how the proposed registration criteria would apply to phased, multi-building, and
multi-tenant Computational Load Sites. Building on the existing Figures 2 and 3,
NERC should illustrate a campus with multiple phases energized over time, shared
substations and cooling infrastructure, separate parcel boundaries, multiple
points of connection and the voltages of the connecting equipment, and tenants
that control only their own computational workloads. The examples should
identify the expected registration outcomes and clarify whether connected load is
evaluated at the site level or by individual phase, owner, operator, or tenant. Such
examples would provide meaningful implementation guidance and help ensure
consistent application of the criteria across a range of common data center
development and ownership structures.

Sincerely,

Morgan A. Sipple
Director, Energy Policy - FERC and RTOs 
Data Center Coalition

My comments are as follows:

defined in Appendix 5B at page 8. Some definitions, but not all, include threshold values.
Appendix 2 is likely to be the first place interested parties would look for threshold values.

2. Appendix 5B, Statement of Compliance Registry Criteria, includes a section on
"Determination of Material Impact" at page 8, which states, "An entity that does not meet (i.e.,
falls below) the criteria may nevertheless be registered if it can be demonstrated that the entity
has a material impact on the reliability of the BPS." Given the robust debate over thresholds, it
would seem prudent for NERC to actively engage stakeholders in reviewing these threshold
values in a public process going forward.

the traditional NERC registration framework characteristics of the load itself. Footnote 5 on
page 4 expressly broadens “users, owners, and operators of the BPS” to include not only
entities using, owning, or operating BES Elements, but also entities “otherwise defined in the
Registry Criteria in this Appendix 5B."

prior registration practice, and no discussion of why direct regulation of an electricity 
consumer is institutionally different from registering utilities, generators, transmission owners, 
planners, or reliability coordinators.  

Including a direct acknowledgement and explanation of this shift in policy seems reasonable.

Thank you again for the opportunity to review these well-crafted documents.

Re: Comments on the August 2026 Proposed Revisions to the NERC Rules of

To whom it may concern, 

EdgeConneX (“ECX”) respectfully files these comments in response to 

the August 19, 2026 notice as to proposed changes to NERC’s Rules of 
Procedure.  Those proposed changes include adding the terms 
“Computational Load Owner” and “Computational Load Operator,” to 
Appendix 2.  The definitions of those terms, however, are inadequate to 
allow implementation of the standards that NERC is contemplating. 

The proposed definition of a Computational Load Owner is simply an 
“entity that owns and maintains a Computational Load Site.”  Similarly, a 
Computational Load Operator is proposed to be “an entity that operates a 
Computational Load Site.”  Neither definition is clear as to whether it 
includes collocated tenants that operate information technology at a 
Computational Load Site.  This lack of clarity is significant because, if 
tenants are not included, it may well be the case that the entities that are 
covered by the proposed standards will not have the ability or information 
necessary to comply with many of those requirements. 

For instance, proposed standard CLO-OO1 anticipates Computational 

Load Owners providing studies and modeling data.  ECX, however, does not 
own or operate any servers that hold or manage computational data.  Those 
are owned by its collocated tenants, so ECX does not have information 
necessary to create forecasts based on those parties’ actual future behavior.  
Beyond that, under its lease agreements with all its tenants, ECX is often 
subject to strict confidentiality agreements that may well prevent it from 
sharing any information it does have as to future usage. 

Similarly, for purposes of communicating real-time operational 
information under proposed CLO-002, ECX can provide information only at 
the level of the full data center, not that of any individual tenant.  Any 
information that relates to tenant data must be released by the tenant, 
rather than ECX.  Even where it has tenant-specific data, existing 
agreements often prevent ECX from releasing that information. 

For these reasons, NERC should clarify whether tenants are 

Computational Load Operators.  If they are not Computational Load 
Operators subject to the proposed reliability standards, NERC should either 

2201 Cooperative Way, Suite 400
Herndon, VA 20171 

add a definition of tenants and include those entities in its standards or 
revise those standards so that they do not inappropriately and unfairly 
impose obligations that regulated entities cannot satisfy.

Proposed Changes to NERC Rules of Procedure 
“Computational Load Owner”

Comments of the Electricity Consumers Resource Council 
(ELCON) 

The  Electricity  Consumers  Resource  Council  (ELCON)  respectfully  submits  these 
Comments in response to the National Electric Reliability Corporation’s (NERC) proposed 
revisions to the NERC Rules of Procedure posted August 19, 20261 incorporating the terms 
“Computational Load Owner,” “Computational Load Operator,” and “Computational Load 
Site.”  

ELCON  is  the  national  association  representing  large  industrial  consumers  of  electricity. 
ELCON member companies create a wide range of products from virtually every segment of 
the  industrial  community—we  own  and  operate  hundreds  of  major  facilities  and  are 
significant consumers of electricity throughout the United States. Reliable electricity supply 
at just and reasonable rates is essential to our members’ operations. 

ELCON appreciates NERC’s careful consideration of the public comments and feedback to 
its April 1, 2026 posting proposing a newly defined “Computational Load Entity” for NERC 
registration. ELCON recognizes that NERC attempted to incorporate ELCON’s feedback to 
add further clarification to the proposed definitions and criteria that directly tie the primary 
electrical operations of a facility or site to the risks posed to the bulk power system (BPS).  

However,  we  remain  concerned  that  the  revised  definitions  and  registration  criteria,  as 
written,  could  capture  industrial  and  other  large  commercial  loads  rather  than  narrowly 
targeting  data  center and  cryptocurrency  loads  identified  in  NERC’s  prior  whitepapers  as 
exhibiting behaviors that pose a risk to the BPS.2 

1 https://www.nerc.com/who-we-are/rules-of-procedure/proposed-changes-to-rules-of-procedure. 

2 See Characteristics and Risks of Emerging Large Loads (July 2025), https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/who-we-
are/standing-committees/rstc/whitepaper-characteristics-and-risks-of-emerging-large-loads.pdf; Assessment of 
Gaps in Existing Practices, Requirements, and Reliability Standards for Emerging Large Loads (March 2026), 
https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/our-work/guidelines/reliability/white-paper---assessment-of-gaps.pdf.  

Appendix 2 – Definitions Used in the Rules of Procedure 

The  August  19  proposed  revisions  to  Appendix  2  of  NERC’s  Rules  of  Procedure  replace 
“Computational Load” and “Computational Load Entity” with three new terms that include 
“Computational Load Owner,” “Computational Load Operator,” and “Computational Load 
Site.” The definition for “Computational Load Site” being: 

one or more buildings, structures, or installations at a single location that 

1) Primarily contains information technology infrastructure used for:

• creating, executing, and delivering software applications and services;
• artificial intelligence training, deployment, and delivery;
• cryptocurrency mining; or
• other computational activities at a data center; and

2) is supplied through electrical equipment that is connected to the BPS.

The new definition attempts to capture the primary operations associated with data center, 
artificial intelligence, and cryptocurrency that encapsulates the majority of that facility or 
site’s  electrical  usage  and  demand.  ELCON  is  concerned  that  the  first  bullet  “creating, 
executing,  and  delivering  software  applications  and  services”  could  be  interpreted  as 
extremely  broad  and  could  capture  any  large  facility  with  a  server  room  hosting 
communication processing, monitoring applications, or data storage. It is unclear whether 
all three actions in bullet one – creating, executing, and delivering – must occur at the site 
or  if  any  one  of  those  actions  qualifies  the  building,  structure,  or  installation  as  a 
Computational  Load  Site.  For  example,  if  the  structure  is  only  executing  software 
applications  that  are  ancillary  to  the  electrical  demand  of  the  primary  operations  of  the 
facility, those entities should not meet the definition of a Computational Load Site.  

NERC’s stated intent is to address the unique, highly variable, and unpredictable electrical 
dynamics  associated  with  massive,  dedicated  data-processing  clusters,  not  to  register 
established  commercial  and  industrial  end-users  whose  load  profiles  and  electrical 
demand are already well understood by their host utilities. 

To  reflect  this  intent  without  regulatory  ambiguity,  the  definition  must  clearly  evaluate 
whether a site is dedicated to the full operational cycle of creating, executing, and delivering 
computational services as its core purpose. The definition must explicitly exclude ancillary 
information  technology  usage,  such  as  on-site  server  rooms  hosting  communication  and 
other  data  processing  applications,  that  is  incidental  to  a  facility’s  primary  industrial  or 
commercial operations. 

ELCON recommends that NERC further refine the definition of Computational Load Site to 
specify: 

1) Primarily contains information technology infrastructure used for:

• creating,  executing,  and  delivering  software  applications  and  their  related
services,  not  including  electricity  usage  for  information  technology

2 

infrastructure  that  is  secondary  or  incidental  to  a  facility’s  primary 
electrical demand; 

As another example, ERCOT’s Large Computational Load definition includes a percentage 
of total demand to effectively carve out those loads whose information technology demand 
is incidental. ERCOT defines Large Computational Load as “A Large Load in which 50% or 
greater  of  the  Demand  at  the  site  consists  of  power  electronic  based  load,  specifically 
computational load, such as data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities.” 

With a similar clarification, ELCON is satisfied that large industrial and commercial loads 
will  be  appropriately  excluded  from  the  category  of  “Computational  Load  Site”  and  thus 
exempt from NERC registration and compliance with mandatory reliability standards. 

Appendix 5B – Statement of Compliance Registry Criteria 

In  the  August  19  posting,  NERC  raised  the  originally  proposed  thresholds  for  registering 
computational loads from 20 MW to 50 MW of total connected load at a single 100kv point, 
rather than 69kv. While the newly proposed 50 MW threshold of total connected load more 
appropriately reflects the risk impact of computational load sites,  merely raising the MW 
threshold does not shield large industrial loads from registration requirements on its own. 
Without the recommended clarifications to the definition, the registration criteria presents 
a  similar  broad  stroke  without  addressing  the  operational  characteristics  unique  to  data 
center and crypto loads. 

Should NERC reject the recommended clarifications to the definition of Computation Load 
Site, ELCON recommends adding similar revised language to the Registration Criteria such 
that  “a  site  with  a  total  connected  load  of  50  MW  or  higher,  of  which  50%  or  more  is 
attributable to information technology demand,” or “not including electricity usage for 
information  technology  infrastructure  that  is  secondary  or  incidental  to  a  facility’s 
primary electrical demand” is effectively differentiated from other large loads. 

With the qualifying language applied either to the Computational Load Site definition or the 
Computational Load Owner/Operator registration criteria, ELCON has no specific comment 
as to the appropriateness of the 50 MW or 100kv thresholds other than to recognize FERC’s 
responsiveness to ELCON’s recommendations to the April 1st proposal. 

ELCON strongly recommends that whatever criteria is ultimately approved to be filed with 
FERC,  there  is  a  coordinated  effort  among  FERC,  NERC,  RTOs/ISOs,  and  the  states  to 
develop consistent terms, conditions, and guidelines around large load interconnection and 
integration  that  recognizes  the  potential  risk  impact  of  certain  large  loads.  Absent  such 
coordination,  we  run  the  risk  of  a  patchwork  of  regulations  rife  with  inconsistencies  and 
conflicting  obligations.  The  reliability  of  an  interconnected  BPS  relies  on  consistent, 
predictable,  and  technically  grounded  rules  that  reflect  how  power  actually  flows. 
Regulatory thresholds must logically align with operational performance and the physical 
impact on the bulk electric system. Without a cohesive, coordinated effort across federal 

3 

and state jurisdictions, the industry faces an uncoordinated compliance regime that creates 
jurisdictional  confusion,  inflates  consumer  costs,  and  distracts  from  addressing  genuine 
reliability risks. 

ELCON appreciates the extensive outreach and analysis devoted to ensuring our grid can 
meet the challenges of integrating computational loads and large load technologies. ELCON 
looks forward to continuing our engagement with NERC as we address large load operations 
and the criticality of reliable electricity. 

/s/ Karen Onaran

September 18, 2026 

ERCOT Comments on Proposed Revisions to Rules of Procedure Relating to 
Computational Loads. 

Electric  Reliability  Council  of  Texas,  Inc.  (ERCOT)  provides  the  following 
comments  in  response  to  the  August  19,  2026  posting  of  proposed  revisions  to 
Appendices 2, 5A, and 5B of the NERC Rules of Procedure, relating to the registration of 
Computational Loads.   

ERCOT has concerns that the proposed definition of “Computational Load Site” 
lacks sufficient clarity to provide clear, objective guidance regarding which locations will 
be subject to the proposed standards.  This lack of clarity could substantially complicate 
the  application  of  the  proposed  standard,  which  requires  Planning  Coordinators, 
Transmission  Planners,  Generator  Owners,  Transmission  Owners,  and  Distribution 
Providers—and developers of Computational Load Sites—to know which entities must be 
subject  to  the  required  interconnection  study  processes.      As  written,  the  proposed 
definition leaves room for significant debate about whether a given site with computational 
load should be regarded as a Computational Load Site.  The definition of that term refers 
to “one or more buildings, structures, or installations at a single location that . . . Primarily 
contains  information  technology  infrastructure  .  .  .  .”    Because  the  phrase  “primarily 
contains information technology infrastructure” is presumed to modify the word “location” 
due  to  subject-verb  agreement  rules,  the  essence  of  this  first  half  of  the  definition  is 
whether a “location . . . primarily contains” IT infrastructure.   If “location” is reasonably 
understood  to  refer  to  the  entirety  of  the  site  that  contains  all  of  the  customer’s  grid-
connected  infrastructure,  which  ERCOT  presumes  is  the  intent,  it  must  then  be 
understood what it means for that site to “primarily contain” IT infrastructure.  On its face, 
this appears to require a spatial determination that raises many questions, such as: Is the 
calculation based on square footage of buildings or square footage of IT equipment inside 
those  buildings?    Does  it  consider  volume  of  either  of  those?    Are  items  like  cooling 
equipment, UPS, and dedicated backup generation included?   

Apart from the lack of clarity in scope, a spatial approach likely presents a problem 
in the case of co-located generation. For example, if a 1,000 MW data center co-locates 
with a 2,000 MW generating facility that has a larger total footprint, one might reasonably 
conclude  that  the  location  primarily  contains  generating  infrastructure,  and  not  IT 
infrastructure.  Yet it would make little sense to exempt data centers from these standards 
simply because they are co-locating with generation facilities.  Given the growing interest 
and incidence of co-location of computational loads with generation (whether existing or 
new generation), ERCOT believes it is important to avoid any room for debate under this 
definition.    

Consistent with NERC’s original draft proposal in April 2026, ERCOT recommends 
that NERC establish the regulatory scope based on the amount of computational load at 
the  site—ideally  establishing  scope  based  on  the  percentage  of  computational  load 

1 

relative to the total site load, so long as total site load meets a minimum MW threshold. 
This approach would better align with the underlying reliability interest because it would 
focus on the MW size of the computational load, which is the most significant factor for 
reliability,  as  opposed to  spatial aspects  of  the  facility,  which  are  less  relevant  to BPS 
reliability.    While  the  proposed  registry  criteria  would  impose  a  50  MW  minimum  size 
threshold,  the  use  of  “primarily  located”  in  the  Computational  Load  Site  definition 
introduces ambiguity as to which locations will be subject to registration in the first place.  
ERCOT encourages NERC to reconsider this approach.   

Relatedly, ERCOT also has concerns with the 100kV threshold in the Compliance 
Registry  Criteria  for  Computational  Load  Owners  and  Computational  Load  Operators.  
Larger loads can connect at voltages lower than 100kV.  As noted above, the MW size of 
the load should be the critical factor for determining impact to the BPS.  Introducing a 
voltage  threshold  serves  no  reliability  purpose  and  creates  room  for  creative 
arrangements  designed  to  circumvent  these  requirements.    ERCOT  recommends 
removing this threshold. 

Regarding the definition of “Computational Load Owner,” requiring that the entity 
both  “owns  and  maintains”  the  Computational  Load  Site  introduces  unnecessary 
ambiguity  due  to  the  uncertain  meaning  of  “maintains.”    In  ERCOT’s  view,  ownership 
should be the only material factor to defining a Computational Load Owner.  Whatever 
“maintain”  is  understood  to  mean,  if  an  entity  that  owns  the  facility  arguably  does  not 
“maintain”  the  facility,  this  would  create  a  gap  where  there  is  no  Computational  Load 
Owner  for  a  given  Computational  Load  Site.    Since  a  Computational  Load  Owner  is 
necessary  for  each  Computational  Load  Site,  the  drafting  team  should  delete  the 
reference to “maintains” to ensure at least one entity meets the definition in each case. 

As a more general matter, ERCOT anticipates that it may be difficult to ascertain 
which entity is the Computational Load Operator in some cases. For example, in some 
situations, an entity that owns a large data center may lease out space to multiple entities, 
each of which may be considered an operator of computational load equipment.  Having 
multiple  entities  responsible  for  compliance  at  a  single  site  would  create  uncertainty 
regarding  allocation  of  responsibility  for  complying  with  operational  requirements  and 
could  require  Reliability  Coordinators,  Balancing  Authorities,  and  other  entities  to 
coordinate with multiple entities, creating unnecessary confusion.  In addition, the entity 
that  operates  the  data  center  location  may  differ  from  the  entity  responsible  for  the 
operational behavior of the IT equipment (e.g., real power oscillation).   Which of them 
truly “operates” the IT equipment at the location may not be not facially clear.  One way 
to address these concerns may be to create a single term—perhaps “Computational Load 
Customer”—that subsumes both the ownership and operator obligations and that could 
be  used  throughout  the  standards  in  lieu  of  the  CLO/CLOP  terms.    This  would  more 
clearly assign responsibility to the entity connecting the computational load to the BPS, 
and that responsibility could then be assigned through contractual allocation of liability to 
any third-party tenants or other actors at the site whose activities might implicate NERC 
Reliability Standard requirements.  This approach would avoid complications that might 

2 

arise  from  attempting  to  determine  which  entity  is  truly  the  operator  in  each  case  and 
would ensure a single entity is responsible for each computational load facility.    

3 

Google comments on NERC"s definition of computational loads

Hello NERC,

Google fully supports the DCC's comments on the updated proposed Rules of Procedure 
definitions and registration criteria for Computational Loads. Please see below.
