*****

The Data Center Coalition (DCC) is pleased to submit these comments on NERC’s updated proposed 
Rules of Procedure definitions and registration criteria for Computational Loads.

Like all customers, the data center industry depends on a reliable electricity grid in order to fulfill its 
role as a vital backbone of our modern economy. In turn, data centers offer a number of reliability 
benefits to the grid, including significant investments in new energy resources and next-generation 
technologies. Data centers can also serve as grid assets that help promote reliability during energy 
emergencies caused by extreme weather.

It is critical to ensure proposed definitions and registration criteria by NERC are based on complete 
evidence, the technical capabilities and specifications of data center equipment, and do not 
disregard important developments or information from the industry. The DCC’s comments below 
aim to provide the challenges and concerns with the proposed definitions and registration criteria in 
applying accurately and fairly across the country, while also giving recommendations to improve the 
definitions and criteria to address the stated issues.

Proposed ROP Definition

DCC requests that NERC confirm that it intended to use the term “BPS” in defining 
Computational Load Site as "supplied through electrical equipment that is connected to the 
BPS."  The NERC registration model has historically been based on the BES definition, as 
NERC/REs determine whether or not entities are "Users, Owners, and Operators" of the BES 
for purposes of registration.  Yet Section 215 of the FPA uses the term "BPS," not BES.  FERC 
has said that, even though NERC uses BES, the fact that FPA Section 215 uses BPS is evidence 
that Congress actually intended to give FERC authority beyond NERC's BES definition. See, 
e.g., Mandatory Reliability Standards for the Bulk Power System, 118 FERC P 61,218 at P 76
(2007) (“Therefore, the Commission confirms its statements in the NOPR that the Bulk-Power
System reaches farther than those facilities that are included in NERC's definition of the bulk
electric system.”).  DCC requests clarity on the intent and purpose of using BPS, and how this
use relates to the exclusion in FPA Section 215–namely that the BPS “does not include

facilities used in the local distribution of electric energy.”

DCC is particularly concerned about the potential for confusion regarding the definition of 
“Computational Load Operator” as the entity that “operates” a Computational Load Site, and 
the definition of Computational Load Owner as the entity that “maintains” a Computational 
Load Site.  Given the diversity of business models and responsibility configurations among 
distinct legal entities that may exist at a given Computational Load Site, it may be unclear 
where one entity’s “operation” of a site ends, and where another’s “maintenance” begins.  
DCC suggests striking the phrase “or maintains” from the definition of Computational Load 
Owner to avoid this potential confusion. In addition, the use of the word “owns” in the 
Computational Load Owner definition should also be clarified that this is the owner of the 
physical equipment of the site (UPS, cooling systems, electrical infrastructure, controls/relays, 
etc.), rather than say owners of the real estate/land.

The Computational Load Site definition covers one or more buildings, structures, or 
installations at a “single location, “ and how that term and the term “one or more buildings” 
are read decides whether a phased campus generates one registration or several. The term 
should be defined to track how campuses are actually built, since buildings may be separated 
by roads or parcel lines, energized years apart, and fed from different stations while sharing 
cooling and auxiliary load. If it stays undefined as it currently is in the proposed definition, the 
same physical campus can be read as one location or several depending on the reviewer, and 
each reading carries a different registration count and compliance cost, which is the highest 
leverage cost driver in the package. DCC asks NERC to either define single location by 
reference to the published factors, or to replace it with new text such as the following: 
“buildings, structures, or installations that share common electrical infrastructure or a 
coordinated operating function constitute a single Computational Load Site, without regard to 
parcel boundaries or phased in service dates.”

Proposed MW Threshold Criteria

DCC recommends NERC increase the proposed registration threshold from 50 MW to 75 MW 
while retaining the 100 kV criterion. NERC's own technical analysis provided with the ROP 
changes shows that a 75 MW threshold would still capture approximately 63,960 MW, or 
80%, of current/forecasted computational load, compared to 68,288 MW, or 86%, under the 
proposed 50 MW threshold. The proposed 50 MW threshold therefore captures only 
approximately 4.3 GW of additional load nationwide, representing less than 6% of total 
current/forecasted computational load. DCC does not believe this incremental increase in 
coverage materially changes aggregate BPS reliability risk, and a 75 MW threshold would 
provide a more appropriate balance between reliability and regulatory burden.

In addition, the term “connected Load” in the CLO/CLOP registration criteria should also be 

clarified to ensure it is the contracted load identified/agreed upon in the interconnection 
agreements such that any behind-the-meter generation is accounted for that impacts the 
total load seen by the grid.

Clarification of the term “Primarily”

NERC should revise the proposed Computational Load Site definition to replace the subjective 
term "primarily" with a measurable threshold. Unlike other jurisdictions, the proposed 
definition does not specify what percentage of facility demand must be attributable to 
computational load activities. For example, ERCOT defines a Large Computational Load as a 
facility where 50% or more of demand consists of computational load, while MISO uses a 
threshold based on at least 25 MW of IT equipment demand (essentially the same as a 50% 
threshold). Establishing a clear percentage or MW-based criterion would improve consistency 
of the registration criteria across Regional Entities.

Proposed Voltage Threshold Boundary Concerns

NERC should clarify the application of the 100 kV criterion by establishing a clear boundary for 
when a Computational Load Site is considered to be "supplied through" electrical equipment 
connected at or above 100 kV. As currently drafted, it is unclear whether a facility 
interconnected at 34.5 kV remains subject to registration simply because the serving 
distribution circuit ultimately traces back to a 100 kV or higher transmission source (all 
distribution eventually traces back to a transmission source). Additional guidance is needed to 
distinguish between facilities served by dedicated feeders directly connected to a neighboring 
transmission substation and facilities served through traditional distribution systems with 
many customers.

The proposed ≥100 kV criterion creates ambiguous and inequitable outcomes for data centers 
connected at distribution voltages. Many facilities take service at sub-100 kV (e.g., 34.5 kV) 
through Distribution Provider infrastructure that connects upstream to the transmission 
network at 100 kV or above. In these configurations, the Computational Load Owner has no 
control over, and often no visibility into, how the Distribution Provider connects to the 
transmission system or what other loads share the same bus. The NERC FAQ diagrams suggest 
that registration may hinge on whether other loads happen to be connected to the same 
distribution bus, yet Distribution Providers routinely move loads, open bus ties, and swap 
feeders without notifying connected customers. A facility's registration status could therefore 
change overnight through no action of its own. DCC requests that NERC clarify: (1) how 
applicability is determined when the distribution bus serving a data center also serves other 
customers; (2) what notification obligations the Distribution Provider has when network 
changes affect a facility's registration status; and (3) whether the FERC Order 773 seven-factor 
test for local distribution exclusion applies to large loads consuming power at distribution 
voltage, given that the only sub-100 kV inclusion precedent in that order was for generation 
injecting power, not load withdrawing it. DCC also asks NERC to further clarify and define the 

phrase “common point of connection,” which Figures 2 and 3 in the FAQ both use and treat as 
distinct from the point of connection to the BPS without defining either.

Co-located Campuses & Buildings

NERC should clarify how registration applies to campus developments with multiple 
Computational Load Owners. Under the proposed framework, it is unclear whether 
registration is assessed at the Computational Load Site level, the individual owner level, or 
both. For example, if a campus exceeds 50 MW in aggregate but consists of multiple building 
owners, including some responsible for less than 50 MW of load, it is unclear whether all 
owners would be required to register.

The industry needs clarity up front prior to these new definitions and registration criteria 
getting approved in place, as the industry and future registered entities need to understand 
exactly how these roles and responsibilities will apply to their facilities and existing 
commercial agreements such that flexibility and appropriate planning of these compliance 
responsibilities can be made well in advance of the official NERC registration dates.

Similarly, many Computational Loads operate in a co-located tenant model. It is unclear 
whether tenants are CLOPs in all circumstances or only when they exercise operational 
control over computational equipment. As an example, if a 300 MW Computational Load Site 
contains ten Computational Load Operators, including operators responsible for less than 50 
MW each, it is unclear whether all ten operators would be required to register or whether 
registration would apply only to those entities with a material ownership or operational role 
at the site. Any compliance framework should align responsibilities with the entity that owns 
or controls the relevant equipment and data. NERC should also recognize that colocation 
providers are often subject to confidentiality and commercial agreements that limit their 
ability to obtain, verify, or disclose tenant-specific operational information, and should avoid 
imposing compliance obligations that require one entity to report information controlled by 
another. 

To illustrate the range of delivery models the registration criteria must accommodate, DCC 
offers the following to NERC staff:

DCC’s members develop power infrastructure using the delivery model best suited for 
each location. On some campuses, the serving utility owns and operates the substation 
and provides medium voltage service (typically 34.5 kV or 12.5 kV) directly to the 
owner’s facilities. On other campuses, particularly large hyperscale developments 

requiring significant capacity, the owner takes service at transmission voltage (typically 
100 kV and above) and owns the high voltage substation that transforms power to 
medium voltage for campus distribution. In these cases, the owner owns and manages 
the transmission interconnection, substation assets, and medium voltage distribution 
infrastructure. Power is delivered to the tenants at low voltage (typically 480 V), and 
each tenant controls only their own computational workload.

Single Registration Language in ROP

NERC should clarify the treatment of multi-tenant facilities and expressly identify when a 
single entity may serve as the accountable Computational Load Operator for an entire 
Computational Load Site in the ROP. While NERC has indicated that a centralized or shared 
operating function may serve as the single accountable Computational Load Operator at a 
multi-tenant site, that concept is not reflected in the proposed registration criteria or 
supporting definitions.

This matters because a campus is typically owned by one legal entity, operated by staff 
or an affiliate or a shared services entity, and leased to tenants who control only their 
own workloads, so without a stated rule, affiliates or tenants risk being pulled onto the 
Compliance Registry alongside the owner. Left as drafted, a registrant cannot tell a 
tenant with confidence that the tenant is outside the registry, which complicates 
leasing. DCC requests that NERC clarify where owner and operator functions are split, 
when a single accountable operator may register as CLO for the entire site, and provide 
confirmation that a tenant controlling only its own workload is or is not itself a 
Computational Load Operator where a shared operating function has registered

Phased Campus Buildouts

NERC should also clarify how these requirements apply to phased campus developments. 
Registration obligations should be clarified on how current energized and operational capacity 
may be phased over time leading to the ultimate buildout capacity, as campuses are 
commonly developed and placed into service over multiple phases and years. Clear guidance 
is needed to ensure consistent treatment of multi-owner campuses while allowing 
registration and compliance obligations to align with the actual load that is in service.

Making the FAQ Document Binding Text

NERC’s FAQ says helpful things, that two or more sites can sit behind the same supply 
equipment, that a single site can be fed from separate stations, and that there can be more 
than one owner and more than one operator of a single site, but an FAQ is not enforceable 
and can be revised or ignored by whoever runs a given registration review. For an owner and 

operator, that means the difference between one registration and several registrations for a 
phased campus is based on informal guidance rather than on the criteria themselves, and 
registration is the gateway to every obligation in all three proposed Reliability Standards. If 
the draft stays as written, each campus gets reviewed on its own facts with no binding text to 
point to, so outcomes vary region to region. DCC recommends NERC to convert the FAQ 
answers into binding text in Appendix 5B or some other enforceable document to keep 
consistency across the entire ERO.

NERC has identified factors – such as ownership, shared or common infrastructure, and 
coordinated use of the computing infrastructure – that bear on how a site is delineated, but 
they currently function as informal guidance rather than as a published test. A published test 
is what lets an owner model registration outcomes at the design stage, when it is deciding 
whether phases share a substation, share cooling, or are separately metered. Without it, the 
registrant has no certainty in advance and invites inconsistent results across regions. DCC asks 
that the factors NERC lists be published as the governing test for site delineation, with the 
further point on how the connected load is measured at the site compared against the future 
maximum build out of load studied in the interconnection process, and how those differences 
will apply for registration and NERC requirements while the projects are built out over time.

FAQ Expansion

DCC requests that NERC add various campus examples to the FAQ illustrating how the 
proposed registration criteria would apply to phased, multi-building, and multi-tenant 
Computational Load Sites. Building on the existing Figures 2 and 3, NERC should illustrate a 
campus with multiple phases energized over time, shared substations and cooling 
infrastructure, separate parcel boundaries, multiple points of connection and the voltages of 
the connecting equipment, and tenants that control only their own computational workloads. 
The examples should identify the expected registration outcomes and clarify whether 
connected load is evaluated at the site level or by individual phase, owner, operator, or 
tenant. Such examples would provide meaningful implementation guidance and help ensure 
consistent application of the criteria across a range of common data center development and 
ownership structures.

Proposed Revisions to Rules of Procedure – NERC is proposing revisions to its Rules of Procedure to develop 
new registered entity types, called Computational Load Owner and Computational Load Operator. In response to 
comments  received  on  its  initial  posting,  NERC  is  posting  proposed  revisions  to  NERC  Rules  of  Procedure 
Appendix 2, Appendix 5A, and Appendix 5B for an additional public comment period for 30 days from August 19, 
2026 to September 18, 2026. Comments must be submitted electronically to ROPcomments@nerc.net.

The proposed revisions address recommendations from the NERC Large Loads Working Group (a subgroup of the 
NERC  Reliability  and  Security  Technical  Committee)  whitepaper  “Assessment  of  Gaps  in  Existing  Practices, 
Requirements, and Reliability Standards for Emerging Large Loads” and are further supported by the findings 
in  the    “NERC  Aggregated  Report  on  NERC  Level  2  Industry  Recommendation:  Large  Load  Interconnection, 
Study, Commissioning, and Operations” analyzing responses to a Level 2 Alert on the interconnection of large 
loads.  The  recommendations  and  findings  indicate  a  need  for  new  registered  entity  types  to  comply  with 
Reliability Standards (currently under development in Project 2026-02 – Computational Loads) to reduce risks to 
the reliability of the Bulk Power System.

In pursuing its mission to assure the effective and efficient reduction of risks to the reliability and security of the 
grid,  NERC  works  with  owners,  operators,  users,  and  consumers  as  well  as  federal,  state,  and  provincial 
regulators  across  North  America.  To  that  end,  NERC  welcomes  input  from  all  stakeholders  on  the  proposed 
revisions and values the opportunity to engage with stakeholders on how the proposed revisions can contribute 
to the reliability of the Bulk Power System.

For more information or assistance, please contact Marisa Hecht via email.

LADWP supports NERC’s objective to revise Appendix 2 (Definitions Used in the Rules of Procedure), Appendix 
5A (Organization Registration and Certification Manual), Appendix 5B (Statement of Compliance Registry Criteria) 
and requests NERC to further clarify some of the proposed changes. 

1. Appendix 2 (Definitions Used in the Rules of Procedure)

LADWP recommends

ii) Clarification regarding which software applications and services to consider. For example, blockchain
technology would fall under the intended scope for the proposed definition of “Computational Load Site”,
whereas an antivirus software service would not fall under the intended scope of the proposed definition.

iii) LADWP requests clarification on the meaning of “at a single location”. The current definition could be
interpreted to mean at a single physical location, or at a single electrical connection which can potentially
lead to all the CLO standards being applicable beyond the intended facilities.

2. Appendix 5A (Organization Registration and Certification Manual)

LADWP supports NERC’s revisions to Appendix 5A of the Rules of Procedure – Organization
Registration and Certification Manual.

3. Appendix 5B (Statement of Compliance Registry Criteria)

The proposed registry criteria for Computational Load Owners (CLOs) and Computational Load
Operators (CLOPs) are ambiguous regarding the point of connection. The Frequently Asked Questions
(FAQ) include example diagrams illustrating scenarios that are intended to be within and outside the
scope of the proposed criterion. However, based solely on the proposed applicability language, it is not
apparent why certain Computational Load Sites are excluded. In particular, the proposed language
appears broad enough that all of the example configurations in Figures 1 through 7 could reasonably be
interpreted as satisfying the criterion that the Computational Load Site is “supplied through the electrical
equipment connected at a voltage level greater than or equal to 100kV.”

For example, in Figure 3, if a Computational Load Site is electrically supplied through multiple

 Page 1 of 3

transformation stages (e.g., 230 kV to 69 kV to 34.5 kV), the proposed language does not clearly identify 
what makes Figure 3 non-applicable. It is unclear whether the disqualification is based on multiple voltage 
transformation levels considering that some utilities only have a single transformation level, or if it is the 
TO or DP serving non-computational load (the example in Figure 3 includes "Local Distribution Load"), or 
some other criteria. Does the inclusion of the "Local Distribution Load" in Figure 3 have a material 
impact on the evaluation for registering? 

Because the language is open to interpretation with or without the use of diagrams, LADWP recommends 
NERC to provide additional clarity on the distinctions revolving around the common point of connection at 
the distribution level (e.g. 34.5 kV) by adding specificity to the registry criteria for CLOs and CLOPs. 
Alternately or in conjunction, NERC should provide a comprehensive set of diagrams via the FAQ to 
encompass varying configurations seen across different utilities. 

4. Additional Comments

LADWP requests NERC to confirm that the responsibility remains with the Computational Load Sites to
register as a CLO/CLOP upon notification from the TO and DP that their equipment connects to the BPS
at 100 kV or greater.

SUBJECT:  Small End-Use Sector (9) Response to 

Proposed Computational Load Rules of Procedure Revisions 

The representatives to the NERC Member Representatives Committee for the Small 
End-Use  Customer  Sector (9)  provide  these  comments  in response  to  the  Proposed 
Computational Load Rules of Procedure Revisions.  

We appreciate the work of the NERC Large Load Working Group (LLWG), NERC 
Staff, and the commenters who have shaped these proposed revisions to the NERC 
Rules of Procedure. Large computational loads are being proposed across the 
country, and the need to consider the reasonableness of integrating them into the 
bulk electric system is real. NERC's Level 2 Industry Recommendation and the 
LLWG whitepaper advance a schedule that looks to proactively address any current 
barriers to entry for these entities prior to them receiving their first electric bill.  By 
moving these efforts through the current system, we are undoubtedly shifting the 
make-ready costs of the grid and the processes that govern its operation to current 
ratepayers, to the benefit of an unproven and highly speculative industries.   

NERC does not set retail rates or render bills, but its compliance, reporting, and 
planning requirements create substantial unfunded mandates for Transmission 
Owners, Planners and Coordinators, Operators, Distribution Providers, and 
Reliability Coordinators. Those costs are passed through to retail bills of existing 
customers often when they are incurred. The September 2025 NERC Alert gave 
entities four months to develop large load integration policies and procedures, 
diverting labor, time, and capital from local system improvements that would have 
delivered reliability benefits to existing customers. Because this work is driven 
entirely by a potential future ratepayer, rather than an existing one, there is no 
feasible way to recover the costs from future large loads entities at the retail level.  
The only real option for recovery of NERC compliance costs, which are difficult to 
argue are not prudent, is to subsidize them across the current customer base.   

The proactive elimination of barriers for future large loads is not speculative; it is 
intentional and mentioned throughout the Level 2 and Level 3 recommendations 
and the Proposed Rules of Procedure Revision summary.   

• 

• 

• 

"enhance their load commissioning activities to establish a comprehensive 
commissioning process that ensures operational readiness for large loads." 

"establish operating protocols and the necessary communication 
infrastructure to support reliable ongoing operations after large load facilities 
enter into commercial operations." 

“The goal is to ensure that as more industrial-scale consumers connect to the 
grid, they actively participate in practices that protect grid stability. These 
steps highlight that proactive planning and participation can enable even 
more of these facilities to come online reliably and quickly.” 

•  To expeditiously address these risks, NERC initiated the Large Loads Action 

Plan. 

These enhancements may be sound planning and engineering principles, but they 
will be at the cost of current customers.  This conflicts with a national and many 
state level goals to require large energy users to cover the full cost of their grid 
integration, which must include overhauls to the regulatory, planning, and 
compliance environments to accommodate their entry to the BES.   

Registering Large Computational Loads without strong ratepayer protections as 
proposed in these revisions gives deep-pocketed tech firms direct influence over 
NERC standards development and balloting, allowing them to potentially shift 
market entry costs onto households in a forum where small customers and customer 
advocates have been disenfranchised because of their lack of adequate resources to 
participate fully.    

While we welcome thoughtful economic growth, large loads must not access the 
Bulk Electric System until NERC, FERC, and state regulators can ensure 
computational loads bear 100% of their costs, including every network upgrade, 
administrative mandate, and resource expansion.

Re: Comments on Project 2026-02 Computational Loads 

The National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA) appreciates the opportunity to comment 
on Project 2026-02 Computational Loads. NEMA represents more than 300 electrical equipment 
manufacturers that make safe, reliable, and efficient products and technologies that power, 
connect, and light our world. Together, our members contribute a full 1% of U.S. GDP and directly 
provide more than 590,000 American jobs, adding over $375 billion to the U.S. economy. 

Of particular importance to Project 2026-02 Computational Loads, NEMA members produce 
technologies supporting the generation, transmission, distribution, control, and end use of 
electricity throughout North America, including critical infrastructure deployed in data centers and 
other large computational load facilities. 

NEMA supports NERC's efforts to address emerging reliability risks associated with the growth of 
computational loads. We are also aligned with the staged approach NERC has outlined: first 
establishing the registration, modeling, data exchange, and monitoring framework, and then 
focusing on dynamic performance, power quality, and ride-through requirements. Clarifying the 
modeling, data submission, disturbance monitoring, and event reporting obligations in CLO-001 
and CLO-003 can help support smoother compliance with technical standards later. 

As NERC advances this initiative, NEMA encourages continued engagement with the electrical 
manufacturing industry to ensure that future Reliability Standards are informed by evolving 
equipment capabilities, facility design practices, manufacturing considerations, and technology 
trends. 

NEMA's 2026 update to A Reliable Grid for an Electric Future projects that U.S. electricity demand 
will increase by more than 55 percent by 2050, with data centers accounting for approximately 38 
percent of net electricity consumption growth through 2037. These trends underscore the 
importance of developing durable, practical reliability requirements that support both system 
reliability and the timely deployment of critical electrical infrastructure. 

General Comments 

NEMA appreciates NERC's responsiveness to stakeholder feedback since its April 2026 proposal. 
The transition from the proposed “Computational Load Entity” concept to a more targeted 
“Computational Load Owner” and “Computational Load Operator” framework, together with 
revisions to the proposed registration criteria, represents a meaningful refinement of the proposal 
and provides a stronger foundation for future standards development. 

As computational load facilities, power architectures, and supporting technologies continue to 
evolve, NEMA encourages NERC to maintain ongoing engagement with electrical manufacturers 
throughout future phases of this initiative. Manufacturers possess unique expertise regarding 

1     |     Comments on Project 2026-02 Computational Loads 

 
equipment design, testing, production, deployment, and operational capabilities that can help 
inform both standards development and implementation considerations. Overall, we support the 
upward revision to a 50 MW connected-load threshold at 100 kV and above, which we believe better 
focuses the framework on facilities with meaningful bulk power system impacts. 

However, as this process moves forward, it is important to continue examining varying thresholds 
and remain flexible as they evolve. For instance, ERCOT's Large Load Interconnection Process uses 
a 75 MW threshold with its own study, model, and performance expectations. Other regions differ 
as well. As a result, the same facility may face multiple applicability triggers and overlapping 
submission requirements. 

Recognizing that these thresholds will evolve as more experience is gained and lessons are learned, 
NEMA members recommend that NERC develop and publish a crosswalk identifying where NERC, 
regional, Planning Coordinator, and Transmission Owner requirements overlap; how conflicts are 
escalated; and when a single study, model, test, or report satisfies equivalent obligations. 
Manufacturers and other providers supplying equipment into multiple regions would find value in 
requirements strategically converging rather than multiplying. 

Definitions and Applicability 

NEMA supports NERC's efforts to establish clear definitions and applicability criteria for 
computational load entities. As definitions and future Reliability Standards evolve, NEMA 
encourages NERC to preserve clear distinctions among: 

•

•

Information technology (IT), operational technology (OT), industrial control systems (ICS),
and other connected management systems that facilitate the operation and administration
of computing loads throughout the grid;
Facility infrastructure supporting those loads, including electrical distribution systems,
backup power systems, cooling systems, and related equipment; and

• Utility-owned and utility-operated assets interconnected with the Bulk Power System.

Maintaining these distinctions will help ensure that reliability obligations are assigned appropriately 
and that future standards accurately reflect the operational responsibilities of the relevant entities. 

CLO-001: Computational Load Interconnection, Studies, and Modeling Data 

NEMA supports efforts to improve planning and operational visibility through enhanced modeling 
and data exchange requirements. 

At the same time, computational load technologies and the electrical infrastructure supporting 
artificial intelligence and high-performance computing applications continue to evolve rapidly. 
NEMA therefore encourages NERC to focus on the performance objectives and reliability 
information needed to support planning and operations while avoiding technology-specific 
requirements that may become outdated as computing architectures and facility designs change. 
As it looks to strengthen reliability performance, NERC could examine areas such as fault and 

2     |     Comments on Project 2026-02 Computational Loads 

 
voltage ride-through, managed load recovery following a disturbance, load ramp-rate management, 
disturbance monitoring, and operational communications. 

Ultimately, performance-based and technology-neutral requirements are more likely to remain 
effective over time while supporting innovation and maintaining reliability objectives. 

Additionally, the drafting team should consider clarifying that the model verification requirements 
in R11.2.2 apply to changes that materially affect a site's aggregate dynamic response at the point 
of interconnection. For large facilities subject to routine hardware, software, firmware, and settings 
updates, applying verification requirements to every individual change may not provide additional 
reliability value where there is no material impact on aggregate electrical performance. 

We also encourage NERC to consider documented change-management processes and periodic 
review for routine changes that do not materially affect electrical performance. Representative 
verification approaches may likewise be appropriate for equipment with materially identical 
configurations and operating characteristics. 

More broadly, firmware and controls updates are a routine part of the equipment lifecycle and, by 
themselves, may not materially affect reliability-relevant electrical behavior. Similarly, the 
determination of a "qualified change" under R7 should focus on changes to a facility's electrical 
characteristics and performance rather than the specific computational workload being performed. 

CLO-002: Operational Data and Communications 

NEMA supports efforts to improve operational visibility and communications between 
computational load facilities and reliability entities and appreciates NERC's recognition of their 
importance. As these requirements are developed, NEMA encourages NERC to consider 
establishing common baseline expectations for operational data, communications, and 
information exchange where practical. 

Consistent approaches to data definitions, timing conventions, quality requirements, and secure 
communications can promote interoperability, reduce implementation complexity, and support 
efficient deployment of communications and monitoring technologies across jurisdictions. NEMA 
also encourages implementation schedules that appropriately reflect the time required to engineer, 
procure, deploy, and validate new communications and monitoring infrastructure. 

CLO-003: Computational Load Protection Coordination and Disturbance Monitoring 

NEMA supports NERC's focus on protection coordination, controls, disturbance monitoring, and 
the reliability impacts associated with rapid load changes. 

As standards development progresses, NEMA appreciates NERC’s effort to broaden engagement 
with electrical manufacturers and original equipment manufacturers, in addition to traditional 
utility and operating stakeholders. Manufacturers have substantial technical expertise related to 

3     |     Comments on Project 2026-02 Computational Loads 

 
protection systems, communications technologies, power electronics, controls, and integrated 
facility equipment that can help inform practical and effective reliability requirements. 

We continue to encourage NERC to prioritize performance-based requirements over prescriptive 
technology selections or specific protection schemes. Such an approach allows flexibility as 
technologies evolve while continuing to support the desired reliability outcomes.  

As NERC further develops disturbance monitoring requirements, NEMA believes it should continue 
evaluating whether the proposed requirements will provide sufficient visibility into the behavior of 
rapidly evolving computational load facilities during system disturbances. NERC should also 
consider practical implementation factors, including equipment capabilities and the collection, 
storage, and management of disturbance data. 

Implementation Considerations 

As NERC advances future standards and implementation plans, it is important that compliance 
schedules and implementation expectations recognize the realities associated with equipment 
engineering, manufacturing, procurement, testing, and deployment. 

The electrical manufacturing industry is experiencing significant transformation as digitalization, 
advanced automation, artificial intelligence, and increasing demand for grid infrastructure reshape 
production and deployment practices. At the same time, the entire electric sector—utilities, 
operators, and suppliers—is responding to unprecedented growth in electricity demand and data 
center development.  

Since grid impacts are often driven by aggregate electrical behavior at the point of interconnection, 
NEMA members encourage reliability measurement and accountability to be addressed generally 
at the interconnected site or campus level. NERC's standards development process will benefit 
from continued dialogue with manufacturers regarding equipment capabilities, supply chain 
considerations, and implementation timelines. We also encourage continued consideration of the 
cumulative burden of evolving or new requirements to avoid creating misaligned incentives for 
computational loads to move toward fully islanded operation. The standards should recognize grid-
tied facilities that invest in visibility, controllability, storage, advanced energy management, and 
flexible load capabilities in a way that values the broader system reliability benefits these 
enhancements can provide. 

In June 2026, NEMA, ASHRAE, and Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) released the AI 
Data Center Energy Performance Framework (Framework), which provides guidance for the 
planning, design, operation, and modernization of next-generation data centers. The Framework 
reflects the industry's ongoing efforts to support resilient, reliable, and efficient computational load 
infrastructure and may serve as a useful resource as NERC's work in this area continues. It also 
references more than ten data center design consideration documents that NEMA developed on 
technologies such as energy storage, switchgear, and microgrids. 

Conclusion

We look forward to continued engagement with NERC and other industry stakeholders as this effort 
progresses and stand ready to provide technical expertise regarding electrical equipment,

relevant to computational load integration and reliability.

To the North American Electric Reliability Commission: 

PG&E wishes to provide the following comments on the Rules of Procedure posting 
regarding the registration thresholds and aggregation matters for Computational Load 
Owners and Computational Load Operators.   

PG&E is concerned about potential load aggregation impacts. Under the proposed 
criteria, several computational load facilities below the registration threshold could be 
interconnected to a common bus, common point of interconnection, or common 
supplying facility and collectively exhibit behavior comparable to a single registrable 
Computational Load Site. Because the proposed registration criteria are applied on a site-
by-site and owner-by-owner basis, these aggregated configurations may fall outside the 
registration framework despite presenting material reliability impacts to the Bulk-Power 
System. 

To address this concern, PG&E recommends that NERC explicitly clarify the availability 
and application of the existing materiality pathway contained in Appendix 5A, Section 
III(D). Specifically, PG&E requests that NERC state in Appendix 5B or the ERO 
Registration Reference Document that: 

1. Regional Entities may consider the aggregate reliability impact of computational
load connected to a common point of interconnection, common bus, or common
supplying facility, including individual sites that fall below the Appendix 5B
registration thresholds;

2. Transmission Owners and Distribution Providers may bring potential aggregation
concerns to the attention of their Regional Entity, along with guidance concerning
the information necessary to support such a review;

3. Registration determinations involving Computational Load Sites are

communicated to the interconnecting Transmission Owner or Distribution
Provider, in addition to the affected entity; and

4. A target timeframe is established for Registration Review Panel determinations.

The reliability basis for this recommendation is that multiple sub-threshold computational 
load facilities are increasingly developed in close electrical proximity and may 
collectively produce reliability impacts similar to those of a single large Computational 
Load Site. PG&E does not recommend expanding the registration criteria themselves to 
capture every such configuration. Rather, PG&E believes the existing materiality process 
is the appropriate mechanism for addressing these situations, but that the circumstances 
under which it may be invoked should be more clearly articulated.

Prologis Comments on Computational Load Definitions and Registration Criteria for 
Proposed Rules of Procedure Revisions  

Prologis appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the NERC’s Computational 

Load Definitions and Registration Criteria, and we acknowledge the significant amount of work and 
attention that went in to developing definitions that will allow NERC to address reliability concerns 
connected to computational load facilities. However, at this time, Prologis does not believe that the 
proposed definitions are sufficiently clear, and we recommend several changes to avoid potential 
confusion in the implementation of these requirements. 

Specifically, defining a Computational Load Owner (CLO) as the entity that “owns and 
maintains” a Computational Load Site implies that the owner of a site is always the same entity that 
maintains the site. In practice, these are often different entities. For example, as a real estate 
provider, Prologis may own the land and building that houses computational load equipment, but the 
operator of the equipment may be responsible for maintenance of the site and associated 
infrastructure. In this respect, the entity that “maintains” the site may actually be the Computational 
Load Operator, creating overlap between these two definitions that may lead to confusion as to 
which entity is responsible for a particular requirement in NERC’s standards. Prologis recommends 
striking the word “maintains” from the definition to avoid confusion. 

In addition, NERC should provide more clarity around what scale and level of ownership is 
needed to establish an entity as a CLO. Is a CLO the entity that owns the land, the building, or the 
computational load equipment in the building? These could be different entities, as real estate 
companies like Prologis may own the land/building while their tenants may own, install, and maintain 
the associated equipment within the building. Prologis recommends clarifying this definition to 
identify that the CLO is the owner of the land/building rather than the equipment, and that 
“ownership” means an ownership stake (i.e. >50% equity) to avoid having minority owners identified 
as CLOs. Finally, NERC should clarify how these definitions will apply in situations where multiple 
buildings or facilities are located on the same site or within the same load pocket on the grid but are 
owned and/or operated by different entities.   

Respectfully submitted, 

Collin Smith 
Energy Policy Manager 
Prologis 
Pier 1, Bay 1 
San Francisco, CA 94111

ROPComments (SM)

Comments of QTS Data Centers on Proposed Revisions to Rules of Procedure Appendices 2, 5A, and 5B 
(Computational Loads), posted August 19, 2026
Friday, September 18, 2026 2:39:28 PM
image.png

To the North American Electric Reliability Corporation:

QTS Data Centers develops, owns, and operates data center campuses across the 
United States and participates in the Registered Ballot Body in Segment 7. QTS owns the 
electrical infrastructure at its campuses, provides a shared operating function for them, 
and expects to register under the criteria NERC adopts.

QTS supports registration and supports a definition of Computational Load Site broad 
enough to capture the aggregate behavior that drives the risk NERC has identified. These 
comments address six provisions where the text would produce different registration 
outcomes for identical electrical facts. QTS files separately from the Data Center 
Coalition and supports the Coalition’s filing.

1. Appendix 2: the extent of a Computational Load Site

Provision at issue: the phrase “at a single location” in the proposed definition of 
Computational Load Site.

Position: NERC should state the electrical and operating facts that place buildings at a 
single location, and should state that total connected Load aggregates across every 
building and every point of connection at that site.

Reason: The extent of a site determines both who registers and whether the 50 MW 
threshold is met, and the current text answers neither question for a campus built in 
phases. A campus reaches full build over several years. Its buildings may sit on separate 
parcels, energize years apart, and draw from more than one point of connection while 
sharing one substation and one auxiliary system.

Read narrowly, the phrase divides that campus. A 300 MW campus served through four 
points of connection reads as four sites of 75 MW, or as twelve buildings each below the 
threshold, and the aggregate behavior NERC’s technical work identifies as the risk driver

falls outside the criteria entirely. Read broadly, the same campus registers once. Both
readings are available on the current text.

The result matters to the Transmission Planner as much as to the Computational Load
Owner. The Transmission Planner models the campus at its points of connection as one
electrical entity. A criterion that fragments it produces several partial models of that
entity, and leaves the largest single contributor to the planning case unregistered.

The factors NERC has already identified – ownership, shared or common infrastructure,
and coordinated use of the computing infrastructure – resolve this without narrowing
NERC’s judgment on application. The proposed text below requires shared electrical
infrastructure in every case, so buildings that share only a cooling system but connect
separately are not aggregated. Appendix 5A leaves every determination reviewable by
the Registration Review Panel.

Proposed redline to Appendix 2, definition of Computational Load Site:

“Computational Load Site” means one or more buildings, structures, or
installations at a single location that 1) Primarily contains information technology
infrastructure used for: creating, executing, and delivering software applications
and services; artificial intelligence training, deployment, and delivery;
cryptocurrency mining; or other computational activities at a data center; and 2)
is supplied through electrical equipment that is connected to the BPS. Buildings,
structures, or installations are at a single location where they share common
electrical infrastructure and are under common ownership or a common
operating function. Parcel boundaries, public rights of way, separate
metering, and differing in service dates do not place them at separate
locations.

Proposed redline to Appendix 5B, Section III, Computational Load Owner or
Operator criterion:

Computational Load Owner or Operator of a Computational Load Site with a total
connected Load greater than or equal to 50 MW that is supplied through
electrical equipment connected at a voltage level greater than or equal to 100 kV
from one or more points of connection. Total connected Load is the sum of the
connected Load of all electrical equipment at the Computational Load Site,
aggregated across all buildings, structures, and installations at the site and
across all points of connection serving the site.

2. Appendix 5B: registration of a site that energizes in phases

Provision at issue: the same criterion, applied to a campus that reaches full build over
several years.

Position: NERC should state that a Computational Load Site is registered once, and that
placing a later phase in service does not create an additional registration where the site
continues to meet the Appendix 2 definition.

Reason: The consequence of the alternative falls on the operating entities. Registering
each phase produces several registrants behind one point of connection, several annual
data submissions describing one electrical facility, and several sets of protection
settings coordinated against one another rather than against the system. During an
event, the Transmission Operator issuing an instruction to that campus would need to
identify which of several registrants controls which portion of the load.

Registration attaches to the site as Appendix 2 defines it. The threshold in Section 1
above continues to operate on the site as a whole, so a campus that grows beyond the
shared infrastructure defining it is assessed against the criteria as it then exists. What
the text below prevents is a second registration for the same electrical facility, not a
registration for a facility that has changed.

Proposed redline to Appendix 5B, Section III, Computational Load Owner or
Operator criterion, second added sentence:

A Computational Load Site is registered once. Placing additional buildings,
structures, or installations in service at a registered Computational Load Site
does not create an additional Computational Load Site or an additional
registration, provided the site continues to meet the definition in Appendix 2.

3. Appendix 2: the Computational Load Operator at a site with divided operating
functions

Provision at issue: “Computational Load Operator” means the entity that operates a
Computational Load Site.

Position: NERC should state that where operating functions are divided, the entity that
controls the electrical demand at the site’s points of connection is the Computational

Load Operator for the site.

Reason: The obligations that attach to this function are operational. A Computational
Load Operator receives an Operating Instruction and changes demand at the points of
connection within the time the instruction allows. The entity able to perform that
function is the one holding the equipment that changes demand, which at a campus
with divided functions is the shared operating function rather than a party controlling a
workload behind low voltage distribution.

The current text does not say this. Read to reach every party that operates equipment at
a site, it registers entities that cannot perform the function the registration exists to
secure, and it leaves the Transmission Operator without a single accountable contact
during an event. NERC replaced “end user or the entity that hosts end users” with two
functions in order to address differing organizational arrangements more clearly. Tying
the operator function to control of demand at the points of connection completes that
work, and it produces the correct answer under any arrangement: where a party does
control demand at a point of connection, it is the operator for that site regardless of how
the campus is leased.

Proposed redline to Appendix 2, definition of Computational Load Operator:

“Computational Load Operator” means the entity that operates a Computational
Load Site. Where operating functions at a Computational Load Site are
divided among more than one party, the Computational Load Operator is the
entity that controls the electrical demand of the site at its point or points of
connection.

4. Appendix 2: the Computational Load Owner where the serving utility owns the
substation

Provision at issue: “Computational Load Owner” means the entity that owns and
maintains a Computational Load Site.

Position: NERC should replace the conjunctive test with ownership of the site’s
electrical infrastructure.

Reason: Campuses take service under two models. On some, the serving utility owns
and operates the substation and delivers medium voltage service to the owner’s
buildings. On others, the owner takes service at transmission voltage and owns the high

voltage substation that transforms power for campus distribution.

The conjunctive “owns and maintains” resolves the second model and not the first.
Where the utility owns and maintains the substation, the entity that maintains the
supplying equipment is not the entity that owns the site. Read to reach the utility, the
criterion registers a Transmission Owner a second time for one asset. Read to reach
neither, a 300 MW campus has no registered Computational Load Owner and no entity
holds the data submission, modeling, and protection coordination duties the proposed
Reliability Standards assign to that function.

Ownership of the site’s electrical infrastructure produces the assignment the standards
use. CLO-003 assigns monitoring and protection duties to whichever entity owns the
equipment on which each duty operates, and a criterion tied to the same fact produces
one consistent answer under either service model.

Proposed redline to Appendix 2, definition of Computational Load Owner:

“Computational Load Owner” means the entity that owns and maintains the

electrical infrastructure of a Computational Load Site.

5. Appendix 5B: the point at which the voltage criterion is measured

Provision at issue: “supplied through electrical equipment connected at a voltage level
greater than or equal to 100 kV from one or more points of connection.”

Position: NERC should state that the voltage is measured where the equipment
supplying the site connects to the BPS.

Reason: The criterion does not say where the measurement is taken, and the answer
determines whether a site registers at all. Consider two 50 MW sites drawing from the
same 230 kV system. One connects at 230 kV. The other sits behind a utility owned 230
to 69 kV transformer and connects at 69 kV. The load behaves identically at both. The
first registers and the second does not.

The difference rests on the serving utility’s upstream configuration, which the site owner
does not control and which the utility may change after the site is built. A site can
therefore move onto or off the Compliance Registry without any change to its own
facilities or its own behavior.

NERC retained the voltage criterion because voltage identifies the most impactful
connections to the BPS. That purpose requires a stated measuring point, because the
criterion otherwise produces different answers for the same equipment depending on
how far upstream the reviewer looks. The text below measures at the connection to the
BPS, which is the point NERC’s Frequently Asked Questions diagrams use, and it does
so without regard to the voltage recited in a service or interconnection agreement.

Proposed redline to Appendix 5B, Section III, Computational Load Owner or
Operator criterion, third added sentence:

The voltage level is the voltage at which the electrical equipment supplying
the Computational Load Site connects to the BPS, without regard to the
voltage recited in any service or interconnection agreement.

6. Appendix 2: the measure of “primarily”

Provision at issue: “Primarily contains information technology infrastructure.”

Position: NERC should state how “primarily” is measured, and should use connected
Load.

Reason: “Primarily” can be measured by floor area, by equipment count, or by load, and
the three produce different answers at the same site. Connected Load is the quantity the
rest of the criterion already uses, and it is the quantity that bears on the reliability
question, since floor area devoted to information technology infrastructure tells the
planner nothing about the demand the site places on the system. Measuring against
connected Load keeps one denominator throughout the criterion.

Proposed redline to Appendix 2, definition of Computational Load Site, clause 1:

Primarily contains information technology infrastructure, meaning information

technology infrastructure accounting for more than 50 percent of the connected
Load at the site, used for:

Thank you for your consideration of the foregoing.

Respectfully submitted,

Jeremy Stout
Senior Manager, Regulatory Compliance

September 17, 2026 

Mr. Jim Robb 
President and CEO  
North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) 
1401 H Street NW, Suite 410 
Washington, DC 20005 

Re: 

Project 2026-02 – Comments on Computational Load Definitions 
(Appendix 2) and Registration Criteria (Appendix 5B)  

Dear Mr. Robb: 

The  Real  Estate  Roundtable  (www.rer.org)  (“RER”)1  appreciates  this 
opportunity  to  comment  on  NERC’s  Definitions  and  Registration  Criteria 
proposed  on  August  19  as  part  of  Project  2026-02.  We  commend  NERC’s 
external  engagement  and  “Large  Computational  Loads”  teams  for  their 
proactive, excellent outreach to many stakeholders, including RER, throughout 
the process.  

Summary of Comments 

We  support  NERC’s  objective  of  addressing  grid  reliability  impacts  of 
Large Computational Loads. NERC’s new regulatory framework should reflect 
how  data  centers  are  actually  owned  and  operated  in  the  real  estate 
marketplace—particularly  at  colocation  and  other  leased  facilities,  where 
ownership of the site is typically separate from control over the computational 
equipment and its electrical load. Our comments recommend that NERC better 
clarify:  

 The  distinction  between  Computational  Load  Owners  (“CLOs”)  and
Computational  Load  Operators  (“CLOPs”)  in  the  Appendix  2  definitions
considering  their  respective  ownership,  control,  leasing  arrangements,
activities, responsibilities, and operational functions at data centers.

1 The last page of the Addendum to this letter provides more information on RER and real 
estate’s impact to the U. S. economy.  

Letter to Mr. Jim Robb 
September 16, 2026 
Page 2 

 What  constitutes  a  “Computational  Load  Site”  in  the  first  instance.  Our  recommended
definition would clarify that a property may use a lot of electricity (≥ 50MW) – but may not
be  a  “Computational  Load  Site”  and  thus  fall  outside  of  NERC’s  registration  regime.  We
suggest that only properties “primarily used by IT infrastructure to process, store, transmit,
or  manipulate  digital  information”  for  computer-based  activities  (like  creating  software
applications, delivering cloud services, training AI models, and mining crypto assets) should
qualify as “Computational Load Sites” for purposes of NERC registration.

 The amount of a Site’s “Total Connected Load” (≥ 50MW) as critical to determine whether a
CLO  and/or  CLOP  must  register  with  NERC.  We  recommend  a  separate  Appendix  2
definition  of  the  term  “Total  Connected  Load”  as  the  amount  of  electricity  that  includes
computational  load  –  plus  the  rest  of  a  facility’s  electrical  consumption  needed  to  run
HVAC,  lighting,  non-computer  equipment  and  appliance  plug  loads,  and  loads  to  support
other non-computational building systems like elevators, security, and fire/safety.

 The  term  “Single  Location”  as  necessary  to  establish  the  physical  boundaries  of  a
“Computational  Load  Site.”  A  separate  Appendix  2  definition  of  “Single  Location”  will
guide CLOs and CLOPs in determining when they must aggregate “Total Connected Loads”
from individual buildings and leased spaces at the Site, for purposes of meeting the 50-MW
registration threshold.

 How Appendix 5B’s  Registration Criteria  apply  to  various data center leasing  scenarios. A
CLO  may  lease  an  entire  Site  and  all  of  its  power  capacity  to  a  single  hyperscaler-CLOP
tenant.  Or,  at  a  colocation  Site,  a  CLO  may  lease  physical  space  and  allocate  contracted
amounts  of  MW  usage  to  numerous  tenant  CLOPs  each  consuming  relatively  smaller
amounts  of  electricity.  There  are  many  variations  of  site  ownership  and  tenant  operational
arrangements  in  between.  NERC  should  provide  a  range  of  hypothetical  examples  to
illustrate how CLOs, CLOPs, and other stakeholders should apply the Registration Criteria in
practice to various owner-landlord/operator-tenant arrangements.

 Offer  an  objective  physical  point  where  voltage  should  be  measured  to  meet  the  100-kV
Registration Criterion. We defer to NERC, and Transmission Owners and Generator Owners,
as to where that precise point should be. As a guiding principle, we think that point should be
reasonably  attributable  to  electricity  usage  by  the  Site,  as  opposed  to  a  point  too  far
“upstream” along the transmission pathway from the Bulk Power System to the Site.

Ideally,  the  refinements  we  suggest  to  the  Appendix  2  Definitions  and  Appendix  5B 
Registration  Criteria  may  encourage  NERC  to  establish  reciprocal,  two-way  data  and 
information sharing responsibilities among CLOs and CLOPs. In this manner, responsibilities to 
comply  with  Standards  CLO-001,  -002,  and  -003  (and  future  Computational  Load  Standards) 
should follow the entity that controls the relevant equipment, activity, and information. 

Letter to Mr. Jim Robb 
September 16, 2026 
Page 3 

Importantly, NERC should avoid imposing  compliance responsibilities on one entity where 
another  party  possesses  the  information  or  operational  capability  needed  to  satisfy  that 
obligation.  Where  a  CLO’s  compliance  depends  on  information  or  actions  within  a  CLOP’s 
possession or control – and vice versa – the Reliability Standards should impose a corresponding 
affirmative obligation for each party to share with the other necessary data and information in a 
timely and confidential manner. This principle is particularly important at colocation Sites, and 
should provide the foundation for NERC’s treatment of data centers as definitions and standards 
evolve—including  any  future  “ride-through”  performance  requirements  for  data  centers  to 
remain connected to the BPS through grid disturbances and voltage oscillations. 

We  believe  our  recommendations  will  help  preserve  clear  regulatory  accountability  while 
also ensuring that NERC receives the ownership and operational cooperation necessary to protect 
the  U.S.  electric  grid.  More  detailed  comments  are  provided  in  the  attached  Addendum.  For 
further  information  regarding  these  comments,  please  contact  Duane  J.  Desiderio,  Senior 
Vice President and Counsel with The Real Estate Roundtable.

Jeffrey D. DeBoer
