Comments on Definition of Computational Load Owner (“CLO)” 

(Appendix 2 Definitions) 

 NERC  Proposed  Definition:  “The  entity  that  owns  and  maintains  a  Computational  Load

Site.”

 RER Recommended Definition:

“Computational  Load  Owner  (CLO)  means  a  corporation,  limited  liability  company,
partnership,  or  other  legal  entity  organized  under  applicable  State,  Tribal,  or  other  law
that directly owns the real property at a Computational Load Site, including the land and
building(s). Ownership of stock, partnership interests, beneficial interests, or other equity
or financial interests in such legal entity shall not, by itself, constitute direct ownership of
the Computational Load Site.

“A CLO may: (1) also qualify as a Computational Load Operator (CLOP); or (2) lease or
otherwise  provide  physical  space,  equipment,  and/or  load  capacity  through  contractual
agreement(s) with one or more unrelated CLOP tenant(s).”

 Explanation:

 Stating that a CLO “owns” a Computational Load Site is circular. NERC should clarify
that “owns” refers solely to the particular business entity that directly owns the real estate
– that is, land and buildings – at the Computational Load Site. NERC should make clear
that  “owns”  does  not  reach  businesses,  shareholders,  and  investors  that  simply  have  an
equity  stake  or  other  financial  interest  in  the  CLO  entity  holding  title  to  the  Site’s  real
property. Much like office buildings, hotels, apartments, warehouses and other types of
commercial buildings, data centers may be held through special purpose entities – such as
project-level  LLCs,  subsidiaries,  joint  ventures,  and  other  multi-tiered  property
ownership structures. Because CLO status triggers registration and mandatory Reliability
Standard  compliance,  NERC’s  definition  should  cover  only  the  particular  project-level
legal entity that directly owns the Site’s real property.

 NERC should avoid the term “owns and maintains” in defining a CLO. A facility-owning
entity  may  satisfy  its  maintenance  responsibilities  through  a  separate  property
management  contractor  or  other  service  provider.  Thus,  the  entity  that  “maintains”  the
property may be different from the entity that “owns” the property. The fact that the Site
owner  does  not  itself  employ  the  personnel  performing  maintenance  work  should  not
negate its status or obligation to register as a CLO. In fact, in many cases, the entity that
maintains the facility may also be the one that  operates it. Thus, the phrase “owns and
maintains” should not be used to avoid overlap between the CLO and CLOP definitions,

2 

and minimize confusion where NERC’s Reliability Standards direct the CLO to fulfill a 
requirement that should fall to the CLOP instead. 

 The  CLO  definition  should  expressly  recognize  distinct  “ownership”  and  “operation”
entities  may  own  different  equipment  at  a  Computational  Load  Site,  particularly  in  the
property leasing context. A CLO may own the underlying land and building(s) at the Site,
as  well  as  HVAC  and  mechanical,  electrical,  and  plumbing  equipment  and  systems  in
common  service  to  the  Site’s  separate  buildings.  Meanwhile,  individual  tenant(s)  may
own  servers,  racks,  processing  units,  UPS  equipment,  batteries,  and  other  equipment
within the leased spaces where they operate.

 Just because a CLO may lease space to data center tenants, or a tenant owns and controls
its own computing systems at the Site, should not make it difficult to readily identify the
CLO  –  or  result  in  each  tenant  becoming  an  additional  CLO  merely  because  it  owns
equipment  located  within  the  Site’s  boundaries.  We  believe  our  recommendations  can
provide a clearer foundation for allocating separate obligations to  CLOs – distinguished
from  CLOP  tenant(s)  that  lease  space  –  with  definitional  reference  to  “who  controls
what” functions,  systems, equipment,  information,  and data within  lessors’ and lessees’
respective spheres of possession and control.

Comments on Definition of Computational Load Operator (“CLOP)” 

(Appendix 2 Definitions) 

 NERC Proposed Definition: “The entity that operates a Computational Load Site.”

 RER Recommended Definition:

“Computational Load Operator (“CLOP”) means a corporation, limited liability company,
partnership,  or  other  legal  entity  organized  under  applicable  State,  Tribal,  or  other  law
that  exercises  day-to-day  control  and  decision-making  authority  over 
the  use,
management,  and  functioning  of  computers,  processing  units,  servers,  and  other
information  technology  equipment  and  systems  that  consume  electric  power  and
contribute to the computational load at the Computational Load Site.

“A CLOP may: (1) also qualify as a Computational Load Owner (“CLO”); or (2) lease or
otherwise  obtain,  through  contractual  agreement(s)  with  an  unrelated  CLO,  physical
space,  equipment  and/or  load  capacity  to  perform  computational  load  activities  and
functions.”

3 

Explanation: 

 Stating  that  a  CLOP  is  the  “entity  that  operates”  a  Site  is  circular.  Given  that  CLOP
registration  would  carry  mandatory  Reliability  Standard  obligations  distinct  from  a
CLO’s  compliance  responsibilities,  businesses  should  be  able  to  determine  with
reasonable  certainty  which  particular  legal  entity(ies)  perform  independent  functions
unique to CLOP status.

 NERC can improve definitional clarity if it states that CLOPs possess day-to-day control
and  decision-making  authority  to  use,  program  and  configure  the  servers,  processing
units,  microchips,  batteries,  networking  equipment,  and  other  IT  infrastructure  whose
electricity consumption constitutes the Site’s computational load.

 Our  recommended  phrase  –  “exercises  day-to-day  control  and  decision-making
authority”  –  draws  from  an  analogous  context  to  help  define  CLOP  status.  The  U.S.
Supreme  Court  emphasized  that  an  “operator”  for  purposes  of  Superfund  sites  is
“someone  who  directs  the  workings  of,  manages,  or  conducts  the  affairs  of  a  facility.”
United States v. Bestfoods, 524 U.S. 51, 66 (1998). The Court tailored that inquiry to the
particular  regulated  activity—in  that  case,  focusing  on  the  “operator”  as  the  party  that
controls  the  day-to-day  management,  direction,  and  conduct  of  business  operations
specifically related to hazardous waste management:

To  sharpen  the  definition  for  purposes  of  [the  Superfund  law’s]  concern 
with  environmental  contamination,  an  operator  must  manage,  direct,  or 
conduct  operations  specifically  related  to  pollution,  that  is,  operations 
having to do with the leakage or disposal of hazardous waste, or decisions 
about compliance with environmental regulations. 

Id.  at  66–67.  See  also  id.  at  72  (evidence  that  the  facility’s  operator  “actively 
participated  in,”  “exerted  control  over,”  and  “issued  directives  regarding,”  the 
facility’s environmental impacts).  

 NERC  should  apply  the  reasoning  from  Bestfoods  and  adopt  a  similar  control-based
approach  here,  tailored  to  a  CLOP’s  actions  affecting  grid  reliability.  Accordingly,  an
“operator” is not determined by “ownership” of the real estate or data center building(s)
within a Site’s boundaries. CLOP responsibilities should rest instead with the entity that
manages,  directs,  or  controls  activities  specifically  related  to  the  electrical  loads  from
“computers,  processing  units,  servers,  batteries,  and  other  information  technology
equipment and systems,” as we propose.

4 

 Our suggested CLOP definition is phrased in a manner to encompass wide varieties of

leasing arrangements that occur at data centers. For example, a CLO may lease the entire
Site and all of its electrical load to a single unrelated hyperscaler tenant that also owns its
own computing equipment. Or, a CLO may lease square footage, equipment, and
electrical capacity to many unrelated “smaller” tenants at a colocation site.

 Whatever  the  scenario  (or  some  variation  in  between),  we  believe  it  is  important  for
NERC to contemplate data center leasing arrangements where CLOs may have limited or
no  control  over  CLOP  tenants’  energy  consumption  activities,  especially  regarding
computer  use.  Because  the  CLO  may  be  responsible  for  the  building  while  lacking
control  over  the  equipment  driving  a  significant  portion  of  its  energy  consumption,  we
recommend  that  the  CLOP  definition  incorporate  similar  language  that  mirrors  our
proposed  CLO  definition  –  to  acknowledge  that  a  data  center  owner  and  a  data  center
operator  could  be  the  same  entity,  but  are  commonly  separate  entities  with  different
regulatory obligations and responsibilities.

Comments on Definition of “Computational Load Site” 

(Appendix 2 Definitions) 

 NERC Proposed Definition: “[O]ne or more buildings, structures, or installations at a single

location that:
“(1) Primarily contains information technology infrastructure used for:

• creating, executing, and delivering software applications and services;
• artificial intelligence training, deployment, and delivery;
• cryptocurrency mining; or
• other computational activities at a data center; and

“(2) Is supplied through electrical equipment that is connected to the BPS.” 

 RER Recommended Definition: “ ‘Computational Load Site’ means one or more buildings,

structures, or installations at a single location that is:

(1) Primarily  contains  used  by  information  technology  infrastructure  to  process,  store,

transmit, or manipulate digital information, including:
• creating, executing, and delivering software applications and cloud services;
• artificial intelligence training, deployment, and delivery; and
• cryptocurrency mining; and
• other computational activities at a data center; and

“(2) Supplied through electrical equipment that is connected to the BPS.” 

4 

 Add a new Appendix 2 definition for “Single Location”:

“The term ‘Single Location’ includes separate buildings, structures, or installations that—
(1) Are located on the same parcel of land, or adjacent or contiguous parcels of land,

as recorded with the relevant local government authority; and

(2) Meet any of the following criteria:

(a) owned by the same CLO;
(b) operated by the same CLOP;
(c) have the same street address;
(d) developed pursuant to a common land-use or master construction plan;
(e) share significant electrical integration to the BPS, such as receipt of electricity
from  the  same  step-down  transformer  that  reduces  transmission-level  voltage
for delivery to the Site; or

(f) are served by the same cooling, water, or other site-level infrastructure.

RER Comments: 

 NERC should separately define the term, “Single Location,” in Appendix 2.

 CLO  and  CLOP  registrants  will  benefit  from  greater  clarity  as  to  what  constitutes  a
“Single  Location”  under  the “Computational  Load Site” definition.  As discussed below
regarding the 50-MW threshold in the “Registration Criteria,” NERC intends that electric
loads of individual buildings – at a “Single Location” – will be aggregated at campuses or
similar  properties  where  separate  structures  are  integrated  in  terms  of  their  ownership,
operations,  management,  and  receipt  of  electricity  from  the  grid.  “Single  Location”
should be defined with objective and consistently applicable criteria to guide when CLOs
and  CLOPs  may  need  to  add  the  loads  of  physically  separate  buildings  at  a
Computational Load Site that are nonetheless related by ownership or function.

 The  U.S.  Department  of  Treasury,  through  the  Internal  Revenue  Service  (“IRS”),
provides  helpful  guidance.  For  purposes  of  a  1-MW  threshold  that  determines
qualification for energy project tax incentives, IRS Notice 2018-59 lists relevant factors
to determine when multiple energy properties “are operated as part of a single project.”2
Treasury and the IRS have consistently relied on these same criteria to define a “single
project.”3

2 Section 7.01(2)-(4) of Notice 2018-59 (at pp. 21-24) discusses when multiple energy properties are treated as a 
“single project” to determine the “start of construction” for federal renewable energy tax credit purposes. Section 
7.01(2) sets forth eight criteria based on whether separate energy properties: (1) are owned by a single legal entity; 
(2) are constructed on contiguous pieces of land; (3) are described in a common power purchase agreement(s); (4)
have a common intertie; (5) share a common substation; (6) are described in one or more common environmental or
other regulatory permits; (7) constructed pursuant to a master construction contract; or (8) are financed pursuant to
the same construction loan agreement.

3 Treasury Department regulation, 26 C.F.R. 1.48-13(d)(1); IRS Notice 2025-42 (August 20, 2025). 

5 

 Our recommended definition here parallels factors in the Treasury/IRS criteria – namely,
common  ownership,  operations,  addresses,  master  development  plans,  and  receipt  of
electricity from the same step-down transformer – to assist NERC’s definitional exercise
for  a  “Computational  Load  Site.”  The  IRS’s  Guidance  may  inform  a  more  predictable
framework  from  NERC  to  help  registered  CLOs  and  CLOPs  decide  when  they  must
combine electric loads from separate buildings located at a “master” Site.

 NERC  should  avoid  describing  a  Computational  Load  Site  as  one  that  “primarily
contains” IT infrastructure – and instead define the Site as one that “primarily  uses” IT
infrastructure to perform various computational activities.

 NERC’s  use  of  the  phrase  “primarily  contains”  is  ambiguous.  It  is  not  clear  what  must
“primarily contain” IT infrastructure – the Computational Load Site as a whole, or each
individual  building  at  the  Site?  It  is  also  unclear  what  “primarily”  measures:  Square
footage? “Computational” load? “Total” load? Equipment count?

 We thus recommend that NERC should instead employ a more functional test regarding
IT infrastructure used at the Site for computational activities– as opposed to whether the
Site “contains” IT infrastructure.

 Our  recommended  definition  of  “Computational  Load  Site”  encourages  NERC  to
illustrate  –  but  not  prescribe  –  the  types  of  computer-based  functions  performed  by  IT
equipment  including  (but  not  limited  to)  activities  like  processing  software,  providing
cloud  services,  developing  and  training  AI  models,  and  mining  crypto  assets.  Our
suggested  text  expresses  these  activities  as  non-exhaustive  types  of  computational
functions  that  “process,  store,  transmit,  or  manipulate  digital  information.”  We  aim  to
reflect  the  wording  and  spirit  of  NERC’s  Level  3  “Action  Alert”  which  immediately
presaged the proposed Reliability Standards at issue for Large Computational Loads.4

Comments on New Compliance Registry Threshold Criteria 

for CLOs and CLOPs  (Section III(c), Appendix 5B) 

 NERC  Proposal:  Computational  Load  Owners  and  Operators  must  register  with  NERC,

regarding a Computational Load Site:
 With a “Total Connected Load” greater than or equal to 50 MW;
 That is supplied through electrical equipment; and

4 NERC’s Level 3 “Action Alert” (May 4, 2026), is aimed to remedy “specific deficiencies with the treatment 
of computational loads. Examples of this load include artificial intelligence training, cryptocurrency mining, 
and traditional data center uses” (emphasis added). 

6 

 Connected at a voltage level greater than or equal to “100 kV from one or more points”

of connection.

RER Comments: 

 NERC should add a new Appendix 2 definition for the term, “Total Connected Load,” as

follows:

“  ‘Total  Connected  Load’  means  ‘Computational  Load’  plus  electricity  used  for  HVAC,
lighting,  non-computer  equipment  and  appliance  plug  loads,  and  loads  to  support  other
non-computational building systems like elevators, security, and fire/safety equipment at a
Computational Load Site.”

 A  separate  glossary  definition  of  “Total  Connected  Load”  will  be  helpful  to  CLO  and
CLOP registrants. Defining the term independently will make clear that “Total Connected
Load”  is  the  relevant  metric  of  magnitude  for  purposes  of  the  50-MW  Registration
Criterion.  It  will  help  property  owners  understand  what  types  of  real  estate  facilities
NERC intends to reach through its Registration Criteria and Reliability Standards.

 At this juncture, NERC does not intend to impose standards on large loads per se – but
only  on  owners  and  operators  of  “Large  Computational  Loads,”  considering  their
impacts on grid reliability.5

 E.g.: A factory, hospital campus, large office park, laboratory complex, or casino may
each consume a lot of energy and individually exceed 50 MW per property. But they
may  not  need  to  register  with  NERC  because  they  may  not  qualify  as  a
“Computational Load Site.”

 We urge NERC to state this point clearly as it finalizes the Registration Criteria.

5 “NERC is proposing foundational Reliability Standards with accompanying glossary updates that align w ith 
updates to the registry criteria to support computational load integration while maintaining reliability of the 
bulk power system.” NERC website, “Large Load Action Plan”. NERC’s Level 3 “Action Alert” (May 4, 
2026), presaging the development of the Reliability Standards at issue, intends to remedy “specific 
deficiencies with the treatment of computational loads. Examples of this load include artificial intelligence 
training, cryptocurrency mining, and traditional data center uses.”  The Level 3 Alert “was issued as NERC 
observed customer-initiated large load reductions and significant oscillations that occur in seconds, leaving little 
or no room for real-time responses, threatening BPS reliability.” NERC press release (May. 4, 2026). See also 
NERC, Reliability Insights, “Large Computational Load Risks Due to Voltage Sensitivity” (Sept. 2026) 
(“[I][nterconnection of large computational loads has implications for BPS reliability,” as “several incidents 
involving computational loads … have been shown to impact BPS operations when the loads remove themselves 
from the system during disturbances”).   

7 

 NERC  should  provide  hypothetical  scenarios 

to  distinguish  between  CLO/CLOP

“registration” and Total Connected Load “aggregation.” For example:

 Data center owner delivers and interconnects a facility with 70 MW of “Total Connected

Load.” A single hyperscaler leases the entire facility.
 The owner must register as a CLO because the site connects at a capacity ≥ 50 MW.
 The hyperscaler tenant must register as a CLOP because its operations use ≥ 50 MW.

 Data center owner delivers and interconnects a colocation facility with 70 MW of “Total
Connected Load.” Seven (7) different tenants each use 10 MW in the spaces they lease in
multiple buildings across the Site.
 The owner must register as a CLO because the data center site in aggregate exceeds

the 50-MW threshold.

 None  of  the  tenants  need  to  register  as  CLOPs.  None  of  their  contracted  electricity

usage is ≥ 50 MW.

 Data center owner delivers and interconnects a facility with 70 MW of “Total Connected
Load.” Tenant A uses 50 MW. Tenant B uses 14 MW. Tenants C and D each use 3 MW.
 The owner must register as a CLO because the data center in aggregate exceeds the

50-MW threshold.

 Tenant  A  must  register  as  a  CLOP.  Its  contracted  electricity  usage  pursuant  to  its

lease with the CLO is equal to NERC’s 50-MW registration threshold.

 Tenants  B,  C,  and  D  do  not  need  to  register  as  CLOPs.  None  of  their  contracted

electricity usage pursuant to their distinct leases meets the 50-MW threshold.

 Data center owner delivers and interconnects a facility with 70 MW of “Total Connected
Load.”  Tenant  A  uses  30  MW  in  Building  X,  and  20  MW  in  Building  Y  at  the  Site.
Tenant B uses 10 MW in Building X, and 20 MW in Building Y.
 The owner must register as a CLO because  “Total Connected Load” in aggregate at

the Computational Load Site exceeds the 50-MW registration threshold.

 Tenant A must register as a CLOP. Its aggregate energy usage in both buildings at the
Site,  as  contracted  with  the  CLO  through  a  lease,  equals  50MW  –  at  NERC’s
threshold.

 Tenant  B  does  not  need  to  register  as  a  CLOP.  Its  aggregate  energy  usage  in  both

buildings at the Site is 30MW – under NERC’s threshold.

 NERC should clarify how far “upstream” on the electrical path, between the BPS and the

Computational Load Site, the 100 kV level should be measured.

8 

 The  proposed  Registration  Criteria  apply  to  a  Computational  Load  Site  with  50  MW
“Total Connected Load” – that is “supplied through electrical equipment connected at a
voltage  level  greater  than  or  equal  to  100  kV  from  one  or  more  points  of  connection.”
While the 50-MW threshold  addresses  magnitude, the separate 100-kV  criterion serves
another  screening  function  to  support  NERC  registration,  by  establishing  a  sufficiently
close electrical nexus along the transmission route between the BPS and the Site.

 We  encourage  NERC  to  specify  the  voltage  measurement  point  as  one  reasonably
attributable  to  electricity  usage  by  the  Computational  Load  Site,  rather  than  remote
upstream  points  on  the  grid  that  distribute  electricity  to  customers  and  properties
unrelated to the CLO.

 When  the  CLO  applies  for  interconnection,  the  Transmission  Owner  and  applicable
Generator  Owners  (longstanding  registrants  in  NERC’s  regime)  are  likely  the  best
entities  to  identify  for  the  CLO  the  specific  voltage  measurement  point  to  ascertain
whether the 100-kV criterion is satisfied.6

 We  urge  NERC  to  adopt  a  reasonable  limiting  principle  to  the  100-kV  threshold  in
identifying  a  point  along  the  BPS’s  transmission  route  that  is  proximate  to  the
Computational  Load  Site.  Furthermore,  our  intent  is  not  to  allow  CLOs  (and  CLOPs)
posing grid reliability impacts to evade registration with NERC. Our recommendation is
intended to appropriately balance grid reliability concerns with the need for an objective
and administrable registration criterion that considers the Site’s actual relationship to and
receipt of electricity from the BPS.

Impacts of Our Recommended Definition and Registration Criteria Refinements on 

Proposed Reliability Standards CLO-001-1, -002-1, and -003-1 



Ideally, the revisions we propose to the Definitions and Registration Criteria will avoid
potential regulatory mismatch whereby one entity bears responsibility for compliance with a
Standard, but another entity possesses the information or functional capacity to achieve it.

 Clearly delineating compliance responsibilities is especially relevant at leased data centers. A

CLO-landlord may know what is occurring at the site and interconnection level, while
individual CLOP-tenant(s) may know what is occurring with the computational equipment
and operational load. Neither necessarily has the complete picture. NERC should not assume

6 Reliability Standard FAC-001-05, regarding “Facility Interconnection Requirements,” states as its “Purpose”: “To 
avoid adverse impacts on the reliability of the Bulk Electric System, Transmission Owners and applicable 
Generator Owners must document and make Facility interconnection requirements available so that entities 
seeking to interconnect will have the necessary information.” (Emphasis supplied.) 

11 

that information automatically flows between them merely because they own and operate at 
the same Site.  

 Thus, where a CLO bears the compliance obligation – but satisfaction depends upon

information within the possession or control of a CLOP(s) – then NERC should impose a
corresponding affirmative obligation on the CLOP(s) to timely provide the CLO with all
information and data necessary to meet the pertinent Standard.

 Likewise, CLOP(s) should bear compliance responsibilities where a Reliability Standard

imposes an obligation directly concerning information, equipment, or operations regarding
computational load functions and activities that it controls and manages on a day-to-day
basis.

 Applying these principles to the proposed Reliability Standards:

 Standard CLO-001-1 should require CLOPs to provide CLOs with equipment data,

operating characteristics, modeling information, model-verification information, and
notice of potentially material changes within CLOPs’ possession or control – so a CLO
can discharge its own responsibilities under the Standard. At least some of the modeling,
change-notification, verification, and study-coordination duties logically belong on the
CLOP—because the operator-tenant(s) may control the very equipment and operating
practices that determine how the facility behaves electrically.

 Standard  CLO-002-1  addresses  the  operational  data,  communications,  and  instructions
necessary  to  support  reliable  operation  of  Computational  Load  Sites  and  the  BPS.  It
imposes obligations on both CLOs and CLOPs. It requires each to share operational data
with grid entities, comply with operating instructions, maintain lines of communication,
provide  notification  of  specified  changes  in  load  or  operations,  and  implement
instructions from grid operators to address BPS reliability needs. NERC should expressly
require  CLOs  and  CLOPs  at  the  same  Site  to  confidentially  share  with  each  other  the
information  necessary  to  satisfy  their  respective  compliance  responsibilities.  NERC
should establish reciprocal compliance obligations on CLOs and CLOPs to confidentially
exchange  data  and  information  as  needed  for  each  to  meet  their  respective  CLO-002
responsibilities.

 Standard CLO-003-1 lays the foundation for eventual, substantive “ride-through”

performance requirements. At this juncture, NERC should impose an affirmative reporting
obligation on the CLOP operating the electrical equipment. A CLO might own a
substation and lease it to tenants, in which case the CLO may not have direct access to the
information NERC needs. In addition, NERC’s Standard should direct CLOs and CLOPs
to confidentially exchange and provide relevant protection and disturbance data with each
other, rather than assuming one possesses the other’s information essential for compliance.
It will be critical to get the monitoring and information-sharing architecture correct now—

12 

because NERC will eventually regulate how CLOs and CLOPs must actually perform 
during “ride-through” events.

18 September 2026 
Thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback on the draft language to the NERC Rules of 
Procedures. 

Before articulating the individual comments to the various appendices included within the NERC 
Rules of Procedure that will be updated as a result of this process, we felt it important to outline 
the principles by which NERC should evaluate success in drafting forthcoming reliability 
standards for large computational users. While these five principles are relevant to the drafted 
ROP language, they also transcend that change and should be applied wherever NERC is 
establishing regulatory, procedural, or policy structures to address and respond to 
computational load entities. 

Principles for Evaluating NERC Draft Reliability Standards and 
Related Revisions for Large Computational Loads

1. Forthcoming Reliability Standards (inclusive of the Registry Criteria) must
comprehensively address the nature of the risk that computational loads pose. 
NERC remains tasked with the singular responsibility of developing, implementing, and 
enforcing reliability standards for computational loads like data centers that pose unique risks to 
the bulk power system. This should be done carefully and comprehensively upfront. Articulating 
the balance between protecting existing systems and fostering an environment of innovation is 
challenging, yet we are confident that NERC is up to the challenge and is poised to develop 
standards that meaningfully address the unprecedented nature of the risk. 

2. While the need for reliability requirements is undeniable, NERC must ensure that
proposed requirements are robust and fully vetted through the stakeholder process. 
Despite claims of urgency from both industry and political stakeholders, the "need for speed” 
cannot undermine the imperative for quality. Stakeholders can and consistently have 
demonstrated the ability to adapt; developing comprehensive standards correctly is more 
important than doing so quickly. The NERC staff, stakeholder bodies, and volunteer contributors 
are working incredibly quickly, and that initiative should be lauded. But compromising the quality 
of the standards to satisfy demands for speed undermines the role of NERC as the entity 
responsible for developing standards to mitigate reliability risks. 

3. First movers in AI data center development must not be rewarded with exemption from
forthcoming requirements. The risk of being an early adopter is just that - higher risk; this 
remains true across the technological innovation spectrum. Technology companies and 
innovators understand this, and it is not NERC’s responsibility to mitigate that risk. Technology 
companies who had (and have) the capital and appetite to pursue rapid development of 
hyperscale data centers did so with knowledge that there could be forthcoming Reliability 
Standards. This should not grant them exemption from the requirements necessary to protect 
the reliability of the bulk power system. Weak retroactivity provisions or broad exemptions 
cannot be used to avoid or delay compliance. 

1 

2101 Webster St. 
Suite 1300 
Oakland, CA 94612 

SierraClub.org 

Instead, NERC and ERO-designated entities have clear procedures for updating, revisiting, and 
evaluating standards in response to ongoing and evolving industry needs. If the need arises to 
evaluate the impact of the standards, such processes can be utilized. Codifying legacy 
exemption or acquired rights does not meaningfully address the concerns raised by industry 
stakeholders about the significant impacts computational loads can have on the bulk power 
system. To manage a period of dramatic change with responsible regulation, NERC must 
propose universally applicable standards. 

4. Greater transparency throughout the standards development process is required for
successful, long-term reliability. Transparency requires clear signposting of standards 
development to utilities, states, and the broader stakeholder community. Many entities including 
RTOs, state regulatory commissions, and utilities are developing large load regulations, tariff 
provisions, and operational policies while NERC is still developing computational load reliability 
standards. NERC clarity regarding expected standard topics and finalization timelines is critical 
to enabling regulators, policy makers, and asset owners to adapt to eventual NERC regulation 
quickly and seamlessly. While NERC must not shy away from a necessary standard if it 
diverges from a previously posted roadmap, clear signposting can help mitigate friction 
associated with these concurrent processes.  NERC should also make clear which 
stakeholders are providing what feedback to support a more open and transparent stakeholder 
process. What NERC is already rolling out with public comment period(s), and use of broader 
communication channels, demonstrates what this can look like in practice. 

5. Reliability Standards must support sensible cost allocation. While NERC’s focus for
Reliability Standards is–and must continue to be–ensuring reliability, how reliability standards 
are set can impact the ability to cleanly allocate costs associated with risk mitigation to the cost-
causers. In plain language, outages cost money, and mitigating the risk imposed by large loads 
has a meaningful impact on long-term cost. NERC should focus standards on how large loads 
can mitigate their reliability risks, and ensure operational actions that other load and unaffiliated 
generation can take to mitigate computational load risk are clearly noted as secondary 
mitigation strategies. 

Utilization of these principles throughout the LLWG and associated processes will ensure that 
the output of the NERC working groups meaningfully and thoroughly addresses and creates 
responsive guardrails to the nature of the risks posed by these system users. To demonstrate 
the gravity of this effort, an additional 313 individual Sierra Club members signed onto these 
principles to demonstrate the importance of NERC’s role in ensuring that standards for large 
computational loads meaningfully address the risks posed (see Signatories at end of 
Comments). 

Sincerely, 
Jessi Eidbo, Senior Advisor, 
Sierra Club

Comments on Updates to the NERC Rules of Procedure

We applaud the care of the Large Loads Working Group to treat the inclusion of Computational 
Loads within the Rules of Procedure (ROP) with the gravity it merits, and appreciate the 
attention being taken to respond to stakeholder concerns throughout the process. We spent 
time reviewing the draft materials and now offer the following for consideration. Our comments 
are organized by Appendix. It’s helpful to note at the onset that three values underpin our 
comments: clarity, consistency with the existing ROP, and reliability as a foundational metric to 
evaluate appropriateness of the proposed changes to the ROP. 

Appendix 2 (Definitions Used in the Rules of Procedure) 

We support the updated definitions in Appendix 2. With regard to the specific definitions: 



“Computational Load Operator” and “Computational Load Owner” are helpful to
keep distinct, appreciating that there are likely to be many instances where they are
distinct actors, though there could be instances where they are the same. When we seek
to find precedent in the existing NERC Rules of Procedure, we appreciate that this
definition retains consistency with the definition for Generation Owner and Generation
Operator. However, there is departure from precedent in that the classification for
Generation Owner immediately incorporates a size classification (20 MW and connected
at a common point of connection greater than or equal to 60 kV). The decision to treat
the size threshold for Computational Load Sites outside of the actor (CL Operator or CL
Owner) creates inconsistency with how this is handled within the ROP for generation.
We recommend including the size threshold in the definition(s) for both the
definition of CL Operator and CL Owner for consistent treatment.

 Computational Load Site. The clarity that the new definition offers is incredibly helpful
and will ensure that ambiguity is mitigated in the compliance and enforcement down the
road. However, the introduction of the word “primarily” in the term “computational load
site” regarding what the site contains could introduce ambiguity. To address this, it may
be helpful to either expound how “primarily” is measured, or change the language to “the
majority of the site’s load consists of information technology infrastructure used for…”
We recognize that the use of the term “primarily” is common in the Rules of Procedure,
and so while this may not be something that NERC can address via these comments
alone, it should be considered in the long-term.

Appendix 5A (Organization Registration and Certification 
Manual) 
We support the inclusion of the two entity types (Computational Load Owner and Computational 
Load Operator) to the list of functional entity types to which mandatory and enforceable 
Reliability Standards apply.  

Appendix 5B (Statement of Compliance Registry Criteria) 

1. The determination of whether a Computational Load Site (CLS) is or is not
beholden to the NERC Reliability Standards must consider more than the size 
and voltage at interconnection of the site. 

The use of size and voltage at interconnection is a somewhat crude delineation of true risk 
posed by a CLS (and relatedly, from multiple CLS) to the BPS.1 An expanded set of holistic 
criteria should be used to determine if a CLS should be subject to the reliability standards. Such 
expansion must address the actual electrical behavior of CLS and the risk profile they present to 
the bulk power system.  

We propose the following characterization schema for criteria registry that builds on the Idaho 
National Lab evaluation of large load risk behavior variables:2 



Load size. Metrics used to define load size should be expanded and include:

o Minimum absolute amount based on peak demand (not cumulative, can be

applicable to only IT equipment).

o Monthly total consumption (cumulative, inclusive of all metered load at

Computational Load Site, not just IT equipment).



Load variability. This could be measured in a number of ways:

o Maximum ramp rate. For example, the Long Island Power Authority evaluates the
amplitude variation at various frequencies and defines an angle under which
large load operations must remain.3

o Frequency of instances of ramp by category (for example, number of daily

instances of ramps exceeding 10 MW/min).

 Load flexibility. This should include both technical ability to be flexible, and elective
flexibility (i.e., when CLS elect to participate in curtailment product offerings within an
RTO).

 Presence of co-located generation. Both the size and the ramping capability of co-

located generation should be considered, as both influence how rapidly a facility could
elect to switch power source(s).

 CLO/CLS’ purchase bid mechanism. This metric should evaluate when a CLO elects
to participate in, for example, a price-adaptive power purchase program. In Southwest
Power Pool (SPP), the regional grid operator is currently outlining provisions for a Price
Adaptive Load (PAL) scheme that would allow customers to only procure power through
the bulk power system when prices are above or below a certain value.4 The
participation in this type of a program could meaningfully impact the behavior of the
facility as it interfaces with the bulk power system.

2. If a site undergoes significant change (i.e., material modification), the
applicability of the reliability standards must be re-evaluated. 

The current language simply reads: “An entity which is not initially placed on the Compliance 
Registry, but which is identified subsequently as having a material impact on the BPS, will be 
added to the Compliance Registry.” 5  Even clearer guidance on what constitutes a change 
significant enough to merit notifying the regional entity should be spelled out. This is especially 
critical given the possibility for certain computational loads to be exempted from the 
requirements.  

While we feel strongly that there should be no wholesale retroactive exemptions (i.e., no 
legacy exemptions or grandfathering provisions), we recognize that in some past instances, 
NERC has adopted legacy exemptions for other entities as they begin participation in the 
registry process. However, we submit any exemptions should be (a) time limited and (b) 
designed to account for legitimate logistical constraints that would impede the facility meeting 
the new standards. 

Further, if exemptions are offered (i.e., legacy exemption or retroactive status provision), then it 
must be made clear when a change to an existing site is sufficient to merit (a) notification of the 
change, and (b) change in compliance status from exempt to no longer exempt. The criteria for 
material modification should include the following. Note that these characteristics are coincident 
with the expanded registry criteria introduced above.

3. We do not support the updated threshold size minimums. As long as size 
alone is being used to evaluate requirements for site compliance, we suggest a 
reversion to the original size threshold for the registry criteria.  

Many would argue there is a need for simplicity in reporting which dictates the use of simplified 
metrics to evaluate the risk that a CLS poses to the bulk electric system.7 However, the criteria 
used to evaluate the true risk of a CLS should be expansive to represent the behavioral profile 
of the load, not just its size, as we argue in (1) above. But we acknowledge that when seeking 
which characteristics offer the most meaningful insight into what degree of risk a CLS 
introduces, size and voltage at interconnection are often the easiest variables to quantify. 
Therefore, should NERC opt to use simpler metrics at the expense of comprehensive metrics, 
the original threshold of 20 MW and 60 kV should be used for the following reasons:  

6  See supra, fn 3.  
7  Characteristics and Risks of Emerging Large Loads, NERC Large Load Task Force, July 2025,

A. Part of the justification for the change to 50 MW and 100 kW was that “unintended

entities were included.” 8 But the number of impacted entities is not a useful metric when
considering reliability impacts to the BPS. While the August 19th update offered
justification for the change based on the number of entities that would or would not be
affected, this does not meaningfully measure the change in system impact from the
revised size and kV threshold definition.9 This importance of mitigating risk associated
with load size is underscored in the current draft NERC white paper, “Large Load
Disturbance Performance – Impact Analysis and Ride-Through Recommendations,” in
which authors acknowledge that: “The capacity of a large load site at its point of
interconnection is a direct factor in both its BPS impact when a CILR occurs and in the
design rigor typically applied to its protection and power systems.”

B. The change to 50 MW and 100 kV introduces a departure from the standards that
already exist for generation, where 20 MW is the current threshold for standard
applicability (see PRC-029). As a result, some elements of PRC-029-1, such as the
defaults for FRT and RoCoF criteria, were extended to large computational loads, while
other parts of PRC-029-1 were not (i.e., size threshold minimums). The departure from
PRC-029 for minimum size threshold is as yet unsubstantiated.

C. Because size and voltage at interconnection are such crude determinants of true risk to
the system, using more conservative thresholds is necessary to protect the integrity and
reliability of the bulk power system. Lowering the thresholds captures the risk which
smaller, lower voltage systems pose to BPS reliability as a function of their behavior,
even if their size alone does not pose a risk. Thus, a more comprehensive and
responsive standard reliant on size alone must revert to the 20 MW and 60 kV
threshold.

To further support lower thresholds, we look to the precedent set by Southwest Power Pool, in 
their recently FERC-approved definition of High-Impact Large Loads (HILL): 

“(1) 10 MW or more if connected to the Transmission System at a 
voltage level less than or equal to 69 [kilovolts (kV)]; 
or (2) 50 MW or more if connected to the Transmission System at a 
voltage level greater than 69 kV.” 

SPP’s approved definition therefore goes one step further than the original NERC draft 
threshold, by requiring a 10 MW minimum size threshold under certain voltage ratings at point of

interconnect. Given that this has already been approved at FERC, there is clear support for

4. If lower thresholds are not restored, then CLS in the 20 MW to 50 MW range
and those connected below 100 kV must be further screened to ensure they do

If necessary, the criteria could allow for sites between 20 MW and 50 MW or below 100 kV to

 EMT models showing detailed risk analysis.


In the interim as EMT modeling of data center risk is being developed, a proxy metric for
risk could be proximity to other CLS. NERC should work with industry to determine a
reasonable threshold for proximity that would indicate that the site seeking waiver does

However, because these EFT models require further refinement to offer value, it is difficult to 
articulate ways to evaluate risk beyond just requiring compliance. We offer this comment insofar 
as we cognizant that the current draft is preferred by some. This does not change our 
preference to require that 20MW serve as the threshold, and therefore that these sites are 
simply beholden to the standards and registered.  

Finally, if no change is made to the thresholds, additional detail (beyond the technical reasoning 
currently provided) around the modeling and inputs used in the decision-making process by 
NERC to justify the change should be made available to all stakeholders and relevant parties. 
This should include model validation and assurance that detailed thought was given to the 
implication of the change on reliability risks, and not just the number of entities impacted.

ISO/RTO Council Standard Review Committee’s Comments 
on Proposed Computational Load Entity ROP Revisions 

September 18, 2026 
The ISO/RTO Council (IRC) Standards Review Committee1 (SRC) offers the following comments on the 
proposed revisions to the NERC Rules of Procedure (ROP) to  define Computational Load and register 
Computational Load Owner (CLO), Computational Load Operators (CLOP), and Computational Load Sites 
(CLS), released on August 19, 2026. The SRC appreciates this opportunity to  provide feedback on  the 
proposed ROP revisions.  

Summary of SRC Comments 

•

Incorporate  clearer  requirements  for  registration  to  address  distributed  Computational  Load
Sites.

• Utilize “and/or” in the enumerated list under Computational Load Site to address potential hybrid

implementations.
Provide examples for entities and scenarios that would require registration.

•
• Complete  CORES  updates  to  enable  notification  to  Distribution  Providers,  Reliability
Coordinators,  Planning  Coordinators,  Transmission  Planners,  and  Transmission  Operators  to
inform them that a CLO/CLOP has notified the RE of the designation.
Formalize criteria for commissioning and interconnection registration requirements that occur
before the CLOP is operational.

•

SRC Comments 

Clearer registration requirements 

The new and revised definitions are necessary to reduce the reliability risks that large computational 
loads pose to the Bulk Power System. The SRC sees value in the inclusion of the 50MW threshold. 

However, the SRC recommends removing the voltage threshold for registration because retaining the 
threshold could: 

• Create confusion among tariff requirements, local state requirements, and others.
•

Prevent the inclusion of distributed (meshed) computational loads that utilize unused electrical
capacity across residential circuits to power discrete nodes at scale, achieving performance and
load sizes analogous to larger, consolidated data centers.

1 For purposes of these comments, the SRC comprises the California Independent System Operator Corporation (California ISO), ISO New England Inc. 
(ISO-NE), PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM), Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., (MISO), New York Independent System Operator, Inc. 
(NYISO), and Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (SPP).   

1 

•

Prevent identification of  distributed networks with a potential for gigawatt-scale load growth
creating risk that could be hidden through jointly defined MW thresholds and defined voltage
levels.

The 50 MW threshold provides a clear delineation for assets that must meet NERC standards and allows 
for the flexibility of the other jurisdictions to manage thresholds for interconnecting.  Alternatively, the 
ROP could utilize a lower interconnection voltage of 60kV, rather than 100kV.   Per NERC’s Technical 
Reasoning2 changing the threshold from 100kV to 60kV would only result in a two percent increase in 
the computational loads identified.  Based on this, setting the threshold to 60kV will not cause additional 
burden on existing computational loads and prevents future computational loads from opting to connect 
at a lower voltage level and bypassing compliance and oversight.  Also, remaining at 60kV aligns with the 
current Category 2 Generator Owners/Operators which ensures NERC registration due to the increasing 
prevalence of inverter-based resources connected at a lower voltage level.  PJM is requesting the same 
oversight and registration as the proliferation of computational loads continues.    

Computational Load Site (CLS) definition 

The currently proposed CLS definition may limit the applicability to a narrower set of resources than 
intended based upon incorrect interpretation to the reference to a “single location.”  As business models 
evolve, the limitation of a single point may obfuscate the actual impact that a distributed resource could 
  These  evolving  applications3  are  demonstrating  a  common  CLOP  controlling  smaller 
have. 
computational  loads,  potentially  in  gigawatts,  that  are  distributed  across  multiple  lower  voltage 
interconnections.    The  net  result  from  the  CLS  is  an  equally  impactful  load  to  frequency.    To  avoid 
excluding materially impactful distributed deployments, replace ‘single location’ with ‘single location or 
served  by  a  single  transmission  bus  or  electrically  contiguous  bus  configuration,’  ensuring  resources 
distributed  across  lower-voltage  interconnections  that  present  aggregate  frequency  impact  are 
appropriately captured. 

The SRC also recommends modifying the list of computational activities associated with a Computational 
Load Site which should use "and/or" instead of "or". As written, it appears a facility could have 20MW 
for cryptocurrency mining and 30MW designated as artificial intelligence training, thus not containing 
50MW of one or the other. This enables hybrid facilities performing multiple tasks to claim the definition 
does not apply to them. Furthermore, the phrase "primarily contains IT infrastructure" is vague for co-
located  sites;  the  drafting  team  should  clarify  how  to  handle  edge  cases,  such  as  a  site  that  is  51% 
generation and 49% data center.  

2 https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/who-we-are/rules-of-procedure/proposed/august-posting-technical-reasoning.pdf 
3 SPAN® Blog | SPAN Announces XFRA, a Distributed Data Center Solution to Close the Speed-to-Power Ga… 

2 

Provide examples and model the Category 2 Generator Owner/Operators process 

Registration Implementation should be modeled after Category 2 Generator Owner (GO) and Generator 
Operator (GOP) registrations with industry outreach and education for these new and existing Registered 
Entities, new NERC Reliability Standards, and new NERC/modified Glossary Terms remains paramount 
to  achieving  the  reliability  objective  of  such  efforts.  It  is  essential  to  publish  numerous  scenarios 
illustrating  Computational  Load  deployments  and  registrations  to  educate  industry  on  how  to  apply 
these  new  criteria.  These  would  include  scenarios  that  identify  configurations  and  deployments  to 
ensure  various  approaches  used  by  industry  would  clearly  define  which  entities  would  need  to  be 
included in the registration process. 

Complete CORES updates 

The  confusion  regarding  registration  has  become  increasingly  apparent,  especially  during  the 
introduction of the new Category 2 GO/GOP functions, where some entities claiming others to serve in 
roles where no formal agreement between both parties exist. This is occurring more frequently as the 
newer  entities  are  registering  with  NERC;  therefore,  declaration  of  the  relationship  to  the  Regional 
Entities during the registration process should include notification reflexively to all entities under such 
declaration to serve in a role under the standards.  For instance, a CLO may declare a certain entity to 
be their Reliability Coordinator (RC).  This creates obligations under the standards to perform certain 
functions or communications that the RC  may not be aware of without notification by NERC  and the 
respective CLO that an entity is claiming to perform its RC function. The declaration of one party alone 
should not be sufficient to create obligations unless all entities affirm their respective functions. 

Formalize criteria for activity before CLO/CLOP operations 

Lastly, upon registration of a CLO/CLOP, the CLO/CLOP must include an affirmation that the CLO/CLOP 
has provided (as requested) the necessary data and information to its host Balancing Authority (BA), 
Transmission Operator (TOP), and Reliability Coordinator (RC).  Coordination between the CLO/CLOP and 
its host BA, TOP, RC is needed prior to registration to ensure reliable operations and compliance to the 
proposed  CLO  Standards.  Nothing  in  the  registration  process  should  preclude  Balancing  Authorities, 
Transmission  Operators,  and  Reliability  Coordinators  from  obtaining  all  necessary  information  and 
adopting additional requirements on computational loads through their own processes.   

Conclusion 

The  SRC  appreciates  the  opportunity  to  comment  on  the  proposed  ROP  revisions.  The  SRC  would 
welcome the opportunity to further discuss these comments or other Computational Load-related topics 
with NERC as appropriate and looks forward to engaging in the remainder of the ROP revision process.

18 September 2026 

Thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback on the draft language to the NERC Rules of Procedures. 

Before articulating the individual comments to the various appendices included within the NERC Rules of Procedure that 
will be updated as a result of this process, we felt it important to outline the principles by which NERC should evaluate 
success in drafting forthcoming reliability standards for large computational users. While these five principles are 
relevant to the drafted ROP language, they also transcend that change and should be applied wherever NERC is 
establishing regulatory, procedural, or policy structures to address and respond to computational load entities. 

Principles for Evaluating NERC Reliability Standard Revisions 
for Large Computational Loads 
1. Forthcoming Reliability Standards (inclusive of the Registry Criteria) must comprehensively address the nature
of the risk that computational loads pose. NERC remains tasked with the singular responsibility of developing,  
implementing, and enforcing reliability standards for computational loads like data centers that pose unique risks to the 
bulk power system. This should be done carefully and comprehensively upfront. Articulating the balance between 
protecting existing systems and fostering an environment of innovation is challenging, yet we are confident that NERC is 
up to the challenge and is poised to develop standards that meaningfully address the unprecedented nature of the risk.  

2. While the need for reliability requirements is undeniable, NERC must ensure that proposed requirements are
robust and fully vetted through the stakeholder process. Despite claims of urgency from both industry and political 
stakeholders, the "need for speed” cannot undermine the imperative for quality. Stakeholders can and consistently have 
demonstrated the ability to adapt; developing comprehensive standards correctly is more important than doing so 
quickly. The NERC staff, stakeholder bodies, and volunteer contributors are working incredibly quickly, and that 
initiative should be lauded. But compromising the quality of the standards to satisfy demands for speed undermines the 
role of NERC as the entity responsible for developing standards to mitigate reliability risks.  

3. First movers in AI data center development must not be rewarded with exemption from forthcoming
requirements. The risk of being an early adopter is just that - higher risk; this remains true across the technological 
innovation spectrum. Technology companies and innovators understand this, and it is not NERC’s responsibility to 
mitigate that risk. Technology companies who had (and have) the capital and appetite to pursue rapid development of 
hyperscale data centers did so with knowledge that there could be forthcoming Reliability Standards. This should not 
grant them exemption from the requirements necessary to protect the reliability of the bulk power system. Weak 
retroactivity provisions or broad exemptions cannot be used to avoid or delay compliance.  

Instead, NERC and ERO-designated entities have clear procedures for updating, revisiting, and evaluating standards in 
response to ongoing and evolving industry needs. If the need arises to evaluate the impact of the standards, such 
processes can be utilized. Codifying legacy exemption or acquired rights does not meaningfully address the concerns 
raised by industry stakeholders about the significant impacts computational loads can have on the bulk power system. To 
manage a period of dramatic change with responsible regulation, NERC must propose universally applicable 
standards. 

4. Greater transparency throughout the standards development process is required for successful, long-term
reliability. Transparency requires clear signposting of standards development to utilities, states, and the broader 
stakeholder community. Many entities including RTOs, state regulatory commissions, and utilities are developing large 
load regulations, tariff provisions, and operational policies while NERC is still developing computational load reliability 

standards. NERC clarity regarding expected standard topics and finalization timelines is critical to enabling regulators, 
policy makers, and asset owners to adapt to eventual NERC regulation quickly and seamlessly. While NERC must not shy 
away from a necessary standard if it diverges from a previously posted roadmap, clear signposting can help 
mitigate friction associated with these concurrent processes.  NERC should also make clear which stakeholders are 
providing what feedback to support a more open and transparent stakeholder process. What NERC is already rolling out 
with public comment period(s), and use of broader communication channels, demonstrates what this can look like in 
practice.  

5. Reliability Standards must support sensible cost allocation. While NERC’s focus for Reliability Standards is–and
must continue to be–ensuring reliability, how reliability standards are set can impact the ability to cleanly allocate costs
associated with risk mitigation to the cost-causers. In plain language, outages cost money, and mitigating the risk imposed
by large loads has a meaningful impact on long-term cost. NERC should focus standards on how large loads can mitigate
their reliability risks, and ensure operational actions that other load and unaffiliated generation can take to mitigate
computational load risk are clearly noted as secondary mitigation strategies.

Utilization of these principles throughout the LLWG and associated processes will ensure that the output of the NERC 
working groups meaningfully and thoroughly addresses and creates responsive guardrails to the nature of the risks posed 
by these system users. To demonstrate the gravity of this effort, an additional 10,979 individual Union of Concerned 
Scientists supporters signed onto these principles to demonstrate the importance of NERC’s role in ensuring that 
standards for large computational loads meaningfully address the risks posed (see attached signatories). 

Comments on Updates to the NERC Rules of Procedure 
We applaud the care of the Large Loads Working Group to treat the inclusion of Computational Loads within the Rules of 
Procedure (ROP) with the gravity it merits, and appreciate the attention being taken to respond to stakeholder concerns 
throughout the process. We spent time reviewing the draft materials and now offer the following for consideration. Our 
comments are organized by Appendix. It’s helpful to note at the onset that three values underpin our comments: clarity, 
consistency with the existing ROP, and reliability as a foundational metric to evaluate appropriateness of the proposed 
changes to the ROP. 

Appendix 2 (Definitions Used in the Rules of Procedure) 
We support the updated definitions in Appendix 2. With regard to the specific definitions: 

“Computational Load Operator” and “Computational Load Owner” are helpful to keep distinct, appreciating that 
there are likely to be many instances where they are distinct actors, though there could be instances where they are the 
same. When we seek to find precedent in the existing NERC Rules of Procedure, we appreciate that this definition retains 
consistency with the definition for Generation Owner and Generation Operator. However, there is departure from 
precedent in that the classification for Generation Owner immediately incorporates a size classification (20 MW and 
connected at a common point of connection greater than or equal to 60 kV). The decision to treat the size threshold for 
Computational Load Sites outside of the actor (CL Operator or CL Owner) creates inconsistency with how this is handled 
within the ROP for generation. We recommend including the size threshold in the definition(s) for both the 
definition of CL Operator and CL Owner for consistent treatment.  

Computational Load Site. The clarity that the new definition offers is incredibly helpful and will ensure that ambiguity 
is mitigated in the compliance and enforcement down the road. However, the introduction of the word “primarily” in the 
term “computational load site” regarding what the site contains could introduce ambiguity. To address this, it may be 
helpful to either expound how “primarily” is measured, or change the language to “the majority of the site’s load consists 
of information technology infrastructure used for…” We recognize that the use of the term “primarily” is common in the 
Rules of Procedure, and so while this may not be something that NERC can address via these comments alone, it should 
be considered in the long-term.  

Appendix 5A (Organization Registration and Certification Manual) 
We support the inclusion of the two entity types (Computational Load Owner and Computational Load Operator) to the 
list of functional entity types to which mandatory and enforceable Reliability Standards apply.  

Appendix 5B (Statement of Compliance Registry Criteria) 

1. The determination of whether a Computational Load Site (CLS) is or is not beholden to the
NERC Reliability Standards must consider more than the size and voltage at interconnection
of the site.
The use of size and voltage at interconnection is a somewhat crude delineation of true risk posed by a CLS (and relatedly, 
from multiple CLS) to the BPS.1 An expanded set of holistic criteria should be used to determine if a CLS should be 
subject to the reliability standards. Such expansion must address the actual electrical behavior of CLS and the risk profile 
they present to the bulk power system. We propose the following characterization schema for criteria registry that builds 
on the Idaho National Lab evaluation of large load risk behavior variables:2 

Load size. Metrics used to define load size should be expanded and include: 

• Minimum absolute amount based on peak demand (not cumulative, can be applicable to only IT equipment).
• Monthly total consumption (cumulative, inclusive of all metered load at Computational Load Site, not just IT

equipment).

Load variability. This could be measured in a number of ways: 

• Maximum ramp rate. For example, the Long Island Power Authority evaluates the amplitude variation at various

•

frequencies and defines an angle under which large load operations must remain.3
Frequency of instances of ramp by category (for example, number of daily instances of ramps exceeding 10
MW/min).

Load flexibility. This should include both technical ability to be flexible, and elective flexibility (i.e., when CLS elect to 
participate in curtailment product offerings within an RTO).  

● Presence of co-located generation. Both the size and the ramping capability of co-located generation should be

considered, as both influence how rapidly a facility could elect to switch power source(s).

● CLO/CLS’ purchase bid mechanism. This metric should evaluate when a CLO elects to participate in, for

example, a price-adaptive power purchase program. In Southwest Power Pool (SPP), the regional grid operator is
currently outlining provisions for a Price Adaptive Load (PAL) scheme that would allow customers to only
procure power through the bulk power system when prices are above or below a certain value.4 The participation
in this type of a program could meaningfully impact the behavior of the facility as it interfaces with the bulk
power system.

2. If a site undergoes significant change (i.e., material modification), the applicability of the
reliability standards must be re-evaluated.
The current language simply reads: “An entity which is not initially placed on the Compliance Registry, but which is 
identified subsequently as having a material impact on the BPS, will be added to the Compliance Registry.” 5 Even clearer

guidance on what constitutes a change significant enough to merit notifying the regional entity should be spelled out. 
This is especially critical given the possibility for certain computational loads to be exempted from the requirements. 

While we feel strongly that there should be no wholesale retroactive exemptions (i.e., no legacy exemptions or 
grandfathering provisions), we recognize that in some past instances, NERC has adopted legacy exemptions for other 
entities as they begin participation in the registry process. However, we submit any exemptions should be (a) time limited 
and (b) designed to account for legitimate logistical constraints that would impede the facility meeting the new standards. 

Further, if exemptions are offered (i.e., legacy exemption or retroactive status provision), then it must be made clear 
when a change to an existing site is sufficient to merit (a) notification of the change, and (b) change in compliance status 
from exempt to no longer exempt.  

The criteria for material modification should include the following. Note that these characteristics are coincident with 
the expanded registry criteria introduced above. 

Any change to load size. Metrics for characterizing change in load size should include at least:  

● A minimum absolute amount, i.e., 10 MW by peak (not cumulative, can be applicable to only IT equipment).
● Change in monthly total consumption (cumulative, inclusive of all metered load at Computational Load Site, not

just IT equipment).

● Change in monthly peak consumption (cumulative, inclusive of all metered load at Computational Load Site, not

just IT equipment).

Change to load variability. This could be measured in a number of ways: 

● Change in maximum ramp rate. As discussed above, the Long Island Power Authority methodology could serve as

a basis for this standard.6

● Changes in frequency of instances of ramp by category (for example, an increase in the number of daily instances

of ramps exceeding 10 MW/min).

Change to load flexibility. This should include both technical ability to be flexible, and elective flexibility (i.e., when CLS 
elect to participate in curtailment product offerings within an RTO). 

● Change to co-located generation assets. Changes to both the size and the ramping capability of co-located

generation should be considered, as both influence how rapidly a facility could elect to switch power source(s).

● Change to a CLO/CLS’ purchase bid mechanism. This should include changes to the bid parameters if the
market mechanism has not changed, and a reassessment of bids if the market mechanism has changed.

3. We do not support the updated threshold size minimums. As long as size alone is being used
to evaluate requirements for site compliance, we suggest a reversion to the original size
threshold for the registry criteria.
Many would argue there is a need for simplicity in reporting which dictates the use of simplified metrics to evaluate the 
risk that a CLS poses to the bulk electric system.7 However, the criteria used to evaluate the true risk of a CLS should be 
expansive to represent the behavioral profile of the load, not just its size, as we argue in (1) above. But we acknowledge 
that when seeking which characteristics offer the most meaningful insight into what degree of risk a CLS introduces, size 
and voltage at interconnection are often the easiest variables to quantify. Therefore, should NERC opt to use simpler 
metrics at the expense of comprehensive metrics, the original threshold of 20 MW and 60 kV should be used for the 
following reasons:  

6 See supra, fn 3.  
7 Characteristics and Risks of Emerging Large Loads, NERC Large Load Task Force, July 2025, 
https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/who-we-are/standing-committees/rstc/whitepaper-characteristics-and-risks-of-emerging-large-
loads.pdf  

1.  Part of the justification for the change to 50 MW and 100 kW was that “unintended entities were included.”8  But 
the number of impacted entities is not a useful metric when considering reliability impacts to the BPS. While the 
August 19th update offered justification for the change based on the number of entities that would or would not 
be affected, this does not meaningfully measure the change in system impact from the revised size and kV threshold 
definition.9  This importance of mitigating risk associated with load size is underscored in the current draft NERC 
white paper, “Large Load Disturbance Performance – Impact Analysis and Ride-Through Recommendations,” in 
which authors acknowledge that: “The capacity of a large load site at its point of interconnection is a direct factor in 
both its BPS impact when a CILR occurs and in the design rigor typically applied to its protection and power 
systems.” 10 

2.  The change to 50 MW and 100 kV introduces a departure from the standards that already exist for generation, 
where 20 MW is the current threshold for standard applicability (see PRC-029).11 As a result, some elements of 
PRC-029-1, such as the defaults for FRT and RoCoF criteria, were extended to large computational loads, while 
other parts of PRC-029-1 were not (i.e., size threshold minimums). The departure from PRC-029 for minimum 
size threshold is as yet unsubstantiated.12 

3.  Because size and voltage at interconnection are such crude determinants of true risk to the system, using more 
conservative thresholds is necessary to protect the integrity and reliability of the bulk power system. Lowering 
the thresholds captures the risk which smaller, lower voltage systems pose to BPS reliability as a function of their 
behavior, even if their size alone does not pose a risk. Thus, a more comprehensive and responsive standard 
reliant on size alone must revert to the 20 MW and 60 kV threshold.  

To further support lower thresholds, we look to the precedent set by Southwest Power Pool, in their recently FERC-
approved definition of High-Impact Large Loads (HILL): “(1) 10 MW or more if connected to the Transmission System at 
a voltage level less than or equal to 69 [kilovolts (kV)]; or (2) 50 MW or more if connected to the Transmission System at a 
voltage level greater than 69 kV.” 13 

SPP’s approved definition therefore goes one step further than the original NERC draft threshold, by requiring a 10 MW 
minimum size threshold under certain voltage ratings at point of interconnect. Given that this has already been approved 
at FERC, there is clear support for more conservative thresholds to mitigate potential risk.  

4. If lower thresholds are not restored, then CLS in the 20 MW to 50 MW range and those 
connected below 100 kV must be further screened to ensure they do not pose meaningful risks.  
If necessary, the criteria could allow for sites between 20 MW and 50 MW or below 100 kV to apply for a waiver if they 
feel they should not be included in the registry. In other words, this would allow the “unintended facilities” to apply for 
exemption. We are supportive of the language spelled out under “Determination of Material Impact” in the Statement of 
Compliance Registry Criteria (Revision 9),” but feel that additional information could be helpful. Examples of the type of 
information that could further be evaluated in the wavier: 

●  EMT models showing detailed risk analysis.

In the interim as EMT modeling of data center risk is being developed, a proxy metric for risk could be proximity

v 

 
 
Summary of Proposed Revisions Posted for Comment 
The following section summarizes the proposed revisions to  the  NERC  Rules of Procedure  posted for comment  from August  19  - September 18, 2026 
regarding registry criteria for computational loads. 

NERC Rules of Procedure Appendix 2 – Definitions Used in the Rules of Procedure 
Appendix 2 to the NERC Rules of Procedure includes defined terms used throughout the Rules of Procedure. The proposed revisions add the following three 
terms: 

•  “Computational Load Operator” means the entity that operates a Computational Load Site. 
•  “Computational Load Owner” means the entity that owns and maintains a Computational Load Site. 
•  “Computational Load Site” means one or more buildings, structures, or installations at a single location that 

1)  Primarily contains information technology infrastructure used for: 

•  creating, executing, and delivering software applications and services;  
•  artificial intelligence training, deployment, and delivery;  
•  cryptocurrency mining; or  
•  other computational activities at a data center; and 

2)  is supplied through electrical equipment that is connected to the BPS. 

NERC Rules of Procedure Appendix 5A – Organization Registration and Certification Manual 
Appendix 5A contains the process used by NERC and the Regional Entities to register certain functional entity types to which mandatory and enforceable 
Reliability Standards apply. The proposed revisions to Appendix 5A add “Computational Load Owner (CLO)” and “Computational Load Operator (CLOP)”as 
types of entities that are required to register on the NERC Compliance Registry. In addition, proposed revisions to Appendix 5A include minor 
administrative corrections. 

NERC Rules of Procedure Appendix 5B – Statement of Compliance Registry Criteria 
Appendix  5B  contains  the  specific  criteria  NERC  and  the  Regional  Entities  use  to  identify  which  organizations  may  be  candidates  for  registration  for 
functional entity types. In accordance with the Federal Power Act, NERC must identify the owners, operators, and users of the Bulk Power System (BPS) 
who have a material impact on the BPS. To that end, the proposed revisions in Appendix 5B add threshold criteria to identify those organizations that 
should be registered as Computational Load Owners and Operators, summarized below: 

•  Computational Load Owner or Operator of a Computational Load Site with a total connected Load greater than or equal to 50 MW that is 

supplied through electrical equipment connected at a voltage level greater than or equal to 100 kV from one or more points of connection.  

Candidates must meet all the criteria in the proposed revisions in Appendix 5B to be registered as a Computational Load Owner or Computational Load 
Operator.

Response  

While the proposed registry criteria provide the generally applicable 
criteria necessary for identifying entities that should be registered as a 
CLO or CLOP, NERC understands that each entity and Computational 
Load Site may have unique characteristics and that entities want to 
understand how the criteria apply in these specific circumstances. NERC 
and the Regional Entities recognize the need for consistency among 
regions and across the continent with respect to which entities are 
subject to registration. To promote this consistency in applying the 
NERC Registry Criteria, the ERO Enterprise develops “Registration 
Reference” documents that provide guidance to ERO Enterprise staff in 
applying criteria to scenarios. NERC will develop a registration reference 
for the CLO and CLOP functions and will update as needed or 
appropriate. Several of the examples provided in the standard drafting 
team’s FAQ document, as well as examples provided in these 
comments, will be considered for inclusion in the reference document.

system to appropriately register the responsible party and to initiate 
contact with compliance staff at NERC and the Regional Entities. NERC 
proactively will seek to reach out to entities to help them start the 
registration process, but NERC encourages possible CLO/CLOP 
candidates, or those who are unsure whether their site may qualify 
them as CLO/CLOP, to engage early with NERC and the Regional Entities 
for the best outcomes. The ERO Enterprise Registration Procedure

campus developments have multiple owners or
