Response  
To that end, there are several mechanisms within the NERC registration 
process available to accommodate these different constructs and 
ensure responsibility for applicable requirements is assigned to the 
appropriate entity or entities, such as Joint Registration Organizations, 
Coordinated Functional Registration, or use of third-party agreements 
to explicitly assign responsibility.  NERC clarifies that a Computational 
Load Site could have multiple CLOs or CLOPs, although the various 
mechanisms described below can help an entity to assign responsibility 
for compliance to one or more entities when there may be tenants or 
multiple owners or operators. 

In Section II of the NERC Registry Criteria Appendix 5B, which includes 
the proposed CLO and CLOP definitions, Footnote 6 reads as follows: 
“Exclusion: An entity will not be registered based on [Section II] criteria 
if responsibilities for compliance with approved NERC Reliability 
Standards or associated Requirements including reporting have been 
transferred by written agreement to another entity that has registered 
for the appropriate function for the transferred responsibilities, 
including bilateral agreements and Sections 501, 507, and 508 of the 
NERC Rules of Procedure.”  

As an example of how this language could apply, an entity that may own 
a Computational Load Site but contracts out its maintenance, and that 
contractor would more appropriately be responsible for the applicable 
requirements, may instead have that contractor register as the CLO of 
the Computational Load Site by demonstrating the responsibility for the 
Reliability Standards requirements has been transferred via a bilateral 
agreement that explicitly transfers such responsibility. Such an 
agreement may also be appropriate for CLOs with tenants who may 
take on the responsibility for all or some of the functional requirements. 

While there may be various types of agreements that achieve the 
intended result, an entity may consider a Joint Registration Organization 
(JRO) relationship (section 507 of the Rules of Procedure) or a 
Coordinated Functional Registration (CFR) relationship (section 508 of

4

the Rules of Procedure). A JRO is when parties agree that a lead entity 
takes full responsibility for a particular function (e.g., Computational

lead entity takes full responsibility for one or more Reliability Standards 
for a particular function. 

These mechanisms and types of acceptable agreements may vary for 
entities depending on facts and circumstances, but Regional Entities 
during the registration process will assist candidate Computational Load 
Owners on the appropriate registration structure for their particular 
circumstance so that the entities on the NERC Compliance Registry are

Commenters questioned the use of “owns and 
maintains” as part of the Computational Load Owner 
definition. Some commented that maintenance and 
operation may be difficult to distinguish in the data 
center context. Others questioned how it applies to 
entities who may own a site, but other entities 
maintain the site or may have the information needed 
to comply with applicable standards. Some suggested 
to remove “and maintains” from the definition. 

NERC acknowledges that the business structures and relationships 
within computational loads are varied or multi-layered and that 
compliance responsibilities should fall on those who have the authority 
or capability to carry them out. However, NERC declines to further 
revise the Computational Load Owner language because commenters 
suggested inclusion of such a function during the first set of comments, 
and the “owns and maintains” language is consistent with other owner 
functions on the NERC Compliance Registry.  

In comments on the April 1st posting, commenters recommended the 
proposed criteria use the same “Owner” and “Operator” Model for 
Computational Loads to remain consistent with the registration criteria 
currently in the NERC Rules of Procedure for Transmission Owner (TO), 
Transmission Operator (TOP), Generator Owner (GO), and Generator 
Operator (GOP). Commenters stated that this structure is in place 
because for Transmission and Generation facilities, there are often 
situations that occur where the owner of the facilities is different from 
the operator of the facilities. This registration criteria structure allows 
the different entities to be responsible only for the activities that they 
are contractually set up for as the owner or operator.  

NERC has been applying the “owns and maintains” language to the 
Transmission Owner and Generator Owner functions, and the various 
organizational structures of those entities, for many years. Accordingly, 
within the NERC registration process, there are mechanisms available to 
help those generation or transmission projects, for example, understand 
which entity should be registered as a Generator Owner or Transmission 
Owner. Under the existing registration construct, entities may wish to 
establish bilateral contracts with other entities to take responsibility for 
the requirements applicable to the GO function, as appropriate. Chapter 
2 of the ERO Enterprise Registration Procedure provides the options for 
a registered entity in using third-party agreements. The ERO Enterprise 
Registration Procedure is available at 
https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/programs/registration/registration-
documentation/ero-enterprise-registration-procedure.pdf.

In the context of computational loads, the Computational Load Owner 
who “owns and maintains” the Computational Load Site helps establish 
that it is intended to be the entity that plays a more active role in 
ownership rather than a passive role. Specifically, the inclusion of 
“maintains” helps better define the role of the entity that will be 
considered as a candidate for registration so that NERC is not registering 
every passive owner with only a small financial interest in a CLS.  

NERC developed Computational Load Owner and Computational Load 
Operator functions based off comments from the first posting that two 
functions better reflected the structure of the industry and who should 
be responsible for applicable requirements.  While entities will need to 
work with Regional Entities to ultimately determine the appropriate 
entity to place on the NERC Compliance Registry, generally speaking a 
CLOP can impact the day-to-day control of the CLS’s electrical 
operations or has communications capabilities with their transmission 
or reliability entities, as appropriate, or both, among other 
considerations as to operations.  
NERC registers entities, not facilities or sites. Accordingly, NERC will 
register an entity that is responsible for the CLO as well as the CLOP 
functions, as appropriate. For phased projects, NERC and the Regional 
Entities will register a CLO and a CLOP as soon as the site, regardless of 
whether there will be future phases, meets the Computational Load Site 
definition and the registry criteria thresholds for that site. Then, should 
that site continue to expand, the CLO and CLOP would not need to 
register again, only update their registration information with the 
Regional Entity. To do so, the CLO and CLOP must notify the Regional 
Entities of changes to its site for compliance purposes or if those 
changes could lead to de-registration or other appropriate changes. 
Once an entity is initially registered as a CLO and CLOP for one site, any 
additional Computational Load Sites only requires the CLO and CLOP to 
notify the Regional Entity of such additions.

Response  
The definition of Computational Load Site provides a list of the types of 
computational activities as well as a “catch all” category intended to 
capture those activities that would be performed at a data center, 
which inherently includes data storage, transmitting/delivering data, or 
data manipulation. The list of activities within the CLS definition 
clarifies that the purpose of the buildings, etc. are for housing IT 
infrastructure used in computational activities, but it is not intended to 
include a server room or building that may be part of a large industrial 
worksite.  

The list of the activities is intended to be illustrative but is not 
exhaustive for every case should a computational activity present an 
impact to the BPS but is not otherwise defined in the list. Further, these 
activities are not treated separately. Any computational type activities, 
including the non-computational ancillary loads (e.g., air conditioning, 
lighting, network switches, etc.), contribute toward the CLS total 
connected Load. In NERC documents, the use of “or” includes “and/or.” 
While several commenters suggest more quantitative measures of how 
much IT infrastructure is part of a site, the use of “primarily” is 
intended to indicate that entities with the infrastructure performing 
computational activities that contribute to the unique impacts to the 
BPS are registration candidates, whereas load that is more industrial or 
manufacturing but may have large IT infrastructure is excluded. NERC 
declines to impose a numerical threshold as that may arbitrarily 
exclude entities with the same reliability impact based on a percentage 
despite the entities performing the same computational activities that 
pose an impact to the BPS.  

NERC does not anticipate the lack of a numerical threshold will indicate 
an issue in defining Computational Load Sites. for instance, the LLWG 
Whitepaper #1 identified that data centers and other computational 
loads’ IT-related equipment that consists of servers, storage, and 
networking gear driven by power electronics, “generally comprise at 
least half of the data center’s energy consumption. Data center 

Consideration of Comments – ROP Appendices 2, 5A, and 5B Revisions (September 2026) 
8 

 
 
 
 
Entity 

Summary of Stakeholder Comments 

Response  
industry experts state that IT-related equipment may make up 60–95% 
of a data center’s total energy demand.” See Whitepaper #1 at page 4, 
https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/who-we-are/standing-
committees/rstc/whitepaper-characteristics-and-risks-of-emerging-
large-loads.pdf. 

Regarding the question on Computational Load Sites co-located with 
generation, the use of “primarily” is not considered in the context of 
on-site generation next to the buildings, structures, or installations at a 
single location. For instance, in the example provided by ERCOT 
regarding the 1,000 MW data center co-located with the 2,000 MW 
generating facility, the buildings, structures, or installations that 
comprise the computational load would be considered in the context of 
the Computational Load Site definition as well as the additional registry 
criteria of the applicable MW and kV thresholds, not the generation 
which could require its owner and operator to register with NERC as a 
Generator Owner or Generator Operator.  

To that end, as entities are registered, the site associated with their 
functions would be considered on a case-by-case basis such that 
Regional Entities reviewing each site would not look to register 
manufacturing facilities or generating facilities that may have certain 
computational equipment that helps run their manufacturing processes 
or generating operations. Rather, the Regional Entities would look to 
whether the buildings, structures, or installations on the site primarily 
contain IT infrastructure, which has been a driver of the unique 
characteristics of computational load with a reliability impact on the 
BPS.

ATC 

NERC developed the Computational Load Site definition in response to 
comments from the first comment period requesting clarity on the site 
boundaries or definition to determine who owned or operated the site 
and how to calculate the total connected Load. While a load site is 
different than generation in many ways, the “single location” concept 
has been used in other regulatory contexts, such as PURPA, where FERC 
may consider certain physical or ownership characteristics of 
generation facilities to determine separate sites for Qualifying Facilities 
purposes. While NERC does not borrow all regulatory concepts from 
PURPA given the distinctions between load sites and generation, NERC 
determined that the use of “single location” in this instance was 
appropriate to convey that the 50 MW was not aggregating possibly 
geographically close but unrelated sites that share CLS characteristics. 
As noted in the standard drafting team’s FAQ document, as part of the 
NERC registration process for CLOs and CLOPs, each Computational 
Load Site will be reviewed based on its specific factors to determine 
applicability. The registration process may consider many factors 
pertaining to the buildings, structures, or installations; including, but 
not limited to ownership, shared or common infrastructure (e.g., 
auxiliary or cooling load), or coordinated use across the information 
technology infrastructure to perform its computational activities. 

In addition, NERC clarifies that single location does not necessarily refer 
to real estate boundaries such as parcels, etc. For example, in the 
standing drafting team FAQ document, it states that it is possible to 
have two or more Computational Load Sites connected to the same 
source equipment because they represent distinct sets of buildings, 
structures, or installations at a single location. In that instance, both 
owners and operators of two Computational Load Sites would be 
subject to registration and be applicable to one or more NERC 
Reliability Standards. In that instance, the two sites could sit on the 
same real estate parcel, but they would be deemed two sites based on 
other operating factors.  

NERC is retaining the existing language as the Computational Load Site 
definition reasonably characterizes one or more buildings, structures,

or installations at a single location as the first condition of registration 
without limiting factors related to land parcel, address assignment, 
roads or rights-of-way, selected site name (e.g., a campus), shared 
utility or other infrastructure, interconnection, etc. Furthermore, while 
NERC appreciates that some commenters may want more specificity in 
the criteria on “single location,” such as the factors NERC may consider 
in determining a Computational Load Site for purposes of identifying 
Computational Load Owners and Computational Load Operators, NERC 
notes that these factors would not be exclusive because of the differing 
site characteristics, ownership structures, topologies, etc. of 
Computational Load Sites. NERC plans to develop a Registration

Commenters requested confirmation that NERC 
intended to use “BPS” and not “BES” and how that 
relates to the exclusion from the BPS of facilities used in 
the local distribution of electric energy. 

BPA 

Under a specific scenario, the commenter suggested 
that some Computational Load Sites would be 
connected to elements excluded from the BES under E1 
or E3. The commenter suggested that the BES should be 
revised to not permit use of E1 or E3 if a Computational 
Load Site is connected to it. 

Response  
NERC confirms its intentional use of the term “BPS” instead of “BES” in 
the proposed Computational Load Site definition. NERC’s reliability 
authority as the ERO under the Federal Power Act extends to all users, 
owners, and operators of the BPS. NERC’s registry criteria identify the 
appropriate users, owners, and operators subject to Reliability 
Standards based on their potential material impact to the BPS. The 
proposed registry criteria are designed to regulate users with an impact 
on BPS reliability and are not designed to regulate users to ensure the 
reliability of local distribution facilities. 

In this instance, the impacts of computational loads as assessed by the 
LLWG and NERC engineering staff are not limited to those solely 
connected to the BES Facilities; rather, as load, the size of the large 
load, unique characteristics of the computational activity, and the 
number of these large loads contribute to the material impact 
identified on the BPS. Accordingly, BES was not an appropriate measure 
for determining which Computational Load Sites would lead to 
registration for entities. Nevertheless, the 50 MW and 100 kV 
thresholds ensure BPS-connected entities are subject to registration 
while excluding entities that have not been seen to negatively impact 
BPS reliability. These thresholds are also intended to remove confusion 
about whether a Computational Load Site is served by what may be 
considered “local distribution”.  

At this time, NERC has not identified a need to revise the Bulk Electric 
System definition. To the extent a need is identified in the future, 
revisions to the BES definition would be considered through NERC’s 
open and transparent standards development process.

Some commenters suggest raising the MW threshold to 
75 MW while some support lowering to 20 MW. Others 
encouraged NERC to consider more than size or voltage. 
Some suggested if no change, additional justification 
beyond the technical reasoning provided be made 
available to stakeholders. Others encouraged NERC to 
continue to monitor how thresholds in regional 
interconnection processes may relate to the NERC 
Reliability Standards. 

Response  

As noted in the response to comments in the first posting and the 
technical reasoning accompanying the second posting, NERC 
determined the 50 MW threshold appropriately addressed the risk 
identified while ensuring smaller, less impactful entities were 
excluded. Based on comments and ongoing analysis during and after 
the April 1-May 15, 2026 posting, NERC was able to refine its 
understanding of the aggregate risks associated with data center sites 
and clusters connected throughout the BPS. Further analysis was 
expanded to sites planned to be operational by the end of 2027. From 
the ongoing and expanded analysis, NERC determined that the 
threshold could be raised to 50 MW (from the first posting’s 20 MW) 
while still addressing the risks. In addition, NERC reviewed Regional 
Transmission Organizations (RTO) and Independent System Operator 
(ISO) definitions of large loads and considered whether those would 
be appropriate for continent-wide reliability purposes. NERC found 
that 50 MW is generally in alignment with some RTO/ISO large load 
definitions.  

The threshold analysis considered available CLS information and their 
association with BPS facilities and encompassed those CLS of the size 
and connected voltage that can create unforeseen and difficult-to-
explain dynamic behaviors impacting the BPS. The analysis further 
determined that CLS less than 50 MW and under 100 kV are generally 
smaller, dispersed across the BPS, and would contribute less aggregate 
risk. While there are locations under 50 MW and 100 kV, these 
locations have not been seen to negatively impact BPS reliability. Also, 
by not including these CLS removes confusion about what may be 
considered being connected to local distribution. NERC will continue to 
monitor the aggregate risks of applicable CLS and reserves the right to 
propose additional ROP Registry Criteria changes in the future to 
address any risks to the BPS. Lastly, NERC further concluded that 
increasing the threshold to 75 MW would decrease the number of CLS 
that are similar in size that have been seen to create unforeseen and

Response  

NERC recognizes that this marks the first instance in which NERC has 
determined to register end users of the BPS for compliance with 
mandatory Reliability Standards. While NERC’s statutory authority 
expressly provides that NERC may register users, owners, and operators 
of the BPS, NERC has not heretofore identified a specific reliability need 
to register end users. The rapid growth of computational end users, the 
unique way in which such end users interact with the BPS, and multiple 
system incidents involving such end users have caused NERC to 
reevaluate. Further, FERC has directed NERC to register such users.  

While the proposed registry criteria itself may not further discuss the 
differences of Load from other existing functional entity types, 
throughout NERC’s Large Load Action Plan, such discussions have 
occurred through various forums and written material. For instance, 
NERC’s Large Loads Working Group (LLWG) Whitepaper #2 discusses 
how existing registered entities cannot address the gaps identified and 
that a new function for Load should be developed. In addition, NERC has 
filed comments in the FERC ANOPR docket discussing that users of the 
BPS have rarely been identified on the NERC compliance registry, but it 
is within NERC’s authority to register users of the BPS and FERC has 
contemplated in the past that a large load could be such a user of the 
BPS.

A commenter suggested revisions to the factors in 
considering materiality in Appendix 5B. Another 
suggested the NERC-led Registration Review Panel 
process to review case-by-case materiality be public. 

Sierra Club 
UCS 

Commenters noted that there should be no wholesale 
retroactive exemptions for in-service units. 

Response  

The assessment of material impact for entities that may either be 
excluded or included from the NERC Compliance Registry is completed 
by a NERC-led Registration Review Panel, which consists of NERC staff 
and Regional Entity staff. Should a panel review such a request, 
decisions are posted on the NERC web site for entities to review, 
providing the necessary level of transparency while protecting 
confidentiality of the materials that may be provided to assess 
materiality. In addition, the non-exclusive factors included in assessing 
materiality are based on certain activities that may or may not be 
applicable to a certain function. These factors help ensure a consistent 
approach to assessing materiality; however, only a sub-set of these 
factors, or other additional factors, may be applicable to a particular 
functional registration category or specific entity. Accordingly, NERC 
declines to further revise Appendix 5B factors that would apply to other 
functions. 
The implementation plans for each Reliability Standard applicable to 
CLO and CLOP provide the timelines when requirements become 
effective and are developed under Project 2026-02 in an open and 
transparent NERC standards development process. As such, the 
standard drafting team can more appropriately address when entities 
would be expected to comply with requirements. However, NERC notes 
that while there may be different timelines for entities depending on in-
service or new loads, there are not planned blanket exceptions for 
entities that are registered as CLO and CLOP based on whether they are 
already in-service. 

Changes in a Computational Load Site that affect an entity’s registration 
status or factors used in its registration determination (e.g., change in 
total connected Load, connection voltage, etc.) are handled through 
Regional Entity processes.

on cost allocation due to the cost of outages. Other 
commenters indicated that the costs of Reliability 
Standards will be at the cost of current customers. 

Response  

NERC recognizes the need for RCs, BAs, and TOPs to coordinate with 
CLOs and CLOPs before and during the registration process. In addition, 
NERC recognizes the impacts of CLO/CLOP registration on the 
compliance obligations for RCs, BAs, and TOPs. As NERC initiates the 
registration process for CLO/CLOP prior to the effective date of 
applicable Reliability Standards, the proposed implementation plans for 
the proposed CLO-001, -002, and -003 Reliability Standards provide the 
timing of associated compliance obligations affecting the new 
registrants and existing registered entities.  
NERC appreciates the recognition of its transparency in stakeholder 
processes and coordination with other regulatory, policy, or reliability-
focused entities while addressing computational loads expediently. 
NERC plans to continue extensive engagement and outreach to 
stakeholders to ensure appropriate entities provide input into any 
future computational load projects. NERC also asserts that any speed 
with which it has moved comports with its regulatory process, and that 
NERC has used its consensus-building processes to develop quality 
products. 
While setting rates and cost allocation are outside of NERC’s purview, 
comments on cost considerations for standards may be submitted to 
any standards development project for consideration in assisting NERC 
to achieve its reliability goal effectively and efficiently, although, 
consistent with FERC Order No. 672, such proposed standards should 
not achieve less than excellence in system reliability solely to protect 
against reasonable expenses for supporting the grid.

For entities that fall below registry criteria, NERC confirms that the 
NERC-led Registration Review Panel under Appendix 5A, Section III(D) 
could assess the materiality of an entity for purposes of registering the 
entity as a CLO or CLOP. While Appendix 5B lists factors for 
consideration in materiality, NERC notes that the factors are non-
exclusive, and the panel could consider the aggregate reliability impact 
of computational load. NERC publicly posts the decisions of the panel. 
NERC can consider whether target timeframes on decisions may be set 
but declines to set timeframes other than those listed in the Rules of 
Procedure at this time. Finally, NERC confirms that an entity may submit 
a request regarding another entity.

Re: Proposed Computational Load Entity Registry 

On behalf of the Industrial Energy Consumers of America (IECA), we urge you not to move 
forward with the proposed Computational Load Entity Registry. Manufacturing self-generation 
units (CHP/WHP) operate as stable, predictable resources that do not present the reliability 
risks this proposal is intended to address. There is no evidence to suggest that these units are a 
threat to the grid.   

The proposed rule is intended to address reliability gaps associated with emerging 
computational loads but does not identify a demonstrated reliability gap for CHP/WHP 
resources. We are not data centers. We do not operate like data centers and we should not be 
treated like them under contemplated regulations.  

The proposed criteria appropriately focus on large, high-density computational loads 
comprised of information technology equipment with distinctive and less predictable electrical 
behavior, which is not characteristic of CHP/WHP facilities driven by thermal and industrial 
processes. Unlike computational loads, which can fluctuate rapidly, CHP/WHP units are 
thermal-following and operate with stable, continuous output that supports grid stability. 
Industrial facilities typically fall within conventional load profiles and may only include de 
minimis levels of information technology equipment, consistent with NERC’s distinction based 
on differing electrical behavior. The proposed changes unnecessarily increase our costs and 
economic and regulatory uncertainty.  

One hundred percent of IECA’s members are manufacturing companies from every industry. 
Many of these companies have been generating their own power and steam since the late 
1970s, using CHP and/or heat to power systems.      

According to EIA there are over 900 CHP units across the U.S. that have a rated capacity of 
about 60,000 MW. They have operated successfully day and night without any negative impacts 
to grid reliability. Some of them provide valuable balancing benefits to the grid by producing 
less at night and buying power from the grid when demand by other sectors are low. This 
predictable behavior supports grid balancing and supports frequency stability through 
continuous operation that differs fundamentally from the volatility of data center loads.  

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Page 2 
Industrial Energy Consumers of America 

Importantly, some of these units have a history of being called upon to provide power in times 
of power shortages, thereby supporting grid reliability.     

Existing NERC reliability standards and interconnection requirements, including FAC-001 and 
FAC-002, already provide appropriate oversight and study requirements for industrial facilities 
and their interaction with the Bulk Power System. No additional regulatory gap has been 
identified that would justify expanding registration to CHP/WHP under a new functional entity 
classification. 

We are a resource and we look forward to working with you to help ensure any new registry is 
appropriately scoped to address emerging, high-variability computational loads while avoiding 
unintended inclusion of stable, conventional industrial generation. 

Sincerely, 

Paul N. Cicio 
Paul N. Cicio 
President & CEO

ELECTRICITY CUSTOMER ALLIANCE 

To: 

North American Electricity Reliability Council 
ROPComments@nerc.com  

Re: 

Comments on Proposed Computational Load Entity Rules of Procedure Revisions 

The Electricity Customer Alliance (ECA), on behalf of itself and the undersigned customer groups, is 
pleased to submit comments on NERC’s proposed changes to its Rules of Procedure to create a new 
functional entity type, called “Computational Load Entity”, and deﬁne the criteria that will require 
such entities to register with NERC and comply with current or future mandatory and enforceable 
Reliability Standards. ECA appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and the efforts that 
NERC and its staff have made to engage with customers through the course of its analysis of the 
impacts of emerging large loads on bulk power system reliability. For the reasons discussed below, 
ECA asks that NERC decline to move forward with the proposal at this time and instead 
conduct further examination of the most cost-effective and efﬁcient means of addressing the 
reliability risks it has identiﬁed with respect to emerging large loads. 

ECA is a growing national coalition dedicated to advancing customer-centric solutions that 
modernize the grid, support economic growth and the development of digital infrastructure and 
advanced manufacturing, and keep electricity affordable and reliable for all users. Members and 
participants in ECA include a diverse range of customers and customer groups, from large 
customers in the technology, industrial, and manufacturing segments, to smaller commercial 
customers and residential ratepayer advocates. ECA works to elevate customer perspectives and 
coalesce and align customer segments to identify and advance common ground approaches to the 
challenges of load growth, grid expansion and modernization, electricity market governance and 
accountability, and rising electricity affordability concerns.  

Creating the proposed new functional entity type, “Computational Load Entity,” would mark a 
dramatic departure from historic practice by, for the ﬁrst time, subjecting end use customers to 
mandatory and enforceable reliability standards. To date, the mandatory and enforceable reliability 
standards framework has focused on the planning and operational activities of entities that generate, 
transmit, or deliver electricity to end use customers to ensure that these activities support reliable 
operation of the bulk power system. This includes, among other things, planning, operational 
practices, communications, training, and system protection standards that these entities must 
individually and collectively perform to ensure reliable operations in accordance with the 
requirements of Section 215 of the Federal Power Act. In short, the existing reliability standards 
framework is focused on the entities that have operational control of the bulk power system and that 
regularly engage in coordinated planning and communications protocols to ensure reliable 
operations. 

Page 1 of 4 
www.electricitycustomers.com 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
ELECTRICITY CUSTOMER ALLIANCE 

NERC has not demonstrated why bringing end use customers into this framework for the ﬁrst time 
would be the most effective and efﬁcient means of solving the emerging reliability challenges it has 
identiﬁed. NERC’s Large Load Working Group (LLWG) has found that emerging large loads (which it 
proposes to deﬁne as “Computational Loads” like data centers or cryptocurrency operations) may 
pose certain new risks to reliable operations, including operational risks from sudden load drops, 
ramping characteristics, and inability to ride through disturbances. In addition, the LLWG identiﬁed 
gaps in existing reliability standards and requirements that do not account for the unique 
characteristics of these emerging loads, such as planning and interconnection obligations and 
modeling and study requirements. With respect to large load interconnection processes, the LLWG 
identiﬁed the lack of consistent interconnection requirements among current registered entities to 
ensure the identiﬁcation of potential impacts to the bulk power system, such as requirements related 
to voltage/frequency disturbance ride-through, sensitive protection settings, ramping, power quality, 
and oscillation. The LLTF also noted gaps in the assignment of responsibility among existing 
registered entities for assessing and mitigating these potential risks.  

NERC has not fully explained why an unprecedented expansion of registration requirements to end 
use customers is the most effective strategy for ﬁlling these gaps in requirements and assignments of 
responsibility. The LLTF’s gap assessment’s ﬁrst recommendation notes that “[t]here are multiple 
high-impact risks to the [bulk power system] from large loads that NERC registered entities cannot 
adequately address,” a statement followed by a stark conclusion that NERC should “pursue 
registration of a type of entity (or types of entities) that is able to perform speciﬁc functions to 
address the risks.”1 NERC repeats this conclusion in the “Technical Reasoning” document 
accompanying the proposed revisions to the Rules of Operating Procedure, stating that “[d]ue to the 
number of existing and anticipated large loads needing power to support computational processes 
and the unforeseen and difﬁcult-to-explain dynamic electrical behavior of these users of the [bulk 
power system] as identiﬁed by the LLWG, NERC determined that it was appropriate to propose a 
new functional entity type that focuses on loads with these characteristics.”2 

These broad statements do not answer the fundamental question of why existing NERC registered 
entities could not adequately address these impacts with changes to the existing reliability 
standards, or the development of new reliability standards, to ﬁll the information, modeling, study, 
and operational coordination gaps that have been identiﬁed. The two Large Load Task Force (LLTF) 
white papers that form the basis for the recommendation to create a new functional entity, and the 

1 NERC, “Assessment of Gaps in Existing Practices, Requirements, and Reliability Standards for Emerging Large 
Loads: NERC Large Loads Working Group White Paper” at 53 (March 2026), available at 
https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/our-work/guidelines/reliability/white-paper---assessment-of-gaps.pdf. 
2 NERC, “Technical Reasoning: Proposed Computational Load Entity” at 2 (April 2, 2026), available at 
https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/who-we-are/rules-of-procedure/proposed/cle-technical-reasoning-april-
2026-posting.pdf. 

Page 2 of 4 
www.electricitycustomers.com 

 
 
 
 
 
 
ELECTRICITY CUSTOMER ALLIANCE 

other available evidence, including the two industry alerts NERC has issued urging existing 
registered entities to take additional steps to address large load impacts, likewise do not answer this 
question.   

This fundamental question should be answered before taking the unprecedented step of expanding 
the universe of registered entities beyond those with direct operational control of the bulk power 
system. Adding end use customers to the NERC registry and the framework of mandatory and 
enforceable reliability standards would add new complexities to the compliance regime and could 
create unintended consequences for that regime. For example, end use customers do not have the 
same operational control over the bulk power system or visibility into operations that existing 
registered entities possess, nor are they integrated into the communications and protocols that have 
long existed between these entities. These realities will likely create added complications for end use 
customers in complying implementing operational controls in real-time when compared to existing 
registered entities. In addition, integrating an entirely new set of registered entities for the ﬁrst time 
could result in new process or analysis gaps or require new modes of communication, requiring 
additional work that could detract from or stall progress in addressing the emergent reliability 
concerns identiﬁed by the LLWG. Moreover, deﬂecting a subset of reliability obligations to end use 
customers instead of the entities with direct bulk power system operational control could fragment 
and weaken existing accountability structures. 

Reforming the existing reliability standards or developing new standards to ﬁll the information, 
modeling, study, and operational coordination gaps that have been identiﬁed would not mean that 
emerging large loads are free of any responsibility for contributing to the reliable operation of the 
bulk power system. Load interconnection requirements and communication protocols implemented 
by registered entities would place appropriate obligations on those large load customers while 
retaining the focus of the NERC standards framework on those entities who have direct operational 
control of the bulk power system. The difﬁculty of deﬁning “Computational Loads” and the fact that 
customer loads are not a monolith and have different operational proﬁles and potential grid impacts, 
both of which NERC has acknowledged, makes it all the more appropriate to focus on 
interconnection requirements implemented through existing registered entities rather than 
expanding the registered entities that must be involved.     

In addition, before taking such a signiﬁcant step to expand the universe of registered entities, NERC 
should solicit the views of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), states, and other key 
policymakers, and engage them in further examination of the most effective approach to address the 
identiﬁed reliability risks. FERC is ultimately responsible for implementation of the mandatory 
reliability standards framework envisioned by Congress in Section 215 of the Federal Power Act, 
including determining the jurisdictional reach of Section 215 to “users, owners and operators of 
the bulk-power system.” NERC’s proposed criteria directly implicate jurisdictional questions, 
particularly its proposal to apply registration requirements based on aggregated load at a single 

Page 3 of 4 
www.electricitycustomers.com 

 
 
 
 
 
ELECTRICITY CUSTOMER ALLIANCE 

point of interconnection at a voltage of 60 kV or higher, which is above the 100 kV threshold for 
determination of bulk power system facilities. FERC guidance on these questions before taking 
additional steps to extend the NERC compliance framework well beyond where it has been 
historically, and beginning the process of placing the obligations of that framework on end-use 
customers, is critical. Moreover, other federal and state policymakers likely have views on the efﬁcacy 
of such a change and how it could impact consumer costs. Additional process (perhaps convened by 
FERC) is important to transparently address these issues before moving forward.         

Finally, while NERC has identiﬁed important reliability considerations of emerging large loads that 
require immediate attention, it is not clear that expanding the universe of registered entities is 
necessary on the aggressive schedule NERC is pursuing. We understand that the initial reliability 
standards developed under the draft Standards Authorization Request issued in April will not apply 
to the proposed new Computational Load Entities. In addition, the Level 2 and 3 Alerts that NERC 
has issued in the past several months have identiﬁed important steps that existing registered entities 
should take now to address emergent reliability concerns identiﬁed by the LLWG. As a result, there is 
ample time to engage in additional examination and fact ﬁnding before ﬁnalizing a decision on 
registration of Computational Load Entities.   

For these reasons, we urge NERC to reconsider adding additional registered entities at this time and 
instead examine whether reforming existing standards and the responsibilities placed on existing 
registered entities would be a more effective and efﬁcient approach to address the identiﬁed gaps. 
We look forward to further engaging with NERC and stakeholders on these important reliability 
issues.   

Sincerely, 

Electricity Customer Alliance (ECA) 
Electricity Consumers Resource Council (ELCON) 
Industrial Energy Consumers of America (IECA)

American Electrics Power Comments on Proposed Revisions to 
NERC Rules of Procedure for Computational Load 
American Electric Power (AEP) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed 
revisions to the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) Rules of Procedure 
(ROP) related to Computational Load. AEP supports NERC’s objective of protecting the 
Bulk Power System (BPS) from reliability risks associated with large Computational Loads 
and understands the need to develop registration criteria for owners and operators of 
Computational Load. 

AEP offers the following comments and recommended modifications to help ensure the 
proposed changes are clear, consistent with existing NERC registration models, and 
appropriately focused on Computational Loads that pose a material risk to BPS reliability. 

AEP Proposes the Following Modifications: 

Appendix 2 (Definitions Used in the Rules of Procedure) 

1.  Addition of New Definition Computational Load Facility (CLF) 

AEP supports the Trade Associations’ recommendation to add a new definition 
Computational Load Facility (CLF):  

“Computational Load Facility” means a collection of electrical equipment located 
at one or more buildings, structures, or installations that is designed to receive 
power, has an aggregate connected maximum peak demand of Computational Load 
greater than or equal to 75 MW, and is served through electric facilities at a voltage 
level greater than or equal to 100 kV from one or more points of connection. 

A clear definition of a Computational Load Facility is essential to the success of Project 
2026-02. Existing Standards that address similar types of essential actions being proposed 
for data centers but are applicable to other comparable equipment (like generators) 
consistently rely on a Facility-type definition. This is consistent with how Generator 
Owner/Operator and Generating Facility are treated, defined, and included in the 
registration criteria. 

2.  AEP agrees with the Trade Associations’ recommendation to replace CL Entity (CLE) 

with CL Operator (CLOP) and CL Owner (CLO): 

“Computational Load Owner” means the end-user entity that owns and maintains a 
Computational Load Facility, and/or the entity that owns and maintains a Computational 
Load Facility that hosts end-users that receive electric power at a Computational Load 
Facility. 

Page 1 of 3 

 
 
 
 
“Computational Load Operator” means the end-user entity that operates a 
Computational Load Facility, and/or the entity that operates a Computational Load Facility 
that hosts end-users that receive electric power at a Computational Load Facility. 

AEP recommends the same “Owner” and “Operator” Model for Computational Loads to 
remain consistent with the registration criteria currently in the NERC Rules of Procedure for 
Transmission Owner (TO), Transmission Operator (TOP), Generator Owner (GO), and 
Generator Operator (GOP). This structure is in place because for Transmission and 
Generation facilities, there are often situations that occur where the owner of the facilities 
is different from the operator of the facilities. This registration criteria structure allows the 
different entities to be responsible only for the activities that they are contractually set up 
for as the owner and/or operator.  

3.  AEP supports the Trade Associations’ recommendation to clarify the Computational 

Load (CL) definition: 

“Computational Load” means Load comprised primarily of electric power demand from 
power electronic-based information technology equipment.  

Appendix 5A (Organization Registration and Certification Manual) 

4.  As discussed in Comment 2 above, AEP agrees with the Trade Associations’ 

recommendation to replace CL Entity (CLE) with CL Operator (CLOP) and CL Owner 
(CLO) to align with existing NERC Owner/Operator registration frameworks. 

Appendix 5B (Statement of Compliance Registry Criteria) 

5.  AEP supports the Trade Associations’ recommendation to either (a) increase the 

proposed Computational Load thresholds or (b) pursue an approach comparable to the 
Category 1/Category 2 registration structure currently used for Generation. 

a.  Increase Computational Load Threshold  

AEP recommends that NERC increase the proposed thresholds from 20 MW and 60 
kV to 75 MW and 100 kV for Computational Load Facilities and eliminate the 1MW 
Computational Load criterion.  

The proposed thresholds are set unnecessarily low and would result in the 
registration of a substantial number of facilities that do not pose a material risk to 
the reliability of the Bulk Power System (BPS) and, thus, do not justify the burden of 
NERC registration. The current Rules of Procedure, Registration Criteria, and 
Standard Drafting efforts related to Computational Loads should focus on those 
loads that pose the most meaningful risk to the BPS. 

Page 2 of 3 

 
 
 
 
Accordingly, AEP recommends establishing a threshold of greater than or equal to 
75 MW connected at greater than or equal to 100 kV for Computational Load 
Facilities and elimination the 1MW Computational Load criterion. 

b.  Category 1/Category 2 Registration Approach 

NERC should pursue a Category 1/Category 2 approach for Computational Loads. 

If a threshold lower than 75 MW is deemed necessary, AEP recommends that NERC 
enhance the Technical Reasoning document to reflect the analysis and supporting 
evidence demonstrating the need for the lower facility threshold for BPS reliability. 
In addition, AEP recommends that NERC adopt the same registration criteria model 
that was developed for Inverter-Based Resources (IBRs) with the Category 1 
GO/GOP and establish a new Category 1 and Category 2 structure with the 
proposed definitions: 

•  “Computational Load Facility” means a collection of electrical equipment 
located at one or more buildings, structures, or installations that is designed 
to receive power, is served through electric facilities from one or more points 
of connection and meets the criteria in either Category 1 or Category 2 
Computational Load Owner/Operator registration categories. 

•  “Category 1 CLO/CLOP” should be aligned with the BES criteria, which 
would be entities who own/operate Computational Load Facilities (CLFs) 
that are greater than or equal to 75 MW of Computational Load connected 
at greater than or equal to 100 kV. 

•  “Category 2 CLO/CLOP” should be aligned with the lower threshold value 
supported by NERC and industry, which would be entities who own/operate 
Computational Load Facilities that are greater than or equal to 20 MW of 
Computational Load connected at greater than or equal to 60 kV. 

This structure would allow the Electric Reliability Organization enterprise to focus its 
initial entity registration, Standards Development efforts, and compliance education 
activities on the highest-risk CLOs/CLOPs first. This framework also establishes a more 
manageable path to subsequently address lower-risk Category 2 CLOs/CLOPs in future 
work phases.

NERC Rules of Procedure Team —

AIONTRACKS, Inc. respectfully submits the following comments on the proposed Rules of 
Procedure changes establishing the Computational Load Entity (CLE) functional entity type 
and the registration criteria in proposed Appendix 5B.

Comment 1 — The proposed registration criteria are well-calibrated for the threshold class.

The proposed criteria — aggregate connected load capability ≥ 20 MW at a single point of 
interconnection at ≥ 60 kV, hosting ≥ 1 MW of computational load-appear well-aligned with 
the BPS-impact threshold for which mandatory Reliability Standards are appropriate. 
AIONTRACKS supports the proposed thresholds.

Comment 2 — The criteria may benefit from a class of-service descriptor captured at 
registration.

Computational loads vary substantially in workload composition. A facility hosting 
predominantly artificial intelligence training workloads has materially different electrical and 
operational characteristics from facility hosting predominantly inference workloads, or from a 
mixed-workload facility. The class of service hosted at the facility affects both the demand 
profile under normal conditions and the response capability during
disturbances. NERC may wish to consider whether the registration form should capture a 
class-of-service descriptor (e.g., training-dominant, inference-dominant, mixed, batch-
dominant, or other) to support downstream standard application and audit. Capturing this 
information at registration imposes minimal burden on the registrant and provides NERC and 
the Regional Entities with material context for compliance review.

Comment 3 — The criteria should anticipate facilities hosting computational loads on behalf 
of multiple end-users.

Some computational load facilities operate as multi-tenant infrastructure, hosting 
computational workloads on behalf of multiple end-user customers under contractual 
arrangements. The proposed criterion that the CLE must be "the end-user or the entity that 
hosts end-users that receives electric power" appropriately captures this case, but NERC may 
wish to clarify in
guidance whether the multi-tenant facility operator is the registered CLE or whether each end-
user is registered separately. Clarification of this point will reduce registration ambiguity for 
the operator class likely to host the largest aggregate computational load.

AIONTRACKS appreciates the opportunity to comment and offers to serve as a technical 
resource to NERC staff in finalizing the registration criteria.

Respectfully,

Re:  Comments of Alphataraxia on Proposed Revisions to NERC Rules of Procedure Appendices 2, 5A, and 5B 
(Computational Load Entity Registry Criteria) 

Dear NERC Staff: 

Alphataraxia Management LP (“ATX”) submits these comments on NERC’s April 1, 2026 posting of proposed 
revisions establishing a “Computational Load Entity” (“CLE”) functional entity type. ATX is engaged in energy 
trading in domestic ISO/RTO markets and, as a wholesale market participant, has a direct interest in the 
accuracy of load data and planning models that underpin locational marginal prices, congestion revenue rights, 
and reserve margin determinations. Accurate classification and registration of computational loads is not merely 
a technical compliance matter—as large-scale data center and AI infrastructure loads increasingly stress 
transmission systems and distort reserve margin calculations, failures to properly account for their magnitude 
and consumption profiles risk cascading reliability events that ultimately harm end-use consumers through price 
volatility, inadequate capacity procurement, and, in the most severe cases, supply shortfalls.  ATX supports the 
CLE initiative and submits these comments to urge NERC to require, as a registration condition, transparency 
about load qualification criteria and disclosure of historical consumption data. 

I.  Background 

In September 2025, NERC issued its Level 2 Industry Recommendation on Large Load Interconnection, Study, 
Commissioning, and Operations. The Level 2 Alert responded to a series of grid disturbances in which more than 
1,000 MW of large-load output was unexpectedly reduced across multiple events in 2024 and 2025. NERC’s 
Aggregated Report on the Level 2 Alert responses (the “Aggregated Report”) identified a central, recurring 
deficiency: load data for large commercial and industrial customers is “often incomplete, aggregated, or lacks 
necessary granularity, such as hourly or daily usage trends for use in short-term load forecasting.” The LLWG’s 
March 2026 white paper confirmed that existing Reliability Standards and industry processes are inadequate for 
reliable large load integration. The proposed registry criteria represent the correct structural location to address 
this deficiency—before downstream standards development locks out a data-first approach. 

II.  Historical Consumption Data Must Be a Registration Condition 

NERC has recognized that computational loads can exhibit electrical behavior that is “distinctive and often less 
predictable than conventional loads.” The Aggregated Report confirmed that forward-looking projections 
submitted at interconnection bore little resemblance to actual operational profiles. AI training and high-

1911 N. Fort Myer Dr., Suite 800, Arlington VA 22209 | P:571.207.8399 | F:571.482.6999 | www.alphataraxia.com 

 
 
 
 
 
performance compute workloads have been specifically identified as among the load types most likely to 
introduce forced oscillations into the grid. 

ATX recommends that the criteria require CLEs, as a condition of initial registration, to commit to submitting 
metered consumption data at hourly intervals, including observed peak demand, minimum demand, and 
average load factor. For newly commissioned facilities, the most complete available observed data plus a 
validated dynamic load model should be required, as well as a commitment to post metered consumption data 
to a nationwide database that is publicly available.  Public posting of such data has huge value.  There is already 
a nationwide database for generators posted by the US Energy Information Administration (available at 
https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data.php), which has supported significant analysis and research; a similar 
database for CLEs would add immense value to research into reliability and optimization. 

III.  Load Modeling and Market Integrity Require Actual Consumption Data 

Level 2 Alert Recommendation 5 directed Transmission Planners, Resource Planners, and Planning Coordinators 
to incorporate large loads into near-term and long-term demand forecasts, accounting for intra-minute 
variability, cyclical ramping, and aggregate load disconnections during contingencies. That recommendation 
presupposes access to actual consumption data. Without it, the planning models that underpin wholesale 
market prices in PJM, MISO, SPP, and ERCOT will continue to degrade in accuracy as CLE penetration grows. 

When load models do not reflect actual CLE consumption profiles, the resulting distortions affect locational 
marginal prices, create unanticipated transmission congestion, and affect the financial settlement of FTRs and 
virtual transactions. ATX accordingly recommends that the criteria explicitly require CLEs to provide historical 
consumption data to a nationwide database. 

IV.  Transparent Qualification Criteria Are Necessary to Prevent Registration Arbitrage 

Opaque CLE qualification criteria create incentives for registration arbitrage. Entities with borderline facilities, 
like data centers co-located with conventional operations, multi-metering-point campuses, or facilities with 
significant on-site backup generation, have incentives to structure their operations to minimize reported 
interconnection load and avoid registration, reducing compliance costs while continuing to affect grid 
conditions. NERC should publish detailed guidance on how the 20 MW aggregate connected load threshold is 
measured across shared substations, co-located generation, and mixed-use facilities, and how “single point of 
interconnection” is applied to campus configurations. Consistent, data-grounded application across all Regional 
Entities is essential to preventing regulatory gaps and preserving the competitive integrity of wholesale markets. 

As data centers are projected to be more than 10% of total U.S. electricity consumption by 2028, the aggregate 
market impact of unmodeled or under-modeled CLE consumption will be substantial. Wholesale market 
participants that hold financial transmission rights and manage load-serving obligations in CLE-concentrated 
load zones are entitled to rely on planning models that reflect actual CLE consumption behavior. 

V.  Conclusion 

1911 N. Fort Myer Dr., Suite 800, Arlington VA 22209 | P:571.207.8399 | F:571.482.6999 | www.alphataraxia.com 

 
 
 
ATX urges NERC to strengthen the proposed CLE registry criteria by incorporating the idea of a nationwide 
database of CLEs.  In particular, (i) requiring submission of consumption data at hourly intervals; (ii) defining load 
qualification criteria with sufficient specificity to enable consistent Regional Entity application and prevent 
registration arbitrage; and (iii) explicitly requiring that historical consumption data flow be provided so that it 
can be posted publicly (ideally, in a national database) so as to allow Transmission Planners, Planning 
Coordinators, Balancing Authorities, and RTOs/ISOs to incorporate into planning models. These measures are 
necessary to give practical effect to the Aggregated Report’s findings, to enable existing registered entities to 
fulfill their planning standards obligations, and to preserve the competitive integrity of the wholesale markets 
NERC’s reliability framework supports.

Ameren comments on the NERC Proposed Computational Load Entity ROP Revisions 

Ameren agrees with EEI's comments on the revisions. 

May 15, 2026 

North American Electric Reliability Corporation 
Rules of Procedure Comments 

Via Electronic Submission: ROPcomments@nerc.net 

Re: Comments on Proposed Revisions to NERC Rules of Procedure — Computational Load Entity 
(Appendices 2, 5A, and 5B) 

I. Introduction 

Arevon Energy, Inc. (Arevon) appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the proposed revisions 
to the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) Rules of Procedure (“RoP”) establishing a 
new Computational Load Entity (“CLE”) functional category and associated registration criteria in 
Appendices 2, 5A, and 5B. These comments are submitted in response to NERC’s April 1, 2026 posting 
and the 45-day public comment period closing May 15, 2026. 

Arevon recognizes that emerging large computational loads — including data centers, AI compute 
clusters, and cryptocurrency mining facilities — present genuine reliability challenges that require 
proactive action. While NERC’s Large Loads Action Plan objectives are valid, we urge NERC to reﬁne the 
proposed RoP revisions to ensure that (1) deﬁnitions are precise and risk-calibrated, (2) registration 
thresholds capture only those entities whose behavior drives the identiﬁed reliability risks, (3) the 
obligations that follow registration are proportionate and appropriately assigned, and (4) the 
implementation timeline is realistic for entities that are entirely new to NERC’s compliance framework. 

The comments included in this document are organized into four sections: Appendix 2 (Deﬁnitions), 
Appendix 5A (Registration Process), Appendix 5B (Registry Criteria), and Cross-Cutting Process and 
Implementation Considerations. 

II. Appendix 2 — Deﬁnitions Used in the Rules of 
Procedure 

A. The Proposed “Computational Load” Deﬁnition Requires Greater 
Precision 

As proposed, “Computational Load means Load comprised of electric power demand from information 
technology equipment, such as servers, storage, and networking hardware.” While we agree with NERC 
staﬀ that a term other than “Large Load” is appropriate — since “Large Load” can connote many 
diﬀerent types of loads on the Bulk Power System (“BPS”), such as large process facilities, education and 
medical campuses, pharmaceutical loads, and manufacturing loads — the proposed deﬁnition 
introduces several ambiguities that should be resolved before adoption. 

Page 1 of 10 

1. The phrase “such as” is non-inclusive and open-ended. It creates uncertainty about what equipment 
falls within scope. Virtually all BPS-connected facilities may contain some information technology 
equipment (PLCs, RTUs, SCADA systems, routers, personal computers). Without a clear, inclusive list or a 
quantitative threshold tied to the proportion of IT-related demand, the deﬁnition risks capturing facilities 
that were never the intended subject of NERC’s Large Load Action Plan. NERC should replace “such as” 
with “including, but not limited to” or provide a closed-form deﬁnition anchored to the types of facilities 
actually driving reliability risk (data centers, AI compute clusters, cryptocurrency mining). 

2. “Storage” should be amended to “data storage.” As drafted, “storage” is ambiguous and could be 
interpreted to include Battery Energy Storage Systems (“BESS”), which are separately governed under 
existing NERC registration criteria for inverter-based resources. The intent is clearly to reference Network 
Attached Storage (“NAS”), Hard Disk Drives (“HDDs”), and Solid-State Drives (“SSDs”). This clariﬁcation is 
essential to avoid unintended overlap with generation-side registration criteria. 

3. The term “Computational” may be too narrow. Some referenced equipment — particularly 
networking hardware — has minimal computational capability compared to CPUs and GPUs. As power 
electronic equipment (e.g., solid-state transformers) is deployed at customer sites, the deﬁnition may 
become even more misaligned with the actual risk drivers. NERC should consider a broader term such as 
“Electronic Load,” consistent with ERCOT’s adoption of “Large Electronic Load” in NPRR 1308, which 
extends beyond purely computational activities and better captures the full spectrum of loads driving 
the identiﬁed reliability risks. 

B. The Deﬁnition Excludes Non-IT Large Loads with Identical Reliability 
Risks 

The proposed deﬁnition captures only loads from information technology equipment. Yet NERC’s own 
Large Loads Working Group (“LLWG”) reports identify hydrogen electrolyzers, industrial heat pumps, 
advanced manufacturing facilities, and other energy-intensive loads as posing identical reliability risks — 
rapid demand changes, voltage sensitivity, and forecasting diﬃculty. 

By limiting the deﬁnition to “information technology equipment,” NERC would need to repeat the entire 
RoP revision process when these load types reach scale — delaying the reliability protections that the 
Large Loads Action Plan was designed to deliver. NERC should either broaden the deﬁnition now to 
encompass all large loads exhibiting the identiﬁed risk behaviors, or explain in its technical reasoning 
why the identiﬁed reliability risks are unique to computational equipment and do not apply to other 
emerging large loads. 

C. The “Computational Load Entity” Deﬁnition Has Structural 
Ambiguities 

As proposed, “Computational Load Entity means the end-user or the entity that hosts end-users that 
receives electric power for Computational Load.” This deﬁnition raises several structural concerns: 

Page 2 of 10 

1. Owner/Operator Distinction. NERC’s existing registration framework distinguishes between owners 
and operators (e.g., GO/GOP, TO/TOP). Many computational load facilities will have separate ownership 
and operating structures — particularly in the colocation and multi-tenant data center market. The 
proposed single “Computational Load Entity” functional type does not accommodate this reality and 
should adopt a parallel Owner/Operator structure (e.g., CLO/CLOP) to properly assign diﬀerentiated 
reliability responsibilities. 

2. Ambiguity in “end-user or the entity that hosts end-users.” Where both an end-user and a hosting 
entity exist at a single facility, the deﬁnition does not clarify which party bears registration obligations — 
or whether both must register. This is a critical gap given the prevalence of colocation and multi-tenant 
data center arrangements. 

3. Potential Third-Party Registration Obligations. The use of “end-user” could introduce lessee or tenant 
entities as separately registrable parties, creating a three-tier registration structure (owner, operator, 
tenant) that is unprecedented in NERC’s framework and operationally unworkable without further 
guidance. NERC should clarify whether registration follows facility ownership, operational control, or 
electrical metering boundaries. For example, if Company A and Company B lease a warehouse owned by 
Company C that hosts the equipment creating the demand for electricity (load), who should register? 
Company A, B, or C or all of them? There could be several permutations and combinations of such 
scenarios.  

D. The “Users of the BPS” Legal Authority Does Not Compel Registration 
of All Load Customers 

NERC’s Technical Reasoning grounds the proposed CLE registration in the Federal Power Act’s grant of 
authority over “users, owners, and operators of the Bulk Power System.” 16 U.S.C. § 824o, Section 
215(b); 18 C.F.R. § 39.2(c) (2026). However, the existence of jurisdictional authority does not, by itself, 
determine where the registration threshold should be set. NERC acknowledges this materiality principle 
by proposing thresholds rather than blanket registration of all BPS-connected loads. The critical question, 
therefore, is not whether NERC has authority to register computational load entities — it does — but 
whether the proposed thresholds are appropriately calibrated to capture entities whose behavior 
materially impacts BPS reliability. As discussed in Section IV below, the proposed 1 MW Computational 
Load threshold is set so low that it captures entities whose electrical behavior does not implicate the 
reliability risks identiﬁed in NERC’s own technical analysis.  

Page 3 of 10 

III. Appendix 5A — Organization Registration and 
Certiﬁcation Manual 

A. The Registration Process Requires a Reasonable Transition and 
Implementation Timeline 

The addition of “Computational Load Entity (CLE)” as a registrable entity type represents a historic ﬁrst. 
The registration process should include a reasonable implementation period and clear guidance on the 
registration workﬂow, particularly for entities that have no institutional familiarity with NERC’s 
compliance obligations, audit expectations, or the ERO Enterprise framework. It is recommended that a 
clear communication be developed for outreach to entities that would potentially fall under this 
registration type, as well as the ecosystem supporting those entities.  

B. Registration Must Be Coordinated with Project 2026-02 Standards 
Development 

Registration should not outpace the development of applicable Reliability Standards. Registering CLEs 
before the standards they must comply with are ﬁnalized creates a compliance gap — entities would be 
on the NERC Compliance Registry with no clear obligations, or worse, subject to enforcement actions for 
standards still under development. NERC’s Standards Committee accepted the Project 2026-02 SAR on 
March 18, 2026, and a Standards Drafting Team has been appointed. The current project timeline targets 
Board adoption in December 2026. Accordingly, the eﬀective date for CLE registration should be no 
earlier than the eﬀective date of the ﬁrst mandatory Reliability Standard applicable to CLEs. 

C. A Clear De-Registration Process Is Needed 

The proposed criteria deﬁne when an entity must register but are silent on what happens when an entity 
falls below the threshold — e.g., a facility reduces IT load below 1 MW, or aggregate load drops below 20 
MW due to decommissioning or facility reconﬁguration. 

Appendix 5A should include a clear de-registration process for CLEs that no longer meet the threshold 
criteria. The current RoP provisions for de-registration of other functional entities (e.g., GOs, TOPs) may 
not translate directly to CLEs, given the dynamic nature of computational load facilities. NERC should 
specify the evidentiary requirements, timeline, and Regional Entity review process for CLE de-registration 
to avoid indeﬁnite registration of entities that no longer pose the identiﬁed reliability risks. 

Page 4 of 10 

IV. Appendix 5B — Statement of Compliance Registry 
Criteria 

A. Registration Thresholds Are Misaligned with Actual Reliability Risk 

As proposed, the three-part threshold requires: (1) aggregate connected Load capability ≥ 20 MW; (2) at 
a single point of interconnection to the BPS at ≥ 60 kV; and (3) hosting ≥ 1 MW of Computational Load. 
This threshold captures facilities that do not present the reliability risks identiﬁed in NERC’s own 
technical analysis. It also appears that these numbers have simply been adopted from the IBR 
registration initiative (aggregation and interconnection thresholds), rather than based on any solid 
engineering or technical analysis demonstrating risk to the BPS.  

The 1 MW Computational Load threshold is disproportionately low. At 20 MW aggregate load, 1 MW of 
Computational Load represents just 5% of total facility demand. A 75 MW industrial facility with 1 MW of 
IT equipment for servers, PLCs, RTUs, routers, and personal computers would be required to register 
despite presenting none of the rapid load-swing, voltage stability, or protection coordination risks 
documented in the LLWG white papers and the Level 3 Alert. Additionally, current Registered Entities 
that may have 1 MW of computational load may also fall under this category – does that mean they 
would have to register as a CLE as well and have the additional administrative burden and cost of 
complying with standards that may be applicable to a CLE? 

ERCOT’s approach may better reﬂects risk. ERCOT’s proposed NPRR 1308 deﬁnition requires that 50% or 
greater of site demand consist of power-electronic-based computational load, with a minimum 
aggregate peak demand of 75 MW. NERC’s criteria, intended to establish the minimum acceptable 
continent-wide requirements, may conﬂict with ISO/RTO- has determined appropriate for its footprint. 

Recommendation. NERC should consider surveying diﬀerent markets or transmission organizations that 
are interconnecting such large loads to determine what the right threshold (e.g., Computational Load 
percentage of 25–50% of aggregate demand) for registration is to ensure only facilities whose electrical 
behavior genuinely poses BPS reliability risks — namely, those with high concentrations of power-
electronic-based load capable of rapid, large-magnitude demand changes are registered. This approach 
would align with the LLWG’s ﬁndings and permit transmission organizations to adopt more stringent 
criteria as appropriate for their systems. 

The aggregate impact doctrine requires careful calibration for load entities. NERC’s Technical Reasoning 
invokes the aggregate impact doctrine, citing 150 FERC ¶ 61,213 at P 58 (2015), which provides that 
“Registry Criteria provide that a class of entities, each of which would be individually excluded, may 
nevertheless be registered based on their aggregate impact on Bulk-Power System reliability.” However, 
the aggregate impact doctrine was originally developed in the context of generation resources and was 
subsequently applied to inverter-based resources (IBRs) under the Category 2 GO/GOP registration 
initiative. Applying this doctrine to load entities requires careful calibration. The aggregate impact of a 
class of computational load entities may not justify registering individual entities within that class whose 

Page 5 of 10 

own characteristics do not pose the identiﬁed reliability risks. A 20 MW mixed-use industrial facility with 
1 MW of IT/computational load equipment may not exhibit the power electronic load (“PEL”) behavior 
that NERC identiﬁes as the risk driver — regardless of how many such facilities exist in aggregate. 

The 1 MW threshold does not eﬀectively serve as a de minimis ﬁlter. NERC’s Technical Reasoning states 
that “the intent behind the ‘1 MW or greater’ of Computational Load threshold is to distinguish that 
those entities, such as industrial manufacturers, with a ‘de minimus’ amount of Computational Load do 
not meet the criteria for registration as a Computational Load Entity.” Howe4ver, 1 MW does not 
eﬀectively serve this de minimis ﬁltering function. Modern industrial facilities routinely may contain well 
over 1 MW of information technology equipment — including server rooms, SCADA systems, industrial 
automation platforms, edge computing infrastructure, and enterprise networking. A large petrochemical 
complex, steel mill, or semiconductor fabrication facility with 1–5 MW of IT equipment would be 
captured by the proposed criteria despite presenting none of the rapid load-swing or voltage sensitivity 
risks associated with data centers. A percentage-based threshold (e.g., 25–50% of aggregate demand 
consisting of Computational Load) would more eﬀectively distinguish facilities whose primary function is 
computational from facilities that simply use computing equipment ancillary to their primary industrial 
process. 

The registration criteria should align with NERC’s own technical risk analysis. Notably, NERC’s Technical 
Reasoning identiﬁes power electronic load (“PEL”) behavior as the actual technical risk driver, citing the 
LLWG’s ﬁnding that “many new large loads are [power electronic loads] (PELs) that use software controls 
to manage the load behavior rather than the mechanical controls used by older motor loads” and that 
“PEL control systems enable loads to rapidly change electricity consumption, creating previously unseen 
load behavior that can cause BPS planning and operational challenges.” Yet the proposed deﬁnition and 
registration thresholds are equipment-type-based, not behavior-based. NERC should align its registration 
criteria with its own technical reasoning by incorporating behavioral characteristics — such as the 
proportion of PEL-based load, rate-of-change capability, or voltage sensitivity — rather than simply 
counting megawatts of “information technology equipment.” This approach would more precisely target 
the entities whose behavior drives the identiﬁed reliability risks. 

B. A Tiered Registration Approach Should Reﬂect Non-Linear Risk 
Scaling 

The LLWG’s own analysis concluded that “the potential impact of several 100 MW loads may be less than 
the impact of a 500 MW load and may require diﬀerent treatment” and that “the emergence of 
gigawatt-scale loads may create exponential complications for study, planning and operations.” Yet the 
proposed criteria apply a single binary threshold — register or don’t. 

The registry criteria should support a tiered or graduated approach to compliance obligations, consistent 
with the LLWG’s ﬁnding that risk scales non-linearly with load size. A 25 MW data center and a 500 MW 
hyperscale campus present fundamentally diﬀerent risk proﬁles, yet the proposed criteria would subject 
both to the same registration status. Consider distinguishing between load sizes (e.g., 20–100 MW, 100–
300 MW, >300 MW) to enable proportional obligations in the standards that follow. 

Page 6 of 10 

C. NERC Should Explicitly Preserve Regional Flexibility — Floor vs. 
Ceiling 

Multiple ISOs/RTOs are developing their own large load frameworks with materially diﬀerent thresholds.
