NERC’s proposed criteria establish a continent-wide ﬂoor, but they should explicitly state that Regional 
Entities and ISOs/RTOs retain the ability to adopt more stringent thresholds and additional criteria 
appropriate to their system conditions — consistent with NERC’s traditional approach to registration. 
Without this clariﬁcation, the proposed criteria could be misinterpreted as preempting more tailored 
regional approaches like ERCOT’s NPRR 1308 or SPP’s HILL framework. 

D. “Single Point of Interconnection” Requires Clariﬁcation for Co-
Located Facilities 

The criterion requiring connection “at a single point of interconnection to the Bulk Power System at a 
voltage greater than or equal to 60 kV” does not address facilities with multiple POIs, shared substations, 
or co-located generation. NERC should clarify: 

•  Whether aggregation occurs across multiple POIs at the same physical site; 
•  How co-located generation (solar, BESS) and computational load at a shared POI are treated for 

purposes of the 20 MW aggregate calculation; 

•  Whether behind-the-meter generation oﬀsets are considered — i.e., whether a 30 MW data center 
with 15 MW of on-site solar has an “aggregate connected Load capability” of 30 MW or 15 MW; and 
•  How phased construction or modular expansion of computational load facilities aﬀects the timing of 

registration obligations. 

Page 7 of 10 

 
 
E. Registration Thresholds Should Align with the Level 3 Essential Action 
Alert 

On May 4, 2026, NERC issued a Level 3 Essential Action Alert identifying seven essential actions that 
registered entities must take to address immediate risks posed by computational loads interfacing with 
the BPS: 

1.  Develop modeling requirements for computational loads; 
2.  Complete system studies and planning improvements; 
3.  Update deﬁnition of “qualiﬁed change”; 
4.  Establish a commissioning process for computational loads; 
5.  Implement protection and coordination enhancements; 
6.  Install dynamic fault recording devices; and 
7.  Create Interpersonal Communication capabilities. 

These seven essential actions provide the clearest preview yet of the obligations CLEs will face. NERC 
should explain how the proposed registration thresholds were calibrated to capture the entities whose 
behavior drives the need for these essential actions. If the thresholds capture entities whose facilities do 
not implicate these actions (e.g., a 20 MW mixed-use industrial facility with 1 MW of IT equipment), the 
criteria are overbroad and should be revised. 

Notably, the two speciﬁc incidents that underpin NERC’s urgency — the January 2025 Eastern 
Interconnection large load loss event and the January 2026 Texas Interconnection voltage-sensitive 
crypto load reductions — both involved facilities with high concentrations of computational load, not 
mixed-use facilities with incidental IT equipment. This further supports a higher percentage threshold 
that targets the facilities whose electrical behavior actually caused these events. 

V. Cross-Cutting Process and Implementation 
Considerations 

A. Protect Against Unintended Scope Creep to Generator Owners and 
Operators 

Any new registration criteria and the reliability standards that follow must clearly delineate which risks 
are attributable to computational load behavior versus generation performance. Risks driven by 
computational load characteristics — volatility, forecasting uncertainty, rapid load changes, and 
protection coordination challenges — should be addressed through CLE-speciﬁc obligations, not through 
expanded requirements on Generator Owners or Generator Operators who do not control load behavior. 

Furthermore, any new or revised Reliability Standards developed as a result of these RoP revisions 
should be applied prospectively and aligned with approved interconnection agreements, study 

Page 8 of 10 

assumptions, and existing facility designs. Retroactive application would introduce compliance risk 
without corresponding reliability beneﬁt, particularly for co-located generation and storage facilities. 

B. Jurisdictional Coordination with FERC’s ANOPR (Docket RM26-4-000) 

NERC’s proposed CLE registration criteria are advancing in parallel with FERC’s Advanced Notice of 
Proposed Rulemaking (“ANOPR”) under Docket RM26-4-000, initiated pursuant to DOE Secretary 
Wright’s rare invocation of Section 403 authority. The ANOPR will establish its own federal large load 
interconnection framework, including standardized study procedures, cost allocation, and protection 
system requirements for loads greater than 20 MW connecting to transmission. 

NERC should explain how CLE registration will coordinate with — and avoid conﬂicting with — FERC’s 
emerging interconnection requirements. The ANOPR’s > 20 MW threshold matches NERC’s proposed 
aggregate load threshold, but FERC’s scope extends to all large loads, not just computational loads. 
Entities may face overlapping, inconsistent, or duplicative obligations unless NERC and FERC explicitly 
coordinate these parallel proceedings. At minimum, NERC’s ﬁling with FERC for approval of the RoP 
revisions should address how the two frameworks will interact. Notably, NERC itself ﬁled comments in 
Docket RM26-4-000 on November 21, 2025, acknowledging the need for coordination between NERC’s 
reliability framework and FERC’s interconnection requirements for large loads. The proposed RoP 
revisions should be consistent with the positions NERC articulated in those comments. 

C. Data Conﬁdentiality Protections for CLE Operational Data 

Many CLEs — particularly hyperscale data centers — consider their power consumption, load proﬁles, 
demand forecasts, and facility conﬁgurations to be commercially sensitive and competitively valuable. 
The proposed RoP revisions do not address how CLE operational data will be protected under NERC’s 
existing conﬁdentiality framework. 

The revisions should clarify how data submitted by CLEs will be treated under NERC’s conﬁdentiality 
classiﬁcations (Public, Limited Disclosure, Conﬁdential, Restricted-Conﬁdential). Without clear data 
protection commitments, entities may resist registration or provide incomplete data, undermining the 
reliability objectives of the Large Loads Action Plan. NERC should develop CLE-speciﬁc data handling 
protocols in coordination with the Regional Entities before the registration process begins. 

D. NERC Should Publish a Clear Implementation Roadmap 

The Level 3 Essential Action Alert (May 4, 2026), the Voluntary Reliability Guideline, the RoP registration 
criteria (comment period closing May 15, 2026), and the Phase 1 bridge standard from Project 2026-02 
are all advancing in parallel on aggressive timelines. NERC should publish a clear implementation 
roadmap that sequences registration, standard development, and enforcement expectations to avoid 
confusion and premature compliance exposure. 

Additionally, NERC and the Regional Entities should develop targeted onboarding materials, compliance 
workshops, and a reasonable ramp-up period before enforcement actions are pursued against newly 

Page 9 of 10 

registered CLEs. These entities are, by deﬁnition, new to NERC’s compliance framework and will require 
structured guidance to achieve meaningful compliance. 

VI. Conclusion 

The Large Loads Action Plan represents an important and timely initiative. However, the proposed RoP 
revisions require reﬁnement in several critical areas to ensure that the new CLE registration framework 
achieves its intended reliability objectives without creating unintended consequences. 

In summary, the comments are organized around four key themes: 

1.  Deﬁnitional Precision: The “Computational Load” and “Computational Load Entity” deﬁnitions 

require greater speciﬁcity to avoid overbroad application, resolve ambiguities regarding 
ownership/operating structures, and close gaps for non-IT large loads with identical reliability risk 
proﬁles. 

2.  Risk-Calibrated Thresholds: The Appendix 5B registration criteria should be revised to increase the 
Computational Load percentage threshold, adopt a tiered approach reﬂecting the LLWG’s ﬁnding 
that risk scales non-linearly with load size, incorporate behavioral characteristics consistent with 
NERC’s own PEL-based technical reasoning, and explicitly preserve regional ﬂexibility for ISOs/RTOs 
to adopt more stringent criteria. 

3.  Implementation Sequencing: CLE registration should not outpace standards development or 

enforcement readiness. NERC should coordinate registration timing with Project 2026-02, FERC’s 
ANOPR under Docket RM26-4-000, and the Level 3 Alert essential actions to avoid overlapping or 
conﬂicting obligations. 

4.  Scope Protection: Risks attributable to computational load behavior should be addressed through 
CLE-speciﬁc obligations — not through expanded requirements on Generator Owners or Generator 
Operators who do not control load behavior.

Comments on  
Proposed Revisions to NERC ROP: Computational Loads 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Comments on  
Proposed Revisions to NERC ROP: Computational Loads 

ATC generally supports the comments presented by the Trade Associations (APPA, EEI, LPPC, 
NRECA, TAPS, and NARUC) including the Section 1 ‘Overarching Principles’; maintaining 
consistency with other NERC Registration Categories; deﬁning Computational Load to avoid 
inadvertent inclusion of previously stable large loads like industrial and commercial processes; and 
Section 4 ‘Comments on NERC’s Proposed Revisions’. 

Additional comments are provided below. 

ATC Proposed Modiﬁcations  

1.  Add a new deﬁnition Computational Load Facility (CLF): 

“Computational Load Facility” means a collection of electrical equipment located at one 
or more buildings, structures, or installations that is designed to receive power, has an 
aggregate connected maximum peak demand greater than or equal to 20 MVA, hosts 50% 
or greater of the peak demand load as Computational Load, and is served through electric 
facilities at a voltage level greater than or equal to 60 kV from one or more points of 
connection. 

A clear deﬁnition of a Computational Load Facility is essential for Project 2026-02 success. 
Existing standards that currently address the same types of essential actions being 
proposed for data centers but are applicable to other comparable equipment (like 
generators) consistently rely on a Facility-type deﬁnition. This is consistent with how 
Generator Owner/Operator and Generating Facility are treated, deﬁned, and included in the 
registration criteria. 

Data center sites can have a signiﬁcant number of physical and electrical conﬁgurations. 
For example, many data center sites can consist of one or more buildings, with each 
building having one or more connections to the Bulk Power System at the same location. In 
some cases, data center owners may consider that each building is an individual data 
center, while in other cases the collection of buildings connected to the grid is viewed as the 
data center. The risk to the BES comes from the aggregate load behavior of facilities at a 
single site. This was emphasized in NERC’s “Characteristics and Risks of Emerging Large 
Loads” whitepaper that, while speciﬁc load types and thresholds to deﬁne Large Loads 
could not be deﬁned across industry at that time, all agreed that any such deﬁnition should 
include “aggregation of load facilities at a single site behind one or more point(s) of 
interconnection that can pose reliability risks to the BPS.”   

2.  Replace CL Entity (CLE) with CL Operator (CLOP) and CL Owner (CLO) 

“Computational Load Operator”: means the end-user entity that operates a 
Computational Load Facility, and/or the entity that operates a Computational Load Facility

4.  Modify Computational Load criteria thresholds in Appendix 5B 

ATC is concerned that NERC’s Appendix 5B definition and criteria for Computational Load 
Entity is too broad and could unintendedly include larger loads that do not pose the same 
reliability risks as data centers. These existing non-data center facilities are not the target of 
these to address the most critical reliability issues associated with integrating these large 
loads onto the BPS in the near-term. It is inefficient to require all facilities 20 MW and 
greater with 1 MW of computation load to register, and difficult to then depend on the 
standard to further delineate between hospitals and data centers for requirements in new 
or existing standards. 

Therefore, ATC proposes that the criteria and definition for Computational Load Entity be 
modified to “1) contributes to an aggregate connected maximum peak demand greater than 
or equal to 20 MVA; 2) hosts 50% or greater of the peak demand load as Computational 
Load; and 3) is served through electric facilities at a voltage level greater than or equal to 60 
kV from one or more points of connection” 

ATC also recommends that NERC considers requiring each applicable Transmission 
Operator and Transmission Owner to perform an entity specific study to determine the MW 
threshold at which a computational load presents reliability risk within its system. 

ATC would consider supporting the Category 1/Category 2 designations proposed by the 
Trade Associations as long as both categories are subject to the same requirements and 
both categories are implemented without delay between them.

The Trades propose the following modiﬁcations: 

1.  Add a new deﬁnition Computational Load Facility (CLF): 

 
 
 
 
 
 
AZPS Comments on Proposed Revisions to NERC ROP: Computational 
Load Entity 

May 8, 2026 

“Computational Load Facility” means a collection of electrical equipment located at one 
or more buildings, structures, or installations that is designed to receive power, has an 
aggregate connected maximum peak demand of Computational Load greater than or equal 
to 75 MW, and is served through electric facilities at a voltage level greater than or equal to 
100 kV from one or more points of connection. 

A clear deﬁnition of a Computational Load Facility is essential for Project 2026-02 success. 
Existing standards that currently address the same types of essential actions being 
proposed for data centers but are applicable to other comparable equipment (like 
generators) consistently rely on a Facility-type deﬁnition. This is consistent with how 
Generator Owner/Operator and Generating Facility are treated, deﬁned, and included in the 
registration criteria. 

Data center sites can have a signiﬁcant number of physical and electrical conﬁgurations. 
For example, many data center sites can consist of one or more buildings, with each 
building having one or more connections to the Bulk Power System at the same location. In 
some cases, data center owners may consider that each building is an individual data 
center, while in other cases the collection of buildings connected to the grid is viewed as 
the data center. The risk to the BES comes from the aggregate load behavior of facilities at a 
single site. This was emphasized in NERC’s “Characteristics and Risks of Emerging Large 
Loads” whitepaper that, while speciﬁc load types and thresholds to deﬁne Large Loads 
could not be deﬁned across industry at that time, all agreed that any such deﬁnition should 
include “aggregation of load facilities at a single site behind one or more point(s) of 
interconnection that can pose reliability risks to the BPS.”   

2.  Replace CL Entity (CLE) with CL Operator (CLOP) and CL Owner (CLO) 

The Trades recommend that the Computational Load Entity deﬁnition be replaced with new 
deﬁnitions that align with the “Owner” and “Operator” Model currently in place in the NERC 
Rules of Procedure for registration criteria. Today we have registration criteria for 
Transmission Owner (TO), Transmission Operator (TOP), Generator Owner (GO), and 
Generator Operator (GOP). This structure is in place because for Transmission and 
Generation facilities, there are often situations that occur where the owner of the facilities 
is different from the operator of the facilities. This registration criteria setup allows for the 
different entities to be responsible only for the activities that they are contractually setup for 
as the owner and/or operator.  

For Computational Load Facilities, these facilities have the same type of structure. There 
are many cases where the owner is different from the operator. Therefore, because of the 
actual structure of the facilities and to align with existing NERC registration criteria, the 

 
 
 
 
AZPS Comments on Proposed Revisions to NERC ROP: Computational 
Load Entity 

May 8, 2026 

Trades recommend replacing of the Computational Load Entity deﬁnition with 
Computational Load Owner and Computational Load Operator, with proposed deﬁnitions 
for each included below. 

“Computational Load Owner” means the end-user entity that owns and maintains a 
Computational Load Facility,  and/or the entity that owns and maintains a Computational 
Load Facility that hosts end-users that receives electric power at a Computational Load 
Facility. 

“Computational Load Operator” means the end-user entity that operates a 
Computational Load Facility, and/or the entity that operates a Computational Load Facility 
that hosts end-users that receives electric power at a Computational Load Facility. 

However, if NERC staff retains only one Registered entity, the Trades suggest the following 
modiﬁcations to the Computational Load Entity deﬁnition: 

“Computational Load Entity” means the end-user and/or the entity that hosts end-users 
that receives electric power for at a Computational Load Facility. 

The risk to the BPS and the gaps in NERC reliability standards, as noted in NERC’s 
“Assessment of Gaps in Existing Practices, Requirements, and Reliability Standards for 
Emerging Large Loads” is driven by Computational Load impacts and behavior, not other 
type of load, and Computational Load Entity should focus only on the amount of data-
centric/information technology type of load. 

3.  Clarify the Computational Load (CL) deﬁnition: 

The Trade Associations recommend that the proposed Computational Load deﬁnition focus on the 
power electronic-based information technology equipment, which is the focus of the risks to the 
BPS as documented by NERC’s Large Loads Task Force and Large Loads Working Group. 

NERC’s “Assessment of Gaps in Existing Practices, Requirements, and Reliability Standards for 
Emerging Large Loads” identiﬁes risks associated with the behavior and impacts of computational 
loads. Those risks arise from the data-centric and information technology characteristics of the 
load, not from unrelated load at the same site. The deﬁnition should therefore focus only on the 
amount of computational load and should not sweep in other types of loads that do not raise the 
same reliability concerns. 

“Computational Load” means Load comprised primarily of electric power demand from 
power electronic-based information technology equipment.  

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
AZPS Comments on Proposed Revisions to NERC ROP: Computational 
Load Entity 

May 8, 2026 

4.  Either (a) increase Computational Load thresholds or (b) pursue an approach 

comparable to the Category 1/Category 2 designations for Generation. 

a.  NERC should increase its 20 MW and 60 kV Thresholds  

The Trades recommend NERC reconsider the registration thresholds proposed in 
Appendix 5B. The proposed 20 MW/60 kV threshold with the 1MW Computational 
Load criteria is set unnecessarily low and sweeps in a substantial number of 
facilities that pose no material impact to the reliability of the Bulk-Power System 
and, thus, does not justify the burden of NERC registration. The current Rules of 
Procedure, Registration, and Standard Drafting efforts related to Computational 
Loads should focus on those loads that pose the most meaningful risk to the Bulk 
Power System. The threshold criteria (20 MW, 60 kV) is too low and we recommend 
the threshold be set to 75 MW connected at >= 100kV for Computational Load 
Facilities, consistent with the NERC Bulk Electric System deﬁnition for dispersed 
power producing resources (i.e., inverter-based resources) – where the current 
criteria is greater than 75 MVA at a common point of connection at >= 100kV is 
utilized. 

Although NERC has developed a Technical Reasoning Proposed Computational 
Load document, it does not provide sufficient explanation or practical examples to 
justify the selected thresholds in the proposed registration criteria. The Trades are 
concerned that NERC’s proposed approach could inadvertently create compliance 
obligations for Distribution Provider (DP) entities by effectively deeming them 
Transmission Owners (TO) or Transmission Operators (TOP). It is critical to ensure 
that DPs do not lose the radial system exemption when solely serving load and not 
operating transmission facilities. Clear justiﬁcation and reﬁnement of the proposed 
thresholds are required to demonstrate that there are identiﬁable and material risks 
to the BES. 

In addition, NERC’s “Characteristics and Risks of Emerging Large Loads” indicated 
that “most of the survey respondents qualiﬁed ‘large’ as greater than 50 MW, and 
the single size number most commonly suggested was 75 MW,” and the NERC Alert 
2 results conﬁrmed this. NERC’s “Assessment of Gaps in Existing Practices, 
Requirements, and Reliability Standards for Emerging Large Loads” refers back to 
the ﬁrst Whitepaper and in the deﬁnition section, and focuses on really large loads 
and how several smaller loads (still much bigger than 20 MW) are not as big of a risk. 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
AZPS Comments on Proposed Revisions to NERC ROP: Computational 
Load Entity 

May 8, 2026 

“The potential impact of several 100 MW loads may be less than the impact of a 500 
MW load and may require different treatment.” 

Furthermore, the NERC “Ten benchmarks of an Effective Reliability Standard” white 
paper emphasizes that “each [NERC reliability standard] requirement is ‘not a 
lowest common denominator’ exercise but instead achieves an objective that is the 
best approach for bulk power system reliability.” The same applies to deﬁnitions and 
reliability criteria. NERC’s decision to select 20 MW appears to be a “lowest 
common denominator” choice, instead of a higher value that the majority of the 
industry agrees with.  

The Trades recommend NERC adopt an initial threshold of 75 MW at a common 
point of connection of 100 kV or higher.  This pairing adheres to the current Bulk 
Electric System deﬁnition and appropriately balances reliability risk to compliance 
burden.  A 75 MW/100 kV starting point focuses computational load entity 
registration on the facilities most likely to have a material impact on Bulk-Power 
System reliability.  It would also give NERC and the Regional Entities time to identify 
entities for registration, develop Reliability Standards, and gain compliance 
oversight experience with a manageable population.  Further, it avoids imposing 
new obligations on facilities whose individual contribution to reliability risk is 
limited.   

b.  NERC should pursue a Category 1/Category 2 approach for Computational 

Loads  

If a threshold lower than 75 MW is deemed necessary by NERC staff, the Trades 
recommend that NERC staff enhance the Technical Reasoning document to reﬂect 
the analysis/evidence demonstrating the lower facility threshold is needed for BPS 
reliability. In addition, in this scenario the Trades also recommend that NERC staff 
adopt the same registration criteria model that was developed for IBRs with the 
Category 1 GO/GOP and Category 2 GO/GOP. NERC should create a new Category 1 
Computational Load Owner/Operator (CLO/CLOP) and Category 2 CLO/CLOP 
deﬁnitions, and structure the MW and voltage criteria for each to align with the 
Category 1 GO/GOP and Category 2 GO/GOP. The Category 1/Category 2 approach 
to address the different security requirements needed for each categories. To create 
this structure, the following deﬁnitions are proposed: 

•  “Computational Load Facility” means a collection of electrical equipment 
located at one or more buildings, structures, or installations that is designed 
to receive power, is served through electric facilities from one or more points 

 
 
 
AZPS Comments on Proposed Revisions to NERC ROP: Computational 
Load Entity 

May 8, 2026 

of connection and meets the criteria in either Category 1 or Category 2 
Computational Load Owner/Operator registration categories. 

•  “Category 1 CLO/CLOP” should be aligned with the BES criteria, which 
would be entities who own/operate Computational Load Facilities (CLFs) 
that are >= 75 MW of Computational Load connected at >= 100kV. 

•  “Category 2 CLO/CLOP” should be aligned with the lower threshold value 

supported by NERC and industry, which would be entities who own/operator 
Computational Load Facilities that are >= 20 MW of Computational Load 
connected at >= 60kV. 

With NERC expected to address computational load risk on an accelerated timeline 
by the end of 2026, this structure would allow the entire ERO to focus its initial entity 
registration, standards development efforts, and compliance education activities on 
the highest-risk CLOs/CLOPs ﬁrst. This framework also establishes a more 
manageable path to subsequently address lower-risk Category 2 CLOs/CLOPs in 
future work phases. Finally, this structure would enable a risk-based compliance 
approach by allowing more stringent reliability and security requirements to be 
applied to Category 1 CLOs/CLOPs compared to Category 2 CLOs/CLOPs. 

5.  Additional Comments 

The draft Computational Load Entity registry criteria uses the word “capability” which can 
be interpreted as the maximum load of a Computational Load Facility (CLF). For example, if 
the CLF facility has a maximum possible load demand of 100 MW, then this is the Load 
“capability” of the CLF. However, this “capability” term as used with Load is likely not widely 
understood or utilized today. We recommend an alternative to the use of “capability” such 
as “maximum peak demand” of a Facility to be clearer. In addition, evaluating a CLF’s 
impact on the BES should not rely solely on its size. Incorporating operational 
characteristics such as interruptibility, load ﬂexibility, and the availability of on-site or 
contracted backup generation will provide a more comprehensive and accurate 
assessment of system impacts. 

Additionally, the proposed registration criteria includes reference to a “point of 
interconnection” at 60 kV. “Point of interconnection” is primarily a term referring to 
generation interconnections – interconnections that most often rely on one generating tie-

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
AZPS Comments on Proposed Revisions to NERC ROP: Computational 
Load Entity 

May 8, 2026 

line. Data centers often have many connections to the Bulk Power System at the same 
location. The ownership of equipment can also vary site to site, in which some connect to 
utilities directly at the high voltage kV bus by owning the high-voltage transformation, while 
others do not own the transformation or equipment greater than 60 kV. 

In NERC’s current proposed Computational Load Entity registration criteria, it states 
“contributes to an aggregate connected Load capability.” How will NERC determine the 
amount of Computational Load or the amount of aggregate connected load thresholds? Will 
it be based on the “nameplate” of the various racks in a data center warehouse or some 
other methodology?  Regardless of the method(s) for determining these values, the Trades 
recommend that this should be conﬁrmed between the CLE and its Regional Entity and 
NERC should not be dependent on other registered entities for providing this information to 
Regional Entities. Critically this criteria states Load, not Computational Load. We believe 
this is incorrect and should be updated to state “Computational Load capability.” In our 
proposed Computational Load Facility deﬁnition, we have included the use of 
Computational Load in the deﬁnition so that the focus is only on data-centric/information 
technology load. The Trades ask “How is a Computational Load fundamentally different 
from other large traditional loads such as steel mills, food processors, or automobile 
manufacturers? All large loads must be studied to ensure their interconnection and 
operation do not create grid reliability issues. There is concern that, as written, it may 
capture facilities that are not data centers or cryptocurrency mining operations, which are 
the business types that NERC has identiﬁed as potentially impacting the reliability of the 
BES. For example, many industrial and commercial facilities may operate more than 1 MW 
of information technology equipment (either now or in the future) such as servers, storage, 
and networking hardware to control and support processes, yet these are not solely or 
primarily computational in nature. In addition, it seems unreasonable that the loss of a 1 
MW load, regardless of load type, would have a signiﬁcant impact on the BES, therefore 
including a de minimis criteria of 1 MW of Computational Load drives signiﬁcant confusion, 
pulls in a signiﬁcant number of entities unnecessarily and has no justiﬁcation pertaining to 
actual risk to the BPS. The 1 MW de minimis threshold conﬂicts with the material impact 
standard applied throughout Appendix 5B and would expand registration beyond entities 
capable of materially impacting BPS reliability. The 1 MW de minimis threshold should be 
removed from the Computational Load threshold. 

To build on the concerns shared and the alternatives provided the Trades ask the following 
questions. 

•  “How will a Computational Load Entity(ies) be identiﬁed for registration under the 

proposed framework?”   

 
 
AZPS Comments on Proposed Revisions to NERC ROP: Computational 
Load Entity 

May 8, 2026 

•  Will the Transmission Owner (TO), Transmission Operator (TOP), or Transmission 

Planner (TP) be responsible for identifying this Load(s) and sharing that information 
with their Regional Entity?  

•  Additionally, will responses to the NERC Level 3 Alert on Computational Loads be 

used to inform or determine registration requirements?   

In addressing these questions, the Trades recommend that the identiﬁcation CLEs for 
potential registration should be the responsibility of the Regional Entity and NERC 
should not be dependent on other registered entities for providing this information to 
Regional Entities. 

Appendix B 
It is unclear on how large load facility topology/interconnection conﬁgurations may impact 
the applicability of the proposed registration criteria. Recommend that the NERC/ERO 
quickly develop a CMEP Practice Guide on this new registration criteria for review by 
industry and DT to ensure no unintended consequences from this new criteria. 

The Trades also note that NERC's document "Summary of Revisions" states candidates for 
CL registration must meet all the criteria in the proposed revisions in Appendix 5B in order 
to be registered as a Computational Load Entity, however, that is not explicitly stated in the 
proposed changes in Appendix 5B and should be stated. 

Bright-line Criteria  
Computational Load Entity (CLE) registration should be based on clear, bright-line criteria 
coupled with a formal exception process similar to the BES deﬁnition framework. Such an 
approach would allow an entity to demonstrate, through documented technical 
justiﬁcation, that its facilities do not have a material impact on the Bulk Electric System 
(BES). This balance is necessary to ensure that registration and compliance obligations are 
applied only where there is a substantiated reliability risk, while avoiding unnecessary 
regulatory burden for entities whose operations do not pose a material threat to BES 
reliability.

BPA understands NERC’s ROP revisions proposal has the following registration qualiﬁers 
for a Computational Load Entity: 

1) contributes to an aggregate connected Load capability greater than or equal to 20 MW;  

2) at a single point of interconnection to the Bulk Power System at a voltage greater than or 
equal to 60 kV; and  

3) hosts 1 MW or greater of Computational Load. 

In BPA’s experience, data center interconnections vary.   

Many large data centers interconnect at High Voltage (HV) level, 230-kV or 115-kV, and own 
step-down transformers and Medium Voltage (MV) equipment, usually 34.5-kV and 12.5-
kV). BPA believes these will clearly ﬁt into the proposed NERC ROP registration criteria. 

However, BPA also sees large data centers that interconnect at the MV level, as illustrated 
below for a 200 MW data center. BPA understands that an interconnecting utility will own 
and operate HV to MV step-down transformers and MV substation and the change of 
ownership between a utility and a data center occurs at 34.5-kV level. BPA recommends 
the deﬁnition clarify that the described interconnection meets the NERC deﬁnition. 

To achieve BPA’s recommendation regarding the Computational Load Entity (CLE) 
deﬁnition, BPA suggests revising the language listed below: 

III(c) Computational Load Entity: 

III.c.1 Computational Load Entity that encompasses all of the following: 

1) One or more facilities at a single site that contributes to an aggregate 

connected Load capability greater than or equal to 20 MW;

greater than or equal to 60 kV; and 
 Connects to the Bulk Power System (BPS) operated at a voltage greater than

Interconnection (POIs) or Service Delivery Points; and

identiﬁed for AGC. BPA understands this to be the threshold for modeling and operational 
monitoring. BPA recommends revising the language to: 

3) hosts 1 3MW or greater of Computational Load.

In addition to supporting the comments submitted by APPA, SVP provides the following 
comments on the Computational Loads SAR and proposed ROP revisions which include a 
new definition for “Computational Load Entity” and registration criteria for CLEs.

COMPUTATIONAL LOAD ENTITY “CLE” REGISTRATION

SVP agrees that registration of Computational Load Entities is necessary to help ensure that 
interconnecting entities commit to meeting baseline reliability expectations, and SVP 
supports the registration criteria proposed in the Rules of Procedure, Appendix 5b [1)load 
capability greater than or equal to 20M; 2) at a single point of interconnection to the 
Bulk Power System at a voltage greater than or equal to 60kV; and 3) hosts 1MW or 
greater of Computational Load.] 

CLE DEFINITION

SVP considers the proposed definition of Computational Load Entity, “the end user or the 
entity that hosts end-users that receives power for Computational Load,” to be 
unnecessarily broad and more likely to result in conflicting accountability and strain any 
coordination efforts between TOPs and the CLEs within their system. SVP recommends that 
the Computational Load Entity be identified as the host/facility owner; this will streamline 
any coordination or Interpersonal Communication requirements that evolve from the Large 
Loads Bridge Standard project. (e.g.:  Level 3 NERC Alert, Essential Action #7 – “TOPs, RCs, 
and BAs should establish Interpersonal Communication capabilities with computational 
loads to improve their situational awareness and joint operating procedures to ensure the 
reliability operation of the BPS. . .”)

SCOPE of STANDARD AUTHORIZATION REQUEST

While the purpose of the Standard Authorization request is generally understood by the 
industry, the SAR itself lacks enough specificity about the reliability risks it intends to 
address. SVP recommends that the SAR identify the risks the Essential Actions are meant to 
mitigate, using the “Essential Actions” in the May 4th Level 3 NERC Alert pertaining to 
Computational Loads as guidance.  This will assist both the drafting team and voting entities 
determine whether the initial bridge standard meets the purpose of the SAR.

Concern Regarding 1 MW Minimum Computational Threshold 

The proposed 1 MW computational load threshold may be too low to reliably indicate the presence of 
system-relevant  computational  behavior.  A  facility  with  1  MW  of  computational  load  within  a  20MW 
aggregated load is unlikely to exhibit the characteristics that NERC is intending to address. We suggest 
evaluating whether a higher threshold or ratio-based threshold would better reflect reliability risk. 

SPP recommend NERC evaluate whether: 

·

A higher computational load minimum (for example, 3–5 MW) better reflects the
threshold at which computational characteristics materially impact system stability, or

·

Additional technical justifications are provided to support the 1 MW cutoff.

Need Precise Definition of “Point of Interconnection at ≥60 kV” 

We request clarification on how the point of interconnection at 60 kV or above is to be determined. This 
is critical for distinguishing true transmission-connected computational loads from distribution-fed 
commercial or mixed-use facilities. A defined measurement methodology would help ensure consistent 
registration and audit application. 

Alan Wahlstrom N.C.S.O
Lead Engineer
Reliability Standards Development Group
Southwest Power Pool

capability greater than or equal to 20 MW of Computational Load; and 2) at a single

60 kV.; and 3) hosts 1 MW or greater of Computational Load.

The reasoning for this is that with the currently proposed definition (hosting 1MW of greater of
Computational Load), a large number of facilities may be pulled into the registration criteria that
are not AI data centers. 1MW of computational load may inadvertently require office buildings,
university campuses, research centers, etc. to register as a Computational Load Entity.

By amending the first item to focus on the required amount of computational load, and not an
aggregate load plus a relatively small portion of computational load, the definition becomes
more salient and succinct.

Thank you,

Eric Mannarino 
Global Design & Construction
Design Delivery Principal, Electrical Engineering

CRUSOE TECHNOLOGIES LLC     |     NERC Computational Load Entity — Comments on Proposed Appendix 5B 

May 12, 2026   |   Via Electronic Filing: ROPcomments@nerc.net 

Comments of Crusoe Technologies LLC 
NERC Rules of Procedure Revision — Computational Load Entity Registration Criteria 
(Appendix 5B) 
45-Day Comment Period  |  April 1 – May 15, 2026  |  Project 2026-02 

I.  Introduction 
Crusoe Technologies LLC ("Crusoe") submits these comments on NERC's proposed Appendix 5B 
registration criteria for a new functional entity type — the Computational Load Entity (CLE). Crusoe 
operates  large-scale  artificial  intelligence  compute  infrastructure  interconnected  to  the  bulk  power 
system (BPS) and participates actively in ERCOT's Batch Zero large load interconnection proceeding. 

Crusoe supports the CLE framework, with more specific definitions. NERC's May  4, 2026 Level 3 
Alert  documented  widespread,  simultaneous 
from 
computational  facilities  —  events  that  create  real  BPS  stability  exposure.  A  registration  and 
compliance  framework  with  mandatory  Reliability  Standards  is  the  right  response.  That  said,  any 
definitions and registration criteria should be grounded in load size and grid impact, applicable to all 
large  load  facilities  regardless  of  industry  type  —  not  targeted  at  a  specific  end  use  of  electricity. 
Crusoe's  comments  address  two  specific  issues:  the  20  MW  threshold  is  too  low  and  will  not 
accomplish what NERC intends, and the proposed definitions are overbroad and require refinement. 

load  reductions  exceeding  1,000  MW 

II.  The 20 MW Threshold Is Too Low — 75 MW Is the Right Number 
The proposed criteria require registration where a facility contributes to aggregate connected load 
capability of ≥ 20 MW at ≥ 60 kV and hosts ≥ 1 MW of computational load. The 20 MW floor does not 
reflect large load impacts on the BPS.  

A 20 MW load tripping offline — even instantly — creates an immeasurable frequency deviation on 
the Eastern or Western Interconnection. Automatic generation control and governor response absorb 
events of this size routinely without any reliability consequence. NERC's own Level 3 Alert identified 
the reliability problem as large-scale, simultaneous drops from clusters of computational facilities — 
not from individual 20 MW sites. Registering 20 MW facilities does not solve that problem. It creates 
an  enormous  administrative  burden  for  the  wrong  population  while  diluting  NERC's  enforcement 
focus. 

ERCOT — the RTO with the largest concentration of emerging computational load in North America 
— set its large load interconnection threshold at 75 MW. This threshold reflects decades of ERCOT 
operational  experience  with  the  load  size  at  which  a  single  facility  begins  to  affect  transmission 
planning  assumptions,  SCED  constraint  dispatch,  and  reliability  coordination.  Crusoe  respectfully 
urges NERC to adopt 75 MW as the CLE threshold and to explain, with technical justification, if it 
believes a different number better reflects BPS material impact. 

Page 1 of 4 

 
 
 
 
 
 
CRUSOE TECHNOLOGIES LLC     |     NERC Computational Load Entity — Comments on Proposed Appendix 5B 

III.  The 1 MW Computational Load Sub-Criterion Sweeps In the Wrong 
Facilities 
The proposed criteria require only that a qualifying facility 'hosts 1 MW or greater of Computational 
Load' — defined as load from servers, storage, and networking hardware. This definition is overly 
broad: it sweeps in hospitals, universities, corporate offices with modest server rooms, and industrial 
facilities  like  steel  mills  with  incidental  on-site  IT  equipment.  None  of  these  are  the  purpose-built, 
utility-scale infrastructure that prompted NERC's Level 3 Alert, and imposing full NERC compliance 
obligations on incidental IT users bears no relationship to the reliability risk NERC is managing 

That is not the population that tripped 1,000 MW simultaneously and prompted NERC's Level 3 Alert. 
The Level 3 Alert, the Level 2 Alert before it, and the Large Loads Working Group white paper all 
focused on purpose-built, utility-scale AI and data center infrastructure. Imposing NERC Reliability 
Standards compliance — with audit obligations and civil penalty exposure up to $1 million per violation 
per day under FPA Section 215 — on incidental IT users bears no relationship to the reliability risk 
NERC is managing.Crusoe recommends that the computational load sub-criterion be set at 50 MW 
of dedicated computational load, or alternatively that computational load constitute at least 50% of 
the facility's aggregate connected load capability. Either formulation limits registration to purpose-built 
computational  infrastructure  —  the  actual  source  of  BPS  risk  —  and  excludes  conventional 
commercial  and  industrial  facilities  with  incidental  IT.  As  such,    Crusoe  recommends  refining  the 
definition  of  Computational  Load  to  capture  only  loads  that  meet  the  MW  threshold  and  are 
"predominantly  comprised  of"  or  where  "the  majority  of  electric  power  demand"  comes  from  IT 
equipment.  

IV.  Proposed Revision to Appendix 5B Criterion 2 

Current Language: 
A Computational Load Entity that (1) contributes to an aggregate connected Load capability greater than or equal 
to 20 MW; (2) at a single point of interconnection to the BPS at a voltage ≥ 60 kV; and (3) hosts 1 MW or greater 
of Computational Load. 

Crusoe's Recommended Language: 
A Computational Load Entity that (1) contributes to an aggregate connected Load capability greater than or equal 
to 75 MW; (2) at a single point of interconnection to the BPS at a voltage ≥ 100 kV; and (3) hosts 50 MW or 
greater of Computational Load [alternative: for which Computational Load constitutes at least 50% of aggregate 
connected Load capability at that point of interconnection]. 

Crusoe also recommends a 100kv voltage threshold instead of the proposed 60kv. Transmission-
level  interconnection  is  a  meaningful  indicator  of  BPS  exposure  and  should  remain  a  necessary 
condition.. 

V.  One Additional Issue: Co-Located Generation and Storage 
The  proposed  CLE  definition  does not  address  facilities  that  combine computational  load  with  co-
located generation or energy storage — the BYOG (Bring Your Own Generation) model increasingly 
common in large AI infrastructure deployments. A facility that must register as a CLE, a Generator 
Owner, and an Energy Storage Resource Owner may face multi-entity compliance obligations that 

Page 2 of 4 

 
 
 
 
 
CRUSOE TECHNOLOGIES LLC     |     NERC Computational Load Entity — Comments on Proposed Appendix 5B 

have  not  been  reconciled.  Crusoe  requests  that  NERC  issue  guidance  on  multi-functional  entity 
registration for co-located configurations before the CLE criteria are finalized. 

VI.

Additional Recommendations

Crusoe supports the comments submitted by the Data Center Coalition (DCC).  As an additional 
recommendation if NERC maintains the 20 MW/60kV thresholds, NERC should adopt the same 
registration criteria model that was developed for Inverter-Based Resources with the Category 1 
and Category 2 GO/GOP definitions and criteria.  This would enable NERC and the industry to 
focus initially on reliability issues created by the larger Category 1 Computational Load 
Owner/Computational Load Operator categories.  

Category 1 CLO/CLOP:  Computational Load Facilities that are >= 75 MW of maximum peak 
demand of Computational Load connected at >= 100kV 

Category 2 CLO/CLOP:  Computational Load Facilities that are >= 20 MW of maximum peak 
demand of Computational Load connected at >= 60 kV 

VI. Summary of Recommendations

1. Raise the aggregate connected Load capability threshold from 20 MW to 75 MW.

2. Raise the Computational Load hosting sub-criterion from 1 MW to 50 MW — or require Computational
Load to constitute at least 50% of aggregate connected load capability.

3. Raise the 60 kV voltage threshold to 100kv

4. Issue guidance on multi-functional entity registration for co-located generation and storage
configurations before the CLE criteria are finalized.

Crusoe  thanks  NERC  for  its  leadership  in  addressing  the  BPS  reliability  implications  of  large 
computational loads. The Level 3 Alert demonstrates that the urgency is real. Getting the threshold 
right — so that mandatory compliance obligations fall on the facilities that actually affect BPS reliability 
—  is  essential  to  making  the  CLE  framework  effective.  Crusoe  is  available  to  provide  additional 
technical input if that would assist NERC's deliberations. 

Respectfully submitted, 

Crusoe Technologies LLC

Data Center Coalition Comments on                                                                                       5/15/2026 
Proposed Revisions to NERC ROP: Computational Loads 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Data Center Coalition Comments on                                                                                       5/15/2026 
Proposed Revisions to NERC ROP: Computational Loads 

The Data Center Coalition is pleased to submit these comments on NERC’s proposed Rules of Procedure 
definitions and registration criteria for Computational Loads. 

Like all customers, the data center industry depends on a reliable electricity grid in order to fulfill its role 
as a vital backbone of our modern economy. In turn, data centers offer a number of reliability benefits to 
the grid, including significant investments in new energy resources and next-generation technologies. As 
recently demonstrated during Winter Storm Fern, data centers can also serve as grid assets that help 
promote reliability during energy emergencies caused by extreme weather. 

It is critical to ensure proposed definitions and registration criteria by NERC are based on complete 
evidence, the technical capabilities and specifications of data center equipment, and do not disregard 
important developments or information from key markets. In Virginia, improved communication between 
NERC, regional entities, utilities, and data center operators have greatly reduced — if not altogether 
eliminated in certain instances — load transfer events in Virginia. In Texas, DCC is unaware of any load 
transfer events that have been caused by data centers, based on ERCOT's reporting. This type of close 
collaboration, communication, and technical information sharing is essential to the upcoming work with 
NERC. 

While NERC has elected to pursue a pathway that conflates and singles out "computational loads," we 
emphasize that any new definitions and registration criteria should be defined by any type of large load 
facility – and the corresponding load size, voltage level, and operational characteristics of any such large 
load facility - not simply by industry type or end use of electricity. With that fundamental concern noted, 
DCC is committed to leaning in as an engaged partner with NERC and transmission entities to help 
ensure a reliable grid for all customers and offers the following comments. In addition, while the DCC 
understands the urgency of the NERC computational load work, the recently released NERC Level 3 Alert 
on Computational Load Modeling, Studies, Instrumentation, Commissioning, Operations, Protection, 
and Control is an important tool that should help get essential actions in place by the electric 
transmission industry. Given the scale and criticality of this Level 3 Alert, it would be prudent to wait for 
the industry response to this Level 3 Alert and corresponding essential action implementation before 
moving forward with the registration criteria and standard development for Computational Loads. The 
DCC also urges NERC to publicly release its legal analysis that NERC stated was ongoing throughout 
2025, which we understand is supporting the conclusion that NERC has the authority under Section 215 
of the Federal Power Act to register Computational Load Entities and impose mandatory reliability 
standards on them. This is a significant expansion of NERC's jurisdictional reach, and the data center 
industry, other computational load industries, and the electric industry all deserve to understand the 
legal reasoning before any registration framework or standard is advanced. Publishing this analysis would 
allow for informed stakeholder engagement, support a more defensible rulemaking record, and ensure 
that the process is lawful and reflects the transparency and due process the industry expects from NERC. 

•  Summary of RoP Changes 

 
 
 
 
 
 
Data Center Coalition Comments on                                                                                       5/15/2026 
Proposed Revisions to NERC ROP: Computational Loads 

o  NERC has decided to target large computational loads, which appears to specifically 
exempt other types of large loads that also have a material impact on the bulk power 
system. Particularly with the relatively low thresholds proposed, it is unclear how a 20 MW 
data center would have a substantially greater impact to the BPS than, say, a multi-
hundred MW mining load or manufacturing facility.  

•  Appendix 2 

o  The definition for “Computational Load” is rather generic and may be difficult to implement 

and enforce due to the ambiguities it contains. Specifically, the terms say that “Load 
comprised of electric power demand from IT equipment…” Thus, if ANY portion of the load 
is IT-based equipment, then this would technically constitute as a Computational Load. 
For some examples: 

▪  A steel mill likely has some servers or computers on site that ultimately are IT 

equipment; however, the vast majority of the load is an industrial process and not 
intended to be captured by this definition.  

▪  Hospitals, large office buildings, colleges/universities are additional examples that 
all are large loads that will have plenty of IT equipment, including servers, storage 
systems, and networking equipment. But all of these facilities should not be 
intended to be captured by this definition. 

Therefore, NERC should consider some improvements to the definition to scope and refine 
it. One example would be to state “Load primarily comprised of electric power demand 
from IT…” or “Load where the majority of electric power demand from IT…”. This captures 
the same intent but provides some clear specifications on how to apply it. 

o  NERC should consider whether the “Computational Load Entity” (“CLE”) is sufficient for 

the purposes of future standards applicability and registration. Does this refer to the owner 
or operator of the facility or the owner and operator of the computational load? Which is 
the main target of standards? What if the owner and operator are different entities, which is 
a common structure in the data center industry? 

o  NERC may want to further clarify what “end-user or the entity that hosts end-users” means 
exactly, with some examples to support registration efforts. The industry generally believes 
this refers to, for example, data center locations that may have multiple tenants, but 
examples/confirmation from NEC on this is critical. 

•  Appendix 5B 

 
 
 
 
 
 
Data Center Coalition Comments on                                                                                       5/15/2026

o  The criteria for CLE is generally missing the overall risks stated by NERC and industry in the 
various reports, as written. The criteria essentially states that a 50 MW load that has only 1 
MW of Computational Load would then need to be registered as a CLE. A 1 MW threshold 
for registration and applicability to NERC standards seems very misaligned with the 
findings in NERC reports. We recommend that the 1 MW threshold requirement be 
removed entirely from the definition. 

o 

In addition, a more straightforward definition would be: “contributes to aggregate 
connected Computational Load greater than 20 MW at a single point of interconnection to 
the BPS at a voltage greater than or equal to 60 kV.” It is unclear why a definition such as 
something like this couldn’t achieve the same outcome and be more aligned with other 
NERC registration efforts (e.g., Category 2 GO/GOPs) and general understanding of BPS 
impact/risks.  

With those general comments provided, DCC would like to propose the following modifications to 
the proposed definitions and registration criteria, while also providing new definitions that provide 
better alignment with existing NERC registration criteria and definitions. 

•  Modify the new term, “Computational Load”, to reference this load being primarily made up of 
power-electronic-based information technology equipment and remove any unnecessary 
examples of that equipment. 

•  “Computational Load”: Load comprised primarily of electric power demand from power 

electronic-based information technology equipment 

•  Create a new definition, “Computational Load Facility”, to align with how existing NERC 

standards apply to Facilities (not entities) and include the updated registration criteria in this new 
definition. The registration criteria include updated MW threshold to 75 MW, updated voltage 
connection to 100kV, and changes the word “capability” to “maximum peak demand.” 

•  Computational Load Facility (“CLF”): a collection of electrical equipment located at one 

or more buildings, structures, or installations that is: 

(1) designed to receive power 

(2) has an aggregate connected maximum peak demand of Computational Load 

greater than or equal to 100 MW 

(3) and is served through electric facilities at a voltage level greater than or equal to 

100kV from a single point of connection. 

•  Modify the new term, “Computational Load Entity”, to reference the CLF definition and add some 

clarifying edits to the definition:

If NERC insists on keeping the 20 MW threshold of Computational Load, we ask that NERC provide 
a detailed explanation and evidence why such a low threshold is needed, as NERC’s own reports 
and white papers do not align with this low threshold. 

o  NERC’s Large Load Task Force (LLTF) White Paper #1 (Characteristics and Risks of 

Emerging Large Loads) states that most survey respondents listed large loads to be in the

o  NERC’s LLTF White Paper #2 (Assessment of Gaps in Existing Practices, Requirements, and

o  NERC’s report on the Level 2 Alert responses (“Aggregated Report on NERC Level 2 Industry

Providers] had thresholds typically below 20 MW.” 

o  All these reports and recommendations lead us to recommending that NERC increase the 
threshold to 100 MW connected at 100kV for the proposed Computational Load Facilities. 

 
 
 
 
 
 
Data Center Coalition Comments on                                                                                       5/15/2026 
Proposed Revisions to NERC ROP: Computational Loads 

If NERC should continue to insist on a lower threshold being needed, we recommend that 
NERC adopt the same registration criteria model that was developed for Inverter-Based 
Resources with the Category 1 and Category 2 GO/GOP definitions and criteria. This would 
allow the industry to first focus our standard development efforts on the larger Category 1 
CLO/CLOP Facilities, and then in time address the lower Category 2 CLO/CLOP Facilities. 
Below are the proposed Category 1 and Category 2 CLO/CLOP definitions that align with 
the current Category 1 and Category 2 GO/GOP thresholds/criteria. 

•  Category 1 CLO/CLOP: 

•  Computational Load Facilities that are >= 100 MW of maximum peak 

demand of Computational Load connected at >= 100kV 

•  Category 2 CLO/CLOP: 

•  Computational Load Facilities that are >= 20 MW of maximum peak 

demand of Computational Load connected at >= 60 kV 

There are two primary types of data centers relevant to this discussion: (1) self-perform and enterprise 
data centers, in which the business owns and controls its servers and peripheral equipment and may or 
may not own the physical facility; and (2) multitenant and build-to-suit data centers, in which the facility 
owner leases space to one or more tenants, potentially encompassing both critical and non-critical load 
behind the same meter,  where those tenants bear direct responsibility for the computational load 
activity occurring within their leased space. Reference the CIP-002-5.1a ERO Endorsed Implementation 
Guidance document that also defines Tenants and considers Tenants in the aspects of the standard. 

Any attempt by NERC to define Computational Loads and Computational Entities must be cognizant of 
the complex and varied operational structures, agreements, contracts, and lease arrangements that 
currently exist between the owners, operators, and tenants of computational load facilities. These 
relationships were established under existing regulatory frameworks and commercial constructs that did 
not anticipate the definitional boundaries now being proposed. Accordingly, it is essential that NERC 
incorporate a clearly defined exception process to accommodate computational load facilities that were 
designed, contracted, and operationalized prior to the effective date of these rule changes; facilities that, 
through no fault of their own, may not align with new definitions or satisfy new requirements without 
significant operational or contractual disruptions and substantial retrofit costs. A blanket application of 
new definitions and requirements without such a process risks penalizing facilities for non-compliance 
with standards they had no reasonable basis to anticipate and could create unintended consequences 
for grid reliability if affected entities are forced into reactive operational changes. 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Thank you for providing an opportunity to comment on the proposed Computational Load Entity Registry Criteria.

NERC should use the information it collects to provide greater transparency regarding large computational loads 
to the wider electricity market.  Currently, market participants are struggling to understand where new large 
computational loads will interconnect, their size, and basic operational characteristics.  Without this information, 
project developers, generators, power marketers and other electricity industry participants cannot forecast and 
plan for future grid conditions accurately and efficiently.   

Large computational loads affect grid operations and locational electricity prices to a similar extent as generation 
resources of equivalent size.  Yet, there is far less information available regarding large computational loads than 
there is for generation resources.  For example, the Energy Information Administration publishes a public data 
base with basic information on the interconnection location and characteristics of generation resources (i.e., Form 
EIA-860 Data Base), but does not maintain an equivalent data base for large computational loads. 

Private actors across the industry cannot make efficient investments in transmission and generation to serve the extraordinary 
demand forecasted from large computational loads without greater transparency, stifling investment and, ultimately, 
jeopardizing reliability.  Electricity market participants should have access to certain information regarding each large 
computational load via a database of approved loads, their sizes, and the locations at which they plan to interconnect with the 
grid.  In addition, market participants should have information regarding the portion of the load that will be firm or in another 
category.  NERC should also provide basic information on the type of load, for instance, whether the studied load is for a data 
center or crypto mining, and whether the load will include new or existing co-located generation.  

Justin R. Cockrell
Assistant General Counsel

DPN Comments on NERC Proposed Rules of Procedure Revision:  

Computational Load Entities (CLEs) 

As NERC considers revisions to the Rules of Procedure Appendix 2 (Definitions Used in the 
Rules of Procedure) to add new Computational Load Entities (CLEs), the Digital Power 
Network (DPN) offers the following comments and recommendations to ensure the 
continued operational viability of large, flexible computing loads as the standards are 
drafted. 

DPN is the largest coalition of Bitcoin miners and digital infrastructure providers, 
representing facilities with a significant footprint in the grid and energy sector. Bitcoin 
mining facilities and data centers are increasingly critical components of modern 
infrastructure that support financing buildout and providing demand flexibility. Any 
standards framework should therefore balance reliability objectives with the need to 
support the safe, secure, and economically viable operation of these facilities. 

I. Appendix 2 (Definitions Used in the Rules of Procedure) Comments 

Ensure Clear Statutory Authority 

NERC should clearly articulate the statutory basis for creating the Computational Load 
Entity (CLE) category and the proposed definition to ensure the framework remains legally 
grounded. 

While Section 215 of the Federal Power Act (FPA) authorizes NERC to develop mandatory 
reliability standards for the Bulk-Power System (BPS), subject to FERC approval, that 
authority is not based on the identity of a particular industry or type of end-user. Rather, it is 
based on whether an entity materially affects the reliable operation of the BPS. 

Accordingly, NERC should continue to focus on functional reliability impacts rather than 
establishing a fixed, industry-specific category of “Computational Load Entity.” Historically, 
NERC registration and compliance obligations have been tied to reliability functions and 
material impacts on the BPS, rather than a facility’s status as a particular type of electricity 
consumer. 

Further, whether a computational load materially impacts BPS, reliability may need to be 
evaluated on a case-by-case basis given regional and operational differences. At the same 

 
 
time, other non-CLE load entities may also materially affect BPS reliability but would not 
fall within the proposed definition. 

NERC should also clarify its statutory basis for imposing direct reliability standards on 
“end-users” of the BPS. Section 215 applies to “users, owners, and operators” of the BPS, 
but NERC has historically applied registration and compliance obligations based on an 
entity’s reliability function and material impact on BPS operations, rather than solely on its 
status as an electricity consumer. 

Historically, crypto miners and data centers have generally been treated as end-users of 
electricity rather than entities directly subject to mandatory reliability standards. While 
NERC and applicable reliability entities may exercise indirect oversight through 
transmission operators, planners, balancing authorities, interconnection processes, and 
operating requirements, these facilities have not traditionally been subject to direct 
compliance obligations under the FPA solely by virtue of being large electricity consumers. 

Further, NERC’s jurisdiction extends only to entities and activities affecting the BPS and 
does not extend to purely local distribution facilities or other systems outside the statutory 
definition of the BPS. 

While DPN supports NERC’s mission to reduce risks to BPS reliability, expanding reliability 
standards through the BPS to directly regulate end-users raises broader legal and practical 
concerns that warrant careful consideration. 

II. Foundational Principles for Initial Standards  

Prioritize Coordination Before Compliance Requirements 

The current standards drafting process appropriately emphasizes process-based 
standards. It is important that NERC promote coordination between large loads and 
relevant authorities. 

Early and structured coordination will: 

-  Ensure stakeholder input is incorporated into standards development 
-  Reduce the risk of infeasible or misaligned requirements 
- 

Improve overall implementation outcomes 

 
 
Large loads should be active participants in the standards-setting process, not only 
subjects of compliance. 

Streamline and Standardize Data Requests 

As standards evolve, multiple entities (e.g., Transmission Planners, Planning Coordinators, 
Reliability Coordinators) may request similar data from large loads. 

To avoid duplicative and burdensome requirements: 

-  Data requests should be standardized and streamlined across entities 
-  A coordinated framework should minimize repetitive submissions 
-  A lead authority or centralized process should be designated when possible 

Protect Proprietary and Sensitive Information 

Data centers and Bitcoin mining facilities frequently handle proprietary or third-party data. 
Energy usage and operational characteristics are integral to their business models and may 
be competitively sensitive. 

NERC should incorporate clear data protection standards, including: 

-  Recognition of this data as Critical Energy Infrastructure Information (CEII) 
-  Robust protections for CEII 
-  Safeguards for commercially sensitive information such as: 

o  Pricing strategies 
o  Customer relationships 
o  Capacity plans and expansion timelines 
o  Technical specifications 

Increased data-sharing requirements must be paired with equally strong data protections. 

Stakeholder Process and Governance 

To ensure operationally and economically viable compliance with the requirements of 
relevant authorities, NERC should: 

-  Require relevant authorities to engage directly with large load operators when 

developing standards 

-  Establish clear stakeholder participation processes that prioritize entities with 

direct operational relevance 

 
 
III. Looking Ahead: Future (Technical) Standards 

As NERC moves beyond initial “bridge” standards toward technical requirements, DPN 
emphasizes the importance of maintaining operational feasibility. 

Voltage Ride-Through Standards 

Future low-voltage ride-through (LVRT) requirements must be carefully designed to reflect 
current technological capabilities.  

-  Requirements that are too stringent could necessitate significant new technologies 

and impose substantial costs 

-  Poorly calibrated standards risk driving facilities out of certain markets  

Ramp Rate Requirements 

Ramp rate standards should account for real-world constraints, including: 

-  Supply chain limitations 
-  Permitting timelines 

Overly rigid requirements could unintentionally limit deployment and flexibility 

Preserve Operational Viability 

Across all future standards should: 

-  Maintain flexibility for large loads to continue participating in demand response and 

curtailment programs 

-  Avoid requirements that undermine the economic or technical feasibility of 

operations 

-  Ensure standards are developed in partnership with industry 
-  Evaluate the impact of changing resource mixes and inverter-based resources on 
essential reliability services such as frequency response, voltage support, and 
system inertia  

Conclusion 

 
 
 
DPN supports NERC’s efforts to improve coordination and visibility around large loads. 
However, the definition must only pertain to loads that have actual reliability impacts on 
the system rather than a targeted scope focused on industry rather than impact.  

Beyond the definition, DPN recognizes that process-based standards are an appropriate 
first step. 

However, success will depend on: 

-  Early and meaningful coordination with industry 
-  Streamlined and consistent data requirements 
-  Strong protections for sensitive information 
-  A continued focus on operational feasibility as standards evolve 

A balanced approach will strengthen grid reliability while enabling the continued growth of 
critical digital infrastructure. 

 
Proposed Changes to NERC Rules of Procedure 
“Computational Load Entity” 

Comments of the Electricity Consumers Resource Council 
(ELCON) 

The  Electricity  Consumers  Resource  Council  (ELCON)  respectfully  submits  these 
Comments in response to the National Electric Reliability Corporation’s (NERC) proposed 
revisions to the NERC Rules of Procedure posted April 1, 20261 incorporating defined terms 
and registration criteria for “Computational Load Entities.”  

ELCON  is  the  national  association  representing  large  industrial  consumers  of  electricity. 
ELCON member companies create a wide range of products from virtually every segment of 
the  industrial  community—we  own  and  operate  hundreds  of  major  facilities  and  are 
significant consumers of electricity throughout the United States. Reliable electricity supply 
at just and reasonable rates is essential to our members’ operations. 

ELCON has been engaged in the work of the NERC Large Load Task Force (now Large Load 
Working Group or LLWG) since its inception in August 2024 and appreciates the efforts of 
NERC staff and industry to quickly anticipate and mitigate emerging risks to the Bulk Power 
System (BPS) posed by massive new loads interconnecting to the BPS at speeds our current 
system was not designed for.  

Following  the  completion  of  two  whitepapers,2  NERC  determined  that  “unforeseen  and 
difficult-to-explain  dynamic  electrical  behavior”  made  it  appropriate  “to  propose  a  new 
functional entity type that focuses on loads with these characteristics [and] further define 
the entities that will be subject to registration based on their individual characteristics as 
well  as  the  aggregate  impact  of  multiple  Computational  Loads  meeting  the  Registry

are/standing-committees/rstc/whitepaper-characteristics-and-risks-of-emerging-large-loads.pdf (Whitepaper #1); 
Assessment of Gaps in Existing Practices, Requirements, and Reliability Standards for Emerging Large Loads (March
