Criteria.”3  NERC  further  correctly  identified  the  need  to  incorporate  certain  minimum 
thresholds “to distinguish [  ] those entities, such as industrial manufacturers, with a ‘de 
minimus’ [sic] amount of Computational Load do not meet the criteria for registration as a 
Computational Load Entity. This distinction is based on these entities’ differing electrical 
behavior historically.”4 

As explained below, ELCON is concerned that, despite NERC’s clear intent to register only 
those loads that exhibit certain behaviors that risk BPS stability and reliability, the proposed 
definitions in the Rules of Procedure and registration criteria in Section III of Appendix 5B 
(separately and jointly) could capture some traditional loads and, by requiring registration 
by end users, do not effectively target the entities responsible for ensuring reliable usage of 
the BPS. 

In  fact,  nothing  in  the  definition  or  registration  criteria  addresses  the  behaviors  that 
introduce risk to the BPS, but rather focus on ancillary usage of a broad set of IT equipment 
that  may  or  may  not  introduce  those  risks.  Industrial  and  manufacturing  large  load 
customers  are  fundamentally  different  from  the  data  center  and  computational  facility 
activities that precipitated NERC’s large load work. In contrast, traditional manufacturing 
and  industrial  customers  operate  predictable,  process-driven  load  profiles;  are  already 
subject  to  existing  power  quality  expectations  under  IEEE  519;5  have  decades-long 
interconnection histories with their host utilities; and do not exhibit the behaviors the LLWG 
identified as the primary drivers of BPS reliability risk. As proposed, the CLE definition and 
registration criteria do not adequately target those entities and behaviors identified in the 
whitepapers and the CLE Technical Reasoning. 

Appendix 2 – Definitions Used in the Rules of Procedure 

The  proposed  revisions  to  Appendix  2  of  NERC’s  Rules  of  Procedure  introduce  two  new 
terms: 

“Computational  Load”  means  Load  comprised  of  electric  power  demand  from 
information  technology  equipment,  such  as  servers,  storage,  and  networking 
hardware.  

“Computational Load Entity” means the end-user or the entity that hosts end-users 
that receives electric power for Computational Load.  

As an initial matter, both proposed definitions are anchored exclusively to equipment type—
“information technology equipment, such as servers, storage, and networking hardware”—
rather  than  to  any  of  the  behavioral  characteristics  that  NERC’s  own  LLWG  analysis 

3 CLE Technical Reasoning, p. 2 (Apr. 2, 2026), https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/who-we-are/rules-of-
procedure/proposed/cle-technical-reasoning-april-2026-posting.pdf.    

4 Id., p. 3 (emphasis added).  

5 IEEE Standard for Harmonic Control in Electric Power Systems. 

2 

 
 
 
 
 
 
identified as the source of BPS reliability risk.6 NERC’s technical work consistently grounds 
the  large  load  reliability  concern  in  specific  operational  behaviors:  second-to-second 
demand oscillation tied to AI training workloads, voltage-sensitive customer-initiated load 
reductions  (CILR),  and  synchronized  cross-facility  demand  reductions.  A  definition 
anchored  to  equipment  type  rather  than  demonstrated  or  expected  behavior  cannot 
effectively distinguish load facilities that pose reliability risks from those that do not. ELCON 
urges NERC to anchor the definition to behavioral criteria, or at a minimum incorporate a 
substantial-proportion threshold as detailed below. 

The “Computational Load Entity (CLE)” definition is independently problematic and overly 
broad.  As  worded,  any  user  of  electric  power  demand  from  information  technology 
equipment satisfies this definition and is a candidate for registration. Taken to its extreme, 
anyone with a computer is a potential NERC registrant.  

The phrase “the entity that hosts end-users” could capture a landlord or owner of a multi-
tenant industrial park that has no direct control over individual tenants’ electrical behavior. 
Similarly, an industrial manufacturer that operates a vendor-managed server room could be 
registered  as  a  CLE  even  though  it  has  zero  operational  control  over  that  equipment’s 
electrical behavior or demand variability. ELCON recommends that  NERC revise the CLE 
definition to require that the entity have operational control over the computational load at 
the facility. An entity that passively receives electric power for use by a third-party operator 
of information technology equipment should not bear registration obligations arising from 
that operator’s equipment and behaviors. 

In addition to the overly broad nature of the proposed definitions, it is unclear whether the 
definition and registration criteria are to be considered separately or jointly. In other words, 
must an entity first meet the explicit definition  of a  (CLE) before applying  the  registration 
criteria  to  determine  if  they  are  subject  to  registration?  Is  there  a  scenario  where  a 
“computational  load  entity”  would  not  meet  the  MW  and  voltage  registration  criteria  as 
defined in Appendix 5B of NERC’s Rules of Procedure?  

For example, Company X manufacturers widgets with a load profile of 28 MW and uses 1.6 
MW  of  that  demand  to  power  its  internal  communications  server  (email),  file  database, 
internal management systems, process controls, and onsite data processing. Based on the 
definition alone, Company X could be considered a “Computational Load Entity” as some 
of its demand is used to power its information technology equipment.  

However, if NERC’s intent is to directly tie the characteristics and behaviors of certain loads 
that  pose  a  risk  to  the  BPS  and  then  apply  the  specific  size  and  voltage  thresholds  to 
determine their registration eligibility, it is not entirely clear as written.  

If NERC does not intend to capture traditional loads hosting informational technology that 
is  ancillary  to  its  primary  industrial  process,  ELCON  recommends  that  NERC  modify  the 
proposed  definition  of  “Computational  Load”  to  include  the  qualifying  language  “load 
comprised primarily of electric power demand from information technology equipment… .” 

6 See Whitepaper #2.  

3 

 
 
Alternatively,  NERC  could  include  a  percentage  threshold  to  the  definition.  For  example, 
“Computational Load means Load comprised of at least 50% of total electric power demand 
coming from information technology equipment… .”  

With the clarification proposed by ELCON, traditional loads such as large commercial and 
industrial loads would not qualify for registration as the first criteria, the CLE definition, is 
not applicable. Thus, the proposed registration criteria in Appendix 5B would be irrelevant. 

Appendix 5B – Statement of Compliance Registry Criteria  

If, however, NERC intended to cast a broad net initially, as currently proposed in the CLE 
definition, with the registration criteria being more narrowly targeted to size impacts, the low 
thresholds in the proposed revisions to Appendix 5B of NERC’s Rules of Procedure would 
still inadvertently capture a wide swath of large loads that do not exhibit the characteristics 
and  behaviors  identified  in  the  whitepapers  and  supporting  documentation.  Such  broad 
implementation would be extremely inefficient and would distract industry from focusing on 
mitigating the behaviors that pose actual risk to BPS reliability. 

Applying  the  proposed  registration  criteria  in  our  Company  X  example,  after  meeting  the 
broad criteria in the CLE definition of load with “electric power demand from information 
technology equipment,” Company X would then apply the registration criteria proposed in 
the revisions to Appendix 5B which specifies that a CLE must contribute at least 20 MW in 
aggregate load at a single point of interconnection at a voltage of 60 kV or higher where it 
hosts at least 1 MW of load attributable to information technology equipment. 

Here again, Company X (28 MW load, connects at 60 kV, where 1.6 MW of its power demand 
is used for internal information technology equipment) would meet each of the proposed 
criteria merely because of its size, not its operational characteristics. According to NERC’s 
Technical Reasoning supporting document, the 1 MW of computational load represents a 
de  minimis  amount  that  would  distinguish  traditional 
industrial 
manufacturers.”7 It is not clear how a facility with only 1 MW of computational load (defined 
only  as  “informational  technology  equipment”)  would  exhibit  any  of  the  variable  load 
patterns  attributed  to  reliability  risks  that  precipitated  NERC’s  large  load  work.  Even  in 
aggregate where that 1 MW load was located with 19 other facilities with at least 1 MW of 
computational load (i.e. 20 MW in aggregate), there is no direct link that ties the risk of the 
behavior and the impact to the grid due to its size. This approach risks including traditional 
industrial, manufacturing, and commercial facilities—many of which utilize computational 
processes  as  an  ancillary  component  of  their  operations—but  whose  load  profiles, 
operating characteristics, and system impacts are well understood and already adequately 
addressed through existing planning, interconnection, and operational frameworks. 

load  “such  as

Critically, the proposal does not establish a clear, evidence-based nexus between the mere 
presence of “computational” activity and an increased or unique reliability risk to the BPS. 
Absent such a showing, expanding mandatory registration to these facilities would impose 
significant  compliance  obligations  without  a  commensurate  reliability  benefit.  NERC’s 
registration framework has historically been grounded in functional distinctions that align 
with demonstrated reliability impacts. Departing from that principle here could dilute the 
effectiveness  of  the  registry  by  including  entities  that  do  not  meaningfully  affect  system 
reliability. 

Further, the 60 kV voltage threshold requires explicit legal and technical justification that 
NERC has not provided. FERC’s definition of the Bulk Electric System establishes 100 kV as 
the general bright line, with narrow exceptions justified by specific demonstrated reliability 
impacts.  NERC’s  prior  extension  to  60  kV  for  generator  registration  was  grounded  in 
documented technical analysis of sub-100 kV generation impacts on the BPS. NERC should 
be required to provide equivalent technical justification for applying load registration at 60 
kV, and absent such justification, ELCON recommends the voltage threshold be set at 100 
kV. Similarly, NERC should publish the reliability analysis, if any, that supports the 20 MW 
aggregate threshold, as the LLWG guideline itself explicitly states that no MW threshold is 
specified  in  that  document.  Registration  thresholds  must  be  grounded  in  demonstrated 
reliability impact, not arbitrary size proxies. Finally, the proposed aggregation approach—
measuring load across a single point of interconnection—does not correspond to the actual 
reliability risk that NERC seeks to address. The LLWG’s documented concern is with cross-
facility synchronized demand reductions across geographically dispersed facilities. A single 
28 MW industrial facility with 1.6 MW of internal IT equipment presents no such cross-facility 
synchronization  risk  regardless  of  its  size,  and  the  proposed  criteria  fail  to  make  this 
distinction. 

Should  NERC  reject  the  proposed  qualifying  language  in  Appendix  2  and  adopt  the  CLE 
definition  as  written,  ELCON  requests  that  NERC  adjust  the  MW  and  voltage  thresholds 
proposed in Appendix 5B to more closely align with actual risk impact to the BPS.8

these loads and their variable behavior, but that the proportion of computational loads in

Finally, the breadth of the definition and registration criteria creates uncertainty for entities 
that may not reasonably have considered themselves subject to NERC jurisdiction, leading 
to potential over-reporting, administrative burden, and inefficient allocation of compliance 
resources—for both industry and NERC. Absent these refinements, the proposed criteria 
risk being both overinclusive and insufficiently tied to the reliability concerns it is intended 
to address. We respectfully urge NERC to revise the proposal to ensure that any expansion

Registration of End-Users 

NERC’s jurisdiction over “users, owners and operators” was established by section 215 of 
the Federal Power Act as enacted through the Energy Policy Act of 2005. Since 2005, NERC 
has  asserted  that  authority  through  its  registration  requirements,  mandatory  reliability 
standards,  compliance  and  monitoring  programs,  and  enforcement  at  the  transmission 
level for those responsible for operating and planning the bulk power system. Although there 
has  been  some  consideration  of  NERC’s  jurisdiction  over  certain  distribution  functions, 
there has never been an instance where NERC’s authority over “users” has been challenged 
or more narrowly defined. Specifically, as “users” are typically under retail (state and local) 
jurisdiction, where does NERC’s authority over “users” begin and end?  

Size  and  voltage  thresholds  offer  little  protection  when  defining  NERC  jurisdiction  as  the 
end-user continues to evolve as does NERC’s scope. The generally accepted bright-line for 
NERC  jurisdiction  has  traditionally  been  100  kV  and  above  as  memorialized  in  the  Bulk 
Electric  System  definition  in  NERC’s  Rules  of  Procedure.  With  the  introduction  and 
increased  penetration  of  variable  resources,  NERC  determined  that  it  needed  to  assert 
jurisdiction at the 60 kV in some instances10.  

Here again, NERC is proposing jurisdiction at the 60 kV level without addressing the retail v. 
wholesale,  bulk  electric  system,  transmission  v.  distribution  divide.  Further,  it  is 
questionable to what extent an entity whose chief function falls well outside of electric grid 
service should be required to manage grid operations and protocols. The reliability concerns 
cited  in  the  proposal—such  as  large,  rapidly  changing  load  profiles  or  novel  operational 
characteristics—can be more appropriately and lawfully addressed through entities that are 
already  subject  to  NERC  oversight.  Transmission  Owners,  Transmission  Operators, 
Balancing  Authorities,  and  Load-Serving  Entities  are  already  responsible  for  planning,

registered entities are already positioned and obligated to manage.

Reliability is essential to all of us and time is critical as our Nation’s energy system evolves

NERC Rules of Procedure Team –

Please see below for the comments from AECC’s SMEs regarding the proposed revisions to 
the Rules of Procedure:
Computational Load Definition:

The Standards Drafting Team should consider revising the definition of Computational

Load to ensure it clearly reflects the explicit exclusion of equipment that is used by

direct physical/local interaction (e.g., laptop computers).

The Standards Drafting Team should consider revising the definition of Computational

Load to ensure it is clearly restricted to server type hardware only (which would include

“workstation” type hardware that is operated in a server mode or arrangement) whose

power usage from the transmission system can be directly or indirectly controlled. This

control can be due to the inherent processing source for the equipment between the

transmission system and some other on-site source (e.g., generator, UPS, etc.). The

ability to control the load seen by the transmission system will likely be an important

component in future NERC Reliability Standards. If the owner cannot control the

equipment, NERC will not be able to mandate any requirements that seek to control it.

To summarize: Computational Loads should be non-portable, fixed, server type

information technology equipment whose transmission system power usage can be

controlled.
Other Thoughts:

The Standards Drafting Team should reconsider the 1 MW threshold. 1 MW of load

seems too low, and it may pull smaller data centers which do not pose a problem for the

transmission system into scope. NERC should explain its reasoning and provide a

justification for this specific threshold. The criteria should focus on the amount of

computational load only, and not the amount of other traditional loads.

Is NERC’s intention to focus on the type of equipment or the type of load, and not the

characteristics of the load? Are the concerns based more upon the fluctuations and fast

ramp rates of loads regardless of load type? NERC should consider creating a “volatile

loads” definition that is defined by the speed and degree to which the load magnitude

changes instead of creating a “computational load” definition.

Thanks,
Ayslynn McAvoy

Dear NERC Team,

Thank you for the opportunity to provide stakeholder input on the Proposed Revisions to the 
Rules of Procedure and for NERC’s continued efforts to address reliability considerations 
associated with emerging large/computational loads.

As outlined in the attached OEB–NERC MOU and IESO–NERC–NPCC MOU, these agreements 
define the framework for administering NERC reliability standards in Ontario, including clear 
roles and compliance accountabilities. Under this framework, the IESO is solely accountable 
to NERC, while Ontario market participants/entities comply through the IESO in accordance 
with the Market Rules rather than through direct registration with NERC. Given that changes to 
the Rules of Procedure may require direct registration in the NERC Compliance Registry, it is 
important that any revisions preserve this established compliance structure.

The following are our comments:

Any revisions to NERC Registration Criteria to require registration of Computational
Load Entities with NERC should respect existing jurisdictional registration frameworks
for non-US entities.
Clarification is needed regarding the meaning and intended application of “single point
of interconnection,” since a Computational Load Entity that receives multiple supplies
from the BPS may not meet the definition.
Further clarification would be helpful regarding registration of multi-tenant and
colocation facilities where the host facility and end-use tenants may have different
levels of control over IT load behavior, such as a data centre owner operating the
electrical infrastructure while tenants control server dispatch or workload migration.
It would be helpful to understand the technical and/or reliability rationale for the
proposed registration thresholds, including the 20 MW aggregate connected load
threshold and the 1 MW Computational Load criterion, and whether these values are
based on BPS impact analysis, operational experience, historical disturbance data,
alignment with existing registration thresholds, or specific reliability risks intended to be
screened.
Clarification would be helpful regarding applicability to distribution-connected
computational loads, including cases where the IT load is connected below 60 kV but
the distribution system is supplied from transmission at or above 60 kV; consideration

could be given to whether applicability should be based on the immediate customer
connection point, the upstream transmission connection point, or demonstrated BPS
impact.
Additional clarity would be helpful on the treatment of behind-the-meter generation,
self-supply, and export-capable facilities for registration purposes. Depending on
whether registration is based on gross load, net load, maximum connected load
capability, or another metric, registration criteria may or may not be met.  
Clearly defining registration boundaries between CLEs and existing registered entities
would help avoid uncertainty, duplication, or conflicting obligations, including
interactions with Transmission Planners, Transmission Operators, Distribution
Providers, Planning Coordinators, and Load-Serving Entities.
Looking beyond the current effort to revise the ROP, additional clarity would be helpful
on registration timelines, transition periods, and expectations for existing versus new
computational load facilities.

In closing, we thank NERC for its continued attention to these important matters. We welcome 
further discussion should any points require clarification or additional consideration.

Sincerely,
Independent Electricity System Operator (IESO)
Compliance Assurance

Invenergy Comments on Proposed Computational Load Entity RoP Revisions 

NERC, 

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on this important matter. Invenergy believes 
the proposed registration criteria for Computational Load Entities is overly broad, and the low 
MW thresholds may unintentionally require industrial manufacturers or other non-data center 
loads with a de minimis amount of Computational Load to register with NERC. This will place an 
unnecessary burden on both the newly registered entities and the Regional Entities as critical 
resources are dedicated to smaller facilities that do not present the same risk to the Bulk Power 
System as larger data centers. 

Invenergy recommends NERC revise the proposed registry criteria to better align with the 
existing, and in development, thresholds established by RTOs and ISOs. Their criteria better 
reflect the load capabilities that they consider impactful to their systems and will ensure that 
resources are not spread thin. If NERC is determined to include loads of 20 MW or greater, we 
recommend a ratio-based threshold for the Computational Load capability that limits registration 
to those entities whose primary purpose is Computational Load. 

Sincerely,

ISO/RTO Council Standard Review Committee’s Comments 
on Proposed Computational Load Entity ROP Revisions 

May 15, 2026 
The ISO/RTO Council (IRC) Standards Review Committee1 (SRC) offers the following comments on the 
proposed revisions to the NERC Rules of Procedure (ROP) to  define Computational Load and register 
Computational Load Entities (CLEs), released on April 1, 2026. The SRC appreciates this opportunity to 
provide feedback on the proposed ROP revisions.  

Summary of SRC Comments 

•  Consider developing additional definitions for Bulk Electric System-level Computational Loads, 

• 

analogous to Category 1 Generator Owners and Generator Operators. 
Increase the 1 MW  Computational Load threshold in the CLE registration criteria or replace it 
with a threshold based on what percentage of the CLE’s total Load is Computational Load.  
•  Align the Distribution Provider (DP) registration threshold with the CLE registration threshold. 
•  Evaluate the best way to ensure NERC-level obligations apply to the interconnection of a CLE that 

pushes a distribution entity above the DP registration threshold. 

•  Revise the Computational Load definition to read as follows: “Computational Load” means Load 
that uses electric power for equipment needed for operation of computers or computer programs. 
Examples of such equipment include, but are not limited to, processors, memory,  data storage 
devices, and networking equipment. 

•  Revise  the  CLE  definition  as  follows:  “Computational  Load  Entity”  means  the  end-user  or  the 
entity operator  of  a facility  that  hosts  end-users  that  receives  uses  electric  power  for 
Computational Load. 

SRC Comments 

CLE Registration Threshold  
The  ROP  revisions  propose  to  require  a  CLE  to  register  with  NERC  if  the  CLE  contributes  to  an 
aggregate connected Load capability greater than or equal to 20 MW at a single 60 kV or greater 
point of interconnection to the Bulk-Power System and hosts 1 MW or more of Computational Load. 
The SRC offers no comment on the MW value used in the proposed 20 MW threshold, as a variety of 
thresholds exist in RTO/ISO-specific definitions of what constitutes a large load or CLE-type entity. 

1 For purposes of these comments, the SRC comprises the California Independent System Operator Corporation (California ISO), Electric Reliability Council 
of Texas, Inc. (ERCOT), ISO New England Inc. (ISO-NE), Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., (MISO), New York Independent System Operator, 
Inc. (NYISO), PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM), and Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (SPP).   

1 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The  SRC  notes  the  proposed  threshold  appears  to  align  with  the  threshold  used  for  Category 2 
Generator Owners and Generator Operators. Consequently, NERC may wish to consider whether it 
would be prudent to also establish a higher set of thresholds for CLEs that might be considered part 
of the Bulk Electric System, analogous to Category 1 Generator Owners and Generator Operators.  

However, the SRC believes the 1 MW Computational Load threshold as proposed is too low and could 
result  in  registration  requirements  being  imposed  on  entities  that  do  not  primarily  perform 
Computational Load-type activities and cannot reasonably be considered Computational Loads (for 
example,  a  200  MW  manufacturing  facility  that  happens  to  have  1.5  MW  of  on-site  computing 
equipment). Establishing a higher threshold or a threshold based on a percentage of the total Load 
(e.g.,  more  than  60%  of  the  Load  at  the  facility  is  Computational  Load)  would  help  prevent  the 
definition from being overinclusive.  

DP Registration Threshold 
While the proposed ROP revisions do not presently address the DP registration threshold, the SRC 
recommends revising the DP threshold as part of this project. The original DP threshold was 25 MW, 
and  the  threshold  was  increased  to  75  MW  in  2015  to  reduce  the  regulatory  burden  on  smaller, 
lower-risk  distribution  systems. However,  as  the  Standards  Drafting  Team  in  Project  2026-02  has 
recognized, DPs have an important role to play in reliably interconnecting CLEs to the Bulk-Power 
System.  To  avoid  a  scenario  in  which  a  CLE  attempts  to  interconnect  with  an  entity  that  is  not 
registered  as  a  DP  and  therefore  has  no  NERC-level  obligation  to  fulfill  the  DP’s  role  in  reliably 
interconnecting CLEs (for example, a 25 MW CLE seeking to interconnect with an entity that operates 
a  40  MW  distribution  system,  resulting  in  a  total  system  size  of  65  MW,  which  is  still  below  the 
current  75  MW  DP  threshold),  the  DP  registration  threshold  should  be  revised  to  match  the  CLE 
registration  threshold,  regardless  of  whether  that  threshold  is  ultimately  20  MW  or  some  other 
value.   

Regardless  of  which  registration  thresholds  are  ultimately  used  for  CLEs  and  DPs,  NERC  and  the 
Project 2026-02 Standard Drafting Team will need to carefully consider the most effective way to 
address  a  scenario  in  which  a  CLE  interconnection  pushes  a  distribution  system  above  the  DP 
registration threshold (for example, under current thresholds, a 50 MW CLE seeking to interconnect 
with  a  50 MW  distribution  system, resulting  in a  total  system  size of  100  MW).  System  reliability 
would  be  best  served  if  the  distribution  entity  were  registered  as  a  DP  to  fulfill  the  relevant 
NERC-level DP obligations before interconnecting the CLE. Achieving this result would likely require 
additional revisions to the DP registration criteria.  

2 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Computational Load Definition 
The  proposed  Computational  Load  definition  seem  underinclusive  and  vulnerable  to  arguments 
about whether the examples provided (servers, storage, and networking hardware) limit the scope 
of  the  definition,  thereby  potentially  excluding  hardware  used  for  advanced  computing  (such  as 
computational  accelerators  or  quantum  computing  hardware)  or  hardware  that does not  serve  a 
traditional server-type role, such as hardware used in a peer-to-peer architecture instead of a server-
client  architecture.  To  better  futureproof  the  definition  and  clarify  the  scope  and  role  of  any 
examples provided, the SRC recommends the Computational Load definition to be revised to read as 
follows:  

“Computational  Load” means  Load that uses  electric power for  equipment  needed  for 
operation of computers or computer programs. Examples of such equipment include, but 
are not limited to, processors, memory, data storage devices, and networking equipment. 

CLE Definition2 
In the proposed CLE definition, the phrase “entity that hosts end-users” is somewhat vague, and the 
phrase “end-user or the entity that hosts end-users” creates ambiguity as to whether the end user 
or the facility host would be the CLE for a given facility, which in turn creates ambiguity about who 
is required to register if the facility meets the applicable CLE registration thresholds. It would be less 
ambiguous to assign registration responsibility to the facility operator in all cases, since the operator 
is best situated to ensure the facility complies with all applicable Reliability Standards. Consequently, 
the SRC recommends revising the definition as follows:  

“Computational Load Entity” means the end-user or the entity operator of a facility that 
hosts end-users that receives uses electric power for Computational Load. 

Conclusion 

The SRC appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed ROP revisions. The SRC would 
welcome the opportunity to further discuss these comments or other Computational Load-related 
topics with NERC as appropriate and looks forward to engaging in the remainder of the ROP revision 
process.  

2 PJM is also submitting separate comments regarding the CLE definition and associated registration criteria.  

3 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Microsoft Comments on Proposed Revisions to NERC ROP: Computational Loads 
5/15/2026 
INTRODUCTION 

Microsoft operates more than 400 data centers across North America and five continents. A reliable 
grid is essential to our ability to serve customers and support United States leadership in artificial 
intelligence. We welcome NERC’s efforts to address the reliability risks posed by large 
computational loads and submit these comments to ensure the proposed framework is well-
calibrated to that goal. 

These comments build on Microsoft’s prior submission on NERC’s Standard Authorization Request 
for Project 2026-02, filed April 30, 2026, and focus specifically on whether the proposed definitions 
and registration criteria appropriately reflect system impact and reliability considerations. 
COMMENTS 

A.  Existing Registered Entities Can Provide the Quickest Path to Mitigating Identified 

Risks 

The existing reliability framework already provides effective tools for managing large load risks. 
Transmission Owners and Operators hold federal and state tariff authority that can be used to 
impose requirements on large load customers directly, i.e., no new registration category is required 
to close any accountability gap. Expanding the obligations of existing registered entities is faster to 
implement, avoids the complexity of bringing an entirely new class of entities into NERC 
compliance, and builds on processes that are already operational. 

To make that approach effective, however, registered entities need to do their part. Microsoft 
recommends the drafting team establish clear expectations for existing entities to coordinate with 
large loads on telemetry standards, modeling data requirements, and grid-side monitoring—so that 
any compliance obligations placed on large loads are grounded in information that is available and 
actionable. 

B.  NERC Should Include All Large Loads That Impact the Bulk Power System, Not Only 

Computational Loads 

Singling out “computational” load risks creating a framework that addresses one category of risk 
while leaving comparable risks from other large load types unaddressed. Large electrified 
industrial processes, battery manufacturing facilities, and similar loads can present the same 
reliability challenges—high ramp rates, concentrated interconnection, potential for correlated loss 
events—without falling within the proposed definition. A standard grounded in behavior and 
system impact rather than end-use would be more durable and more effective. At a minimum, NERC 
should commit to addressing other large load types in Phase 2. 

C.  The Definitions of “Computational Load” and “Computational Load Entity” Should Be 
Revised to Distinguish Between Differing Facility Operations and Load Behaviors 

The definition of “Computational Load” as power demand from “information technology equipment, 
such as servers, storage, and networking hardware” is broad enough to capture hospitals, 

 
 
 
universities, industrial facilities, and commercial buildings that use IT equipment as part of 
ordinary operations. These are stable, predictable loads that bear no resemblance to the reliability 
risks NERC has documented. The open-ended “such as” language compounds the problem by 
leaving the scope of the definition unclear for both registrants and auditors. NERC should ground 
the definition in the operational characteristics—load variability, ramp rate, power factor 
behavior—that actually drive reliability concerns and should include a clear exclusion for 
traditional loads that happen to use similar equipment. 

The “Computational Load Entity” definition also does not reflect how data centers are actually 
structured. In many deployments, the entity that owns and finances the facility is entirely separate 
from the tenant that installs and operates the computational equipment, and it is the tenant’s 
operational decisions that drive the load behavior of reliability concern. The single “CLE” 
designation obscures this distinction and risks misallocating compliance obligations between 
parties that have very different relationships to the grid. 

Microsoft recommends that NERC establish separate Computational Load Owner (“CLO”) and 
Computational Load Operator (“CLOP”) functional entities, modeled on the existing Generator 
Owner/Operator and Transmission Owner/Operator frameworks.  

For example, the CLO, the entity that owns and maintains the facility and its interconnection 
infrastructure, would bear responsibility for facility-level obligations: design specifications, 
interconnection compliance, and equipment standards. The CLOP: the entity that controls real-time 
load behavior, would bear responsibility for operational obligations: load ramp management, 
communications with the Transmission Operator and Balancing Authority. A single entity can hold 
both registrations where it owns and operates the same facility. Where ownership and operation 
are split, as is common in co-location and wholesale lease arrangements, each party’s obligations 
would be delineated by function. This structure does not eliminate compliance responsibility for 
large load customers, but it ensures that each requirement attaches to the entity actually in a 
position to fulfill it, and creates a commercially workable framework for allocating grid compliance 
responsibilities between landlords and tenants. 

D.  The Aggregate Capacity and Load Thresholds Are Too Low and Risk Increasing 

Administrative Burden for Little Corresponding Reliability Benefit 

The proposed 20 MW aggregate threshold captures a very wide range of facilities, many of which 
will have no meaningful impact on BPS reliability. NERC has not provided a technical basis for why 
a load at that level presents material risk, and the documented reliability incidents—involving load 
rejection events of 1,000 MW or more—do not support a 20 MW floor. The 1 MW computational 
load sub-threshold makes this worse: a facility with 1 MW of servers within a 20 MW footprint 
simply does not exhibit the characteristics NERC is trying to regulate. It is also important to note 
that what is observed at the point of interconnection is not the same as what is measured at the 
facility level. A load that appears behaviorally significant at the facility may present as routine 
variation at the POI on a larger system.  

Microsoft recommends that NERC either raise the thresholds to levels supported by technical 
analysis and demonstrated material impact on the Bulk Power System or simplify to a single 
Computational Load threshold that directly reflects the characteristic driving reliability risk to the 
Bulk Power System.
the Bulk Power System level, not just the size of the facility. 

Registration thresholds should reflect what is observable and meaningful at 

 
 
 
 
E.  Any New Category of Registered Entity Should Include Explicit Exclusions for Existing 

Facilities and Facilities in Advanced Design 

Facilities that are already in service, under construction, or in advanced development were 
designed and financed without any expectation of NERC registration or technical requirements, 
which may have meaningful impacts on sites that are operational or in advanced design. Applying 
new requirements to them retroactively risks stranded investment and project disruption. 
Microsoft recommends that NERC includes a clear mechanism for requesting an exemption from 
reliability standards or clear grandfathering provisions covering facilities currently in service; 
facilities under active construction; facilities in design, permitting, or procurement; and facilities 
with executed interconnection or service agreements. Where new requirements do apply, 
compliance timelines should be developed in consultation with affected entities before they are 
finalized. 

Microsoft recognizes that certain existing large computational loads may present genuine near-
term reliability risks that NERC has a legitimate interest in addressing promptly. We do not 
categorically dispute that proposition. Our concern is with the remedy, not the risk assessment. 
The proposed framework applies registration and compliance obligations broadly, without 
distinguishing between facilities that present material BPS risk and those that do not. A 500 MW 
hyperscale AI training cluster interconnected directly to the transmission system presents a 
fundamentally different risk profile than a 25 MW colocation facility serving mixed commercial 
tenants. Applying the same retroactive compliance mandates to both, on the same timeline—is not 
proportionate to the actual reliability exposure involved. 

The primary position is that any new registration requirements should apply prospectively, with 
existing and in-development facilities protected by clear grandfathering provisions. Facilities 
currently in service, under active construction, in design or procurement, or with executed 
interconnection or service agreements were designed and financed without any expectation of 
NERC registration; retroactive application risks significant stranded investment or substantive 
additional investment to bring facility into compliance. 

In the alternative, if NERC determines that some existing facilities must be brought into compliance, 
Microsoft urges that the compliance pathway be tightly calibrated to the risk each facility actually 
poses to the Bulk Power System. Obligations and timelines should reflect the facility’s size, 
interconnection voltage, load variability characteristics, and proximity to grid constraints - not a 
uniform mandate applied to every facility above a low MW threshold. This approach is consistent 
with the definitional precision we advocate in Sections B, C, and D: a framework that is 
appropriately scoped to the problem NERC has identified will be more durable, more defensible, 
and more likely to achieve its reliability objectives. 

F.  The “Point of Interconnection at ≥ 60 kV” Criterion Requires Clarification to Prevent 

Inconsistent Application 

The proposed criterion—interconnection “at a single point to the Bulk Power System at a voltage 
≥ 60 kV”—is ambiguous in common facility configurations where a step-down transformer sits 
between the load and the transmission system. A load entity could plausibly argue it interconnects 
at the lower secondary voltage and falls outside the registration threshold, even where the 
functional BPS connection is clear. NERC should close this gap by adopting language modeled on the 
existing Category 2 inverter-based resource definition, which captures facilities “connected through 

 
 
 
 
 
a system designed primarily for delivering capacity to a common point of connection at a voltage 
≥ 100 kV.” That language is already accepted by industry and regulators and would apply 
straightforwardly here.  A 100 kV threshold also aligns with NERC’s existing Bulk Electric System 
definition framework and provides greater consistency across reliability registrations. 
CONCLUSION 

Microsoft appreciates NERC’s consideration of our comments and a shared focus on addressing 
reliability issues in an expedited manner. Microsoft’s recommendations are designed to encourage 
a framework that is based on material risk, existing regulatory structures, and technical rigor. 

In summary, Microsoft respectfully recommends NERC: 

•

•

•

•

•

•

Maximize the use of existing Registered Entities to mitigate large load reliability risks, 
ensuring those entities provide the data, telemetry, and technical guidance that large load 
compliance will require; 

Expand the scope of the ROP revisions to address all large loads with material BPS impact, 
or commit to doing so in Phase 2; 

Revise the definitions of “Computational Load” and “Computational Load Entity” to reflect 
operational behavior and system impact rather than equipment type, and adopt a 
Computational Load Owner/Operator framework consistent with established NERC 
functional entity structures; 

Recalibrate the aggregate MW and Computational Load sub-thresholds upward, supported 
by clear technical analysis demonstrating material BPS impact at the selected levels; 

Include explicit grandfathering provisions covering in-service, in-construction, and in-
design facilities, as well as those with executed agreements, with realistic compliance 
timelines developed in consultation with affected entities; and 

Clarify the “point of interconnection at ≥ 60 kV” criterion using language modeled on the 
existing Category 2 IBR definition to prevent inconsistent application and registration 
avoidance, while aligning the threshold with NERC’s existing BES framework.

Background to the following comments: In PJM’s experience, many of the entities 
that build and own data centers are essentially landlords, who lease out the data 
center facility to an anchor tenant or multiple tenants. As a result, the entity that 
owns the physical facility and interfaces/contracts with the distribution utility may 
be separate and distinct from the entity that controls the computational 
equipment therein. The draft ROP changes to Appendix 5B appear to capture 
this concept better than the definition in the currently drafted Computational Load 
Standard Authorization Request1, by defining Computational Load Entity as “[t]he 
end
Computational Load.” Whichever definition is ultimately adopted, the goal should 
be the same—to provide the Regional Entity with clear authority to ensure that 
contractual relationships between the computational load and the host do not 
frustrate the Regional Entity’s ability to register the party who presents the actual 
risk to the BES.

PJM notes that the draft revisions to Appendix 5B establish that a Computational 
Load Entity will be registered only if it: 1) contributes to an aggregate connected 
Load capability greater than or equal to 20 MW; 2) at a single point of 
interconnection to the Bulk Power System at a voltage greater than or equal to 
60 kV; and 3) hosts 1 MW or greater of Computational Load. PJM recommends 
increasing the load threshold from 20 MW to 50 MW. This is the threshold by 
which PJM defines a large load and will “right size” any subsequent compliance 
obligations to avoid capturing a wide range of entities that do not present the 
same risk to BES reliability as larger data centers. Increasing this threshold will 
also permit Regional Entities to focus their resources on auditing only those 
Computational Load Entities that present the most risk to the BES, in line with the 
overall policy trajectory of the risk-based Reliability Assurance Initiative. PJM 
correspondingly recommends reducing the DP threshold to greater than 50 MW 
of peak Load that is directly connected to less than or equal to 60kV. The original 
DP threshold was 25 MW, and the threshold was increased to 75 MW in 2015 
with the aim of reducing the regulatory burden on smaller, lower-risk distribution 
systems. While this may have made sense in 2015, PJM is now dealing in real 
time with the challenges of the increased DP threshold, such as collecting IBR 
and DER data now required by MOD Standards (and soon to be TOP and IRO

Good morning,
Consumers Energy is submitting comment on the Proposed Computational Load Entity 
ROP Revisions.

Neither NERC’s Assessment of Gaps in Existing Practices, Requirements, and Reliability 
Standards for Emerging Large Load nor the findings in the NERC Aggregated Report on NERC 
Level 2 Industry Recommendation: Large Load Interconnection, Study, Commissioning, and 
Operations provide sufficient justification for establishing the proposed registration 
thresholds of an aggregate load of 20 MW with a 1 MW Computational Load component.

While NERC’s publications to date have demonstrated the potential reliability risks associated 
with large loads—particularly Computational Loads—Consumers Energy agrees that the 
creation of a new registered entity is appropriate. However, Consumers Energy does not agree 
with the proposed thresholds. Rather than defining both an aggregate load threshold and a 
Computational Load sub‑threshold, NERC should simplify the criteria by establishing a single 
threshold based on total Computational Load, as this load characteristic has been identified 
by NERC as posing the greatest potential risk to the Bulk Power System (BPS).

The Level 2 Alert report indicates that approximately 90–95 percent of existing industry-
defined large load thresholds are at or above 20 MW. However, the report does not 
demonstrate that a load at or near 20 MW, in and of itself or in reasonable local aggregation 
with similar loads, presents a material risk to BPS reliability. NERC recently revised their Rules 
or Procedure to include IBR generators 20 MW or larger interconnecting at 60 kV or higher and 
demonstrated that, in aggregate, these units could impact the BPS. Therefore, it is logical that 
NERC would propose a similar threshold for Computational Load Entities, however, NERC 
must acknowledge the fundamental difference in quantity and magnitude of interconnections 
between dispersed IBR generation resources expected to interconnect to the system and 
Computational Loads expected to interconnect to the system. Consumers Energy 
recommends that NERC consider increasing the proposed threshold to better align with 
thresholds already established—or currently being proposed—by Regional Transmission 
Organizations.

As currently defined, Consumers Energy does not believe the proposed criteria sufficiently

distinguish between traditional industrial customers with de minimis Computational Load and
entities whose primary business purpose is Computational Load. While the proposed 1 MW
Computational Load threshold may have been derived from responses to NERC’s Level 2 Alert
questionnaire, this value is unreasonably low if the intent is to capture entities whose
Computational Loads are expected to have a meaningful impact on the BPS.

If the Computational Load threshold is increased to a more appropriate level, Consumers
Energy recommends removing the proposed 60 kV voltage threshold for clarity. The reliability
gaps identified by NERC are not inherently tied to a specific interconnection voltage level, but
rather to the size and characteristics of the aggregated load. If NERC determines that retaining
a voltage threshold is necessary, Consumers Energy recommends including clarifying
language such as: “at a single point of interconnection directly to the Bulk Power System, or
through facilities primarily designed to deliver power to the Computational Load Entity from a
common point of connection, at a voltage greater than or equal to XX kV.” This clarification
would mitigate potential interpretation issues. For example, scenarios exist where the
Transmission Owner owns a networked transmission system, the Distribution Provider
interconnects one or more 138/34.5 kV transformers, and the Computational Load Entity
could assert that its facilities interconnect at 34.5 kV and are therefore exempt from
registration. Incorporating language similar to NERC’s BES Inclusion I4 would help prevent
such gaps in interpretation.

Regards,
Eric R. Sutlief

Comments on Proposed Changes to NERC Rules of Procedures Regarding 
Computational Loads 

The Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) values the opportunity to provide comments on 
proposed changes to NERC Rules of Procedures (ROP) regarding Computational Loads. 

SEIA is a trade organization of over 1,200 members in the solar PV and storage industry.  Many of 
our members are involved in creating solutions that provide electric power to Computational 
Loads. This includes solar PV and Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) which operate through 
Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs), market participation, and co-location with Computational 
Loads.  It also includes the stand-alone supply of BESS co-located with Computational Load, 
which can provide multiple value streams to Computational Load.  In addition, some members are 
evaluating if resources co-located with Computational Load can provide services to the grid. 

SEIA and its members are committed to working with NERC to maintain Bulk Power System (BPS) 
reliability.  

We offer the following comments, arranged by ROP section. 

Appendix 2 
Proposed Terminology “Computational Loads” 

As proposed, “Computational Load means Load comprised of electric power demand from 
information technology equipment, such as servers, storage, and networking hardware.”  We agree 
with NERC staff that a term other than “Large Load,” without including additional descriptors for the 
electronic loads like data centers, AI centers, and crypto-currency mining, is not a satisfactory 
term. “Large Load” also applies to large process facilities, oil and gas loads, education and medical 
campuses, pharmaceutical loads, and manufacturing loads. These large loads do not contain the 
same amount of servers, data storage, and networking equipment, nor the same operational 
characteristics as the loads which are the subject of NERC’s “Large Load Action Plan.” 

However, the term “Computational Load” to describe loads such as data centers, AI training and 
inference facilities, and cryptocurrency mining facilities may not be sufficient.  The proposed 
“Computational Load” definition includes “Load comprised of electric power demand from 
information technology equipment.” However, most Bulk Electric System (BES) loads contain a 
Computational Load component and would therefore be included in the definition, which is not the 
intention of the “Large Load Action Plan”. 

The definition also contains the term “such as servers, storage, and networking hardware.”  The 
term “such as” is non-inclusive and introduces ambiguity as to the equipment that may, or may not 
be, included in the definition. 

In addition, the term “storage” should be amended to “data storage”, to clarify that it is referring to 
information technology equipment such as Network Attached Storage (NAS), Hard Disc Drives 
(HDDs), and Solid State Devices (SSDs) and not “energy storage” such as BESS.   

May 15, 2026 | Page 1 

 Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) 

1425 K Street, NW, Suite 1000, Washington, DC | seia.org 

Furthermore, the use of “Computational” is too inclusive for some of the provided examples, 
particularly “networking hardware” and “data storage”.  These types of equipment have very 
minimum “computational” capability as compared to central processing units (CPUs) and graphical 
processing units (GPUs).   A broader term such as “electronic load” would be more appropriate for 
NERC’s definition, like ERCOT’s adoption of the term “Large Electronic Load,” which extends 
beyond purely computational activities.  Having a uniform definition across industry also facilitates 
standards and compliance activities.  Regardless of the term selected to represent computational 
loads, it also needs to be clear that Inverter-based Resources such as solar PV, battery energy 
storage systems (BESS), and modern wind turbines are not included under the term. 

Proposed Terminology “Computational Load Entity” 

As proposed, “Computational Load Entity means the end-user or the entity that hosts end-users 
that receives electric power for Computational Load.”  We believe it would be beneficial to include 
the same entity naming structure that is used for Generation and Transmission Owners and 
Operators (e.g., GO’s/GOP’s).  In many cases, data center owners and operators will be separate 
entities and could have different reliability responsibilities. 

There is some uncertainty in the phrase “end-user or the entity that hosts end-users.”  At a given 
facility, if both exist, is the Computational Load Entity inclusive of both of those parties?  Or if both 
exist, is it just the end-user with compliance obligations, and the entity that hosts the end-users 
has no compliance obligations? 

In addition, the use of “end-user” introduces some ambiguities.  Traditionally, end-user has been 
thought of as the entity which uses electricity for a given purpose.  End-users could be entities that 
are lessees of facilities in the computation load facility. Holding an end-user/lessee of 
computational facilities responsible for compliance seems to be intractable. As end-users/lessees 
rent computational capabilities, the lessees can frequently change, they could be difficult to 
identify, and there could be very large numbers of end-users who shouldn’t have any compliance 
obligations on the BPS. 

Appendix 5A 
No comments. 

Appendix 5B 
The proposed criteria is “III.c.1 Computational Load Entity that 1) contributes to an aggregate 
connected Load capability greater than or equal to 20 MW; 2) at a single point of interconnection to 
the Bulk Power System at a voltage greater than or equal to 60 kV; and 3) hosts 1 MW or greater of 
Computational Load.” 

With the proposed criteria, there is a risk that certain facilities interconnected at a single point of 
interconnection greater than 60 kV may be required to register even though they do not pose a risk 
to the BPS. For example, if a manufacturing facility is 75 MWs, and has 1 MW of Computational 
Load at the facilities (used in servers for process control, data storage, personal computers, PLC’s, 
RTU’s, routers, etc.), that facility would need to be registered, even though it does not pose the 

May 15, 2026 | Page 2                                                                             Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) 

1425 K Street, NW, Suite 1000, Washington, DC | seia.org 

 
 
 
 
 
same operational characteristics and risks that were identified in the NERC white papers, alerts 
and guidelines. 

The 1 MW of Computational Load compared to 20 MW of aggregate load is 5%.  As the aggregate 
load becomes larger, the percentage of computational load that would be subject to the criteria is 
reduced, as shown by the example above. Other entities have proposed higher percentages, 
reflective of the risk on the BPS.  For example, ERCOT’s proposed definition of Large Electronic Load 
in NPRR 1308 is “A Large Load in which 50% or greater of the Demand at the site consists of power 
electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and cryptocurrency 
mining facilities,” and the accompanying definition of Large Load is “One or more Facilities at a 
single site with an aggregate peak Demand greater than or equal to 75 MW behind one or more 
common Points of Interconnection (POIs) or Service Delivery Points.” 

As NERC develops reliability standards for all North America, it should establish minimum 
acceptable requirements, which would support significantly higher percentage thresholds of 
computational loads. Having computational loads which are 5% or lower of the total aggregate 
demand is not reflective of the minimum acceptable level of requirements consistent with some 
ISOs/RTOs.  While we understand that FERC mandated loads greater than 20 MW in their ANOPR, 
we believe this definition requires further discussion.  It is suggested that NERC leverage the 
LLWG’s conclusions to date to develop load criteria aligned with actual reliability risk, while 
permitting transmission entities to adopt more stringent requirements, if appropriate for their 
systems.
