Trade Association’s Comments on Proposed Revisions  
to NERC Rules of Procedure: Computational Loads 

Trade Associations Comments 

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the draft proposed revisions to the North American 
Electric Reliability Corporation’s (NERC) Rules of Procedure (ROP) on the registration of large 
computational loads. The Trade Associations,1 on behalf of their members, support NERC’s 
objective of protecting the bulk electric system from reliability risks associated with large 
computational loads. The Trades understand there are various considerations needed in developing 
registration criteria and mechanisms for the owners and operators of computational loads.  

To achieve our shared objective, the Trade Associations provide these comments in four parts: 

I. 

II. 

III. 

IV. 

Overarching Principles: We describe core principles that form the basis for our 
proposed and alternative solutions in sections II and III, as well as our comments to 
NERC’s proposal in section IV. We urge NERC to consider these principles when drafting 
the registration criteria for new entities.  

Proposed Solution: We propose changes to deﬁnitions and registration criteria that 
focus on the highest priority risks. 

Alternative Solution: We propose alternate deﬁnitions and registration criteria that 
would deﬁne two categories of large computational loads. 

Comments with NERC’s Proposal: If NERC does not accept the Trade Associations’’ 
proposed or alternative solutions, we describe the concerns we have with NERC’s draft 
proposal that we urge NERC to address. 

I. 

OVERARCHING PRINCIPLES 

DATA CENTER REGISTRATION SHOULD BE RISK-BASED. 
Treating different-sized facilities the same would depart from NERC’s longstanding risk-based 
approach to registration. Registration criteria should focus on the loads most likely to have a 
material impact on bulk electric system (BES) reliability and should avoid imposing unnecessary 
compliance obligations on facilities that do not present comparable reliability risks. 

1 The Trade Associations are the: American Public Power Association (APPA), Edison Electric Institute (EEI), 
Large Public Power Council (LPPC), National Rural Electric Cooperative Association (NRECA), Transmission 
Access Policy Study Group (TAPS), and the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners 
(NARUC) as a member association. 

1 

 
 
 
 
 
 
Trade Association’s Comments on Proposed Revisions  
to NERC Rules of Procedure: Computational Loads 

THE DEFINITION SHOULD CAPTURE LARGE DATA CENTERS AND CRYPTO MINES BUT NOT 
CAPTURE TRADITIONAL COMMERCIAL OR INDUSTRIAL LOADS.  
The registration criteria should focus on the category of large computational loads that NERC has 
identiﬁed as potentially presenting material reliability risks. They should not inadvertently capture 
traditional commercial or industrial loads that contain information technology equipment but do 
not operate primarily as computational load facilities, because such loads do not pose material risk 
to the BES. 

For example, large office buildings with server rooms, defense infrastructure (e.g., the Pentagon), 
and industrial facilities (e.g., aluminum smelters or automobile manufacturing plants) should not 
be registered merely because they use servers, storage, networking hardware, or other information 
technology equipment in support of their ordinary operations. The criteria should distinguish 
facilities whose primary load characteristics raise the reliability concerns identiﬁed by NERC from 
facilities that use information technology equipment only as an incidental part of a broader 
commercial or industrial process. 

RESPONSIBILITY FOR IDENTIFYING NEWLY REGISTERED ENTITIES SHOULD NOT FALL ON 
EXISTING REGISTERED ENTITIES. 
Transmission Owners (TO), Transmission Operators (TOP), Transmission Planners (TP), Distribution 
Providers (DP), and other existing registered entities do not always have—and may lack legal 
authority to obtain—the information necessary to determine whether a particular customer meets 
the criteria for registration as a computational load owner or operator. NERC and the Regional 
Entities should therefore retain responsibility for identifying large computational loads that may 
meet the registration criteria. 

The registration framework should not impose new, open-ended data collection obligations on 
existing registered entities or require them to determine whether a customer’s facilities meet the 
proposed computational load criteria. Existing registered entities may have relevant system 
information, but they should not become the default mechanism for identifying, classifying, or 
certifying customers for registration. 

NEW REGISTRATION CRITERIA SHOULD NOT CREATE COMPLIANCE OBLIGATIONS FOR SMALL 
DISTRIBUTION UTILITIES OR RESULT IN CHANGES TO THE DEFINITION OF BULK ELECTRIC 
SYSTEM. 
Any new registration criteria for large computational load should not directly or indirectly change 
the criteria for registering distribution providers, nor should it result in changes to the BES 
deﬁnition. For example, if a large computational load interconnects to a non-BES line, that should 
not inadvertently convert that line into a BES facility and cause the owner of that facility to become 
a Transmission Owner.  

2 

 
 
 
 
 
Trade Association’s Comments on Proposed Revisions  
to NERC Rules of Procedure: Computational Loads 

II. 

TRADE ASSOCIATIONS’ PROPOSED SOLUTION 

The Trade Associations propose that NERC deﬁne computational load facilities as facilities with at 
least 75 megawatts (MW) of computational load connected at 100 kilovolts (kV)2 or higher, and that 
NERC register the owners (e.g., the landlords) and operators of the computational load facilities.  

CONSISTENT WITH OTHER REGISTRATION CATEGORIES, NERC SHOULD DEFINE FACILITIES 
AND THEN REGISTER THE OWNERS AND OPERATORS OF THOSE FACILITIES. 
A. Add a deﬁnition of “Computational Load Facility”: A clear deﬁnition of a Computational Load 
Facility is essential for Project 2026-02 success. Existing standards that currently address the same 
types of essential actions being proposed for data centers but are applicable to other comparable 
equipment (like generators) consistently rely on a Facility-type deﬁnition. This is consistent with 
how Generator Owner/Operator and Generating Facility are treated, deﬁned, and included in the 
registration criteria. 

Data center sites can have a signiﬁcant number of physical and electrical conﬁgurations. For 
example, many data center sites can consist of one or more buildings, with each building having 
one or more connections to the Bulk Power System (BPS) at the same location. In some cases, data 
center owners may consider that each building is an individual data center, while in other cases the 
collection of buildings connected to the grid is viewed as the data center. The risk to the BES comes 
from the aggregate load behavior of facilities at a single site. This was emphasized in NERC’s 
“Characteristics and Risks of Emerging Large Loads” whitepaper that, while speciﬁc load types and 
thresholds to deﬁne large loads could not be deﬁned across industry at that time, all agreed that 
any such deﬁnition should include “aggregation of load facilities at a single site behind one or more 
point(s) of interconnection that can pose reliability risks to the BPS.”   

We therefore recommend the following deﬁnition of “Computational Load Facility” – A  
collection of electrical equipment located at one or more buildings, structures, or installations that 
is designed to receive power, has an aggregate connected maximum peak demand of 
Computational Load greater than or equal to 75 MW, and is served through electric facilities at a 
voltage level greater than or equal to 100 kV from one or more points of connection. 

B. Replace “Computational Load Entity” with “Computational Load Owner” and “Computational 
Load Operator” or alternatively make changes to “Computational Load Entity.” 

The Trade Associations recommend that the Computational Load Entity deﬁnition be replaced with 
new deﬁnitions that align with the “Owner” and “Operator” Model currently in place in the NERC 
Rules of Procedure for registration criteria. Today we have registration criteria for TO, TOP, Generator 
Owner (GO), and Generator Operator (GOP). This structure is in place because for transmission and 
generation facilities, there are often situations that occur where the owner of the facilities is 

2 NARUC’s position is 115kV or higher as opposed to 100kV or higher. 

3 

 
 
 
 
 
 
Trade Association’s Comments on Proposed Revisions  
to NERC Rules of Procedure: Computational Loads 

different from the operator of the facilities. This registration criteria set up allows different entities 
to be responsible only for the activities for which they are contractually obligated as the owner 
and/or operator. For Computational Load Facilities, these facilities have the same type of structure. 
There are many cases where the owner is different from the operator.  

Therefore, because of the actual structure of the facilities, and to align with existing NERC 
registration criteria, the Trade Associations recommend replacing the Computational Load Entity 
deﬁnition with Computational Load Owner and Computational Load Operator, with proposed 
deﬁnitions for each included below. 

“Computational Load Owner” means the end-user entity that owns and maintains a 
Computational Load Facility, and/or the entity that owns and maintains a Computational Load 
Facility that hosts end-users that receives electric power at a Computational Load Facility. 

“Computational Load Operator” means the end-user entity that operates a Computational Load 
Facility, and/or the entity that operates a Computational Load Facility that hosts end-users that 
receives electric power at a Computational Load Facility. 

However, as discussed in more detail below, if NERC staff retains only one registered entity, the 
Trade Associations suggest the following modiﬁcations to the Computational Load Entity deﬁnition: 

“Computational Load Entity” means the end-user and/or the entity that hosts end-users that 
receives electric power for at a Computational Load Facility. 

The risk to the BPS and the gaps in NERC’s reliability standards, as noted in NERC’s “Assessment of 
Gaps in Existing Practices, Requirements, and Reliability Standards for Emerging Large Loads” are 
driven by computational load impacts and behavior, not other type of loads, so the Computational 
Load Entity deﬁnition should focus only on the amount of data-centric/information technology type 
of load. 

COMPUTATIONAL LOADS SHOULD BE DEFINED AS LOADS MADE UP PRIMARILY OF POWER 
ELECTRONICS-BASED INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY EQUIPMENT. 
Clarify the Computational Load deﬁnition: The Trade Associations recommend that the proposed 
Computational Load deﬁnition focus on the power electronic-based information technology 
equipment, which is the focus of the risks to the BPS as documented by NERC’s Large Loads Task 
Force and Large Loads Working Group. 

NERC’s “Assessment of Gaps in Existing Practices, Requirements, and Reliability Standards for 
Emerging Large Loads” identiﬁes risks associated with the behavior and impacts of computational 
loads. Those risks arise from the data-centric and information technology characteristics of the 
load, not from unrelated load at the same site. The deﬁnition should therefore focus only on the 
amount of computational load and should not sweep in other types of loads that do not raise the 
same reliability concerns. 

4 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Trade Association’s Comments on Proposed Revisions  
to NERC Rules of Procedure: Computational Loads 

Therefore, we urge NERC to update it as follows: “Computational Load” means Load comprised 
primarily of electric power demand from power electronic-based information technology 
equipment.  

THE REGISTRATION THRESHOLD SHOULD BE SET TO 75 MW/100 KV. 
The Trade Associations recommend that NERC revise the proposed thresholds in Appendix 5B. The 
proposed 20 MW/60 kV threshold with the 1MW Computational Load criteria is set unnecessarily 
low and sweeps in a substantial number of facilities that pose no material impact to the reliability of 
the BPS and, thus, does not justify the burden of NERC registration. The current Rules of Procedure, 
Registration, and Standard Drafting efforts related to Computational Loads should focus on those 
loads that pose the most meaningful risk to the BPS. The threshold criteria (20 MW, 60 kV) is too low 
and we recommend the threshold be set to 75 MW connected at >= 100kV for Computational Load 
Facilities, consistent with the NERC BES deﬁnition for dispersed power producing resources (i.e., 
inverter-based resources) – where the current criteria is greater than 75 mega volt amperes (MVA) at 
a common point of connection at >= 100kV is utilized. 

Although NERC has developed a Technical Reasoning Proposed Computational Load document, it 
does not provide sufficient explanation or practical examples to justify the selected thresholds in 
the proposed registration criteria. The Trade Associations are concerned that NERC’s proposed 
approach could inadvertently create compliance obligations for DP entities by effectively deeming 
them TO or TOP. It is critical to ensure that DP do not lose the radial system exemption when solely 
serving load and not operating transmission facilities. Clear justiﬁcation and reﬁnement of the 
proposed thresholds are required to demonstrate that there are identiﬁable and material risks to 
the BES. 

In addition, NERC’s “Characteristics and Risks of Emerging Large Loads” indicated that “most of the 
survey respondents qualiﬁed ‘large’ as greater than 50 MW, and the single size number most 
commonly suggested was 75 MW,” and the NERC Alert 2 results conﬁrmed this. NERC’s 
“Assessment of Gaps in Existing Practices, Requirements, and Reliability Standards for Emerging 
Large Loads” references the ﬁrst Whitepaper and in the deﬁnition section, and focuses on really 
large loads and how several smaller loads (still much bigger than 20 MW) are not as big of a risk. 
“The potential impact of several 100 MW loads may be less than the impact of a 500 MW load and 
may require different treatment.” 

Furthermore, NERC’s “Ten benchmarks of an Effective Reliability Standard” white paper 
emphasizes that “each [NERC reliability standard] requirement is ‘not a lowest common 
denominator’ exercise but instead achieves an objective that is the best approach for bulk power 
system reliability.” The same applies to deﬁnitions and reliability criteria. NERC’s decision to select 
20 MW appears to be a “lowest common denominator” choice, instead of a higher value that the 
majority of the industry agrees with.  

5 

 
 
 
 
 
Trade Association’s Comments on Proposed Revisions  
to NERC Rules of Procedure: Computational Loads 

The Trade Associations recommend NERC adopt an initial threshold of 75 MW at a common point 
of connection of 100 kV or higher. This pairing adheres to the current BES deﬁnition and 
appropriately balances reliability risk to compliance burden. A 75 MW/100 kV starting point focuses 
computational load entity registration on the facilities most likely to have a material impact on BPS 
reliability. It would also give NERC and the Regional Entities time to identify entities for registration, 
develop reliability standards, and gain compliance oversight experience with a manageable 
population. Further, it avoids imposing new obligations on facilities whose individual contribution 
to reliability risk is limited.   

III. 

TRADE ASSOCIATIONS’ ALTERNATIVE PROPOSAL 

As an alternative, the Trade Associations recommend that NERC adopt an approach that mirrors 
the Category 1 and Category 2 Generator Owner and Generator Operator deﬁnitions adopted as 
part of NERC’s Inverter-Based Resources Registration Initiative. 

THE NEW REGISTRATION FRAMEWORK SHOULD STILL DEFINE FACILITIES AND THEN 
REGISTER THE OWNERS AND OPERATORS OF THOSE FACILITIES. 
As with our primary proposal, our alternative proposal retains the structure of deﬁning 
Computational Load Facilities and registering the owners and operators of those facilities. 

THE NEW REGISTRATION SHOULD CONSIST OF TWO CATEGORIES OF COMPUTATIONAL LOAD 
OWNERS AND OPERATORS. 
If a threshold lower than 75 MW is deemed necessary by NERC staff, the Trade Associations 
recommend that NERC staff enhance the Technical Reasoning document to reﬂect the 
analysis/evidence demonstrating the lower facility threshold is needed for BPS reliability. In 
addition, in this scenario, the Trade Associations also recommend that NERC staff adopt the same 
registration criteria model that was developed for inverter-based resources with the Category 1 
GO/GOP and Category 2 GO/GOP. NERC should create a new Category 1 Computational Load 
Owner/Operator (CLO/CLOP) and Category 2 CLO/CLOP deﬁnitions, and structure the MW and 
voltage criteria for each to align with the Category 1 GO/GOP and Category 2 GO/GOP. 

With NERC expected to address computational load risk on an accelerated timeline by the end of 
2026, this structure would allow ERO Enterpriseto focus its initial entity registration, standards 
development efforts, and compliance education activities on the highest-risk CLOs/CLOPs ﬁrst. 
This framework also establishes a more manageable path to subsequently address lower-risk 
Category 2 CLOs/CLOPs in future work phases. Finally, this structure would enable a risk-based 
compliance approach by allowing more stringent reliability and security requirements to be applied 
to Category 1 CLOs/CLOPs compared to Category 2 CLOs/CLOPs. 

Under this alternative structure, the following deﬁnitions are proposed: 

6 

 
 
 
 
 
Trade Association’s Comments on Proposed Revisions  
to NERC Rules of Procedure: Computational Loads 

“Computational Load Facility” means a collection of electrical equipment located at one or more 
buildings, structures, or installations that is designed to receive power, is served through electric 
facilities from one or more points of connection and meets the criteria in either Category 1 or 
Category 2 Computational Load Owner/Operator registration categories. 

“Category 1 CLO/CLOP” should be aligned with the BES criteria, which would be entities who 
own/operate Computational Load Facilities (CLFs) that are >= 75 MW of Computational Load 
connected at >= 100kV. 

“Category 2 CLO/CLOP” should be aligned with the lower threshold value supported by NERC and 
industry, which would be entities who own/operator Computational Load Facilities that are >= 20 
MW of Computational Load connected at >= 60kV. 

IV.  COMMENTS ON NERC’S PROPOSED REVISIONS 

As noted earlier, the Trade Associations have several concerns with NERC’s proposed revisions to 
the Rules of Procedure. If, however, NERC declines to adopt either solution, and proceeds with the 
approach in the April 1, 2026, draft, we urge NERC to address the following concerns before 
ﬁnalizing any revisions. 

REPLACE “CAPABILITY” WITH “MAXIMUM PEAK DEMAND.”   
The draft Computational Load Entity registry criteria use the word “capability,” which can be 
interpreted as the maximum load of a Computational Load Facility (CLF). For example, if the CLF 
facility has a maximum possible load demand of 100 MW, then this is the load “capability” of the 
CLF. However, this “capability” term as used with load is likely not widely understood or utilized 
today. 

We recommend an alternative to the use of “capability” such as “maximum peak demand” of a 
facility to be clearer. In addition, evaluating a CLF’s impact on the BES should not rely solely on its 
size. Incorporating operational characteristics, such as interruptibility, load ﬂexibility, and the 
availability of on-site or contracted backup generation, will provide a more comprehensive and 
accurate assessment of system impacts. 

CLARIFY HOW “POINT OF INTERCONNECTION” APPLIES TO LARGE COMPUTATIONAL LOADS. 
The proposed registration criteria include a reference to a “point of interconnection” at 60 kV. “Point 
of interconnection” is primarily a term referring to generation interconnections – interconnections 
that most often rely on one generating tie-line. Data centers often have many connections to the 
BPS at the same location. The ownership of equipment can also vary site to site, in which some 
connect to utilities directly at the high voltage kV bus by owning the high-voltage transformation, 
while others do not own the transformation or equipment greater than 60 kV. 

7 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Trade Association’s Comments on Proposed Revisions  
to NERC Rules of Procedure: Computational Loads 

CLARIFY HOW TOTAL AGGREGATE LOAD WILL BE CALCULATED. 
NERC’s current proposed Computational Load Entity registration criteria would register an entity 
that “contributes to an aggregate connected Load capability” f 20MW or greater. How will NERC 
determine the amount of Computational Load or the amount of aggregate connected load 
thresholds? Will it be based on the “nameplate” of the various racks in a data center warehouse or 
some other methodology? Regardless of the method(s) for determining these values, the Trade 
Associations recommend that this should be conﬁrmed between the CLE and its Regional Entity 
and NERC should not be dependent on other registered entities for providing this information to 
Regional Entities. Critically this criteria state load, not Computational Load.  The Trade Associations 
believe this is incorrect and should be updated to state “Computational Load capability.” In our 
proposed Computational Load Facility deﬁnition, we have included the use of Computational Load 
in the deﬁnition so that the focus is only on data-centric/information technology load. 

NERC should also clarify how it will calculate the relevant load quantity. For example, NERC should 
explain whether the calculation will rely on the nameplate rating of server racks or other equipment, 
contract demand, projected maximum peak demand, measured demand, or another methodology. 
Clear rules will reduce uncertainty and improve consistency across regions. 

THE 1 MW THRESHOLD SHOULD BE ELIMINATED. 
It is unclear how, in NERC’s April 1 proposal, a Computational Load is fundamentally different from 
other large traditional loads, such as steel mills, food processors, or automobile manufacturers. All 
large loads must be studied to ensure their interconnection and operation do not create grid 
reliability issues. There is concern that, as written, it may capture facilities that are not data centers 
or cryptocurrency mining operations, which are the business types that NERC has identiﬁed as 
potentially impacting the reliability of the BES. For example, many industrial and commercial 
facilities may operate more than 1 MW of information technology equipment (either now or in the 
future), such as servers, storage, and networking hardware to control and support processes, yet 
these are not solely or primarily computational in nature. In addition, it seems unreasonable that 
the loss of a 1 MW load, regardless of load type, would have a signiﬁcant impact on the BES, 
therefore including a de minimis criteria of 1 MW of Computational Load drives signiﬁcant 
confusion, pulls in a signiﬁcant number of entities unnecessarily, and has no justiﬁcation pertaining 
to actual risk to the BPS. The 1 MW de minimis threshold conﬂicts with the material impact 
standard applied throughout Appendix 5B and would expand registration beyond entities capable of 
materially impacting BPS reliability. The 1 MW de minimis threshold should be removed from the 
Computational Load threshold. 

THE TERM “ENTITIES THAT HOST END-USERS” IS UNCLEAR AND SHOULD BE REPLACED. 
The proposed materials use the phrase “entities that host end-users.” That phrase appears 
intended to address data center owners or landlords that host tenants. But the phrase could also 
be read more broadly. 

8 

 
 
 
 
 
Trade Association’s Comments on Proposed Revisions  
to NERC Rules of Procedure: Computational Loads 

For example, a distribution utility may own a substation that serves 20 MW of load, including a 
credit card processing facility with 2 MW of servers. In that circumstance, the distribution utility 
could be described as “hosting” the load on its system, even though it does not own or operate the 
computational load facility. The registration criteria should not create that result. 

NERC should replace or clarify the phrase “entities that host end-users” to ensure that it does not 
include distribution utilities, retail service utilities, TO, TOP, TP, or DP that merely serve, study, or 
interconnect computational load facilities. The registered entity should be the entity that owns or 
operates the Computational Load Facility, not the utility that provides electric service to it. 

As noted above, the Trades suggest the following language to address the concern: 

“Computational Load Entity” means the end-user and/or the entity that hosts end-users that 
receives electric power for at a Computational Load Facility. 

ADDITIONAL TRADE ASSOCIATIONS QUESTIONS REGARDING NERC’S 
APRIL 1 PROPOSAL 

To build on the concerns shared and the alternatives provided the Trade Associations ask the 
following questions 

•  “How will a Computational Load Entity(ies) be identiﬁed for registration under the 

proposed framework?”   

•  Will the TO, TOP, or TP be responsible for identifying this/these load(s) and sharing 

that information with their Regional Entity?  

•  Additionally, will responses to the NERC Level 3 Alert on Computational Loads be 

used to inform or determine registration requirements?   

In addressing these questions, the Trade Associations recommend that the identiﬁcation CLEs for 
potential registration should be the responsibility of the Regional Entity and NERC should not be 
dependent on other registered entities for providing this information to Regional Entities. 

CONSIDER AN EXCEPTION PROCESS FOR LARGE COMPUTATIONAL LOADS THAT MEET THE 
CRITERIA BUT CAN BE SHOWN NOT TO HAVE A MATERIAL IMPACT ON THE BULK ELECTRIC 
SYSTEM. 

Brightline Criteria  
Computational Load Entity (CLE) registration should be based on clear, brightline criteria coupled 
with a formal exception process similar to the BES deﬁnition framework. Such an approach would 
allow an entity to demonstrate, through documented technical justiﬁcation, that its facilities do not 
have a material impact on the BES. This balance is necessary to ensure that registration and 
compliance obligations are applied only where there is a substantiated reliability risk, while 

9 

 
 
 
 
 
 
Trade Association’s Comments on Proposed Revisions  
to NERC Rules of Procedure: Computational Loads 

avoiding unnecessary regulatory burden for entities whose operations do not pose a material threat 
to BES reliability. 

NERC SHOULD DEVELOP A REFERENCE DOCUMENT. 
The proposed criteria raise practical questions about how facility topology and interconnection 
conﬁgurations will affect registration. NERC should develop a reference document addressing the 
new registration criteria. The document should give industry and the drafting team a clear 
opportunity to review how NERC and the Regional Entities expect to apply the criteria. That 
reference document would promote consistent implementation and reduce the risk of unintended 
consequences. 

CANDIDATES MUST MEET ALL CRITERIA TO BE REGISTERED. 
The Trade Associations also note that NERC's document “Summary of Revisions” states candidates 
for Computational Load registration must meet all the criteria in the proposed revisions in Appendix 
5B to be registered as a Computational Load Entity; however, that is not explicitly stated in the 
proposed changes in Appendix 5B and should be stated.

The American  Chemistry  Council  (ACC)1  appreciates  the  opportunity  to  provide  input  on  the 
proposed  revisions  to  the  North  American  Energy  Reliability  Corporation  (NERC)  Rules  of 
Procedures (ROP) to create a new category of registered customer entities, “Computational Load 
Entities,” and associated reliability considerations on the Bulk Power System (BPS). ACC and our 
members  recognize  the  essential  role  NERC  plays  in  ensuring  the  reliability  of  America's 
electricity grid and chemical sector's continuous access to affordable and reliable industrial power. 
NERC's  leadership  is  more  important  than  ever  during  this  pivotal  period  of  rising  demand, 
evolving load and generation characteristics, and the need for rapid deployment of critical energy 
infrastructure.  

ACC represents a diverse set of companies engaged in the business of chemistry, a $673 billion 
enterprise.  The  chemical  manufacturing  industry  is  an  energy  intensive  and  trade  exposed 
cornerstone of American competitiveness, national security, and technological innovation. ACC’s 
members produce a wide variety of chemicals, polymers, and related products that make modern 
life safer, more productive, and more sustainable, supporting over 25 percent of U.S. GDP and 
directly touching nearly all manufactured goods. As a foundational sector of the U.S. economy, 
the  chemical  industry  plays  a  critical  role  in  enabling  domestic  manufacturing,  supply  chain 
resilience, and long-term economic growth.

COMMENTS OF THE AMERICAN CHEMISTRY COUNCIL 
NERC RULES OF PROCEDURES (ROP)
MAY 22, 2026

While  ACC’s  membership  is  diverse,  our  members  share  one  common  characteristic:  heavy 
reliance on reliable, around the clock, affordable energy inputs to drive operations and thermally 
intensive  processes  and,  in  many  cases,  to  serve  as  essential  chemical  feedstocks.  Chemical 
manufacturing  accounts  for  approximately  40  percent  of  industrial  sector  energy  consumption, 
including 20 percent of electricity, 42 percent of natural gas, and 56 percent of purchased steam. 
Over  the  past  15  years,  the  U.S.  chemical  sector  has  become  a  global  leader  in  manufacturing 
competitiveness,  driven  in  significant  part  by  access  to  abundant  and  reliable  energy  supplies, 
including electricity.  

As NERC, its regional partners, and states address the infrastructure and reliability foundations 
needed to support hyperscale computational load and other sources of demand growth, ACC urges 
careful  consideration  of  how  resulting  policies  could  intentionally  or  unintentionally  affect  the 
competitiveness  of American  industrial  customers  and  lead  to  outcomes  that  put  customers  at 
greater financial and compliance risk without achieving commensurate reliability protections. 

ACC offers the following recommendations, beginning with considerations that would be essential 
under any potential path forward, followed by concerns regarding process and statutory authority, 
with a focus on avoiding unintended expansion of regulatory scope and protecting energy‑intensive 
industrial customers from disproportionate impacts. 

Should NERC elect to proceed with regulating electricity customers in any manner, such policy 
should incorporate clear guardrails and limitations. Definitions and registration criteria must be 
narrowly  and  precisely  drawn  to  avoid  inadvertent  overlap  with  traditional  industrial  and 
manufacturing loads and incorporate an explicit limiting principle confirming that the action is not 
intended to establish a precedent or pathway for future expansion of NERC authority to other end 
use  customer  groups. Absent  such  clarity  and  constraints,  the  risk  of  unintended  scope  creep, 
regulatory uncertainty, and collateral impacts on energy intensive industries that may not present 
the same reliability considerations for the BPS would be substantial. 

More fundamentally, ACC urges NERC to reconsider the premise of the proposed Computational 
Load  Entity  ROP  Revisions,  which  would  expand  mandatory  reliability  registration  and 
compliance obligations to end use customer groups. Such an expansion would be unprecedented, 
raising serious questions  regarding the scope and intended reach of Section 215 of the Federal 
Power Act. Extending NERC’s regulatory scope in this manner would introduce a new layer of 
regulatory burden by shifting or diffusing responsibility away from existing registered entities—
those with operational control of the bulk power system, established protocols, and the technical 
workforce  necessary  to  execute  reliability  obligations—toward  users  that  generally  lack  the 
specialized  expertise,  staffing,  systems  visibility,  and  compliance  infrastructure  to  assume  grid 
reliability functions.  

Finally, given the novel expansion of NERC’s regulatory scope, its implications for the scope of 
NERC’s authority under Section 215 of the Federal Power Act, and the resulting application to 
industries not previously subject to NERC oversight, ACC would recommend, NERC expand its 

2

formal  public  consultation  process  and  conduct  a  robust  regulatory  and  economic  impact 
assessment,  consistent  with  the  level  of  scrutiny  that  would  accompany  any  other  significant 
federal regulatory action. That process should include broad outreach to both computational load 
customers and other large-load industries potentially affected by future efforts to register end-use

Consideration of Comments – ROP Appendices 2, 5A, and 5B Revisions (August 2026) 
v 

 
 
 
Summary of Proposed Revisions Posted for Comment 
The following section summarizes the proposed revisions to the NERC Rules of Procedure posted for comment from April 1-May 15, 2026 regarding registry 
criteria  for  computational  loads.  In  response  to  comments,  NERC  is  posting  further  revisions  to  the  proposed  criteria  as  described  in  the  response  to 
comments and is providing this summary on the original proposed language commenters reviewed for convenience. 

NERC Rules of Procedure Appendix 2 – Definitions Used in the Rules of Procedure 
Appendix 2 to the NERC Rules of Procedure includes defined terms used throughout the Rules of Procedure. The proposed revisions add the following 
two terms and definitions:   

• 

• 

“Computational Load means Load comprised of electric power demand from information technology equipment, such as servers, storage, and 
networking hardware.” 

“Computational Load Entity means the end-user or the entity that hosts end-users that receives electric power for Computational Load.” 

NERC Rules of Procedure Appendix 5A – Organization Registration and Certification Manual 
Appendix 5A contains the process used by NERC and the Regional Entities to register certain functional entity types to which mandatory and enforceable 
Reliability Standards apply. The proposed revisions to Appendix 5A added “Computational Load Entity (CLE)” as a type of entity that is required to register 
on the NERC Compliance Registry. In addition, proposed revisions to Appendix 5A include minor administrative corrections. 

NERC Rules of Procedure Appendix 5B – Statement of Compliance Registry Criteria 
Appendix 5B contains the specific criteria NERC and the Regional Entities use to identify which organizations may be candidates for registration for 
functional entity types. In accordance with the Federal Power Act, NERC must identify the owners, operators, and users of the Bulk Power System (BPS) 
who have a material impact on the BPS. To that end, the proposed revisions in Appendix 5B added threshold criteria to identify those organizations that 
should be registered as Computational Load Entities, summarized below:  

1. A Computational Load Entity must be the end-user or the entity that hosts end-users that receives electric power for Computational Load; and  

2. A Computational Load Entity that 1) contributes to an aggregate connected Load capability greater than or equal to 20 MW; 2) at a single point of 
interconnection to the Bulk Power System at a voltage greater than or equal to 60 kV; and 3) hosts 1 MW or greater of Computational Load.  

Candidates must meet all the criteria in the proposed revisions in Appendix 5B in order to be registered as a Computational Load Entity.

Comments  
The following section provides a summary of issues raised in stakeholder comments along with NERC’s response.  

Definitions 

Summary of Stakeholder Comments 

Several commenters recommended NERC use a definition of 
Computational Load Facility to clarify what sort of “site” owners or 
operators are subject to registration. Commenters note this definition 
would assist in the standards development project addressing 
computational loads. Some commenters provided a proposed definition 
for consideration: “Computational Load Facility means a collection of 
electrical equipment located at one or more buildings, structures, or 
installations that is designed to receive power, has an aggregate 
connected maximum peak demand of Computational Load greater than 
or equal to 75 MW, and is served through electric facilities at a voltage 
level greater than or equal to 100 kV from one or more points of 
connection.” Others suggested borrowing concepts FERC uses in 
implementing PURPA through use of the “one-mile” rule to better 
define sites.

Response  
NERC  agrees  that  defining  the  composition  of  a  site 
provides  clarity  to  the  registry  criteria  for  the  owner 
and operator entities that must register. 
Accordingly, NERC is proposing a definition of 
“Computational Load Site.” The proposed definition 
does not include the word “Facility” as proposed by 
some commenters because NERC determined that 
using such a term could lead to confusion. For 
example, a “Computational Load Facility” would 
include the term “Facility”, which is associated with 
Bulk Electric System (BES) Elements, a narrowly 
defined subset of the BPS. In addition, NERC 
determined that the Computational Load Site 
definition does not need the numerical thresholds for 
MW and kV because those will be in the registry 
criteria only, whereas the Computational Load Site 
definition can also be used by the standard drafting 
team in the proposed Reliability Standards. This 
ensures alignment across ROP terms and NERC 
Glossary terms while maintaining registry thresholds 
in the ROP only. See the revised ROP Appendix 2 
posted for comment for the proposed “Computational 
Load Site” definition.

Summary of Stakeholder Comments 
Some commenters suggested that Computational Load definition needs 
clarification on its scope as it may include unintended entities or 
information technology infrastructure. Some commenters suggest it to 
mean “Load comprised primarily of electric power demand from power 
electronic-based information technology equipment.” Other 
commenters noted that some terms used in the definition created 
ambiguity, such as “storage” instead of “data storage” or the use of 
“such as.” Other commenters suggested creating a “volatile loads” 
definition instead of Computational Load. Others suggested 
“Computational Load” means “Load that uses electric power for 
equipment needed for operation of computers or computer programs. 
Examples of such equipment include, but are not limited to, processors, 
memory, data storage devices, and networking equipment.” Others note 
that “electronic load” may be a better description. 

Response  

NERC determined that with the use of the newly 
proposed Computational Load Site definition, the 
definition of Computational Load is no longer needed 
for registry criteria purposes. Where appropriate, 
NERC considered applying the proposals from the 
comments on the Computational Load definition to 
other components of the revised proposed criteria. 
For instance, the use of “primarily” as suggested by 
some commenters in the Computational Load 
definition is now used in the proposed definition of 
Computational Load Site.

Summary of Stakeholder Comments 
Some commenters proposed that Computational Load Entity should be 
Computational Load Owner and Computational Load Operator. Other 
commenters suggested further clarity or guidance on which end-users, 
particularly in a multitenant situation, would be registered as the 
Computational Load Entity. Others suggested to clarify that 
Computational Load Entities are “operators of the facility” that uses 
power for Computational Load. Others suggested clarifying that the 
Load “aggregates” at a point of interconnection “or substation.” 

Response  

NERC agrees that two functions provide more clarity 
on the types of entities subject to registration. 
Accordingly, NERC changed the proposed functional 
entity from “Computational Load Entity” to 
“Computational Load Owner” (CLO) and 
“Computational Load Operator” (CLOP). Additionally, 
NERC removed references to “end-user or entity that 
hosts end-users” from the functional registrations as 
the two separate functions address differing 
organizational arrangements more clearly.

same objective by ensuring those with a small amount 
of computational load that do not pose the same 
impact are not included in the registry criteria through 
a focus on indicating the site “primarily” contains IT 
infrastructure.

definitions.

to refine its understanding of the aggregate risks 
associated with data center sites and clusters 
connected throughout the BPS. As a result, NERC 
determined that the threshold could be raised to 50 
MW.

During registration, NERC should capture a “class descriptor” of the type

Response  
NERC revised the proposed criteria to clarify that large 
industrial or commercial loads historically have not 
posed a material impact to the BPS, such as 
manufacturing facilities or large hospitals, are not 
included. Clarity is accomplished through the removal 
of the term “Computational Load” and the required 1 
MW “de minimus” amount and the addition of the 
Computational Load Site term, which includes the 
word “primarily” to indicate the use of the IT 
infrastructure at the site. Therefore, entities that have 
computational load but are not “primarily” performing 
computational activities do not meet the proposed 
registry criteria. While NERC recognizes the LLWG 
efforts reviewed other large loads in addition to 
computational loads, NERC determined that the risk is 
appropriately addressed at the moment by focusing 
on computational loads due to their aggregate and 
operational impacts on the BPS. 
NERC recognizes computational loads differ, and while 
this information may be captured during the 
registration process, it likely would be more 
appropriately captured by the Regional Entities during 
their risk-based compliance monitoring and 
enforcement processes.

The proposed registry criteria should clarify that it applies to all those

Summary of Stakeholder Comments 

Commenters requested additional technical justification or 
legal basis supporting the proposed registry criteria. To that 
end, some commenters requested additional information on 
why NERC is including certain end-users in the proposed 
registry criteria or why the criteria does not cover all load 
instead of just computational load. 

Some commenters suggested that NERC and the Regional 
Entities be responsible for the identification of entities that can 
meet the new function instead of requesting the information 
from existing registered entities. 

Response  

Consistent with the Federal Power Act section 215, the NERC 
registry criteria identify the set of owners, operators, and users 
who have a material impact on the BPS and must therefore 
comply with applicable Reliability Standards. As NERC noted in 
its technical reasoning document in the first posting of the 
proposed registry criteria, the technical justification for 
proposing to register computational loads is based on their 
aggregate impact to the reliability of the BPS. The assessment 
of this aggregate impact resulted from the work performed by 
the Reliability and Security Technical Committee Large Loads 
Working Group and verified through the Aggregated Report on 
NERC Level 2 Alert and industry confirmation. Further analysis 
identified entities that should be registered to address the 
identified risk based upon their MW capability and voltage 
connection to the BPS.. Upon review of the comments received 
on the initial proposed criteria and further analysis, NERC 
determined to revise the criteria to the higher 50 MW/100 kV 
thresholds and revised the technical reasoning document to 
provide justification for the new proposed thresholds.  
While NERC endeavors to ensure its processes are not overly 
burdensome on entities, there may be instances where existing 
registered entities are best positioned to provide the necessary 
information to ensure identification of appropriate entities to 
support reliability.

Commenters questioned why existing registered entities 
cannot address the risk posed to the BPS instead of a new 
functional registration.  

Existing Reliability Standards provide important precedents and 
framework for maintaining the reliability of the BPS, but they 
were not developed specifically for this type of large load with 
its unique characteristics and aggregate impact. The NERC Large 
Loads Working Group identified gaps in existing Reliability 
Standards in “Assessment of Gaps in Existing Practices, 
Requirements, and Reliability Standards for Emerging Large 
Loads” and recommended development of new and/or updated 
Reliability Standards to address the unmitigated risks to the 
BPS. This need was also underscored in NERC’s Aggregated 
Report on NERC Level 2 Industry Recommendation: Large Load 
Interconnection, Study, Commissioning, and Operations. 
Further analysis identified entities that should be registered to 
address the identified risk based upon their MW capability and 
voltage connection to the BPS. 

When determining the need for new Reliability Standards, the 
LLWG also assessed whether existing registered entities could 
take on the new requirements. Through this assessment, the 
LLWG determined that while a Transmission Owner could 
include requirements such as disturbance ride-through or 
modeling into interconnection requirements via NERC 
Reliability Standard FAC-001.A Transmission Owner does not 
always have the ability to assess performance-based financial 
penalties to better ensure appropriate performance when 
connected to the BPS. Furthermore, the LLWG asserted that if 
computational loads do not have NERC standards directly 
applicable to them, the existing registered entities will then be 
responsible for the performance of that computational load. 
The LLWG noted that while this may have been appropriate for 
historical loads of significant size, emerging large loads are 
comparable to the size of significantly large generators and 
have unique operational characteristics, both of which create 
challenges for having an existing entity be responsible for their 
performance. Accordingly, the LLWG determined that 
requirements applicable to a new functional entity would

Summary of Stakeholder Comments 

Some commenters requested more information on NERC’s 
jurisdiction or statutory authority to register large or 
computational loads. 

Entity 

DCC 
Crusoe 
Corscale 
Google 
Oracle 
DPN 
ELCON 

Response  

Under section 215, the Federal Power Act provides the 
Commission, via the ERO, authority to regulate “users, owners, 
and operators of the Bulk Power System (BPS).” This statutory 
authority to regulate includes: (1) developing and enforcing 
mandatory Reliability Standards that provide for reliable 
operation of the BPS, subject to approval by FERC; and (2) 
assessing BPS reliability and adequacy. Consistent with federal 
jurisdiction over interstate commerce and other sections of the 
Federal Power Act, Congressional authority under section 215 
pertains only to the BPS and “users, owners, and operators” of 
the BPS. As such, under section 215, NERC cannot: (1) develop 
and enforce Reliability Standards for reliable operation of 
facilities used in the local distribution of electric energy, or (2) 
order the construction of additional generation or transmission 
capacity or set and enforce compliance with standards for 
adequacy or safety of electric facilities or services. 

FERC’s regulations echo Federal Power Act section 215 by 
requiring that “each user, owner and operator of the [BPS] 
within the United States…shall register with the [ERO] and the 
Regional Entity for each region within which it uses, owns, or 
operates [BPS] facilities, in such manner as prescribed by the 
Rules of the [ERO] and each applicable Regional Entity. While 
NERC’s reliability authority extends to all users, owners, and 
operators of the BPS, NERC’s registry criteria and Reliability 
Standards identify the appropriate users, owners, and 
operators based on an exercise of reasonable judgment as to 
their potential material impact to the BPS. NERC applies risk-
based engineering judgment, often in coordination with its 
stakeholder technical groups, to assess the impact of a 
particular user, owner, or operator on the BPS and whether any 
action(s) taken by that user, owner, or operator could mitigate 
risks posed by that impact. 

Consideration of Comments – ROP Appendices 2, 5A, and 5B Revisions (August 2026) 
15 

 
 
 
Summary of Stakeholder Comments 

Some commenters suggested NERC develop an exception 
process similar to the BES Exceptions process that allows 
entities without a material impact to be exempt from 
registering despite meeting the criteria. Other commenters 
requested that existing entities be allowed an exception from 
any future rules. 

Response  

NERC already has an established process to handle 
circumstances where an entity does not believe it meets  the 
registry criteria or does not believe its Computational Load Site 
has a material impact on BPS reliability. Under Rules of 
Procedure Appendix 5A, entities may request a review of their 
registration determinations under the NERC-led Registration 
Review Panel. Through that process, NERC and Regional Entities 
review an entity’s materiality to the BPS and may either 
deregister an entity that meets registry criteria or register an 
entity that does not meet registry criteria.  

As for exceptions for existing entities, NERC notes that the 
Project 2026-02 standards drafting team considers appropriate 
implementation time of Reliability Standards. The drafting team 
will consider whether existing facilities are allowed different 
implementation timeframes, or exceptions based on reliability 
risk.

NERC should provide more guidance on how the registry 
criteria applies to entities in differing configurations, such as 
those with co-located configurations among others. In

As was done with the Category 1 and 2 GO/GOP criteria once 
approved, NERC and the Regional Entities plan to develop an 
ERO Registration Reference document that provides additional 
detail on how the registry criteria is applied. This will occur once 
the registry criteria is more finalized, but in the interim, NERC 
registration staff collaborated with the Project 2026-02 drafting 
team to develop a Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) document 
that provides some information on applicability of the registry 
criteria and Reliability Standards. While actual registration 
determinations are made after assessment of an individual 
entity’s configuration compared to the criteria, the FAQ 
document provides some insight into the general application of 
the registry criteria. 

In response to communication and timelines, NERC and the 
Regional Entities will coordinate registration efforts based on 
the anticipated effective date of the newly proposed Reliability 
Standards that will be applicable to the new functional entities. 
As such, once those Reliability Standards are filed and then 
approved at FERC, NERC will base its registration activities 
timeline around the Reliability Standards’ effective dates and 
ensure timely communication and outreach to new entities 
occurs to support a smooth registration process and effective 
dates of registration.

NERC should work with governmental authorities and 
policymakers on the appropriate approach or process to 
addressing the risk posed to the BPS by computational loads. 
Others suggest a more robust regulatory and economic impact

NERC recognizes the importance of collaboration with federal 
and state governmental authorities, policymakers, and 
stakeholders on this matter. To that end, NERC engagement 
with governmental authorities on key issues is a continuous 
high priority. This includes several key engagements with 
critical state and provincial policymakers on large 
computational load entities. NERC has presented on its efforts 
to address reliability risk from large computational loads to 
associations representing the state legislator community, state 
energy officials, state regulators, and other key policymaker 
organizations. 

NERC has engaged several times with the National Association 
of Regulatory Utility Commissioners, also known as NARUC, and 
its relevant committees to discuss major efforts related to the 
Large Loads Working Group (LLWG), including briefings on 
various LLWG white papers and proposed updates to NERC’s 
registration criteria. NERC and NARUC co-hosted two feedback 
sessions between NERC staff and six state commissions that are 
‘first-movers’ addressing reforms to large load rate structure 
and interconnection requirements. In similar ways, the Regional 
Entities are actively engaging with government officials in their 
respective states.  Continued dialogue between NERC, its state 
government representatives on NERC committees, and the 
organizations representing state policymaker interests is 
essential to address risks stemming from integrating large 
computational load entities onto the bulk power system. 

As for FERC input, NERC notes that on July 16, FERC issued an 
order directing NERC, under its section 215(d)(5) authority of 
the Federal Power Act, to “develop and submit new or modified 
Reliability Standards addressing the reliability risks associated 
with the integration of computational loads into the Bulk-Power 
System.” The Commission also directed NERC to “develop 
revisions to its Rules of Procedure, including registry criteria for 
computational load entities.” Accordingly, FERC, through this

NERC affirms its intent to maintain existing compliance

While NERC endeavors to provide as much transparency as 
possible in its regulatory activities, NERC also recognizes the 
sensitive nature of certain Confidential Information submitted 
as part of the registration process or other regulatory 
processes. Accordingly, NERC and the Regional Entities protect 
such information under its Rules of Procedure Section 1500. 
Due to the sensitive commercial nature of consumption data, 
NERC does not plan to collect it on computational loads, and if 
collected, would treat it as Confidential Information and only 
collect such information to aid in registration determinations 
based on the registry criteria. 
At this time, NERC determined the current Appendix 5A 
deregistration process is appropriate for any new functional 
registrations. Therefore, NERC will not create separate de-
registration processes in the proposed ROP revisions. NERC or 
the Regional Entities can develop additional guidance around 
de-registration should issues arise in the future for the new 
entities specific to computational load. 
NERC notes that those comments should be submitted through 
the comment periods conducted by the Project 2026-02 
Computational Loads drafting team, whose web page provides 
information on ways to engage or comment on the 
development of the proposed standards.
